case_summary.text: IT: Income from sale of scrap generated from manufacturing process of industrial undertaking has to be included for purpose of benefit of section 80HH

INCOME TAX : SLP dismissed against order of High Court that income on account of sale of various items of scrap was to be included for purpose of calculation of deduction under sections 80-IA and 80HH
IT : Income on account of sale of various items of scrap is to be included for purpose of calculation of deduction under sections 80-IA and 80HH
IT: For purpose of computation of deduction under section 80HHC proceeds generated from sale of scrap would not be included in 'total turnover'

IT: For purpose of computation of deduction under section 80HHC of manufacturer and exporter of stainless steel utensils, proceeds generated from sale of scrap would not be included in 'total turnover'
IT : Scrap being bi-product of manufacturing activity, there are no expenses which could be excluded from sale of scrap for computing deduction under section 80HHC
IT : Income generated from sale of scrap cannot be included in total turnover under section 80HHC

IT: For purpose of computation of deduction under section 80HHC in case of firm dealing in trading and manufacturing of cycle parts, proceeds generated from sale of scrap would not be included in 'total turnover'
IT : Receipts from sale of scrap cannot be included in total turnover for computing deduction under section 80HHE
IT : Scrap sales is not to be included in total turnover for purpose of computing deduction under section 80HHC
IT : Scrap sale is to be excluded from total turnover while computing deduction under section 80HHC
IT : Sale proceeds generated from sale of scrap would not be included in total turnover for purpose of deduction under section 80HHC

INCOME TAX : Sale of scrap cannot be considered as part of 'total turnover' for purpose of calculation of deduction under section 80HHC in case of assessee engaged in manufacturing of industrial boilers
INCOME TAX : For purpose of section 80HHC, proceeds of sale of scrap would not form part of 'total turnover'
IT: Insurance claim, sale consideration of raw materials, tools, stores, scraps, etc. cannot form part of turnover for purpose of computation of deduction under section 80HHC

IT : Where assessee imported metal scrap and after segregating such scrap, produced various articles including graded brass metal, metal vires, etc., entire process came within meaning of 'manufacture or produce'
Scrap  incidental to manufacture; refusal to reimburse duty of under Budgetary support scheme unjustified: HC
IT : Neither amounts of excise duty and sales tax no receipt from sale of scrap can be included in turnover for computation of deduction under section 80HHC
No infirmity in order of ITAT if it rightly allowed sec. 80-IB deduction on sale of scrap: HC

INCOME TAX : Where scrap was generated from production process and assessee was not in business of sale of scrap, any income from such scrap would tantamount to recoupment of cost of raw material/production and, therefore, was includible in 'profits of business' for purpose of section 80HHC
IT : An assessee is entitled to deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I where process of twisting and texturising of partially oriented yarn amounted to manufacture in terms of section 80-IA
IT: Since products obtained in course of ship breaking activity were usable as such, same would not fall within definition of scrap under section 206C

IT : Where assessee after using material, had sold packing materials/scrap and aggregate amount of scrap sale was credited to profit and loss account (thereby reducing cost of material), amount derived by sale of scrap was eligible for deduction under section 80-IC
IT : Once assessee answers description of an industrial undertaking, it is immaterial for purpose of allowing deduction under section 80HH whether it is manufacturing or producing or processing
IT: Excise duty, sales tax and scrap sales are not includible in total turnover for purpose of deduction under sections 80HHC and 80HHE

IT-V :Where assessee-society sold scrap material such as tin, polythene, iron scrap, drum etc., since none of scrap was generated during manufacturing or mechanical process, provisions of section 206C were not applicable to assessee's case
IT-II: Profits and gains from sale of scraps resulting in manufacturing process were eligible for deduction under section 80-IC
IT : Where assessee did not establish any new industrial unit and had only improved existing unit by adding new machineries, deduction claimed under sections 80HH and 80-I were not allowable
Scrap income generated during manufacturing process would be eligible for deduction under section 80-IC: HC
IT: Conversion of granite boulders into crushed metal granite and also 'M sand' of different size amount to manufacture and also production, eligible for deduction under section 80HH/80-I
Blending of metal scrap to make ‘blended metal  scrap’ amounts to manufacture, rules AAR
IT : Assessee eligible for deduction under section 80-IC on account of sale of scrap.

IT-III : Sale of scrap being part and parcel of activities of assessee-undertaking, gains derived from said activity was required to be taken into consideration for purposes of computation of deduction under section 80-IC

IT: Where assessee put imported scrap to series of manual and mechanical processes and thereby brought into existence entirely new and distinct commodity which was marketable, it was to be regarded as 'manufacturing' activity and, thus, assessee's claim for deduction under section 80-IB was to be allowed
IT: Where cotton waste disposed of by assessee was reused by purchaser was used for manufacture of lower count of cotton yarn, it would not come under meaning of 'scrap' as defined in section 206C

IT : Where assessee had two separate and distinct undertaking, one for manufacturing cement and another for mining of lime that was to be used in cement manufacturing, profit only from manufacturing of cement would be eligible for deduction under section 80HH

IT: Process of bottling of gas into cylinders for domestic use by complex technical process undertaken in plant with machinery amounts to production or manufacture of gas-cylinders for purposes of deduction under sections 80-I, 80-IA and 80HH

IT : Where assessee having imported garments, cut them into smaller pieces and sold to different parties, in view of fact that waste generated in said process such as rags, wipers or chindi were used by buyers in manufacturing other items like blankets, pillows etc., waste so manufactured would not fall within ambit of expression 'scrap' as envisaged in clause (b) of Explanation to section 206C
IT : For purpose of considering deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I, entirety of allowance under section 32AB cannot be included in a routine manner in profits and gains of industrial undertaking
ITC blocked on pipeline laid outside factory premises, not considered as plant and machinery
GST/Excise & Customs: Worn-out conveyor belts sold as waste and scrap was liable to payment of duty
Construction of breakwater wall to protect jetty is not ‘plant & machinery’; ITC is not available: MH AAAR
IT: Where products obtained in course of ship breaking activity are usable as such, they do not fall within definition of scrap for purposes of tax collection at source on their sale

INCOME TAX : Where income generated from sale of spares as scrap actually only reduced cost of new spares purchased and, thus, leads to higher manufacturing profits to assessee, profits commensurate with scrap sold was said to be directly earned from manufacturing activity of assessee and, accordingly, assessee was entitled to claim deduction under section 80-IA on such income generated from sale of spares
AO can’t disallow sec. 80-IA claim merely because old machinery was used in power plant setup by transfer: ITAT
IT : Where job work formed part of main business activity, job work charges received by assessee could not be held as similar to word 'charges' provided in Explanation (baa) of section 80HHC

IT: Where assessee was a manufacturer of yarn out of purchase of cotton and cotton waste on its own and it had also done conversion on job work basis, net conversion charges would also form part of gross total income and 90 per cent of said sum had to be reduced from total income for arriving at business profits for computing deduction under section 80HHC
Clarification by revenue that scrap of used tyre cut into pieces was chargeable to custom duty was invalid: HC

IT : Where Tribunal allowed deductions under sections 80-HH and 80-I by considering gross income from two units of assessee, and said order of Tribunal was challenged on ground of violation of section 80AB, matter was to be remanded back for disposal afresh in light of decision in Synco Industries Ltd. v. Assessing Officer (Income-tax) 168 Taxman 224 (SC)

IT : Where job work charges were integral part of dominant business activity of assessee, same would form part of operational income and would be included in profits of business for computation of deduction under section 80HHC

digest.text:
HEADNOTE: SECTION 80HH OF THE INCOME-TAX ACT, 1961-DEDUCTIONS-PROFITS AND 
GAINS FROM NEWLY ESTABLISHED INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKINGS ETC., IN BACK- 
WARD AREAS-ASSESSEE WAS ENGAGED IN MANUFACTURE AND SALE OF 
DIFFERENT VARIETIES OF METALLIC WIRES AND IN COURSE OF SUCH MANUFAC-TURING ACTIVITY, WASTE MATERIAL, VIZ., SCRAP METAL, WAS OBTAINED-
WHETHER ASSESSEE WAS ENTITLED TO DEDUCTION UNDER SECTION 80HH IN 
RESPECT OF PROFITS FROM SALE OF SUCH SCRAP METAL-HELD, YES-
WHETHER ASSESSEE COULD ALSO CLAIM DEDUCTION UNDER SECTION 80HH IN RESPECT OF PROFITS DERIVED FROM SALE OF DRUMS, USED FOR STORING 
WATER, WHICH HAD BECOME USELESS-HELD, NO

SECTION 41(1) OF THE INCOME-TAX ACT, 1961-REMISSION OR CESSATION OF 
TRADING LIABILITY-WHETHER IN VIEW OF THE FACTS MENTIONED UNDER 
CAPTION 'DEDUCTION - IN RESPECT OF PROFITS AND GAINS OF INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKING, ETC., IN BACKWARD AREAS', SECTION 41(1) WAS NOT 
APPLICABLE INTO PROFITS DERIVED BY ASSESSEE PROM SALE OF SCRAP AND 
DRUMS-HELD, YES

SECTION 41(2) OF THE INCOME-TAX ACT, 1961-BALANCING CHARGE-
WHETHER IN VIEW OF FACTS MENTIONED UNDER CAPTION 'DEDUCTIONS - IN 
RESPECT OF PROFITS AND GAINS OF INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKING, ETC., IN 
BACKWARD AREAS', SECTION 41(2) WAS NOT ATTRACTED TO PROFITS FROM 
SALE OF SCRAP BUT WAS APPLICABLE TO PROFITS FROM SALE OF DRUMS-
HELD, YES

FACT: The assessee was engaged in the manufacture and sale of different varieties of metallic wires and in the course of such manufacturing activity, waste material, viz., scrap metal, was obtained. The assessee's claim for deduction under section 80HH in respect of profits attributable to sale proceeds of scrap and drums and value of scrap at close of the accounting year was rejected by the ITO on the ground that the impugned profits could not be said to have been derived from the industrial undertakings. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the assessee's claim on the ground that scrap metal was a direct offshoot of the manufacturing activity of the assessee and eventually it could not be put into a different category other than the one from which the main product was derived. On appeal, the revenue contended, inter alia, that sections 41(1) and 41(2) were applicable to profits derived from sale of scrap metal and drums.

HELD: Section 41(1 ) brings to tax certain amounts by a fiction of law. Therefore, the operation of such fiction should be limited to the language of the section. Where the assessee has incurred a loss or expenditure or trading liability and this trading liability has been allowed as deduction in an earlier year and something has later on been recovered in respect of such liability or such liability has either been remitted or has ceased to exist, section 41( 1) comes into operation. But according to the facts in the present case, nothing happened as contemplated by section 41(1) . Sale proceeds derived were for the sale of the particular product and not recoupment of earlier purchase. Accordingly, section 41(1) had no application to the facts of the instant case.

Further, the particular receipt under consideration is, insofar as scrap was concerned, realisation from the sale of waste material from manufacturing activity of the assessee-company and it was not a receipt from the sale of some of its old machinery, plant or building resulting in balancing charge as contemplated under section 41(2) . Therefore, section 41( 2) also had no application to the facts of the instant case as far as scrap was concerned. The section could be attracted insofar as the sale price of drums was concerned.

In fact, the assessee was entitled to deduction in respect of profits and gains from newly established industrial undertaking as contemplated under section 80HH in relation to profits from sale of scrap since this scrap, being a waste product which had a commercial value, was directly derived from the industrial undertaking which the assessee was carrying on and was sold in the normal course of running the industrial undertaking.

HEADNOTE: I. Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from hotels or industrial undertakings etc., in backward areas - Assessment year 1979-80 - Whether income from sale of scrap not being relatable to industrial activities of assessee-company, could not be allowed for deduction under section 80HH - Held, yes

FACT: For the assessment year 1979-80, the assessee-company claimed deduction under section 80HH on income from sale of scrap. The Tribunal disallowed the claim of the assessee on ground that income from sale of scrap was not relatable to the industrial activities of the assessee.

On reference :

HELD: This Court in a case concerning the same assessee in Pandian Chemicals Ltd. v. CIT [2002] 254 ITR 562, had held, inter alia, that scrap not being a necessary by product in the process of manufacturer, the income from the sale of scrap could not be regarded as income derived from the industrial undertaking.

Therefore, the Tribunal was right in law in holding that the income from the sale of scrap was not relatable to the industrial activities of the assessee for the purpose of section 80HH.

as far as scrap was concerned. The section could be attracted insofar as the sale price of drums was concerned.

In fact, the assessee was entitled to deduction in respect of profits and gains from newly established industrial undertaking as contemplated under section 80HH in relation to profits from sale of scrap since this scrap, being a waste product which had a commercial value, was directly derived from the industrial undertaking which the assessee was carrying on and was sold in the normal course of running the industrial undertaking. While giving the relief under section 80HH, value of closing stock of scrap would also have to be included. The sale proceeds of drums used for storing water and which had become useless could not, however, be said to be directly derived from the industrial undertaking considering the manufactur-ing activity in which the assessee was involved. This surplus was also of the nature falling under section 41(2 ). Therefore, the assessee was not entitled to relief in respect of profits attributable to sale of drums.

HEADNOTE: II. Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from hotels or industrial undertakings, etc., in backward areas (Computation of deduction) - Assessment years 1993-94 and 1994-95 - Whether scrap generated from manufacturing process has direct and immediate nexus with industrial undertaking and any income from sale of such scrap has to be included for purpose of benefit of section 80HH - Held, yes [Para 15] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: While computing deduction under section 80HH, the Assessing Officer excluded income from the sale of scrap by xerographic equipment unit and toner, developer, photocopier unit holding that income from the scrap could not be said to be income derived from the industrial undertaking.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) directed the Assessing Officer to take income from sale of scrap as income derived from industrial undertaking.

The Tribunal confirmed the order of the Commissioner (Appeals).

On revenue's appeal:

HELD: The word "derived from" under section 80-HH has to be understood as something which has immediate nexus with the industrial undertaking. In the instant case, the scrap generated from the concerned units has direct and immediate nexus with the industrial undertaking since the said scrap has been generated from the manufacturing process itself. Thus, the Commissioner (Appeals) as well as the Tribunal have committed no error in allowing the benefit of section 80-HH to the assessee on the aforesaid income. [Para 15]

HEADNOTE: I. Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from hotels and industrial undertakings, etc., in backward areas - Assessment year 1992-93 - Whether deduction under section 80HH is allowable on profit from sale of scrap in case of an industrial undertaking - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company, an industrial undertaking, had claimed deduction under section 80HH on sale of scrap. The Assessing Officer held that the deduction could be available only on the profits and gains derived from industrial undertaking and not from income incidental to the activity of industrial undertaking. Therefore, for the purpose of determining the deduction, the income shown from sale of scrap should be excluded. In appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that the generation of scrap was independent to manufacturing activity and, therefore, the assessee was not entitled to claim of deduction under section 80HH and the action of the Assessing Officer was confirmed.

On second appeal :

HELD: In Fenner (India) Ltd. v. CIT (No. 2) [2000] 241 ITR 803, the Madras High Court expressed the view that the scrap materials has direct link or nexus with the industrial undertaking and, therefore, profit from the sale of the scrap materials should be eligible for deduction under section 80HH. Following that decision, it was to be held in the instant case that the relief under section 80HH was allowable to the assessee on profit on sale of scrap. [Para 13]

HEADNOTE: Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from hotels or industrial undertaking, etc., in backward areas - Assessment year 1994-95 - Assessee, engaged in running of steel and iron re-rolling mill, derived income from sale of brass scrap which he obtained from dismantling certain guns purchased in auction and which could not be used for re-rolling - He claimed deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I on such income which was denied as it was not considered as income arising from industrial undertaking - Assessee had stated that he dealt in steel scrap and was not aware that inside guns, there was brass scrap which was removed - Thus, it was only a fortuitous circumstance that, in relevant assessment year, assessee had purchased guns without knowledge that brass scrap was inside them which was separated and it could not be said to be a by-product obtained in process of manufacture - Whether since brass was not an essential raw material of industrial unit, in question and brass was not at all connected with steel re-rolling, there was no nexus between brass scrap obtained on dismantling of guns and main activity of assessee of steel re-rolling and, therefore, separation of brass could not be said to be in process of manufacture or a product or by-product of activity of assessee’s industrial undertaking - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, profit on sale of brass scrap could not be said to be profit and gain derived from industrial undertaking so as to be entitled to deduction under sections 80HHC and 80-I - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee, engaged in the manufacture of re-rolled products of iron and steel in his re-rolling mill, filed his return of income which was accepted as such. In the course of the survey conducted under section 133A, the assessee had offered to pay tax on Rs. 10 lakhs. When required to explain the surrender, the assessee submitted that he had purchased certain guns in auction and certain quantity of brass scrap was obtained from breaking and dismantling those guns and the balance was iron scrap. It was contended that the said activity tantamounted to production of goods and, hence, income from industrial undertaking. The Assessing Officer, however, did not consider the income from sale of brass scrap as arising from industrial undertaking for purposes of allowing deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I and allowed the claim only in respect of other income. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) accepted the assessee’s submission. On revenue’s appeal, the Tribunal reversed the impugned order and allowed the revenue’s appeal. It accepted the plea that the assessee had purchased guns and the income from brass scrap which could not be used for re-rolling, thus, was not entitled to deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I.

On appeal to the High Court :

HELD: The assessee in his explanation had stated that he dealt in steel scrap and was not aware of the fact that inside the guns, there was brass scrap which was removed. Thus, it was clear from the reply that brass was not an ingredient used in the process of manufacture in industrial undertaking of the assessee. The brass scrap had no direct nexus with the appellant’s industrial undertaking. It could not be said that brass scrap was a profit or gain which directly flowed, neither it had close connection with undertaking of the assessee. By removal of brass scrap which was not useful for steel rerolling work no different and distinct article came into existence, it was only incidental as was apparent from the assessee’s reply. [Paras 13 and 14]

Further, composition of brass scrap was not at all changed, that was only removed as that was not useful to the assessee for the activity of manufacturing which he was carrying on. It was only a fortuitous circumstance that in the relevant assessment year, the assessee had purchased the guns without the knowledge that brass scrap was inside them which was separated and it could not be said to be a by-product obtained in the process of manufacture. There was no nexus between brass and activity of steel rerolling. Brass was not at all an input in the process of manufacture of steel rerolling. It was not a raw material at all for the process of rerolling in which the assessee was involved. It was purely incidental that brass was found inside guns which were purchased in that year. Guns might have several components, sometimes brass or some other articles which may not be connected at all with the manufacturing process of the industrial undertaking. [Paras 22, 23, 24 and 25]

HEADNOTE: Section 147 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Income escaping assessment - Non-disclosure of primary facts - Assessment years 1979-80 to 1984-85 - Petitioner’s claim for deduction under section 80HH was allowed for some years by Assessing Officer, for other years by Commissioner (Appeals) and Tribunal - Subsequently, Assessing Officer issued notices for reassessment alleging that entire manufacturing activity was not carried on in backward area and petitioner had failed to disclose fully and truly all material facts for making assessment - Petitioner contended that all facts had been disclosed before assessment was made and Assessing Officer was not able to specify exact information which was required and which was not disclosed - Whether, therefore, revenue could claim that there was no true and full disclosure of facts - Held, no

FACT: The petitioner-company, which was carrying on the business of manufacturing and sale of beedies, set up a factory in a backward area. Some of the raw beedies were entrusted to contractors for being manufactured and with that along with raw beedies manufactured by the assessee itself in the industrial undertaking, the further processes of heating, ringing, belleying, wrapping and packing were carried on with the consequence that the finished product was made in the factory which was in the backward area. The petitioner claimed deduction under section 80HH. Deduction was allowed for some years by the ITO, for some years by the Commissioner (Appeals) and for some years by the Tribunal. On the ground that a part of the manufacturing activity was carried on outside the backward area, notices were issued alleging that the petitioner had failed to disclose fully and truly all the material facts for making the assessment. Petitioner questioned the issue of notices contending that they lacked jurisdiction inasmuch as the facts had been disclosed before the assessments were made.

On petition :

HELD: Sub-section (2) of section 80HH lays down certain conditions, one of which is that the industrial undertaking should manufacture or produce articles in any backward area and another condition is that it should employ 10 or more workers in the manufacturing process carried on with the aid of power. It was not the case of the revenue that any of these conditions were not fulfilled. Their only case was that the entire manufacturing activity from beginning to end was not carried on in the backward area and an initial part of it had been entrusted to the contractors who carried on that part of the activity outside the backward area. The contention, therefore, was that the profit shown as the profit of the industrial undertaking in the backward area might actually include a small part of the profit derived from activity outside the backward area and, therefore, there was inflation of the profit and consequentially inflation of the deduction claimed by the assessee, that could be withdrawn by reopening the assessment. [Para 5]

The revenue rejected the assessee’s clam for investment allowance by resorting to the Schedule XI on the ground that all items that were installed in the factory premises, with the exception of tools, jigs, dies and tools were to be aggregated and. consequently, since the value of machinery and plant exceeded Rs. 20 lakhs, the assessee could not be categorised as a small scale Industrial unit.

On second appeal: HELD: The policy of the Government to promote the small scale units by providing various concessions through the Ministry of Industry, considering their contribution to the overall growth and economic development of the country, was echoed in the memorandum explaining the provisions of the Finance Bill, 1986. The benefits as were extended to the small scale units by the Industry Ministry were considered under the Act for the first time in 1976. which was the grant of investment allowance to such units and this continued over the years. In 1986, through the Finance Bill, 1986, it was observed that the upward revision of the value of the machinery and plant was being made in the light of the upward revision made by the Department of industrial Development through the notification dated 17-3-1985, to be effective from 1-4-1985. From the time small scale units were given concessions under the Act, there was never any Explanation or provision added to the Act, as to manner of determination of the aggregate value of the machinery and plant, that was contrary to the. one laid by the Ministry of Industry. Unlike the provisions of sections 80-I, 80HH etc., where the pre-requisites for a new industrial undertaking has been defined, there are no conditions specified in section 32A for grant of recognition as a small- scale unit, other than borrowal of the definition from the one recognised by the Ministry of Industries. This, suggests that the only authority which has the power to grant recognition to a unit as a small-scale unit being the Industry Ministry or the concerned department under that Ministry, so long as a unit ‘is recognised by that authority, for purposes of harmonious construction of the term small-scale unit, the same should be adopted for the purposes of this Act as well. In the absence of any specified Explanation or provision for the determination of the aggregate value of machinery and plant under the Act, it would be only proper that the manner of computation of the aggregate value of the machinery and plant as recognised by that Ministry is also adopted, so that uniformity for the same class or category under different Acts can be maintained. Such uniformity of view is what is intended by the Legislature and will only be proper for achieving the objective of the growth of these units and their contribution to the overall economic development of the country and, last but not the least, to reducing avoidable litigation. Therefore, the assessee’s plea that the aggregate value of machinery and plant should be determined in the like manner as done by the Directorate of Industries was to be accepted. Since the Directorate of Industries had accorded recognition to the assessee as a small scale industrial unit, the assessee’s claim of investment allowance on such items as were installed in the factory premises was upheld.

HEADNOTE: Section 80HHC of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from industrial undertakings in backward area - Assessee-company had set up an industrial undertaking in a backward area and was carrying on business of manufacture and sale of V-belts, oil seals, O-rings, rubber moulded products, etc. - Whether profits and gains from sale of scrap material resulting in manufacturing process were eligible for deduction in an amount equal to 20 per cent under section 80HH, since scrap materials came within manufacturing process of industrial undertaking set-up by assessee - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company, carrying on the business of manufacture and sale of V-belts, oil seals, O-rings, rubber moulded products, etc., set-up an industrial undertaking in a backward area. It claimed deduction of 20 per cent of net profits allowable under section 80HH in respect of profit on sale of scrap which resulted in the manufacturing process. The ITO disallowed that claim. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the assessee's claim. On further appeal, the Tribunal reversed the Commissioner (Appeals)'s order.

On reference :

HELD: Section 80HH is meant to give a tax rebate to certain categories of assessees and one, who wants to claim such a relief, must strictly satisfy the requirements prescribed therein. He must establish that his profits and gains are derived from his industrial undertaking or the business of hotel. Axiomatic proposition of law is that it is not sufficient if a commercial connection is established between the profits earned and the industrial undertaking and the law requires that such profits must have been derived from the industrial undertaking. The industrial undertaking itself must be the source of that profit. The business of the industrial undertaking must strictly yield that profit. It must be the direct source of profit and not a means to earn any other profit.

In the instant case, in the industrial undertaking for the manufacture of V-belts, oil seals, O-rings and rubber moulded products, certain scrap materials resulted, which had a saleable value. To say that the scrap materials had no direct link or nexus with the industrial undertaking, could not at all be expected to commend acceptance, especially, on the facts and in the circumstances of the instant case. The scrap materials came within the manufacturing process of the industrial undertaking in the manufacture of certain products such as V-belts, oil seals, O-rings and certain rubber moulded products, etc. In that view of the matter, profits and gains from the sale of scrap materials were eligible for deduction in an amount equal to 20 per cent under section 80HH, inasmuch as such gains or profits were derived from the industrial undertaking and includible in the gross total income of the assessee and the question relatable to the profit on the sale of scrap was answered in favour of the assessee.

Provisions of section 80HH or 80-I are meant for the benefit of industrial undertakings that carry out the activity of manufacture or production of articles or things and not for the scrap merchants who trade in buying old articles or things and take out their parts to sell them separately. All large scale junk dealers in discarded old and scrapped vehicles who might fish out a horn in working condition from such vehicle or pull out its steering wheel or part of its engine that may have a demand in the market of second hand spares will proclaim themselves to be manufacturers or producers of articles or things. No such startling result is intended by the provisions of sections 80HH and 80-I, having regard to their underlying purpose of encouraging industries for being set up for manufacturing or production of new articles or things. In fact, industrial undertaking formed by transfer of machinery or plant previously used for any purpose is disentitled to such benefits both under sections 80HH(2)(iii) and 80-I(2)(iii). [Para 23]

The ships imported for breaking up are obviously old ships, purchased to retrieve the material, particularly steel plates, for disposal in the market for re-rolling or re-cycling purposes which is the activity done by these ship breakers in the process of ship breaking.

Thus, there is nothing whatsoever in the process of ship breaking activity which can be termed as manufacture or production of any article or thing. The dismantled material is already existing as a component of the old ship. The process of extracting steel plates from it while dismantling the ship will not make such extraction of existing material an activity of manufacture or production of such material nor will the process of cutting extracted steel plates for convenient disposal be manufacture or production of such steel plates. Merely because the ship breaking is considered as an industry, it would not be an industry engaged in manufacture or production of any article or thing. Benefit of the provisions of sections 80HH and 80-I is clearly not intended for such ship breaking activities which do not result in bringing into existence any new article or thing. The word ‘manufacture’ in the context of sections 80HH and 80-I would mean making of articles or things. While dismantling, the ship steel plates are not made but only removed which is not the same thing as making of steel plates. The word ‘production’ in context of these provisions would mean the action of making or manufacturing from components or raw materials an article or thing and not just removing of an existing article or cutting it.

In the instant case, application of mechanical methods only removed the steel plates and other objects which were existing on the ships, which would not mean that the assessee produced those existing articles or things by the process of removing and cutting them. [Para 27]

The word ‘production’ or ‘produce’ when used in juxtaposition with word ‘manufacture’ takes in bringing into existence new goods by a process which may or may not amount to manufacture. The principle of adopting a liberal interpretation which advances the purpose and object of beneficial provisions cannot be carried out to the extent of doing violence to the plain and simple language of the enactment. [Para 27.1]

Therefore, ship breaking is not an activity which gives rise to manufacture and production of altogether new commercial articles or things. The assessees were not entitled to claim deductions under sections 80HH and 80-I and the Tribunal committed an error in upholding such deductions. [Para 27.2]

It was purely incidental that brass was found inside guns which were purchased in that year. Guns might have several components, sometimes brass or some other articles which may not be connected at all with the manufacturing process of the industrial undertaking. HEADNOTE: Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from industrial undertaking in backward areas - Assessment year 1991-92 - Whether business of receiving from clients untreated crank shafts, forgings, castings, etc., and subjecting them to heat treatment, in order to toughen them to requisite standards, so that they could be sold in market, is a manufacturing activity, entitling it to claim deduction as contemplated under sections 80HH and 80-I - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company claimed deductions in respect of profits and gains under sections 80HH and 80-I. The Assessing Officer rejected same on the ground that the assessee had not done any manufacturing activity. However, on appeal, the first appellate authority allowed the assessee’s claim. On the revenue’s appeal, the Tribunal following its earlier order relatable to the same assessee for the assessment years 1984-85 to 1986-87, held that the assessee was engaged in the manufacturing activity and, therefore, affirmed the order of the first appellate authority. The revenue’s application for reference was rejected by the Tribunal.

On application for reference :

HELD: The pivotal point, underlying the questions was as to whether the activity carried on by the assessee, namely, the business of receiving from its clients untreated crank shafts, forgings, castings, etc., and subjecting them to heat treatment, in order to toughen them to the requisite standards, so that they could be sold in market was a manufacturing activity, entitling it to claim the deductions, as contemplated under sections 80HH and 80-I. In the assessee’s own case in Tax Case Petition Nos. 592 to 594 of 1997 for the assessment years 1984-85 to 1986-87 it was held that the activity carried on by the assessee was one of manufacturing activity. The rationale or reasoning projected therein would hold goods here also, and the assessee’s activity could not be anyone other than the one relatable to manufacturing activity entitling it to claim necessary deductions under the original provisions administrated under sections 80HH and 80-I.

Thus, the activity of the assessee was the manufacturing activity entitling it to claim deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I.

Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction - New industrial undertaking in backward areas - Assessment year 1985-86 - Whether assessee’s claim, that technical service charges representing cost of the ‘brain’ - Component of electric typewriter manufactured by it, though billed separately for purposes of excise duty, was to be included as part of profit of undertaking for deduction under section 80HH, had to be allowed -Held, yes.

FACT: For the assessment year 1985-86, the assessee-company claimed that the profit derived from the undertaking for purposes of deduction under section 80HH should be determined on the basis that the Income shown under the head "Services" was from the industrial undertaking. The assessee, while selling the electronic typewriters, had charged for the price of the typewriters separately from the technical service charge that represented the value of the software provided as part of the typewriters, because, according to the assessee, no excise duty was leviable on such software. The excise authorities, however, had levied excise duty on the entire cost, including the cost of the software which represented the ‘brain’ or the central processing unit (CPU) of the typewriter. The Commissioner (Appeals) rejected the assessee’s claim by observing that since the assessee itself had treated the technical service charge separately, It could not be included as part of the profit of the undertaking for deduction under section 80HH.

On second appeal:

HELD: The "brain" or the CPU is the main driving force behind the electronic typewriters and the sale of the typewriters would be incomplete without the "brain" or the CPU. The treatment of the CPU or the "brain" as software services does not in any way change its true nature, which is that it is part of the machine and both of them need each other to form one complete composite unit. The maintaining of separate account for the value of the "brain" as technical service charges does not affect its true classification as the main strength of the electronic typewriters. Therefore, the profit derived from the industrial undertaking had to be worked out including the income from the sale of technical services and on that profit, assessee should be allowed deduction under section 80HH.

EDITOR’S NOTE

The Tribunal also allowed/disallowed certain other claims of the assessee by following the decision dated 28-1-1994 of the Special Bench of the Tribunal in the case of the assessee itself for the assessment year 1984- 85 in IT Appeal No. 3483 (Delhi) of 1983.

FACT: The assessee-company, a small-scale industrial undertaking, was carrying on the business of manufacturing ‘Jarda’ from raw tobacco in a backward area. The processing operations employed by the assessee were that raw tobacco (angad) was stripped off the midrib by manual labour. It was then sand-screened to control the moisture content. The raw tobacco was fed into a vibratory feeder and it was conveyed into a pneumatic pick up duct where heavy stems and stones would drop down. In the pick up duct, the tobacco was lifted up by suction and discharged into first tower classifier. In this tower classifier, the heavier tobacco flakes were separated from lighter ones and left behind. The lighter flakes were carried by air into second tower classifier. Here, the tobacco dust and flakes were differentiated. Finally, the lamina was sent to a sleeve chamber where it was cut and graded to suit the requirement of beedi manufacturer. The pure tobacco flakes came out after the dust was sucked out in the dust collecting unit. The end-product was called ‘Jarda’ or ‘Jardi’. The assessee claimed reliefs under sections 32A, 80HH and 80-I for the assessment years 1984-85 and 1985-86. The assessee also claimed that it should be charged at a concessional rate treating it as an industrial company as defined under section 2(8)(c) of the Finance Act, 1985. The Assessing Officer disallowed the assessee’s claims on the ground that the assessee was not manufacturing or producing any article or any thing. On appeal the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the disallowance.

On second appeal:

HELD: The instant case was not a border line case and a firm conclusion was easily approachable. By subjecting tobacco to treatment beedi patti was produced. By ginning cotton, pure cotton is obtained or pressed cotton is produced. Raw wool subjected to processing to eliminate dirt, grease and other vegetable matter results in production of pure wool. Leather is said to be manufactured when raw hide is treated. In all these cases a different product in commercial realm is said to be produced. In the same strain, it was equally possible to say that ‘Jarda’ or ‘Jardi’ was produced or manufactured from raw tobacco as a result of some manual or mechanical treatment, or both. Anybody could go to the market and purchase the article known as raw tobacco and it is equally possible to go and purchase in the market an article called Jarda or Jardi. The physical property in raw tobacco and Jarda or Jardi might be same. While raw tobacco is unfit for beedi manufacture in the same condition, Jarda or Jardi can ready be used in the beedi manufacture. In commercial parlance Jarda or Jardi is distinctively different from raw tobacco. For the aforesaid reasons, in the instant case, the assessee’s business was one of manufacture or production of an article or thing. The assessee’s business undertaking was in a backward area and there was no dispute about it. Then, if the assessee was manufacturing or producing an article, it must be taken that all the conditions in sub-section(2) of section 80HH were fulfilled. The assessee was having a mechanised tobacco processing plant which was even patented. It was registered as a small scale industrial unit by the Government. The most vital was the schedule of assets which formed part of the balance sheet, which showed that the cost of machinery employed was below the limit placed in Explanation to section 32A(2) or Explanation 3 to section 80-I(2), read with section 80HHA(8). The assessee was, therefore, entitled to the reliefs under sections 32A, 80HHA and 80-I. Since the assessee was found manufacturing an article it should be treated as an industrial company as defined in the Finance Act, though even processing, which the assessee was certainly doing, may be sufficient to justify a claim for concessional rate of tax. Thus, the assessee was also entitled to concessional rate of tax for both the years being an industrial company within the meaning of section 2(8)(c).

HEADNOTE: Section 80HH, read with section 80-I, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from hotels or industrial undertakings, etc., in backward areas - Assessment year 1992-93 - Assessee-company was engaged in manufacture and sale of high tensile fasteners, etc. - It had a unit at 'K', a notified backward area, which manufactured fasteners and sockets - It claimed deduction under section 80HH in respect of forging work done at 'K' on products manufactured by it on sub-contract basis - Admittedly, assessee's 'K' unit had maintained its accounts separately as an independent unit and derived income out of its production process - Whether, on facts, assessee was entitled to deduction under section 80HH on sub-contract receipts of 'k' unit - Held, yes [In favour of assessee]

FACT: The assessee-company was engaged in manufacture and sale of high tensile fasteners, cold extruded parts, etc., in Padi. It had a unit at 'k', a notified backward area, which manufactured fasteners and sockets. The assessee claimed deduction under section 80HH in respect of forging work done in 'k' unit on products manufactured in Padi, which it called as 'sub-contract receipts'. The Assessing Officer rejected the claim for deduction in respect of 'k' unit. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) directed the Assessing Officer to allow relief in accordance with law. Aggrieved, the revenue went in appeal before the Tribunal, which was allowed by a common order holding that the receipt on sub-contract could not be treated as income derived from the industrial undertaking for the purpose of granting relief under section 80HH.

On assessee's appeal :

HELD: The decision in CIT v. Tamilnadu Heat Treatment & Fetting Services [1999] 238 ITR 540/104 Taxman 210 (Mad.) is a case falling under sections 80HH and 80-I wherein the Court upheld the claim of the assessee as a sub-contractor to have the relief granted under sections 80HH and 80-I. The law declared in the above-stated case had direct relevance to the facts of the instant case. [Para 12]

In the subsequent decision in CIT v. Taj Fire Works Industries [2007] 288 ITR 92/[2006] 154 Taxman 380 (Mad.), a case where the assessee doing job work claimed the benefit of sections 80HH and 80-I, the Court held that since the assessee was involved in a systematic activity organized by the employer for the production and distribution of goods, it was entitled to the benefit of sections 80HH and 80-I. [Para 13]

In the instant case, the assessee's unit at 'k' was stated to be the only unit having hot forging machine. It was stated that the assessee, based at 'k', received bolts and nuts from Padi, manufactured using cold forging. The 'k' unit completed hot forging and after the process the products came to Padi where there was further value addition and after assembling nuts and bolts, they were marketed. Thus, it was only after the process was carried on by the 'k' unit, that the commodities reached a stage of marketability. The process of hot forging involved heating of raw materials to 1100 : C cutting, forming and piercing. Those nuts were then cooled and tapped. The nuts were then subject to heat treatment and surface coating, depending on customer's requirement to withstand higher stress. Thus, given the nature of the processing done at 'k' unit, the deduction was rightly considered by the Commissioner (Appeals) in the assessee's favour. [Para 15]

Further, the assessee's unit at 'k' had its own account maintained separately as an independent unit and out of the production process, it had derived income therein. Thus, it satisfied the test as given under section 80HH, which qualified for deduction in respect of receipts on job work done at the 'k' unit. Following the decisions in Tamilnadu Heat Treatment & Fetting Services (P.) Ltd.'s case (supra ) and Taj Fire Works Industries (supra), the order of the Tribunal was to be set aside. Accordingly, the Assessing Officer was to be directed to give effect to the direction of the Commissioner (Appeals). [Para 16]

According to revenue, the sale proceeds from scraps must be included in the 'total turnover' as the assessee was selling scrap and forms part of sales.

On appeal, High Court passed the order in favour of assessee.

On further appeal to the Supreme Court:

HELD: Computation of Section 80HHC deduction

The deduction under section 80HHC, subject to several other conditions, incorporated in the section, is determined as under: Thus, if the total turnover increases, the advantage which the assessee would get under section 80HHC would decrease because the amount deductible substantially depends upon the ratio between the export turnover and total turnover. If the export turnover is higher, comparatively the amount deductible under section 80HHC would be more; or in other words, if compared to total turnover, export turnover is less the amount deductible from the income under section 80HHC would be reduced. [Para 10]

Meaning of the term 'turnover'

The term 'turnover' had neither been defined in the Act nor has been explained by any of the CBDT circulars. [Para 17]

In the aforesaid circumstances, one has to look at the meaning of the term 'turnover' in ordinary accounting or commercial parlance. [Para 18]

Normally, the term 'turnover' would show the sale effected by a business unit. It may happen that in the course of the business, in addition to the normal sales, the business unit may also sell some other things. [Para 19]

In ordinary accounting parlance, as approved by all accountants and auditors, the term 'sales', when reflected in the profit and loss account, would indicate sale proceeds from sale of the articles or things in which the business unit is dealing. When some other things like old furniture or a capital asset, in which the business unit is not dealing are sold, the sale proceeds therefrom would not be included in 'sales' but it would be shown separately. [Para 20]

In simple words, the word 'turnover' would mean only the amount of sale proceeds received in respect of the goods in which an assessee is dealing in. [Para 21]

So far as the scrap is concerned, the sale proceeds from the scrap may either be shown separately in the profit and loss account or may be deducted from the amount spent by the manufacturing unit on the raw material, which is steel in the case of the respondent-assessee, as the respondent-assessee is using stainless steel as raw material, from which utensils are manufactured. The raw material, which is not capable of being used for manufacturing utensils will have to be either sold as scrap or might have to be re-cycled in the form of sheets of stainless steel, if the manufacturing unit is also having its re-rolling plant. If it is not having such a plant, the manufacturer would dispose of the scrap of steel to someone who would re-cycle the said scrap into steel so that the said steel can be re-used. [Para 22]

When such scrap is sold, the sale proceeds of the scrap cannot be included in the term 'turnover' for the reason that the respondent-unit is engaged primarily in the manufacturing and selling of steel utensils and not scrap of steel. Therefore, the proceeds of such scrap would not be included in 'sales' in the Profit and Loss Account of the respondent-assessee. [Para 23]

The situation would be different in the case of the buyer, who purchases scrap from the respondent-assessee and sells it to someone else. The sale proceeds for such a buyer would be treated as 'turnover' for a simple reason that the buyer of the scrap is a person who is primarily dealing in scrap. In the case on hand, as the respondent-assessee is not primarily dealing in scrap but is a manufacturer of stainless steel utensils, only sale proceeds from sale of utensils would be treated as his 'turnover'. [Para 24]

The Institute of Chartered Accountants of India ('ICAI') has published some material under the head 'Guidance Note on Tax Audit under section 44AB'. The said material has been published so as to guide the members of the ICAI. In our opinion, when a recognized body of Accountants, after due deliberation and consideration publishes certain material for its members, one can rely upon the same. Para 5 of the said Note deals with 'Sales', 'turnover' and 'gross receipts'. The meaning given by the ICAI clearly denotes that in normal accounting parlance the word 'turnover' would mean 'total sales' as explained hereinabove. The said sales would definitely not include the scrap material which is either to be deducted from the cost of raw material or is to be shown separately under a different head. There is no reason for not accepting the meaning of the term 'turnover' given by a body of Accountants, which is having a statutory recognition. [Para 25]

If all accountants, auditors, businessmen, manufacturers etc. are normally interpreting the term 'turnover' as sale proceeds of the commodity in which the business unit is dealing, there is no reason to take a different view than the view normally taken by the persons who are concerned with the said term. [Para 26]

HEADNOTE: Section 32A of the Income-tax Act, 1961-Investment allowance-
Whether, assessee was entitled to investment allowance under
section 32A in respect of machinery and plant installed in cold
storage-Held, no

Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961-Deductions-Profits and 
gains from newly established industrial undertaking in backward
areas-Whether, assessee was entitled to relief in respect of cold 
storage, which was situated in backward area, under section 80HH-
Held, no

FACT: The assessee, being an owner of a cold storage situated in a backward area wherein potatoes were kept in the relevant assessment year, claimed investment allowance under section 32A on machinery and plant installed in the cold storage on the ground that the cold storage involved ‘manufac-turing’. The ITO disallowed the assessee’s claim, holding that a cold storage involved only processing and not manufacture or production of an article or thing. He also disallowed the assessee’s claim for deduction under section 80HH, On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order of the ITO.

On second appeal;

HELD: Section 32 A uses the expression ‘business of manufacture or production of any article or thing’. The expression used in section 80HH is similar, namely, ‘to manufacture or produce articles’. There is no reference to ‘processing’ as used in the definition of ‘industrial company’ under section 2(7)(d) of the Finance Act, 1966, and the Finance (No. 2) Act, 1967. Again, unlike section 80J(4)(iii), reference is not made in section 32A or 80HH to the operation of a cold storage plant. This would show that mere processing (even if the potatoes were held to undergo processing in a cold storage) is not recognised under sections 32A and 80HH to amount to manufacture or production of any article or thing. The same expression is used in section 80HHA and 80-I(2)(iii). Again, section 35C, which deals with agricultural development allowance, refers to a company or a co-operative society being engaged in the manufacture or processing of a relevant article or thing There-fore, as neither section 32A nor section 80HH refers to processing of any article or thing, the lower authorities were justified in rejecting the claims of the assessee.

area and an initial part of it had been entrusted to the contractors who carried on that part of the activity outside the backward area. The contention, therefore, was that the profit shown as the profit of the industrial undertaking in the backward area might actually include a small part of the profit derived from activity outside the backward area and, therefore, there was inflation of the profit and consequentially inflation of the deduction claimed by the assessee, that could be withdrawn by reopening the assessment. [Para 5] Sub-section (7) of section 80HH provides for this contingency by stating that where it appears to the Assessing Officer that owing to the close connection between the assessee carrying on the business to which this section applies and any other person, the business between them is so arranged that it produces to the assessee more than the ordinary profit, the profits and gains of this industrial undertaking may be reasonably estimated. In the instant case also, if the Assessing Officer had carefully scrutinised the accounts of the assessee and drawn the inference that because of the entrustment of the initial part of the contract process to contractors, the income from the industrial undertaking was likely to be inflated, with reference to the profit derived from the backward area, he could have reasonably estimated the profit instead of accepting the profit as shown by the assessee. That estimate, he failed to do at the time of the assessment and he sought to do the same by reopening the assessment. The question was whether he could do it by stating that there was an omission on the part of the assessee to disclose fully and truly all material facts. In the case of Parashuram Pottery Works Co. Ltd. v. ITO [1977] 106 ITR 1, the Supreme Court stated that the duty of an assessee in any case does not extend beyond making a true and full disclosure of primary facts. Once he has done that, his duty ends. It is for the ITO to draw the correct inference from the primary facts. It is no responsibility of the assessee to advise the ITO with regard to the inference, which he should draw from the primary facts. If an ITO draws an inference which appears subsequently to be erroneous, mere change of opinion with regard to that inference would not justify initiation of action for reopening assessments. In the instant case, the ITO failed to draw an inference that because of the entrustment of the initial manufacturing activity to contractors, the income derived from the industrial undertaking with reference to the backward area could be inflated and to that extent the income had to be estimated for confining the deduction to that profit which could be said to have been derived only from the backward area. Failing to draw that inference, blame could not be put on the assessee, when at the time of assessment the list of contractors, the quantity of beedies manufactured and the amount paid had been disclosed by the assessee. That disclosure was admitted in the counter affidavit. The ITO was not able to specify what extra information was required by him to have applied his mind to draw that inference for reducing the deduction to which the assessee was entitled. As long as it was not possible for the ITO to specify the exact information which was required and which was not disclosed, it was not possible to accept the claim that there was no true and full disclosure in the case. When that jurisdictional fact was not established, the ITO could not issue a notice under section 147(a). In the circumstances, the impugned notices were quashed. [Paras 6 & 7]

The writ petition was allowed. [Para 7]

Hence, it would be doing violence to the language of the section if it is said that while a ship is being dismantled or broken or destroyed, in effect an article or thing is being manufactured or produced. Hence, the activity of breaking or dismantling of a ship cannot be considered to be an industrial undertaking which manufactured or produced articles or things and, therefore, the assessee was not entitled to deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I. Regarding the contention of the assessee that the Government of India had recognised ship breaking as industry and, hence, the assessee was entitled to deduction claimed, there was no presumption that every industry is engaged in ‘manufacture’ or ‘production of articles or things’. Even if ship breaking is considered as an industry in the light of the definition of section 2(f) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, it will not mean that it would amount to manufacture or production so as to entitle the assessee to claim deductions under the respective sections. The assessee being governed by the Factories Act also would not change the matter in any way because that is broadly meant for welfare of labourers employed. The argument that a ship-breaking industry is labour intensive and that in the process heavy machinery like cranes and winches are employed is not relevant in absence of any manufacturing process involved. Mere application of systematic and sophisticated machines in the process would not treat an activity into manufacture. Thus, ship breaking activity amounts to carrying out the manufacturing process in a reverse order, as originally the ship is built from iron sheets and iron bars and other materials and by process of breaking the same, ship was reconverted into iron scrap and other materials. In view of the above, the findings of the Commissioner (Appeals) were to be reversed.

HEADNOTE: Section 80HHC of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction - Exporter (Computation of deduction) - Assessment year 1999-2000 - Assessee's partnership firm was engaged in making bicycle parts for export - Assessee claimed deduction under section 80HHC - While computing deduction, Assessing Officer excluded amount of sale of scrap from 'total turnover' and proportionate profit on sale of scrap from 'profit of business' - Whether Apex court in case of CIT v. Punjab Stainless Steel Industries [2014] 364 ITR 144/46 taxmann.com 68/[2015] 229 Taxman 423, had finally cleared this issue that proceeds generated from sale of scrap would not be included in 'total turnover' for purpose of computation for deduction under section 80HHC - Held, yes - Whether in view of same, question regarding inclusion of sale of scrap in total turnover was required to be examined afresh by Assessing Officer in factual matrix of case; thus, matter to be remanded to Assessing Officer - Held, yes [Paras 6 and 7] [Partly in favour of assessee/Matter remanded]IT: For purpose of computation of deduction under section 80HHC proceeds generated from sale of scrap would not be included in 'total turnover'

FACT: The assessee, partnership firm was engaged in making of bicycle parts for exports. The assessee filed its return of income declaring total income at Rs. Nil and claimed deduction under section 80HHC. A reopening notice under section 148 was issued and served upon the assessee. Thereafter, the assessee filed return of income declaring Nil income after claiming deduction under section 80HHC. The assessment was finalised by Assessing Officer under section 143(3) and deduction under section 80HHC was restricted to lesser amount as against the claim of the assessee.

While computing deduction under section 80HHC, the Assessing Officer excluded the amount of sale of scrap from the total turnover and the proportionate profit on sale of scrap from the 'profit of the business'.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) decided the issue in favour of the assessee. However, it was clarified that the sale of scrap would not be considered while computing the profits of the business.

On further appeal, the Tribunal recorded that if the sale of scrap was excluded from the purview of 'total turnover', the proportionate profit thereof should also be reduced from the 'Profit of the business' for the purpose of computing deduction under section 80HHC. Thus, the order passed by the Assessing Officer on this aspect was sustained.

On revenue's appeal to the High Court:

HELD: The issue has now been finally decided by the Supreme Court in CIT v. Punjab Stainless Steel Industries [2014] 364 ITR 144/46 taxmann.com 68/[2015] 229 Taxman 423 wherein after considering the relevant statutory provisions and the case law on the point, it was held by the Apex Court that the proceeds generated from the sale of scrap would not be included in the total turnover. It was observed that the intention behind the enactment of section 80HHC was to encourage export so as to earn more foreign exchange. It was concluded that once the Government decides to give some benefit to someone who is helping the nation in bringing foreign exchange, the revenue should also make all possible efforts to encourage such traders or manufacturers by giving such business units more benefits as contemplated under the provisions of law. [Para 6]

In view of the law laid down by the Apex Court in Punjab Stainless Steel Industries's case (supra), for the parties submitted that the question regarding inclusion of sale of scrap in the total turnover is required to be examined afresh by the Assessing Officer in the factual matrix of the case. It was urged that in such circumstances, the orders passed by the Commissioner (Appeals) and the Tribunal be set aside and the matter be remanded to the Assessing Officer for passing fresh order after hearing assessee on this issue in accordance with law. [Para 7]

HEADNOTE: Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from hotels or industrial undertakings, etc., in backward areas - Assessment year 1988-89 - Whether assessee firm engaged in business of breaking ships and obtaining metal which was later on sold in market could be said to be an industrial undertaking engaged in manufacture and production of things and hence entitled for deductions under sections 80HH and 80-I - Held, yes - Whether when one of partners of assessee firm retired and remaining partners took over running business, it did not amount to reconstruction of business already in existence so as to deny deductions under sections 80HH and 80-I - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee firm was in the business of ship-breaking. The assessee’s business consisted of breaking ships and obtaining metal which was later on sold in the market. For the assessment year 1988-89 the assessee’s claims under sections 80HH and 80-I were rejected on the grounds that business of ship breaking did not amount to manufacture or production of an article or a thing and secondly that the assessee had succeeded to the business on retirement of one of the partners and, hence, it was a business formed by reconstruction of a business already in existence.

On second appeal :

HELD: In the light of the decision of the Bombay Court in the case of Ship Scrap Traders (supra) which was delivered after considering the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of CIT v. N.C. Budharaja & Co. [1993] 204 ITR 412/170 Taxman 312, the assessee was to be held as a manufacturer of an article or thing and deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I could not be denied on the ground that they did not manufacture new article or thing.

As regards the alleged reconstruction of business, as contended rightly by assessee, when one partner retired and the remaining partner took over a running business, it did not amount to a case of reconstruction of an existing business but it was a case of succession to an already existing business. In the light of CIT v. Pigot Chapman & Co. [1982] 135 ITR 620/ 9 Taxman 7 the contention raised by the assessee was to be accepted. It was therefore, directed that the deductions under sections 80HH and 80-I should be allowed to the assessee subject to the satisfaction of other conditions laid down in those provisions.

HEADNOTE: Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - In respect of certain incomes of industries in backward areas - Assessment year 1988-89 - One unit of assessee-company manufactured bulk drugs and sold them to Generic Division at market value - Assessing Officer valued them at cost and held that deductions under section 80HH were wrongly inflated by company - Whether section 80HH(7) had no application as it does not deal with intra-unit transfer - Held, yes - Whether assessee had correctly valued goods at market value as directed in section 80HH(6) and had not inflated deduction - Held, yes

FACT: The Ratlam Unit of the assessee-company manufactured bulk drugs which were sold to the Generic Division at market value. The Assessing Officer valued them at cost and held that the deductions under section 80HH were wrongly inflated by the company. The department contended that the Assessing Officer had invoked section 80HH(7). The Tribunal reversed that decision.

On appeal :

HELD: Section 80HH(7) had no application. It does not deal with intra-unit transfer. The Assessing Officer had not invoked section 80HH(7). Moreover, section 80HH(6) directs the Assessing Officer to value the goods at market value. This had been done by the company. Hence, the company had not inflated the deduction under section 80HH. The appeal, was, therefore, dismissed.

HEADNOTE: Section 80HH, read with section 80J of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from hotel or industrial under taking etc., in backward areas - Assessment year 1981-82 - Assessee, an erstwhile partnership firm, was engaged in business of manufacture and sale of black steel tubes of 2 inches diameter - Assessee after having converted into a private limited company set up a project called project No. 2 consisting of milling plant for manufacture of steel tubes of 4 inches diameter - ITO rejected assessee's claim for relief under sections 80HH and 80J on ground that it was a case where new project was formed by splitting up or reconstruction of a business already in existence as machinery and plant were common to both projects or moulding plant - Tribunal, however, held that deductions ware admissible to assessee as assessee had set up a new project for manufacturing of 4 inches diameter black pipe which was different from manufacturing 2 inches diameter black pipe by assessee and merely because some of facilities were common that would not mean reconstruction or splitting up - Tribunal, accordingly, allowed assessee's claim - Whether impugned order of Tribunal was justified-Held, yes

FACT: The assessee a erstwhile a partnership firm, was engaged in manufacturing black steel tube of 2 inches diameter. It was converted into a private limited company, which set up a project called project No 2 consisting of a milling plant for manufacture of steel tubes of 4 inches diameter. The assessee claimed relief under sections 80J and 80HH to the extent of 7½ per cent of the capital employed in the project No. 2 after deduction of loans from UPFC and PICUP.

The ITO rejected the claim on the ground that the condition laid down in section 80J(4)(i) was not satisfied in as much as it was a case where the new project was formed by the splitting up or the reconstruction of a business already in existence as several machinery and plant were common to both the projects or the moulding plants.

The ITO also negatived the claim of deduction under section 80HH on the ground that the claim under section 80J was not admissible. The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the finding of the Income-tax Officer. On further appeal, the Tribunal held that the new project of the assessee was a new industrial unit, which was separate physically from the old one, the capital of which and the profits thereon ware ascertainable. It, accordingly, allowed the assessee's claim.

On reference :

HELD: The Tribunal had found that the assessee had set up a new project for manufacturing of 4 inches diameter black pipe which was different from manufacturing 2 inches diameter black pipe by the assessee. Merely because some of the facilities were common that would not mean reconstruction or splitting up.

The Tribunal had correctly applied the principle laid down by the Apex Court in Textile Machinery Corporation Ltd. v. CIT [1977] 107 ITR 195 , and, accordingly, was justified in holding that deduction under sections 80J and 80HH was admissible to the assessee in respect of the capital employed in Project No. 2.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee
