HEADNOTE: Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction - In respect of incomes of industries or hotels in backward area - Assessee, an exporter of prawns, bought prawns which were processed and thereafter exported - There was a detailed process by which prawns were prepared for export and one of the vital stages of that process was beheading, peeling and deveining of the prawns - Whether assessee was entitled to deduction under section 80HH - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee, an exporter of prawns used to buy prawns which were processed and ultimately exported. The assessee claimed deduction under section 80HH. The ITO disallowed the assessee's claim on the ground that the aforesaid business of the assessee was not one in which either manufacture or production was involved so as to attract the provisions of section 80HH.

On appeal, the Tribunal observed that, there was a detailed process by which prawns were prepared for export and one of the vital stages of that process was beheading, peeling and deveining of the prawns and, thus, allowed the deduction under section 80HH.

On reference:

HELD: Like in section 33, so also in section 80HH, the word 'manufacture' or 'produce' appear. While both the words appear in clause (i ) of sub-section (2) of section 80HH only the word 'manufacturing' appears in clause (iv ) of that sub-section. The benefit of section 80HH is available whenever anew industrial undertaking is started in a backward area and that undertaking begins to manufacture or produce articles. The facts that section 80HH(2)(iv ) refers to the manufacturing process alone does not mean that production process is excluded. Every manufacturing process naturally involves production process for the object of manufacture is the production of goods.

It processed or frozen fish and fish products can be regarded as articles manufactured or produced' for the purpose of the development rebate, it was the Legislature intent to attribute the same meaning to the identical expression appearing in another provision of the same statute, the object of which is to confer a benefit in the newly established industrial undertaking with a view to the advancement of the backward areas. In the instant case, the Tribunal understood the various stages through which prawns were prepared for export and held that process involved production or manufacture. Therefore, its finding was not perverse and was perfectly in harmony with the Legislature intent as disclosed by the scheme of the relevant provision of the statute. Hence, the assessee was rightly allowed the deduction under section 80HH.

P.K.R. Menon for the Applicant. G. Sivarajan for the Respondent.

HEADNOTE: I. Section 80HH, read with  section 80-I, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from hotels or industrial undertakings, etc., in backward areas - Whether ship breaking activity results in production of a distinct and different article and, therefore, assessee doing said activity would be entitled to deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company, engaged in the business of ship breaking, claimed deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I. The Assessing Officer disallowed the assessee's claim. On appeal, the Tribunal allowed the assessee's claim. On the revenue's appeal, the High Court held that when a ship breaking activity is undertaken, the articles, which emerge from the activity of ship breaking, continue to be the part of the ship and such parts do not constitute new goods and, consequently, the assessee was not entitled to claim the benefit under sections 80HH and 80-I as there was neither production nor manufacture of new goods by the process of ship breaking.

On appeal to the Supreme Court :

HELD: The important test, which distinguishes the word 'production' from 'manufacture', is that the word 'production' is wider than the word 'manufacture'. Further, the Legislature has used the words 'manufacture' or 'production'. Therefore, the word 'production' cannot derive its colour from the word 'manufacture'. Further, even according to the dictionary meaning of word 'production', the word 'produce' is defined as something which is brought forth or yielded either naturally or as a result of effort and work. It is important to note that the word 'new' is not used in the definition of the word 'produce'. [Para 8]

Therefore, the Tribunal was right in allowing the deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I to the assessee holding that the ship breaking activity gave rise to the production of a distinct and different article. [Para 10]

HEADNOTE: Section 80-I, read with section 80HH, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from new industrial undertakings after a certain date - Assessment years 1987-88 to 1992-93 - Assessees engaged in dismantling of damaged/unserviceable ships claimed deduction under section 80HH and 80-I - Whether legislature intended to extend benefit of deductions only to industrial undertakings manufacturing or producing articles - Held, yes - Whether as ship-breaking activity amounts to carrying out manufacturing process in reverse order, assessees were not entitled to deduction claimed - Held, yes

FACT: The assessees, engaged in the business of breaking and dismantling of damaged or unserviceable ships and selling the goods obtained therefrom to various parties, claimed deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I. The Assessing Officer rejected the claims on the grounds that the assessee were not industrial undertaking within the meaning of section 80HH and 80-I and they did not fulfil any of the conditions of those sections and that there was nothing like a process of manufacturing done by the assessees. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that ship breaking was an industrial undertaking and, accordingly, the assessees were eligible for the deductions claimed.

On revenue’s appeal :

HELD: The Legislature intended to extend the benefit of deduction under section 80HH only to the industrial undertakings which manufacture or produce articles. This section is not intended to be applied to industrial undertakings which are engaged in ‘processing of goods’ not amounting to manufacture or production of articles. The ship-breaking activity involves buying of damaged and unserviceable ships which are otherwise uneconomic to run, for the purpose of breaking and scrapping and sale of various goods and scrap obtained from such breaking and dismantling of old and used ships. Process is employed for breaking ship for dismantling and selling the scrap and substantial part of the items fitted in the ship and the oil contained in the tankers are sold in the same from without carrying out any further act, except removal of same from the ship and the remaining ship, made mainly of iron and steel, is then broken into different pieces of different sizes and shapes and sold by weight. Therefore, at the end of the process employed by the assessee, what is acquired are iron bars, plating rods, bronze, gunmetal copper and non-ferrous metal which, though marketable and commercial commodities, cannot be said to be manufactured or produced articles or things. For all practical purposes it is scrap. The scrap cannot be called a manufacture product or produced article because they are no new commodities but parts of the old and discarded ship as held by the Bombay High Court in the case of CST v. Delhi Iron & Steel Co. (P.) Ltd. [1995] 98 STC 202 the condemned and unserviceable ship purchased by the dealer is not a ship but re-rollable scrap in the form of an old ship for dismantling, in effect, the dealer acquires only the old materials and articles contained therein which are sold by it in the form in which they are acquired. No process whatsoever is applied to the goods, much less any process of manufacture. The issue stood squarely covered in favour of the revenue by the decision of the Bombay Bench of the Tribunal in the case of Asst. CIT v. Virendra & Co. [1995] 55 ITD 309 which held that ‘the meaning of manufacture and production of articles and things’ would have to be considered in their ordinary plain and natural meaning. Breaking or dismantling a ship would perhaps be just the opposite of manufacturing or production of an article or an thing. When a ship is dismantled or broken, what is obtained by the persons who are engaged in that process are the components by which the ship is constructed or manufactured and if it is possible to reassemble those pieces or parts, the ship may be manufactured or constructed. Hence, it would be doing violence to the language of the section if it is said that while a ship is being dismantled or broken or destroyed, in effect an article or thing is being manufactured or produced. Hence, the activity of breaking or dismantling of a ship cannot be considered to be an industrial undertaking which manufactured or produced articles or things and, therefore, the assessee was not entitled to deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I.

HEADNOTE: Section 80J, read with section 80HH, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from new industrial undertaking , ships or hotels - Assessment year 1987-88 - Assessee-firm carried on business of manufacturing water/air pollution control plant at site of its customers, and its claim for deductions under sections 80J and 80HH was being allowed since its inception - Whether assessee was an industrial undertaking, engaged in manufacturing or producing an article in shape of air/water control plant in a backward area, and Commissioner committed an error in setting aside Assessing Officer’s order allowing deductions under sections 80J and 80HH - Held, yes - Whether since very year of inception of assessee’s business, position had continuously remained same and in absence of any new fact coming to his knowledge or any separate enquiry having been made, it was permissible for Commissioner to start afresh from admitted position of parties on a particular point - Held, no

FACT: For the assessment year 1987-88, the assessee-firm claimed deduction under sections 80J and 80HH and the Assessing Officer allowed the same in the assessment order framed under section 143(3). The Commissioner set aside the assessment order by invoking the provisions of section 263, on the ground that the conditions laid down for allowing deductions under sections 80J and 80HH had not been fulfilled by the assessee.

On appeal:

HELD: The Supreme Court, in the case of Bangalore Water Supply & Sewerage Board v. A. Rajappa AIR 1978 SC 548, has laid down that where there is (i) systematic activity, (ii) organised by co-operation between employer and employees, (iii) for the production and/or distribution of goods and services calculated to satisfy human wants and wishes, prima facie, there is an industry. Absence of profit motive or gainful object is irrelevant. This view of the Supreme Court has been followed by the jurisdictional High Court in the case of CIT v. J.B. Kharwar & Sons [1987] 163 ITR 394 and by Karnataka High Court in the case of Shankar Construction Co. v. CIT [1991] 189 ITR 463. In the case before the Karnataka High Court, the business of constructing dams and channels was taken as that of ‘industrial undertaking’ entitled to investment allowance; while in the case of J.B. Kharwar & Sons (supra) before the Gujarat High Court, the business was that of printing and dyeing of cloths and the work was taken as manufacturing work for the entitlement of deduction under section 80J. On the basis of the above case law, the working of the assessee-firm which was involved in the work of designing, erection and commissioning of water and air pollution control plants, would certainly be falling in the category of an ‘industrial undertaking’, and the assessee-firm was an ‘industrial undertaking’ as used in sections 80HH and 80J.

In the instant case, the activities of the assessee-firm were that of manufacturing or that of producing an article as they were constructing water/air pollution plants. Thus, the assessee-firm was an ‘industrial undertaking’ and was engaged in manufacturing or producing an article in the shape of air/water pollution control. That the assessee was manufacturing or producing the plant in backward area, was one of the requirements of the claim under section 80HH. The contention of the assessee was that only 11.45 per cent of the total receipt had been taken for deduction under section 80HH as that work alone was done in backward area and it was not expected from the assessee to have its office or plant in backward area. The crux of the case laws is that if an industrial undertaking begins to manufacture or produce outside in any backward area, it is entitled to deduction under section 80HH. The assessee-firm set up its own industrial undertaking at the site of its customers for whom water/air pollution control plant was manufactured and of the places which were falling under the backward area declared under the Act, then, naturally the assessee should be getting benefit of the same and the computation made by the assessee-firm of the same was correct one.

Thus the assessee-firm had been able to make out a case in its favour on the guidelines referred to above for qualifying its claim under sections 80HH and 80J and the ITO was justified in allowing its claim from the assessment year 1982-83 onwards till the year under consideration and the Commissioner committed an error in concluding otherwise and the order of Commissioner was to be quashed on this point.

HEADNOTE: Section 80J of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from new industrial undertakings, ships or hotels - Assessment years 1979-80 to 1982-83 - Assessee-company was carrying on business in engineering contracts - During relevant accounting years it had contracts to build hydel projects and to complete this project it had to provide independent items which were manufactured by it - Whether marketability of products, intermediate or final is essential test to be satisfied before article manufactured could be considered as an article entitled to relief under section 80J and in this case that test was not satisfied in respect of articles manufactured by assessee - Held, yes - Whether since end product in this case was underground power house, all other items undertaken by the assessee were only intermediate products supporting end product and consequently they could not be termed as articles as mentioned in sections 80J and 80HH - Held, yes

Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction - Profits from newly established undertaking or hotel business in backward areas - Assessment years 1979-80 to 1982-83 - Whether in view of facts under heading ‘Deductions - Profits and gains from new industrial undertakings’ assessee was entitled to deduction under section 80HH - Held, no

FACT: The assessee was a company doing business in engineering contracts. It had during the relevant years several contracts and manufacturing activities at various sites, one of which was a C Hydel project. At said project an underground power house was to be built with horizontal pressure shafts, butterfly valve chamber, tailrace tunnel, cable and other connected tunnels. The roof of underground power house was supported by heavy steel supports manufactured in the assessee’s own workshops. The entire aggregate required for the concreting was also manufactured with the cruisers and sand processing plants at site owned by the assessee. On appeal to the Tribunal the judicial member held that the assessee was manufacturing articles or things which were independent of the main activity of the assessee at different sites and each of the articles thus manufactured was an end product by itself on the sale of which the assessee received its price, though as a part of the regular bills prepared for other works also. According to him the following were such independent items:

(i) Permanent steel supports; (ii) Rock bolts; (iii) Steel reinforcement work; and (iv) Heavy foundation work. He held that the assessee had manufactured articles and, therefore, was entitled to the claim under section 80J as well as under section 80HH. The Accountant Member held that since the end product in this case was the underground power house, all other items undertaken by the assessee were only intermediate products supporting the end product and consequently they could not be termed as, articles as mentioned in sections 80J and 80HH.

As there was difference of opinion between the members the matter was referred to the Third Member.

HELD [PER ORDER OF THE THIRD MEMBER]

It is no doubt true that neither in section 80J nor in section 80HH there is a stipulation that the things or articles manufactured should be marketable but according to the interpretation placed upon an identical section 84 by the Supreme Court in the case of CIT v. Cellulose Products of India Ltd. [1991] 192 ITR 155, the marketability of the things manufactured becomes the only relevant consideration and has to be assumed to be applied for the grant of relief under section 80J. Therefore, marketability of the commodities manufactured, whether intermediate or final, is the essential test to be satisfied before an article manufactured could be considered as an article entitled to the relief under section 80J.

This can be understood even from a commercial angle. What is the purpose of manufacturing things or articles unless they are to be sold and how can an undertaking yield any income unless the things or articles manufactured by it are sold. Either it may manufacture the articles or things for sale or for eventual consumption as raw material for the manufacture of other products. In the former case the marketability test will naturally become the relevant test. In the latter case the finished product will have to become marketable. Thus, in either case the things manufactured or produced will have to be marketed because it is inconceivable for an industrial undertaking to exist to manufacture articles or things not intended for sale or consumption. If it is the case of the consumption of the articles manufactured, then the ultimate thing, i.e., the final product must become marketable. The High Courts have consistently held that in the case of contractors building bridges, buildings etc., there could not be any manufacture of articles intended for sale otherwise than for consuming them in executing the contract.

HEADNOTE: SECTION 80HH OF THE INCOME-TAX ACT, 1961 - DEDUCTIONS-PROFIIS AND GAINS FROM NEWLY ESTABLISHED INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKINGS, ETC., IN BACK- WARD AREAS -ASSESSEE-COMPANY, WHOSE BUSINESS WAS REPAIRS OF BARGES, WAS NOT ALLOWED DEDUCTION UNDER SECTION 80HH BY ITO, SINCE ITS 
ACTIVITIES COMMENCED PRIOR To 31-12-1970-WHETHER DEDUCTION WAS ALLOWABLE SINCE NO MANUFACTURING ACTIVITY COMMENCED BEFORE THAT 
DATE AND ONLY REPAIRING ACTIVITY WAS DONE-HELD, NO

SECTION 139(8)  OF THE INCOME-TAX ACT, 1961-RETURN OF INCOME- 
INTEREST FOR LATE FILING OF-WHETHER, BEFORE LEVYING INTEREST, ASSESSEE MUST BE PROVIDED OPPORTUNITY OF BEING HEARD-HELD, NO

FACT: For late filing of return, the ITO levied interest while completing the assessment, but the Commissioner (Appeals) cancelled the levy on the ground that the ITO failed to give opportunity of hearing to the assessee.

On second appeal:

HELD: Levy of interest under section 139 is automatic, and the ITO has no discre-tion in the matter. The only remedy available to the assessee is to apply for its waiver, under rule 117A, and the very use, of the word 'reduce' in that rule pre-supposes levy of interest at an anterior stage. The Commissioner (Appeals) was, therefore, not right in cancelling the levy.

HEADNOTE: Section 80HH, read with  section 80J of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profit and gains from hotels or industrial undertakings etc., in backward areas - Assessment years 1979-80 and 1980-81 - Whether business of tyre retreading does not amount to production of new article entitling assessee to relief under sections 80HH and 80J - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company, which was retreader and established its plant in a backward area, claimed deductions under sections 80HH and 80J. The Assessing Officer disallowed the assessee's claim. On second appeal, the Tribunal held that the business of tyre retreading amounted to the production of a new article and that, therefore, the assessee was entitled to the relief under sections 80J and 80HH.

On reference:

HELD: The word "manufacture" or "produce articles" used in the provision to section 80HH have not been defined in the Act. The word "manufacture" has been considered by the Supreme Court and the High Courts on numerous occasions and the common thread which runs in all the decisions is that it is only when a new and distinct commodity commercially accepted as such, comes into existence as a result of the processing, that a commodity can be said to have been manufactured.

Having regard to the fact that the word "article" used in the section is an article which is manufactured or produced and the word "produce" having been used in juxtaposition with the word "manufacture" it connotes the bringing into existence of new goods. The result of production should be the coming into existence of a new article. The terms "production" and "produce" would also take in by-products, intermediate products and residual products. All of them should be products or articles, which are capable of being regarded as new articles. By holding that a "new" article should emerge from manufacture or production new words are not being added to section 80HH. The term new has been employed in the decisions of the courts only to indicate the end result of the process of production or manufacture. It is only when that result can be said to have been achieved, that the industrial undertaking which brings about such a result by its process of production or manufacture, would qualify for the benefits conferred under the section. In view of aforesaid, it could not be said that retreading of tyres resulted in the production of an article for the purpose of section 80HH.

Hence, the Tribunal was not right in holding that the business of tyre retreading amounted to the production of a new article entitling the assessee to the relief under sections 80J and 80HH.

Note: The case has been decided in favour of the revenue.

HEADNOTE: Section 80HH, read with  section 80-I, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from hotels or industrial undertakings, etc., in backward areas - Assessment year 1993-94 - Whether only that income, which has a direct or immediate nexus with industrial undertaking, will be taken into consideration for calculating deduction under section 80HH/80-I - Held, yes - Whether where main business of assessee was to manufacture and sell soyabeen oil, income earned by assessee from sale of old gunny bags could be treated as an income earned from industrial undertaking within meaning of section 80HH/80-I - Held, no

FACT: The assessee-company was engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling soyabean oil. For the relevant assessment year, it claimed deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I on the amount realized by it from sale of the old gunny bags (packing material). The Assessing Officer disallowed the assessee's claim holding that the said income could not be treated as an income derived from an industrial undertaking. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) granted deduction as claimed by the assessee. On the revenue's appeal, the Tribunal upheld the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) holding that the amount earned by the assessee from the sale of old gunny bags was an income derived from industrial undertaking within the meaning of section 80HH/80-I and was eligible for deduction.

HELD: As per the law laid down by the Supreme Court in several decisions, the expression 'derived from' is to be given restricted meaning in section 80HH/80-I while interpreting the section in which this expression is used. [Para 15]

In the instant case, the main and only business of the assessee, for which the plant was set up in the backward area, was to manufacture and to sell soya oil. Hence, all incomes derived from sale of soya oil would be income derived from an industrial undertaking for the purpose of calculating deduction under section 80HH/80-I.

The income earned by the assessee out of sale of gunny bags could not be kept at par or alike the income derived from sale of soya bean oil due to following reasons - Sale of gunny bags was not the main or even ancillary business activity of the assessee; it was not regular or continuous business activity; no investment was made by the assessee for their sale. The gunny bags were never manufactured by the assessee in its plant and merely because some gunny bags were lying in the factory as surplus or unused or as waste material for any reason and such bags were sold to earn income, then it could not be a ground to hold that for the purpose of section 80HH/80-I, such income was the income actually derived from the assessee's industrial undertaking. [Para 16]

In order to derive income from industrial undertaking, the assessee must show that it was earned by sale of goods/commodity which were manufactured/produced in the said industrial undertakings as a part of its main and day-to-day business activity. Only then, the income earned by sale of such goods can be termed as income derived from industrial undertaking within the meaning of section 80HH/80-I. It is for this reason that it has a direct or immediate nexus with the assessee's industrial undertaking established in the backward area. This necessarily follows that income, which has a direct or immediate nexus with the industrial undertaking, alone will be taken into consideration for calculating the deduction under section 80HH/80-I, ibid. Such was not the case in the instant case, because the income earned from sale of gunny bags was not the result of direct or immediate nexus with the business of assessee carried on in the industrial undertaking. [Para 17]

Hence, the Tribunal fell in error in holding that the income earned by the assessee from sale of gunny bags was an income earned from industrial undertaking within the meaning of section 80HH/80-I and, accordingly, the assessee was entitled to claim deduction from total income. That view was to be reversed and order of the Tribunal was to be set aside. [Para 21]

HEADNOTE: Section 80HH, read with section 80I, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from hotels or industrial undertakings, etc. in backward areas - Assessment year 1989-90 - Assessee-company claimed benefits under sections 80HH and 80-I after excluding expenses on research and development carried out by it at its establishment at ‘M’ - Assessing Officer allocated certain sum as expenditure on research and development pertaining to ‘C’ unit, though according to assessee, there was no research and development in that unit - Tribunal upheld allocation of research and development expenses to ‘C’ unit as justified on presumption that any technology about new flavours and essence would automatically be utilised in ‘C’ unit also - Whether apportionment of expenses on activities of research and development to ‘C’ unit merely on presumption that products manufactured at ‘C’ also had benefit of research made at ‘M’ was not proper as assessee had other manufacturing units besides one ‘C’ - Held, yes - Whether for purpose of determining as to whether at all there was research and development undertaken regarding product manufactured in ‘C’ unit, matter was to be remitted back to Tribunal - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company carrying on business in the manufacture and sale of flavours, essence, etc., claimed benefits under sections 80HH and 80I after excluding the expenses on research and development carried out it at its establishment at ‘M’. The Assessing Officer allocated certain sum as expenses for the benefit of the ‘C’ unit as a consequence of which the deductions under sections 80HH and 80I got reduced and the burden of taxation became heavier for the assessee. The assessee submitted before the Tribunal that there was no research and development expenses at ‘C’ unit, and that research and development carried out at ‘M’ was not with regard to the product manufactured at ’C’. The Tribunal, however, upheld the order of the Assessing Officer.

On reference :

HELD: Apportionment of expenses on activities of research and development to ‘C’ unit merely on the presumption that products manufactured at ‘C’ also had the benefit of the research made at ‘M’ by the Research and Development Department was not proper.

The Tribunal had also not gone into this aspect. Instead, there was a presumption made that any technology about new flavours and essence would automatically be utilised in ‘C’ unit also without examining as to whether the research and development actually carried out at ‘M’ was of use for the unit at ‘C’ as the assessee had other manufacturing units besides the one at ‘C’. It was only on such presumption, allocation of the research and development expenses to ‘C’ unit was held by the Tribunal to be justified.

For the purpose of determining as to whether at all there was research and development undertaken regarding the product that was manufactured in ‘C’ unit, the matter was remitted back to the Tribunal. If it did pertain to the product manufactured at ‘C’ only then the allocation of the expense to ‘C’ unit would be justified.

Note : Matter remitted back.

P.P.S. Janardhanaraja and Subbaraya Aiyar for the Appellant.

T. Ravikumar for the Respondent.

HEADNOTE: Section 80HHC of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Exporters - Assessment year 2002-03 - Assessee was a manufacturer of commutators - It also manufactured certain goods on sub-contract basis for others and received service charges; and also received certain sums from sale of copper scrap - Assessee claimed deduction under section 80HHC on whole amount which included latter two receipts also - Assessing authority, however, held that receipts from sub-contract and scrap fell within Explanation (baa) to section 80HHC and, therefore, same could not be included for claiming section 80HHC deduction - Whether since both receipts from sub-contract and scrap had been arisen out of very same business of manufacturing of commutators, said receipts did not fall within Explanation(baa) to section 80HHC - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was a manufacturer of commutators. It also manufactured certain goods on sub-contract basis for others and received services/job charges and besides receipts from sale of copper scrap. They claimed deduction under section 80HHC including the said receipts. The assessing authority held that the receipts from the sub-contract receipts and scrap fell within the Explanation ( baa) to section 80HHC and, therefore, the same could not be included. Aggrieved by the said order, the assessee preferred an appeal. The appellate authority held that as there was a direct nexus between the receipts from special contract as well as sale of scrap material, it did not fall within the Explanation ( baa) and the assessee was entitled to include the said receipts in the income from the business and profits. The revenues appeal to the Tribunal came to be dismissed.

HELD: From the material on record, it is clear that the assessee is in the business of manufacture of commutators and they export the commutators after manufacturing and they have export income. They also manufacture certain products which are sold locally. The scrap which is sold is generated in the course of the manufacturing activity. Therefore, it is clear both the subject matter of the sub-contract and the scrap arises out of the very same business of manufacturing of commutators carried on by the assessee. Therefore, it does not fall within the Explanation (baa) to section 80HHC as rightly held by the Tribunal as well as the appellate authority. [Para 4]

In these circumstances, there is no justification to interfere with the order passed by the Tribunal as it is strictly in accordance with law. Accordingly, the substantial question of law is answered in favour of the assessee and against the revenue. Appeals are dismissed. [Para 5]

M.V. Seshachala for the Appellant. S. Parthasarathi for the Respondent.

-A, like section 80HHC or 80HH. In such a situation the deduction to the extent of such profits and gains shall not be allowed under any sections of 80HH to 80RR and shall in no case exceed the profits and gains of the undertaking or the hotel as the case may be. Thus, there is a total capping on claiming deduction from profits and gains of industrial undertaking, which is equal to 100 per cent of such profits. [Para 16] The question that arose for consideration was whether amount of deduction allowed under section 80-IA will be reduced from the business profit while working out deduction under section 80HHC, i.e., reduction would be made in the business profits before applying the formula of section 80HHC as suggested by the Commissioner (Appeals), or after applying the formula to the profits of industrial undertaking, working out the deduction under section 80HHC and then to reduce the deduction already allowed under section 80-IA. As per the language used in section 80-IA(9A), the deduction allowed under section 80-IA will not be allowed as further deduction under other sections 80HH to 80RRA. That means that deduction under section 80HHC will be worked out independently, without reducing the ‘business profits’ by the deduction under section 80-IA. That is, effect of deduction under section 80-IA will be given after applying the formula and working out deduction under section 80HHC. So deduction under section 80HHC has to be calculated independently and then effect of section 80-IA(9A) has to be given. Where deduction under section 80HHC is more than the deduction under section 80-IA, the figure of deduction under section 80-IA will be reduced from the deduction under section 80HHC. The balance will be the deduction under section 80HHC. Where deduction under section 80-IA is more than the deduction under section 80HHC calculated for the unit, then no deduction under section 80HHC will be separately allowed. Hence, in a case where both the deduction are available to an assessee, than higher of the two would be allowed. [Para 17]

The upper limit of the deductions under sections 80HH to 80RRA has also been laid down under section 80-IA(9A), where it is said that in no case the deductions shall exceed the profits and gains of the undertaking. Thus, in no case deductions under section 80-IA and other sections from 80HH to 80RRA will exceed 100 per cent of the profits of the undertaking. Further, deduction under section 80HHC will have to be calculated unit-wise and not for whole of the business. Thus, it is clear from sub-section (2) that total deductions under Chapter VI-A will not exceed the total income computed before giving deduction under Chapter VI-A. Hence, the deduction under section 80-IA or 80HHC will be computed unit-wise and independent of any deduction allowed in any other section of Chapter VIA. Deductions under section 80-IA and under any other sections from 80HHC to 80RRA together will be available to the extent of higher of the two. Overall deductions in respect of an industrial unit under sections 80-IA and 80HH to 80RRA will be limited to 100 per cent of profits and gains of that industrial undertaking. In no case deduction under Chapter VI-A will exceed gross total income before allowing those deductions. Therefore, the steps 1, 2 and 3(a) suggested by the Commissioner (Appeals) in his order were correct. But for the purpose of computing deductions under other sections, such as 80HHC, no effect of deduction under section 80-IA would be given but after computing deduction under section 80HHC the capping would be done. [Para 18]

EDITOR’S NOTE

1. It was also held by the Tribunal that for computing deduction under section 80HHC not only sale of scrap by the assessee but also sale of steam would be part of ‘business profit’, once it was held by the Commissioner (Appeals) that both sale of scrap and sale of steam would constitute part of turnover.

2. It was further held by the Tribunal that insurance claim received by the assessee would form both parts of the assessee’s business profit as well turnover. Similarly, sale of ammonia, which gave rise to miscellaneous income of the assessee, would also form part of the assessee’s business profit, as well as total turnover to determine deduction under section 80HHC.

HEADNOTE: Section 80HH, read with section 80-I, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from hotels or industrial undertakings, etc., in backward areas - Assessment years 1993-94 to 1995-96 - Whether in case of manufacturing activity inputs and outputs should be commercially different - Held, yes - Whether commercial identity is to be considered in light of respective trade practice, or  if there is no such trade practice, in light of common parlance meaning - Held, yes - Assessee was engaged in manufacture of graded metal (granite rubble of various sizes) - It claimed deductions under sections 80HH and 80-I on ground that it was carrying on a manufacturing activity - Assessing Officer denied deductions holding that conversion of granite boulders into granite rubble of various sizes did not amount to manufacturing, as raw material and final product were same and only difference was in size - Whether since granite rubbles/aggregates of different sizes sold by assessee were commercially different from granite boulders extracted by assessee from quarry, assessee was carrying on a manufacturing activity - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, assessee was entitled to deductions under both sections 80HH and 80-I independently - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was a small-scale industrial unit manufacturing graded metal (granite rubble of various sizes). It claimed deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I on the ground that it was carrying on a manufac- turing activity. The Assessing Officer denied the deductions holding that conversion of granite boulders into granite rubble of various sizes did not amount to manufacturing, as the raw material and the final product were the same and the only difference was in sizes and, therefore, the activity carried on by the assessee could not be held as a manufacturing activity.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that the various processes employed by the assessee ultimately resulted in an end-product (granite aggregate), which had a distinct utilitarian value, which the primary material of boulders did not possess and, therefore, the activity carried on by the assessee was in the nature of manufacturing activity. He, therefore, allowed the assessee’s claim for deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I.

On further appeal by the department :

HELD: It is well settled by the Supreme Court in the case of Pio Food Packers 46 STC 632 that in the case of a manufacturing activity the inputs and outputs should be commercially different. This "commercial identity" is to be considered in the light of the respective trade practice, or if there is no such trade practice, in the light of common partanee meaning. In the instant case, the raw material extracted by the assessee was the granite boulders. What was sold by the assessee was granite aggregate (commonly known as metal) of different commercial sizes of 1.1/2", 1", ½", ¼", etc. These different sizes of granite aggregates were used for different purposes, even though used generally in construction activities. The granite aggregates of different sizes sold by the assessee were commercially different from granite boulders extracted by the assessee from the quarry. There was no doubt that they were commercially different. Therefore, the assessee was carrying on a manufacturing activity and, hence, it was entitled for the deductions available under sections 80HH and 80-I. [Para 11]

The Rajasthan High Court in the case of CIT v. Chokshi Contacts (P.) Ltd. has held that deductions under sections 80HH and 80-I operate independently and the assessee is entitled to deductions under both sections, which is to be simultaneously granted without any order of preference. Therefore, the Assessing Officer was directed to grant the benefit of sections 80HH and 80-I independently on the eligible profits of the assessee. [Para 12]

Hence, the department’s appeal was liable to be dismissed. [Para 13]

FACT: The assessee claimed deduction under section 80HHC stating that it was engaged in the manufacture and sale of harvester combines and its spare parts and components. The Assessing Officer while computing deduction under section 80HHC included warranty claims received by the assessee and the amount realized on sale of scrap as part of total turnover. He, further excluded 90 per cent of the provision written back and 90 per cent of the interest income being received from customers on delayed payments from the profits of business for the purpose of computing deduction under section 80HHC.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the action of the Assessing Officer.

On second appeal :

HELD: SALE PROCEEDS OF SCRAP : NOT PART OF TOTAL TURNOVER

Clause (ba ) of Explanation below sub-section (4C) of section 80HHC provides that 'total turnover' shall not include freight or insurance attributable to the transport of the goods beyond the custom station. The proviso to this definition provides that the expression 'total turnover' excludes various export benefits referred in clauses (iiia ) to (iiie) of section 28. However, there is no provision which defines the words 'total turnover'. The term 'turnover' means the value of goods purchased/sold in the course of carrying of business. The business of assessee was manufacture and sale of harvester combine and its spares. The scrap generated during the manufacturing process was sold as such. The assessee was not engaged in the business of sale of scrap. Thus, the scrap, generated and which was sold, only reduced the cost of material consumed in the manufacturing process. Accordingly, the same could not be considered as part of turnover of the business carried on by the assessee. Therefore, the Assessing Officer was directed to exclude the amount realized on sale of scrap from the total turnover adopted for computing deduction under section 80HHC. [Para 12]

WARRANTY CLAIM : PART OF TURNOVER

Counter claim made by the customers of assessee were also paid. In a way, it was arising in the course of business but could not be considered as part of turnover. Therefore, the warranty claims were not to be included in the total turnover for the purpose of computing deduction under section 80HHC. [Para 13]

manufacture. The associated words are indicative of the mind of Legislature. Where a word is doubtful or ambiguous in nature, the meaning has to be ascertained by considering the company in which it is found and the meaning of the word associated with it. The words 'manufacture' and 'production' have received extensive judicial attention both under the Act as well as the Central Excise Act and the various sales tax laws. The word 'production' has wider connotation than the word 'manufacture'. Applying the principles spelt out by the Apex Court in CIT v. N.C. Budharaja & Co. [1993] 204 ITR 412/ 70 Taxman 312 and the ordinary meaning of the word 'produce' as disclosed by the dictionary and by its ordinary connotation, it could be held that when the word 'manufacture' appears in the company of the word 'production', which has wider connotation than the word 'manufacture', then in that event the word 'manufacture' would have to be interpreted in a wider sense and would have to be understood at par with meaning assigned to the word 'production' and if such approach contemplated by the Legislature is adopted, then in that event it is not difficult to reach the conclusion that the assessees were the industrial undertakings, engaged in manufacture and production of articles and things. Further, the Apex Court in the aforementioned case observed that the word 'production' or 'produce' takes into account all the by-products, intermediate products and residual products which emerge in the course of manufacture of goods. The Apex Court while considering the next word 'articles' occurring in the said clause has noticed that the word 'articles' is preceded by the words 'it has begun or begins to manufacture or produce' and reached to the conclusion that the expressions 'manufacture' and 'produce' are normally associated with movables, i.e., articles and goods, big and small.

Applying the said yardstick adopted by the Apex Court and considering the peculiar nature of the ship-breaking activity, it could be viewed that the ship-breaking activity gave rise to manufacture and production of altogether a new commercial article or thing which is commercially identifiable in the commercial world other than the ship and, therefore, the assessees should be held entitled to claim deductions under sections 80HHA and 80-I.

HEADNOTE: Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - In respect of certain income of hotels or industries in backward areas - Assessment year 1979-80 - Whether industrial undertakings engaged in processing of goods or articles not amounting to manufacture or production are entitled to benefit of section 80HH - Held, no - Whether processing of prawns amounts to manufacture or production of articles within meaning of section 80HH, so as to entitle an assessee, engaged in such processing and sale of prawns, to deduction under section 80HH - Held, no

FACT: The assessee derived income from sale of prawns. The nature of activity carried on by the assessee was purchase of raw prawns, subjecting the same to the process of cutting the heads and tails, cleaning, etc., and thereafter selling the same. In the assessment for the assessment year 1979-80, the assessee claimed deduction under section 80HH from the income from sale of prawns on the ground that the activity of processing of prawns before putting them for sale amounted to 'manufacture' and 'production' of articles within the meaning of section 80HH. The ITO rejected the claim, observing that the activity of processing prawns for the purpose of sale did not amount to manufacture or production of goods or articles within the meaning of section 80HH. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the deduction to the assessee and the Tribunal confirmed the order of Commissioner (Appeals).

On reference :

HELD: Section 80HH applies to those industrial undertakings only which 'manufacture or produce articles'. The manufacturing process mentioned in clause (iv) of sub-section (2) refers to the process undertaken to achieve the above object, i.e., to 'manufacture or produce articles'. Sub-section (4) also uses the same expression 'begins to manufacture or produce articles'. This section nowhere uses the expression 'processes goods or articles'.

On a careful reading of section 80HH in the light of scheme thereof and other provisions of the Act referred to above, it is clear that the Legislature intended to extend the benefit of deduction under section 80HH only to the industrial undertakings which manufacture or produce articles. Manufacture, as observed by the Supreme Court in Dy. CST v. Pio Food Packers [1980] 46 STC 63, is the end result of one or more processes through which the original commodity is made to pass. The nature and extent of processing may vary from one case to another, and indeed there may be several stages of processing and perhaps different kinds of processing at each stage and with each process suffered, the original commodity experiences a change. But it is only when the change, or a series of changes, take the commodity to the point where commercially it can no longer be regarded as the original commodity but instead is recognised as a new and distinct article that a manufacture can be said to take place. Where the commodity retains a continuing substantial identity through the processing stage, it cannot be said that there has been manufacture. Similarly, the word 'production' has a wider connotation than the word 'manufacture'. While every manufacture can be characterised as production, every production need not amount to manufacture. As observed by the Supreme Court in CIT v. B. C. Budharaja Co. [1993] 204 ITR 412, the word 'production' or 'produce' when used in juxtaposition with the word 'manufacture' takes in bringing into existence new goods by a process which may or may not amount to manufacture. It also takes in all the by-products, intermediate products and residual products, which emerge in the course of manufacture of goods. This section was not intended to beapplied to industrial undertakings which are engaged in 'processing of goods' not amounting to manufacture or production of articles. 'Processing' means subjecting a commodity to a process or treatment so as to develop it or make it fit for market. Processing is, thus, an operation on an article so that it undergoes a change. There may be processes undertaken by an industrial undertaking which may result in conversion of the article into a new commercial commodity or may change the nature and character of the article in such a manner that it may lose its original identity and get transformed into an entirely new commodity. In such cases 'manufacture' can be said to have taken place.

HEADNOTE: Sections 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction - Profits and gains from newly established industrial undertakings, etc. in backward areas - Three units belonging to assessee were crushing barytes into powder for hire and receiving crushing charges - Further, assessee had not prepared separate profit and loss accounts and balance sheets for each unit - Whether barytes are distinct not only in form and name but also in use from barytes powder and barytes powder is distinct and separate article produced from barytes and, therefore, barytes powder is an article produced from barytes - Held, yes - Whether sections 80HH and 80-I do not contemplate division of profits and gains in respect of a unit and Assessing Officer may compute such profits and gains under section 80HH on such reasonable basis as he may deem fit - Held, yes - Whether when industrial units satisfied other critiera laid down under sections 80HH and 80-I, assessee was entitled to deduction - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee established three industrial units in backward areas. The units were crushing barytes into powder for hire and receiving crushing charges. The Assessing Officer held that mere crushing of barytes was not a manufacturing activity nor the powder produced could be called a new article. He further found that the assessee had not prepared separate profit and loss accounts and balance sheets in respect of each unit. He, therefore, disallowed the assessee’s claim for deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I. The Commissioner (Appeals) affirmed the order of the Assessing Officer. However, the Tribunal found that the barytes powder so produced got its marketability for its use for the purposes totally different from that of barytes. It further held that irrespective of the fact that there was no division of account, still they were entitled for the benefit of sections 80HH and 80-I as having satisfied the conditions laid down thereunder.

On reference :

HELD: Sections 80HH and 80-I do not contemplate the division of profits and gains in respect of a unit, provided the industrial undertaking satisfies the criteria laid down under section 80HH. The proviso of section 80HH(c ) itself provides that if in the opinion of the Assessing Officer, the computation of the profits and gains of industrial undertaking presents exceptional difficulties, the officer may compute such profits and gains on such reasonable basis as he may deem fit. In other words, it empowers the Assessing Officer to ascertain the profits and gains of a particular unit and make assessment. Therefore, the assessee was entitled to the benefit of sections 80HH and 80-I, provided the criteria laid down were satisfied.

It is not disputed that the barytes were made into powder by using power and the powder is a distinct and separate article from barytes and the use of barytes powder is in the manufacturing of paints while the barytes are used in a different form for different purposes.

Further, the barytes powder is marketed as such. Therefore, barytes are distinct not only in form and name but also in use from barytes powder and barytes powder is distinct and separate article produced from barytes. Therefore, it cannot be said that barytes powder is not an article produced from barytes. As a result, the assessee was entitled to deductions under sections 80HH and 80-I.

J.V. Prasad for the Applicant.

Section 80-IC of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Special provisions in respect of certain undertakings or enterprises in certain special category States (Scrap sale receipt) - Assessment year 2010-11 - Assessee was engaged in manufacture of shampoo products for Hindustan Unilever Ltd. [HUL] on job work basis - It submitted that HUL supplied raw material in drums and corrugated bags, etc. and after use of raw material, it had sold these packing materials/scrap and aggregate amount of scrap sale was credited to profit and loss account (thereby reducing cost of production); that scrap sale activity was entrusted to by HUL by simultaneously corresponding reduction in rates of job work; and therefore, scrap sale receipts qualified for deduction under section 80-IC - Whether since sale of scrap had effect of reducing cost of production, amount derived by sale of scrap was eligible for deduction under section 80-IC - Held, yes [Para 38] [In favour of assessee]

Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from hotels or industrial undertakings etc., in backward areas (Manufacturing activity) - Assessment years 1984-85 to 1987-88, 1991-92 - Assessee, a railway construction company, would be eligible for deduction under section 80HH in respect of income derived from manufacturing of large number of items which were used in fabrication and installation of railway lines/tracks even though such manufacturing activity was insignificant as compared to total turnover of assessee [In favour of assessee]

VI. Section 80HHC of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction - Exporter (Computation of deduction) - Assessment year 2003-04 - Whether sale of scrap cannot be considered as part of 'total turnover' for purpose of calculation of deduction under section 80HHC in case of assessee engaged in manufacturing of industrial boilers - Held, yes [Para 49] [In favour of assessee]

Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from hotels or industrial undertakings, etc., in backward areas - Assessment year 1988-89 - Whether assessee firm engaged in business of breaking ships and obtaining metal which was later on sold in market could be said to be an industrial undertaking engaged in manufacture and production of things and hence entitled for deductions under sections 80HH and 80-I - Held, yes - Whether when one of partners of assessee firm retired and remaining partners took over running business, it did not amount to reconstruction of business already in existence so as to deny deductions under sections 80HH and 80-I - Held, yes

Section 80HHC, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction - Exporter (Computation of deduction) - Whether sale proceeds generated from sale of scrap would not be included in total turnover for purpose of deduction under section 80HHC - Held, yes [Para 2] [In favour of assessee]IT : Sale proceeds generated from sale of scrap would not be included in total turnover for purpose of deduction under section 80HHC

VII. Section 80HHC of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction - Exporters (Computation of deduction) - Assessment years 2002-03 to 2005-06 - Whether internal consumption of power would not form part of total turnover for purpose of computing relief under section 80HHC - Held, yes - Whether scrap sale is to be excluded from total turnover while computing deduction under section 80HHC - Held, yes [Para 60] [In favour of assessee]

Section 2(f) of the Central Excise Act, 1944 - Manufacture - emptying of drum - by taking out its contents - not amounting to manufacture of scrap as the drum after emptying remains drum and no new commercially different product comes into existence
