TRADING LIABILITY-WHETHER IN VIEW OF THE FACTS MENTIONED UNDER 
CAPTION 'DEDUCTION - IN RESPECT OF PROFITS AND GAINS OF INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKING, ETC., IN BACKWARD AREAS', SECTION 41(1) WAS NOT 
APPLICABLE INTO PROFITS DERIVED BY ASSESSEE PROM SALE OF SCRAP AND 
DRUMS-HELD, YES

Section 80HH, read with section 80I, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from hotels or industrial undertakings, etc. in backward areas - Assessment year 1989-90 - Assessee-company claimed benefits under sections 80HH and 80-I after excluding expenses on research and development carried out by it at its establishment at ‘M’ - Assessing Officer allocated certain sum as expenditure on research and development pertaining to ‘C’ unit, though according to assessee, there was no research and development in that unit - Tribunal upheld allocation of research and development expenses to ‘C’ unit as justified on presumption that any technology about new flavours and essence would automatically be utilised in ‘C’ unit also - Whether apportionment of expenses on activities of research and development to ‘C’ unit merely on presumption that products manufactured at ‘C’ also had benefit of research made at ‘M’ was not proper as assessee had other manufacturing units besides one ‘C’ - Held, yes - Whether for purpose of determining as to whether at all there was research and development undertaken regarding product manufactured in ‘C’ unit, matter was to be remitted back to Tribunal - Held, yes

Section 80HHC of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Exporters (Computation of deduction) - Assessment year 1997-98 - Whether for purpose of section 80HHC, proceeds of sale of scrap would not form part of 'total turnover' - Held, yes - Whether where turnover would relate to a turnover of paper manufactured by assessee, turnover of sale of scrap must not be added - Held, yes [Para 5] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : For purpose of section 80HHC, proceeds of sale of scrap would not form part of 'total turnover'

Section 80HHC of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Exporters - Assessment years 1989-90 to 1991-92 - Sale of scrap in India is to be included as part of 'total turnover' of assessee for purposes of calculation of deduction under section 80HHC [In favour of revenue]

Penalty - Rule209A of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - leviable on senior executives of assessee when they gave direction to their subordinates to act in a manner, which rendered the goods liable to confiscation even though they have not physically dealt with the offending goods. (Para 5 (g))  Dutiability - Carbouys and Drums - cleared as scrap - not dutiable as they do not come into existence due to a process of manufacture. (Para 7)  Penalty - Section 11AC of the Central Excise Act, 1944 - need not be equal to duty evaded - appeals disposed of. (Para 7)

Section 80HH of Income-tax Act, 1961
Where part of business activity is carried out in backward area assessee would be entitled only to a proportionate deduction
ITO v. Echel Mehra Forest Ind. (P.) Ltd. [1983] 16 TTJ (Chd.) 324
The assessee company was based in backward areas declared in Schedule VIII. The forests where it fell trees and brought them to its company were situated in non-backward areas. From forests to the depots situated in backward areas, the wood floated through river and floating of the wood in the river to the depot was a mixed process of transport and it passed through backward and non-backward areas. While the  assessee claimed 100 per cent deduction the Income-tax Officer held that no deduction was to be allowed as the assessee was situated in non-backward area. The Commissioner, on appeal, after taking into consideration the length of backward areas the wood travelled through granted 2.5  per cent of the total relief admissible under section 80HH.
Held that the assessee was not entitled to 100 per cent relief but on facts on basis of length of backward area through which the wood travelled  assessee could be allowed 1.5  per cent of relief contemplated in section 80HH.

III. Section 80HH, read with Section 80-I of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from hotels or industrial undertakings etc. in backward areas [Conditions precedent] - Assessment years 1986-87 and 1987-88 - Assessee had claimed deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I on ground that it had established a new factory for manufacturing industrial vanaspathi - Assessing Officer held that assessee did not establish any new industrial unit and had only improved existing vanaspathi unit by adding new machineries and disallowed deductions claimed by assessee - Tribunal, however, reversed order of Assessing Officer based on its earlier order dated 15-6-2006 and 28-4-2003 in assessee's own case for assessment year 1985-86 - Whether since orders passed by Tribunal dated 15-6-2006 and 28-4-2003 were set aside by this Court in IT Appeal No. 128/2007 and assessee did not bring any material on record for seeking deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I, order passed by Tribunal was legally unsustainable - Held, yes [Para 28] [In favour of revenue]

III. Section 80HH,  read with section 80-I of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from hotels or industrial undertakings etc., in backward areas (Computation of deduction) - Assessment years 1994-95 and 1995-96 - Assessee-company's Gehring division was established and located in industrially backward area classified for purposes of sections 80-HH and 80-I - It claimed deductions for said division independently under both provisions - It was found that assessee could not quantify actual amount of expenditure attributable to said division - Whether there was wrong computation of profit of assessee's division and, therefore, assessee could not claim deduction for amount it had not correctly computed - Held, yes [Para 22][In favour of revenue]

Section 80HH, read with section 80-I, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from hotels or industrial undertakings, etc., in backward areas - Assessment years 1993-94 to 1995-96 - Whether in case of manufacturing activity inputs and outputs should be commercially different - Held, yes - Whether commercial identity is to be considered in light of respective trade practice, or  if there is no such trade practice, in light of common parlance meaning - Held, yes - Assessee was engaged in manufacture of graded metal (granite rubble of various sizes) - It claimed deductions under sections 80HH and 80-I on ground that it was carrying on a manufacturing activity - Assessing Officer denied deductions holding that conversion of granite boulders into granite rubble of various sizes did not amount to manufacturing, as raw material and final product were same and only difference was in size - Whether since granite rubbles/aggregates of different sizes sold by assessee were commercially different from granite boulders extracted by assessee from quarry, assessee was carrying on a manufacturing activity - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, assessee was entitled to deductions under both sections 80HH and 80-I independently - Held, yes

Section 80HH, read with  section 80-I, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from hotels or industrial undertakings, etc., in backward areas - Assessment year 1993-94 - Whether only that income, which has a direct or immediate nexus with industrial undertaking, will be taken into consideration for calculating deduction under section 80HH/80-I - Held, yes - Whether where main business of assessee was to manufacture and sell soyabeen oil, income earned by assessee from sale of old gunny bags could be treated as an income earned from industrial undertaking within meaning of section 80HH/80-I - Held, no

Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from hotels or industrial undertakings, etc., in backward areas - Assessment years 1981-82 to 1983-84 - Assessee running a cold storage claimed deduction under section 80HH, which was allowed by ITO - Commissioner in exercise of power under section 263 withdrew deduction under section 80HH - Whether in view of Delhi Cold Storage (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1991] 191 ITR 656/59 Taxman 144, Commissioner was right in withdrawing deduction - Held, yes

Section 80HH, read with section 80HHA, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from hotel and industrial undertakings, etc., in backward areas - Assessment years 1987-88 to 1989-90 - Assessee claimed and was allowed deduction under sections 80HH and 80HHA in respect of its various industrial units - Commissioner passed order under section 263 holding that deduction allowed under sections 80HH and 80HHA was not allowable to assessee - Whether having regard to facts that assessee had not claimed both benefits under sections 80HH and 80HHA in respect of same industrial unit and that Commissioner himself did not dispute that assessee was an industrial unit, Commissioner passed impugned order without going through record and claim of assessee, and reasons given therein were not in accordance with law - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, Commissioner’s order under section 263 on that ground had to be set aside - Held, yes

Section 80HHC of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction - Exporters - Assessment year 1993-94 - Value received by assessee by selling scrap in domestic market has to be included towards its total turnover while calculating deduction under section 80HHC; however, excise duty paid by assessee for selling scrap has to be excluded [Case remanded]

Waste and Scrap of iron and steel - Quantum - determination thereof - arising during manufacture of railway parts from iron  steel material - no allowance for invisible loss to be available while calculating the quantum of such waste  scrap arising during processes of forging, machining, boring, turning, threading, grinding etc. (Para 10)

Section 80HHC of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Exporters - Computation of deduction - Assessment year 2003-04 - Assessee, engaged in manufacturing of goods for export, claimed deduction under section 80HHC - In computation of business profit, value of sale of scrap was included - Assessing Officer took view that total sale of scrap could not be included in business profit but only profit after deducting expenses of generation of scrap - Whether since scrap is bi-product of manufacturing activity there were no expenses which could be excluded from sale of scrap - Held, yes [Para 7] [In favour of assessee]IT : Scrap being bi-product of manufacturing activity, there are no expenses which could be excluded from sale of scrap for computing deduction under section 80HHC

Section 80HHC of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Exporters (Computation of deduction) - Assessment year 2001-02 - Whether excise duty and sales tax can be included in turnover for computation of deduction under section 80HHC - Held, no - Whether receipt from sale of scrap can be included in total turnover for computation of deduction under section 80HHC - Held, no - Whether where assessee engaged in business of export of goods earned fees from foreign enterprise towards development work which had immediate nexus with activity of export, 90 per cent of such fee would not be excluded under clause (baa) of Explanation to section 80HHC in computing profits of business - Held, yes [Para 5] [In favour of assessee]IT : Neither amounts of excise duty and sales tax no receipt from sale of scrap can be included in turnover for computation of deduction under section 80HHC

II. Section 80HHC of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Exporters - Assessment year 2001-02 - Whether scrap, generated during manufacturing process, if sold, only goes to reduce cost of material consumed and for computing deduction under section 80HHC same cannot be considered as part of turnover of business carried on by assessee - Held, yes - Whether where assessee received warranty claims due to provision of warrant avail-able to it in respect of purchases made while counter claim made by customers of assessee were also paid, warranty claims arose in course of business but could not be considered as part of turnover for purpose of computing deduction under section 80HHC - Held, yes - Whether though interest received from customers for delayed payment is to be treated as part of profits of business, in view of clause (baa) of Explanation to section 80HHC, 90 per cent thereof has to be reduced from profits of business irrespective of fact as to whether it is received from banks or from customers - Held, yes - Whether provision written back merely reduces expenditure claimed and, hence, cannot be excluded while computing profits of business under clause (baa) of Explanation to section 80HHC - Held, yes

Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - In respect of certain incomes of industries in backward areas - Assessment year 1988-89 - One unit of assessee-company manufactured bulk drugs and sold them to Generic Division at market value - Assessing Officer valued them at cost and held that deductions under section 80HH were wrongly inflated by company - Whether section 80HH(7) had no application as it does not deal with intra-unit transfer - Held, yes - Whether assessee had correctly valued goods at market value as directed in section 80HH(6) and had not inflated deduction - Held, yes

Section 80HH, read with section 80J of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from hotel or industrial under taking etc., in backward areas - Assessment year 1981-82 - Assessee, an erstwhile partnership firm, was engaged in business of manufacture and sale of black steel tubes of 2 inches diameter - Assessee after having converted into a private limited company set up a project called project No. 2 consisting of milling plant for manufacture of steel tubes of 4 inches diameter - ITO rejected assessee's claim for relief under sections 80HH and 80J on ground that it was a case where new project was formed by splitting up or reconstruction of a business already in existence as machinery and plant were common to both projects or moulding plant - Tribunal, however, held that deductions ware admissible to assessee as assessee had set up a new project for manufacturing of 4 inches diameter black pipe which was different from manufacturing 2 inches diameter black pipe by assessee and merely because some of facilities were common that would not mean reconstruction or splitting up - Tribunal, accordingly, allowed assessee's claim - Whether impugned order of Tribunal was justified-Held, yes

III. Section 80HH, read with section 80-I, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from newly established industrial undertakings or hotel business in backward areas - Assessment year 1995-96 - Whether where freight-collection was at par with job work receipts and was part and parcel of operation of business of assessee and connected to priority industry of assessee, assessee was entitled to deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I on freight collection on depot sales - Held, yes

facts.text: The assessee was engaged in the manufacture and sale of different varieties of metallic wires and in the course of such manufacturing activity, waste material, viz., scrap metal, was obtained. The assessee's claim for deduction under section 80HH in respect of profits attributable to sale proceeds of scrap and drums and value of scrap at close of the accounting year was rejected by the ITO on the ground that the impugned profits could not be said to have been derived from the industrial undertakings. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the assessee's claim on the ground that scrap metal was a direct offshoot of the manufacturing activity of the assessee and eventually it could not be put into a different category other than the one from which the main product was derived. On appeal, the revenue contended, inter alia, that sections 41(1) and 41(2) were applicable to profits derived from sale of scrap metal and drums.

The assessee-company, carrying on the business of manufacture and sale of V-belts, oil seals, O-rings, rubber moulded products, etc., set-up an industrial undertaking in a backward area. It claimed deduction of 20 per cent of net profits allowable under section 80HH in respect of profit on sale of scrap which resulted in the manufacturing process. The ITO disallowed that claim. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the assessee's claim. On further appeal, the Tribunal reversed the Commissioner (Appeals)'s order.

On reference :

For the assessment year 1979-80, the assessee-company claimed deduction under section 80HH on income from sale of scrap. The Tribunal disallowed the claim of the assessee on ground that income from sale of scrap was not relatable to the industrial activities of the assessee.

On reference :

The assessee, being an owner of a cold storage situated in a backward area wherein potatoes were kept in the relevant assessment year, claimed investment allowance under section 32A on machinery and plant installed in the cold storage on the ground that the cold storage involved ‘manufac-turing’. The ITO disallowed the assessee’s claim, holding that a cold storage involved only processing and not manufacture or production of an article or thing. He also disallowed the assessee’s claim for deduction under section 80HH, On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order of the ITO.

On second appeal;

While computing deduction under section 80HH, the Assessing Officer excluded income from the sale of scrap by xerographic equipment unit and toner, developer, photocopier unit holding that income from the scrap could not be said to be income derived from the industrial undertaking.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) directed the Assessing Officer to take income from sale of scrap as income derived from industrial undertaking.

The Tribunal confirmed the order of the Commissioner (Appeals).

On revenue's appeal:

The assessee, engaged in the manufacture of re-rolled products of iron and steel in his re-rolling mill, filed his return of income which was accepted as such. In the course of the survey conducted under section 133A, the assessee had offered to pay tax on Rs. 10 lakhs. When required to explain the surrender, the assessee submitted that he had purchased certain guns in auction and certain quantity of brass scrap was obtained from breaking and dismantling those guns and the balance was iron scrap. It was contended that the said activity tantamounted to production of goods and, hence, income from industrial undertaking. The Assessing Officer, however, did not consider the income from sale of brass scrap as arising from industrial undertaking for purposes of allowing deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I and allowed the claim only in respect of other income. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) accepted the assessee’s submission. On revenue’s appeal, the Tribunal reversed the impugned order and allowed the revenue’s appeal. It accepted the plea that the assessee had purchased guns and the income from brass scrap which could not be used for re-rolling, thus, was not entitled to deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I.

On appeal to the High Court :

The assessee-company, an industrial undertaking, had claimed deduction under section 80HH on sale of scrap. The Assessing Officer held that the deduction could be available only on the profits and gains derived from industrial undertaking and not from income incidental to the activity of industrial undertaking. Therefore, for the purpose of determining the deduction, the income shown from sale of scrap should be excluded. In appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that the generation of scrap was independent to manufacturing activity and, therefore, the assessee was not entitled to claim of deduction under section 80HH and the action of the Assessing Officer was confirmed.

On second appeal :

The assessee dealt in marine products for the purpose of exports. It processed these products, and froze and packed the same as per export specifications. It also bought meat in the market and subjected the same to several processes such as cleaning, removing bones and fat through chemical and scientific methods, bifurcating chunks, trimming and finally packing the same in a fit condition for the export market. For this purpose the assessee used several types of machinery. The assessee claimed deduction under section 80HH which was allowed by the ITO but was later on negatived by the Commissioner under section 263. On appeal, the Tribunal allowed the assessee's claim.

On reference :

The assessee-firm was engaged in the business of constructing dams, etc. The ITO held that the assessee was not entitled to deduction under section 80HH The Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the deduction.

On appeal, the revenue, relied on the order of the Full Bench in the case of ITO v. Hydle Constructions (P.) Ltd. [1983] 6 ITD .575 (Delhi) and contended that the assessee was not entitled to deduction under section 80HH because the end product of the assessee was a dam, which could not be considered to be an article within the meaning of section 80HH(2)(i).

The Assessing Officer included the scrap sales in the total turnover of the assessee for computing deduction under section 80HHC.

The assessee submitted that the scrap sales did not represent the turnover manufactured by the appellant and the said amount would reduce the cost of raw materials consumed.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) as well as the Tribunal upheld the order of the Assessing Officer.

On further appeal:

The assessee-company was engaged in manufacture and sale of high tensile fasteners, cold extruded parts, etc., in Padi. It had a unit at 'k', a notified backward area, which manufactured fasteners and sockets. The assessee claimed deduction under section 80HH in respect of forging work done in 'k' unit on products manufactured in Padi, which it called as 'sub-contract receipts'. The Assessing Officer rejected the claim for deduction in respect of 'k' unit. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) directed the Assessing Officer to allow relief in accordance with law. Aggrieved, the revenue went in appeal before the Tribunal, which was allowed by a common order holding that the receipt on sub-contract could not be treated as income derived from the industrial undertaking for the purpose of granting relief under section 80HH.

On assessee's appeal :

The assessee-company was a manufacturer and exporter of stainless steel utensils.

In the process of manufacturing stainless steel utensils, some portion of the steel, which cannot be used or reused for manufacturing utensils, remains unused, which was treated as scrap and the same was disposed of in the local market.

For the purpose of availing deduction under section 80HHC, assessee was not including sale proceeds of scrap in the 'total turnover' but was showing the same in the profit and loss account.

According to revenue, the sale proceeds from scraps must be included in the 'total turnover' as the assessee was selling scrap and forms part of sales.

On appeal, High Court passed the order in favour of assessee.

On further appeal to the Supreme Court:

The assessee had installed an industrial unit at a notified backward area. During the year in appeal the assessee received a sum on account of job charges for twisting of yarn during the year. The claim of the assessee under sections 80HH and 80-I was rejected by the assessing officer on the ground that separate balance sheet in respect of the unit had not been filed; that the assessee had done job work and was not manufacturing goods on his own account and that, the twisting of year did not amount to manufacturing of goods for the purposes of sections 80HH and 80-I claims. The Commissioner (Appeals) held that the assessee was entitled to a deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I.

On appeal:

The assessee was engaged in manufacture of Iron & Steel products. Credit on Modvat on the duty paid on inputs and capital goods was availed by the assessee. They had availed credit of duty paid on conveyor belts as well which after repeated use were worn-out and became unfit for further use for intended purpose. These belts were sold out as waste and scrap and removed on receipt of consideration.

A show-cause notice was issued by the revenue demanding duty on the clearance of waste of conveyor belts.

The Commissioner confirmed the duty on the assessee along with interest and also a penalty of equal amount was imposed under section 11AC.

On appeal, the Tribunal set aside the Commissioner's order.

On second appeal, the High Court remanded back the matter to the Tribunal for fresh consideration.

Before the Tribunal:

The petitioner-company, which was carrying on the business of manufacturing and sale of beedies, set up a factory in a backward area. Some of the raw beedies were entrusted to contractors for being manufactured and with that along with raw beedies manufactured by the assessee itself in the industrial undertaking, the further processes of heating, ringing, belleying, wrapping and packing were carried on with the consequence that the finished product was made in the factory which was in the backward area. The petitioner claimed deduction under section 80HH. Deduction was allowed for some years by the ITO, for some years by the Commissioner (Appeals) and for some years by the Tribunal. On the ground that a part of the manufacturing activity was carried on outside the backward area, notices were issued alleging that the petitioner had failed to disclose fully and truly all the material facts for making the assessment. Petitioner questioned the issue of notices contending that they lacked jurisdiction inasmuch as the facts had been disclosed before the assessments were made.

On petition :

The assessee, a private trust, carried on the business of purchasing forests, felling the trees and converting them into logs and, subsequently, sawing them into timber of various sizes and varieties fit to be used in construction of buildings and also for being put to other uses inclusive Of manufacture of furniture. The business operations of the assessee were carried on in a backward area. The ITO allowed the assessee’s claim for deduction under section 80HH in respect of the profits and gains derived from the said industrial undertaking. However, the Commissioner held that all the activities of the assessee did not represent manufacturing activities. Accor-dingly, he set aside the assessment under section 263 and directed the ITO to examine each activity and allow deduction under section 80HH only in respect of those activities, which actually represented manufacturing of commodities.

On appeal to the Tribunal:

The assessee was a manufacturer of commutators. It also manufactured certain goods on sub-contract basis for others and received services/job charges and besides receipts from sale of copper scrap. They claimed deduction under section 80HHC including the said receipts. The assessing authority held that the receipts from the sub-contract receipts and scrap fell within the Explanation ( baa) to section 80HHC and, therefore, the same could not be included. Aggrieved by the said order, the assessee preferred an appeal. The appellate authority held that as there was a direct nexus between the receipts from special contract as well as sale of scrap material, it did not fall within the Explanation ( baa) and the assessee was entitled to include the said receipts in the income from the business and profits. The revenues appeal to the Tribunal came to be dismissed.

The assessee established three industrial units in backward areas. The units were crushing barytes into powder for hire and receiving crushing charges. The Assessing Officer held that mere crushing of barytes was not a manufacturing activity nor the powder produced could be called a new article. He further found that the assessee had not prepared separate profit and loss accounts and balance sheets in respect of each unit. He, therefore, disallowed the assessee’s claim for deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I. The Commissioner (Appeals) affirmed the order of the Assessing Officer. However, the Tribunal found that the barytes powder so produced got its marketability for its use for the purposes totally different from that of barytes. It further held that irrespective of the fact that there was no division of account, still they were entitled for the benefit of sections 80HH and 80-I as having satisfied the conditions laid down thereunder.

On reference :

The assessee ran a cold storage and had claimed that it was an industrial undertaking in a backward area and since it had satisfied all the conditions laid down in section 80HH(2), it was entitled to the benefit of the aforesaid section. The ITO rejected its claim as according to him the assessee was not engaged in the manufacture of articles and hence the necessary conditions were not satisfied and, therefore, the claim could not be allowed. On appeal, the Commissioner upheld the order of the assessing authority, which order had been confirmed in further appeal by the Tribunal.

On reference :

The assessee-company was an industrial undertaking set up in a backward area, for the purpose of repairs of barges. It was following the financial year as its accounting year. For the assessment year 1976-77, its claim for deduction under section 80HH was disallowed by the ITO on the ground that its activities commenced prior to 31-12-1970 as was evident from the facts that it was allowed deduction under section 80J for the assessment year 1971-72 and that it had receipts from repairing charges during that year. The Commissioner (Appeals), however, held that the only receipt dur-ing that year being from repairing activity, no manufacturing activity commenced during that year but only in the next year and, hence, the assessee was entitled to the impugned relief.

On second appeal:

The assessee-company was engaged in business of excavating and breaking boulder stones from stone quarries and supplying the same to a construction company for their work. The assessee claimed investment allowance and deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I which were denied by the Assessing Officer on the ground that the assessee was not engaged in any industrial activity. The Commissioner (Appeals) held that the assessee was entitled to investment allowance in respect of dumpers used in the business and directed the Assessing Officer to allow the same as well as to entertain the claim of the assessee under sections 80HH and 80-I.

On revenue’s appeal :

The assessee-company was engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling soyabean oil. For the relevant assessment year, it claimed deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I on the amount realized by it from sale of the old gunny bags (packing material). The Assessing Officer disallowed the assessee's claim holding that the said income could not be treated as an income derived from an industrial undertaking. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) granted deduction as claimed by the assessee. On the revenue's appeal, the Tribunal upheld the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) holding that the amount earned by the assessee from the sale of old gunny bags was an income derived from industrial undertaking within the meaning of section 80HH/80-I and was eligible for deduction.

The assessee was a jeweller engaged in the business of manufacture and sale of ornaments. He claimed deduction under section 80HH for the assessment year 1983-84. The ITO declined the assessee's claim. One of the grounds on which the ITO disallowed the assessee's claim was that the assessee had not employed any worker in the manufacturing process to fulfil the condition prescribed in section 80HH(2)(iv). On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the finding of ITO.

On second appeal, it was contended that the assessee was giving job work to artisans to prepare jewellery as per assessee's requirement for which money was paid to them and as such it was entitled to the deduction.

For the assessment years 1979-80 and 1980-81, the assessee, a private limited company, claimed relief under section 80HH on the gross income in respect of its liquid section which had been newly set up in a backward area. The contention of the assessee was that the relief should be allowed on the gross income and not on the net income. The ITO held that relief could be granted only on the net income of the liquid section. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) affirmed the order of the ITO. On second appeal, the Tribunal also upheld the order of the ITO.

On reference:

The assessee-company, which was retreader and established its plant in a backward area, claimed deductions under sections 80HH and 80J. The Assessing Officer disallowed the assessee's claim. On reference:

The assessee-firm started an industrial undertaking in 1977. The business of the assessee-company was centrifuging rubber latex. held.text:
Section 41(1 ) brings to tax certain amounts by a fiction of law. Therefore, the operation of such fiction should be limited to the language of the section. Where the assessee has incurred a loss or expenditure or trading liability and this trading liability has been allowed as deduction in an earlier year and something has later on been recovered in respect of such liability or such liability has either been remitted or has ceased to exist, section 41( 1) comes into operation. But according to the facts in the present case, nothing happened as contemplated by section 41(1) . Sale proceeds derived were for the sale of the particular product and not recoupment of earlier purchase. Accordingly, section 41(1) had no application to the facts of the instant case.

Further, the particular receipt under consideration is, insofar as scrap was concerned, realisation from the sale of waste material from manufacturing activity of the assessee-company and it was not a receipt from the sale of some of its old machinery, plant or building resulting in balancing charge as contemplated under section 41(2) . Therefore, section 41( 2) also had no application to the facts of the instant case as far as scrap was concerned. The section could be attracted insofar as the sale price of drums was concerned.

In fact, the assessee was entitled to deduction in respect of profits and gains from newly established industrial undertaking as contemplated under section 80HH in relation to profits from sale of scrap since this scrap, being a waste product which had a commercial value, was directly derived from the industrial undertaking which the assessee was carrying on and was sold in the normal course of running the industrial undertaking.

While giving the relief under section 80HH, value of closing stock of scrap would also have to be included. The sale proceeds of drums used for storing water and which had become useless could not, however, be said to be directly derived from the industrial undertaking considering the manufactur-ing activity in which the assessee was involved. This surplus was also of the nature falling under section 41(2 ). Therefore, the assessee was not entitled to relief in respect of profits attributable to sale of drums.

In Fenner (India) Ltd. v. CIT (No. 2) [2000] 241 ITR 803, the Madras High Court expressed the view that the scrap materials has direct link or nexus with the industrial undertaking and, therefore, profit from the sale of the scrap materials should be eligible for deduction under section 80HH. Following that decision, it was to be held in the instant case that the relief under section 80HH was allowable to the assessee on profit on sale of scrap. [Para 13]

The word "derived from" under section 80-HH has to be understood as something which has immediate nexus with the industrial undertaking. In the instant case, the scrap generated from the concerned units has direct and immediate nexus with the industrial undertaking since the said scrap has been generated from the manufacturing process itself. Thus, the Commissioner (Appeals) as well as the Tribunal have committed no error in allowing the benefit of section 80-HH to the assessee on the aforesaid income. [Para 15]

This Court in a case concerning the same assessee in Pandian Chemicals Ltd. v. CIT [2002] 254 ITR 562, had held, inter alia, that scrap not being a necessary by product in the process of manufacturer, the income from the sale of scrap could not be regarded as income derived from the industrial undertaking.

Therefore, the Tribunal was right in law in holding that the income from the sale of scrap was not relatable to the industrial activities of the assessee for the purpose of section 80HH.

The assessee in his explanation had stated that he dealt in steel scrap and was not aware of the fact that inside the guns, there was brass scrap which was removed. Thus, it was clear from the reply that brass was not an ingredient used in the process of manufacture in industrial undertaking of the assessee. The brass scrap had no direct nexus with the appellant’s industrial undertaking. It could not be said that brass scrap was a profit or gain which directly flowed, neither it had close connection with undertaking of the assessee. By removal of brass scrap which was not useful for steel rerolling work no different and distinct article came into existence, it was only incidental as was apparent from the assessee’s reply. [Paras 13 and 14]

Further, composition of brass scrap was not at all changed, that was only removed as that was not useful to the assessee for the activity of manufacturing which he was carrying on. It was only a fortuitous circumstance that in the relevant assessment year, the assessee had purchased the guns without the knowledge that brass scrap was inside them which was separated and it could not be said to be a by-product obtained in the process of manufacture. There was no nexus between brass and activity of steel rerolling. Brass was not at all an input in the process of manufacture of steel rerolling. It was not a raw material at all for the process of rerolling in which the assessee was involved. It was purely incidental that brass was found inside guns which were purchased in that year. Guns might have several components, sometimes brass or some other articles which may not be connected at all with the manufacturing process of the industrial undertaking. [Paras 22, 23, 24 and 25]

Thus, there was no nexus between the brass scrap obtained on dismantling of the guns and the main activity of the assessee of steel rerolling. Gun was not an essential raw material of appellants’ industrial unit, in any case, brass was not at all connected with steel re-rolling. Thus, separation of brass could not be said to be in the process of manufacture or a product or a by-product of the activity of the assessee’s industrial undertaking. There was no direct nexus between the separation of the brass from the guns and the main activity. Thus, considering the provisions of sections 80HH and 80-I, it could not be said to be profit and gain derived from industrial undertaking. Thus, deductions on profits and gains under sections 80HH and 80-I were not admissible and had been rightly disallowed by the Tribunal. [Para 28]

Resultantly, the instant appeal was to be dismissed. [Para 29]

The Legislature intended to extend the benefit of deduction under section 80HH only to the industrial undertakings which manufacture or produce articles. This section is not intended to be applied to industrial undertakings which are engaged in ‘processing of goods’ not amounting to manufacture or production of articles. The ship-breaking activity involves buying of damaged and unserviceable ships which are otherwise uneconomic to run, for the purpose of breaking and scrapping and sale of various goods and scrap obtained from such breaking and dismantling of old and used ships. Process is employed for breaking ship for dismantling and selling the scrap and substantial part of the items fitted in the ship and the oil contained in the tankers are sold in the same from without carrying out any further act, except removal of same from the ship and the remaining ship, made mainly of iron and steel, is then broken into different pieces of different sizes and shapes and sold by weight. Therefore, at the end of the process employed by the assessee, what is acquired are iron bars, plating rods, bronze, gunmetal copper and non-ferrous metal which, though marketable and commercial commodities, cannot be said to be manufactured or produced articles or things. For all practical purposes it is scrap. The scrap cannot be called a manufacture product or produced article because they are no new commodities but parts of the old and discarded ship as held by the Bombay High Court in the case of CST v. Delhi Iron & Steel Co. (P.) Ltd. [1995] 98 STC 202 the condemned and unserviceable ship purchased by the dealer is not a ship but re-rollable scrap in the form of an old ship for dismantling, in effect, the dealer acquires only the old materials and articles contained therein which are sold by it in the form in which they are acquired. No process whatsoever is applied to the goods, much less any process of manufacture. The issue stood squarely covered in favour of the revenue by the decision of the Bombay Bench of the Tribunal in the case of Asst. CIT v. Virendra & Co. [1995] 55 ITD 309 which held that ‘the meaning of manufacture and production of articles and things’ would have to be considered in their ordinary plain and natural meaning. Breaking or dismantling a ship would perhaps be just the opposite of manufacturing or production of an article or an thing. When a ship is dismantled or broken, what is obtained by the persons who are engaged in that process are the components by which the ship is constructed or manufactured and if it is possible to reassemble those pieces or parts, the ship may be manufactured or constructed. Hence, it would be doing violence to the language of the section if it is said that while a ship is being dismantled or broken or destroyed, in effect an article or thing is being manufactured or produced. Hence, the activity of breaking or dismantling of a ship cannot be considered to be an industrial undertaking which manufactured or produced articles or things and, therefore, the assessee was not entitled to deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I.

Regarding the contention of the assessee that the Government of India had recognised ship breaking as industry and, hence, the assessee was entitled to deduction claimed, there was no presumption that every industry is engaged in ‘manufacture’ or ‘production of articles or things’. Even if ship breaking is considered as an industry in the light of the definition of section 2(f) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, it will not mean that it would amount to manufacture or production so as to entitle the assessee to claim deductions under the respective sections. The assessee being governed by the Factories Act also would not change the matter in any way because that is broadly meant for welfare of labourers employed. The argument that a ship-breaking industry is labour intensive and that in the process heavy machinery like cranes and winches are employed is not relevant in absence of any manufacturing process involved. Mere application of systematic and sophisticated machines in the process would not treat an activity into manufacture. Thus, ship breaking activity amounts to carrying out the manufacturing process in a reverse order, as originally the ship is built from iron sheets and iron bars and other materials and by process of breaking the same, ship was reconverted into iron scrap and other materials. In view of the above, the findings of the Commissioner (Appeals) were to be reversed.

R.K. Choudhary for the Appellant. K.C. Patel, M.K. Patel, K.C. Thakker, N.B. Shah, N.B. Dvatia and G.C. Pipara for the Respondent.

Sub-section (2) of section 80HH lays down certain conditions, one of which is that the industrial undertaking should manufacture or produce articles in any backward area and another condition is that it should employ 10 or more workers in the manufacturing process carried on with the aid of power. It was not the case of the revenue that any of these conditions were not fulfilled. Their only case was that the entire manufacturing activity from beginning to end was not carried on in the backward area and an initial part of it had been entrusted to the contractors who carried on that part of the activity outside the backward area. The contention, therefore, was that the profit shown as the profit of the industrial undertaking in the backward area might actually include a small part of the profit derived from activity outside the backward area and, therefore, there was inflation of the profit and consequentially inflation of the deduction claimed by the assessee, that could be withdrawn by reopening the assessment. [Para 5]

Sub-section (7) of section 80HH provides for this contingency by stating that where it appears to the Assessing Officer that owing to the close connection between the assessee carrying on the business to which this section applies and any other person, the business between them is so arranged that it produces to the assessee more than the ordinary profit, the profits and gains of this industrial undertaking may be reasonably estimated. In the instant case also, if the Assessing Officer had carefully scrutinised the accounts of the assessee and drawn the inference that because of the entrustment of the initial part of the contract process to contractors, the income from the industrial undertaking was likely to be inflated, with reference to the profit derived from the backward area, he could have reasonably estimated the profit instead of accepting the profit as shown by the assessee. That estimate, he failed to do at the time of the assessment and he sought to do the same by reopening the assessment. The question was whether he could do it by stating that there was an omission on the part of the assessee to disclose fully and truly all material facts. In the case of Parashuram Pottery Works Co. Ltd. v. ITO [1977] 106 ITR 1, the Supreme Court stated that the duty of an assessee in any case does not extend beyond making a true and full disclosure of primary facts. Once he has done that, his duty ends. It is for the ITO to draw the correct inference from the primary facts. It is no responsibility of the assessee to advise the ITO with regard to the inference, which he should draw from the primary facts. If an ITO draws an inference which appears subsequently to be erroneous, mere change of opinion with regard to that inference would not justify initiation of action for reopening assessments. In the instant case, the ITO failed to draw an inference that because of the entrustment of the initial manufacturing activity to contractors, the income derived from the industrial undertaking with reference to the backward area could be inflated and to that extent the income had to be estimated for confining the deduction to that profit which could be said to have been derived only from the backward area. Failing to draw that inference, blame could not be put on the assessee, when at the time of assessment the list of contractors, the quantity of beedies manufactured and the amount paid had been disclosed by the assessee. That disclosure was admitted in the counter affidavit. The ITO was not able to specify what extra information was required by him to have applied his mind to draw that inference for reducing the deduction to which the assessee was entitled. As long as it was not possible for the ITO to specify the exact information which was required and which was not disclosed, it was not possible to accept the claim that there was no true and full disclosure in the case. When that jurisdictional fact was not established, the ITO could not issue a notice under section 147(a). In the circumstances, the impugned notices were quashed. [Paras 6 & 7]

The writ petition was allowed. [Para 7]

Following the decision of the Division Bench in the case of CIT v. Metal Powder Co. Ltd. [2008] 300 ITR 48/174 Taxman 398 (Mad.) it was to be held that the conversion charges had to be excluded from the turnover for the purpose of calculation of deduction under section 80HHC.

The policy of the Government to promote the small scale units by providing various concessions through the Ministry of Industry, considering their contribution to the overall growth and economic development of the country, was echoed in the memorandum explaining the provisions of the Finance Bill, 1986. The benefits as were extended to the small scale units by the Industry Ministry were considered under the Act for the first time in 1976. which was the grant of investment allowance to such units and this continued over the years. In 1986, through the Finance Bill, 1986, it was observed that the upward revision of the value of the machinery and plant was being made in the light of the upward revision made by the Department of industrial Development through the notification dated 17-3-1985, to be effective from 1-4-1985. From the time small scale units were given concessions under the Act, there was never any Explanation or provision added to the Act, as to manner of determination of the aggregate value of the machinery and plant, that was contrary to the. one laid by the Ministry of Industry. Unlike the provisions of sections 80-I, 80HH etc., where the pre-requisites for a new industrial undertaking has been defined, there are no conditions specified in section 32A for grant of recognition as a small- scale unit, other than borrowal of the definition from the one recognised by the Ministry of Industries. This, suggests that the only authority which has the power to grant recognition to a unit as a small-scale unit being the Industry Ministry or the concerned department under that Ministry, so long as a unit ‘is recognised by that authority, for purposes of harmonious construction of the term small-scale unit, the same should be adopted for the purposes of this Act as well. In the absence of any specified Explanation or provision for the determination of the aggregate value of machinery and plant under the Act, it would be only proper that the manner of computation of the aggregate value of the machinery and plant as recognised by that Ministry is also adopted, so that uniformity for the same class or category under different Acts can be maintained. Such uniformity of view is what is intended by the Legislature and will only be proper for achieving the objective of the growth of these units and their contribution to the overall economic development of the country and, last but not the least, to reducing avoidable litigation. New ships are not meant for demolition or breaking. It is after the operative and useful life of the ship is over that they are scheduled to be sold for demolition. The procedure for demolition of a ship is not just a private affair and involves permission of the authorities under the law to transfer them for demolition. Merely because the ship is able to sail on its own up to the shore where it is to be demolished, it cannot be said that such ship which is sold for demolition is a new ship. Remaining afloat is not a sure test for a ship to be called new, because a condemned ship is not always a sunk ship. An old ship sold for demolition that manages to remain afloat cannot be said to be a new ship. The distinction made on that count is a distinction attempted without any real difference between the old ships which are sold for demolition, for the purpose of considering whether the ship breaking activity is a manufacturing or production activity. [Para 22]

By the nature of its very setting, one has to construe the expression ‘manufacture or produce articles’ in sub-section (2)(i ) of section 80HH and the expression ‘manufactures or produces any article or thing not being any article or thing specified in the list in the Eleventh Schedule’, appearing in section 80-I(2)(iii) in the context of the fact that the deduction under section 80HH is meant to encourage establishment of new industrial undertakings in backward areas when such industrial undertaking ‘has begun or begins to manufacture or produce articles’ and in context of the fact that section 80-I is designed to encourage industrial undertakings to manufacture or produce ‘any articles or thing not being article or thing specified in the list in the Eleventh Schedule’.

Provisions of section 80HH or 80-I are meant for the benefit of industrial undertakings that carry out the activity of manufacture or production of articles or things and not for the scrap merchants who trade in buying old articles or things and take out their parts to sell them separately. All large scale junk dealers in discarded old and scrapped vehicles who might fish out a horn in working condition from such vehicle or pull out its steering wheel or part of its engine that may have a demand in the market of second hand spares will proclaim themselves to be manufacturers or producers of articles or things. No such startling result is intended by the provisions of sections 80HH and 80-I, having regard to their underlying purpose of encouraging industries for being set up for manufacturing or production of new articles or things. In fact, industrial undertaking formed by transfer of machinery or plant previously used for any purpose is disentitled to such benefits both under sections 80HH(2)(iii) and 80-I(2)(iii). [Para 23]

The ships imported for breaking up are obviously old ships, purchased to retrieve the material, particularly steel plates, for disposal in the market for re-rolling or re-cycling purposes which is the activity done by these ship breakers in the process of ship breaking.

Thus, there is nothing whatsoever in the process of ship breaking activity which can be termed as manufacture or production of any article or thing. The dismantled material is already existing as a component of the old ship. The process of extracting steel plates from it while dismantling the ship will not make such extraction of existing material an activity of manufacture or production of such material nor will the process of cutting extracted steel plates for convenient disposal be manufacture or production of such steel plates. Merely because the ship breaking is considered as an industry, it would not be an industry engaged in manufacture or production of any article or thing. Benefit of the provisions of sections 80HH and 80-I is clearly not intended for such ship breaking activities which do not result in bringing into existence any new article or thing. The word ‘manufacture’ in the context of sections 80HH and 80-I would mean making of articles or things. While dismantling, the ship steel plates are not made but only removed which is not the same thing as making of steel plates. The word ‘production’ in context of these provisions would mean the action of making or manufacturing from components or raw materials an article or thing and not just removing of an existing article or cutting it.

In the instant case, application of mechanical methods only removed the steel plates and other objects which were existing on the ships, which would not mean that the assessee produced those existing articles or things by the process of removing and cutting them. [Para 27]

The word ‘production’ or ‘produce’ when used in juxtaposition with word ‘manufacture’ takes in bringing into existence new goods by a process which may or may not amount to manufacture. The principle of adopting a liberal interpretation which advances the purpose and object of beneficial provisions cannot be carried out to the extent of doing violence to the plain and simple language of the enactment. [Para 27.1]

The Supreme Court, in the case of Bangalore Water Supply & Sewerage Board v. A. Rajappa AIR 1978 SC 548, has laid down that where there is (i) systematic activity, (ii) organised by co-operation between employer and employees, (iii) for the production and/or distribution of goods and services calculated to satisfy human wants and wishes, prima facie, there is an industry. Absence of profit motive or gainful object is irrelevant. This view of the Supreme Court has been followed by the jurisdictional High Court in the case of CIT v. J.B. Kharwar & Sons [1987] 163 ITR 394 and by Karnataka High Court in the case of Shankar Construction Co. v. CIT [1991] 189 ITR 463. In the case before the Karnataka High Court, the business of constructing dams and channels was taken as that of ‘industrial undertaking’ entitled to investment allowance; while in the case of J.B. Kharwar & Sons (supra) before the Gujarat High Court, the business was that of printing and dyeing of cloths and the work was taken as manufacturing work for the entitlement of deduction under section 80J. On the basis of the above case law, the working of the assessee-firm which was involved in the work of designing, erection and commissioning of water and air pollution control plants, would certainly be falling in the category of an ‘industrial undertaking’, and the assessee-firm was an ‘industrial undertaking’ as used in sections 80HH and 80J.

In the instant case, the activities of the assessee-firm were that of manufacturing or that of producing an article as they were constructing water/air pollution plants. Thus, the assessee-firm was an ‘industrial undertaking’ and was engaged in manufacturing or producing an article in the shape of air/water pollution control. That the assessee was manufacturing or producing the plant in backward area, was one of the requirements of the claim under section 80HH. The contention of the assessee was that only 11.45 per cent of the total receipt had been taken for deduction under section 80HH as that work alone was done in backward area and it was not expected from the assessee to have its office or plant in backward area. The crux of the case laws is that if an industrial undertaking begins to manufacture or produce outside in any backward area, it is entitled to deduction under section 80HH. The assessee-firm set up its own industrial undertaking at the site of its customers for whom water/air pollution control plant was manufactured and of the places which were falling under the backward area declared under the Act, then, naturally the assessee should be getting benefit of the same and the computation made by the assessee-firm of the same was correct one.

Thus the assessee-firm had been able to make out a case in its favour on the guidelines referred to above for qualifying its claim under sections 80HH and 80J and the ITO was justified in allowing its claim from the assessment year 1982-83 onwards till the year under consideration and the Commissioner committed an error in concluding otherwise and the order of Commissioner was to be quashed on this point.

The second argument of the assessee-firm was that the Assessing Officer examined the case of the assessee in assessment year 1982-83, the first year of its business and for that necessary enquiries as posed by the Commissioner to himself while passing the order under section 263 were raised by the ITO and necessary correspondence held in between the ITO and the assessee-firm. The assessee had made available all the informations required by Assessing Officer who went through the same, examined the same and then found force in the plea of the assessee and allowed its claim under sections 80HH and 80J for the assessment year 1982-83 and that pattern was followed till the year under consideration and now the Commissioner was not justified to pass an order in question as no new fact had emerged out nor any change of circumstances took place to show that findings of ITO were in any way perverse of contrary to legal position.

The above contention of the assessee had got force as since the assessment year 1982-83, the position had been continuously the same and the Commissioner had not given out any reason to show that order of the ITO was in any way perverse nor any new fact came into his knowledge nor any separate enquiry had been made to differ from the earlier stand and, thus, it was not permissible for the Commissioner to start a fresh litigation from admitted positions of the parties on particular point. Thus, the case of the assessee was rightly processed by the Assessing Officer and there was no justification for the Commissioner to make an order under section 263 with direction to the ITO to withdraw the deduction made in favour of the assessee under said sections.

Section 80HH is meant to give a tax rebate to certain categories of assessees and one, who wants to claim such a relief, must strictly satisfy the requirements prescribed therein. He must establish that his profits and gains are derived from his industrial undertaking or the business of hotel. Axiomatic proposition of law is that it is not sufficient if a commercial connection is established between the profits earned and the industrial undertaking and the law requires that such profits must have been derived from the industrial undertaking. The industrial undertaking itself must be the source of that profit. The business of the industrial undertaking must strictly yield that profit. It must be the direct source of profit and not a means to earn any other profit.

In the instant case, in the industrial undertaking for the manufacture of V-belts, oil seals, O-rings and rubber moulded products, certain scrap materials resulted, which had a saleable value. To say that the scrap materials had no direct link or nexus with the industrial undertaking, could not at all be expected to commend acceptance, especially, on the facts and in the circumstances of the instant case. The scrap materials came within the manufacturing process of the industrial undertaking in the manufacture of certain products such as V-belts, oil seals, O-rings and certain rubber moulded products, etc. In that view of the matter, profits and gains from the sale of scrap materials were eligible for deduction in an amount equal to 20 per cent under section 80HH, inasmuch as such gains or profits were derived from the industrial undertaking and includible in the gross total income of the assessee and the question relatable to the profit on the sale of scrap was answered in favour of the assessee.

Meaning of the term 'turnover'

The term 'turnover' had neither been defined in the Act nor has been explained by any of the CBDT circulars. [Para 17]

In the aforesaid circumstances, one has to look at the meaning of the term 'turnover' in ordinary accounting or commercial parlance. [Para 18]

Normally, the term 'turnover' would show the sale effected by a business unit. It may happen that in the course of the business, in addition to the normal sales, the business unit may also sell some other things. [Para 19]

In ordinary accounting parlance, as approved by all accountants and auditors, the term 'sales', when reflected in the profit and loss account, would indicate sale proceeds from sale of the articles or things in which the business unit is dealing. When some other things like old furniture or a capital asset, in which the business unit is not dealing are sold, the sale proceeds therefrom would not be included in 'sales' but it would be shown separately. [Para 20]

In simple words, the word 'turnover' would mean only the amount of sale proceeds received in respect of the goods in which an assessee is dealing in. [Para 21]

So far as the scrap is concerned, the sale proceeds from the scrap may either be shown separately in the profit and loss account or may be deducted from the amount spent by the manufacturing unit on the raw material, which is steel in the case of the respondent-assessee, as the respondent-assessee is using stainless steel as raw material, from which utensils are manufactured. The raw material, which is not capable of being used for manufacturing utensils will have to be either sold as scrap or might have to be re-cycled in the form of sheets of stainless steel, if the manufacturing unit is also having its re-rolling plant. If it is not having such a plant, the manufacturer would dispose of the scrap of steel to someone who would re-cycle the said scrap into steel so that the said steel can be re-used. [Para 22]

When such scrap is sold, the sale proceeds of the scrap cannot be included in the term 'turnover' for the reason that the respondent-unit is engaged primarily in the manufacturing and selling of steel utensils and not scrap of steel. Therefore, the proceeds of such scrap would not be included in 'sales' in the Profit and Loss Account of the respondent-assessee. [Para 23]

The situation would be different in the case of the buyer, who purchases scrap from the respondent-assessee and sells it to someone else. The sale proceeds for such a buyer would be treated as 'turnover' for a simple reason that the buyer of the scrap is a person who is primarily dealing in scrap. In the case on hand, as the respondent-assessee is not primarily dealing in scrap but is a manufacturer of stainless steel utensils, only sale proceeds from sale of utensils would be treated as his 'turnover'. [Para 24]

The Institute of Chartered Accountants of India ('ICAI') has published some material under the head 'Guidance Note on Tax Audit under section 44AB'. The said material has been published so as to guide the members of the ICAI. In our opinion, when a recognized body of Accountants, after due deliberation and consideration publishes certain material for its members, one can rely upon the same. Para 5 of the said Note deals with 'Sales', 'turnover' and 'gross receipts'. The meaning given by the ICAI clearly denotes that in normal accounting parlance the word 'turnover' would mean 'total sales' as explained hereinabove. The said sales would definitely not include the scrap material which is either to be deducted from the cost of raw material or is to be shown separately under a different head. There is no reason for not accepting the meaning of the term 'turnover' given by a body of Accountants, which is having a statutory recognition. [Para 25]

If all accountants, auditors, businessmen, manufacturers etc. are normally interpreting the term 'turnover' as sale proceeds of the commodity in which the business unit is dealing, there is no reason to take a different view than the view normally taken by the persons who are concerned with the said term. [Para 26]

"After the Modvat credit was taken, the status of the goods changed and instead of the goods being considered as duty paid goods these became goods as if these are the manufacture of the appellants' factory. But there is no controversy that what was removed from the appellants' factory were not the goods as these were brought in i.e. Calcium Carbide filled in the drums but only empty drums. The instant case was not a border line case and a firm conclusion was easily approachable. By subjecting tobacco to treatment beedi patti was produced. By ginning cotton, pure cotton is obtained or pressed cotton is produced. Raw wool subjected to processing to eliminate dirt, grease and other vegetable matter results in production of pure wool. Leather is said to be manufactured when raw hide is treated. In all these cases a different product in commercial realm is said to be produced. In the same strain, it was equally possible to say that ‘Jarda’ or ‘Jardi’ was produced or manufactured from raw tobacco as a result of some manual or mechanical treatment, or both. Anybody could go to the market and purchase the article known as raw tobacco and it is equally possible to go and purchase in the market an article called Jarda or Jardi. The physical property in raw tobacco and Jarda or Jardi might be same. While raw tobacco is unfit for beedi manufacture in the same condition, Jarda or Jardi can ready be used in the beedi manufacture. In commercial parlance Jarda or Jardi is distinctively different from raw tobacco. For the aforesaid reasons, in the instant case, the assessee’s business was one of manufacture or production of an article or thing. The assessee’s business undertaking was in a backward area and there was no dispute about it. Then, if the assessee was manufacturing or producing an article, it must be taken that all the conditions in sub-section(2) of section 80HH were fulfilled. The assessee was having a mechanised tobacco processing plant which was even patented. It was registered as a small scale industrial unit by the Government. The most vital was the schedule of assets which formed part of the balance sheet, which showed that the cost of machinery employed was below the limit placed in Explanation to section 32A(2) or Explanation 3 to section 80-I(2), read with section 80HHA(8). The assessee was, therefore, entitled to the reliefs under sections 32A, 80HHA and 80-I. Since the assessee was found manufacturing an article it should be treated as an industrial company as defined in the Finance Act, though even processing, which the assessee was certainly doing, may be sufficient to justify a claim for concessional rate of tax. Thus, the assessee was also entitled to concessional rate of tax for both the years being an industrial company within the meaning of section 2(8)(c).

EDITOR’S NOTE

1. It was also held by the Tribunal that for computing deduction under section 80HHC not only sale of scrap by the assessee but also sale of steam would be part of ‘business profit’, once it was held by the Commissioner (Appeals) that both sale of scrap and sale of steam would constitute part of turnover. 2. It was further held by the Tribunal that insurance claim received by the assessee would form both parts of the assessee’s business profit as well turnover. Similarly, sale of ammonia, which gave rise to miscellaneous income of the assessee, would also form part of the assessee’s business profit, as well as total turnover to determine deduction under section 80HHC.

Section 32 A uses the expression ‘business of manufacture or production of any article or thing’. The expression used in section 80HH is similar, namely, ‘to manufacture or produce articles’. There is no reference to ‘processing’ as used in the definition of ‘industrial company’ under section 2(7)(d) of the Finance Act, 1966, and the Finance (No. 2) Act, 1967. Again, unlike section 80J(4)(iii), reference is not made in section 32A or 80HH to the operation of a cold storage plant. This would show that mere processing (even if the potatoes were held to undergo processing in a cold storage) is not recognised under sections 32A and 80HH to amount to manufacture or production of any article or thing. The same expression is used in section 80HHA and 80-I(2)(iii). Again, section 35C, which deals with agricultural development allowance, refers to a company or a co-operative society being engaged in the manufacture or processing of a relevant article or thing There-fore, as neither section 32A nor section 80HH refers to processing of any article or thing, the lower authorities were justified in rejecting the claims of the assessee.

The case of Indian Metal Traders (supra ) relied upon by the Commissioner (Appeals), was distinguishable on facts because there the Court was considering the definition of ‘manufacture’ within the meaning of section 2(17) of the Bombay Sales Tax Act, 1959 which is very wide and includes within its scope, certain activities which in ordinary parlance cannot be considered to be ‘manufacture’. Therefore, the Court came to the conclusion that scrap iron and steel obtained by the assessee by dismantling and breaking the ship was a different commercial commodity from the ship itself amounting to manufacture. As held by the Supreme Court in CIT v. Sun Engg. Works (P.) Ltd. [1992] 198 ITR 297/ 64 Taxman 442 , the decision of a Court must be read in the context in which it is taken. Keeping in view this principle, the words ‘manufacture of articles and things’ have got to be viewed in the context of section 80-I and section 80HHA and not in the context of the definition of manufacture in section 2(17) of the Bombay Sales Tax Act. As held by the Supreme Court in Dy. CST v. Pio Food Packers [1980] 46 STC 63 commonly manufacture is the end result of one or more process through which the original commodity is made to pass. It was further held that there might be several stages of processing and perhaps a different kind of processing at each stage and with each process the original commodity experiences a change. Moreover, a mere change in the original commodity does not amount to manufacture. The change must be as a result of process or processes through which the original commodity experiences a change. Further, as held by the Supreme Court in Empire Industries Ltd. v. Union of India [1986] 162 ITR 846, manufacture implies a change but every change is not manufacture and yet every change of an article is the result of treatment, labour and manipulation. But something more is necessary and there must be transformation, a new and different article must emerge having distinctive name, character or use.

The assessee, in the instant case, purchased a ship which was not sea-worthy. In other words, what had been purchased was scrap which was constituted of various materials. The assessee simply broke the said ship and segregated the material for sale. There was no process of manufacture involved nor was the original commodity made to pass through any process. There was no transformation and no distinctive character of the material derived by breaking the ship. Therefore, the business of ship- breaking activity could not be said to be manufacture within the meaning of section 80HHA and section 80-I. The assessee was, therefore, not entitled to deductions under those sections.

As per the law laid down by the Supreme Court in several decisions, the expression 'derived from' is to be given restricted meaning in section 80HH/80-I while interpreting the section in which this expression is used. [Para 15]

In the instant case, the main and only business of the assessee, for which the plant was set up in the backward area, was to manufacture and to sell soya oil. Hence, all incomes derived from sale of soya oil would be income derived from an industrial undertaking for the purpose of calculating deduction under section 80HH/80-I.

The income earned by the assessee out of sale of gunny bags could not be kept at par or alike the income derived from sale of soya bean oil due to following reasons - Sale of gunny bags was not the main or even ancillary business activity of the assessee; it was not regular or continuous business activity; no investment was made by the assessee for their sale. The gunny bags were never manufactured by the assessee in its plant and merely because some gunny bags were lying in the factory as surplus or unused or as waste material for any reason and such bags were sold to earn income, then it could not be a ground to hold that for the purpose of section 80HH/80-I, such income was the income actually derived from the assessee's industrial undertaking. [Para 16]

In order to derive income from industrial undertaking, the assessee must show that it was earned by sale of goods/commodity which were manufactured/produced in the said industrial undertakings as a part of its main and day-to-day business activity. Only then, the income earned by sale of such goods can be termed as income derived from industrial undertaking within the meaning of section 80HH/80-I. It is for this reason that it has a direct or immediate nexus with the assessee's industrial undertaking established in the backward area. This necessarily follows that income, which has a direct or immediate nexus with the industrial undertaking, alone will be taken into consideration for calculating the deduction under section 80HH/80-I, ibid. Such was not the case in the instant case, because the income earned from sale of gunny bags was not the result of direct or immediate nexus with the business of assessee carried on in the industrial undertaking. [Para 17]

Hence, the Tribunal fell in error in holding that the income earned by the assessee from sale of gunny bags was an income earned from industrial undertaking within the meaning of section 80HH/80-I and, accordingly, the assessee was entitled to claim deduction from total income. That view was to be reversed and order of the Tribunal was to be set aside. [Para 21]
