Section 65(105)(j) - Clearing and forwarding agents’ services v. Consignment agent

4.3 The assessee had entered into contracts with two steel companies, the TISCO and TRL. As per the said contract the assessee was to take delivery of the steel materials on behalf of the TISCO and TRL from the railway siding. Thereafter, it was to transport said materials to its own premises/godown and sort and stock said materials after weighment in accordance with instructions of the company’s representative. The assessee was to further arrange for and to take all necessary steps for safe custody and protection of steel materials and was to nominate a hub manager in its premises. Further, it had to deliver materials to company’s customers on production of delivery orders and if the hub manager required, the materials would be loaded on the transport vehicles, etc., of the customer or as nominated by the company. The assessee was to bear all the expenses since time of receipt of materials at its premises till these were dispatched and in case of failing to account for the stock, it was liable for consequences. The assessee received consideration of certain sum which comprised of consignment agent service receipts, and receipts towards reimbursement of expenditure, bending and bundling charges and stock verification charges from the said companies in respect of services rendered. The revenue issued a show-cause notice (SCN) on 13-9-2004 and demanded service tax from the assessee for the period 1-9-1999 to 31-3-2004 by stating that services provided by the assessee to its clients fell under the category of ‘Clearing and forwarding agent’. On non-compliance of same the revenue confirmed service tax liability upon the assessee along with penalty and interest. In the instant appeal, the assessee contended that it had acted as a consignment agent which activity was not covered under ‘Clearing and forwarding agent’s service’ and, therefore, it was not liable to pay service tax.

The Tribunal held that according to the Finance Act, 1994, imposing service tax on certain taxable services, any service provided or to be provided by a ‘Clearing and forwarding agent’ to a ‘client’ in relation to ‘Clearing and forwarding operations’ ‘in any manner’ shall be taxable service under section 65(105)(j). Incidence of levy is on the service of ‘Clearing and forwarding operations’, provided measure of tax is ‘value’ of such service. Thus, service provided by a ‘Clearing and forwarding agent’ to his client directly or indirectly in any manner gives rise to a taxable event, provided the service so rendered is ‘Clearing and forwarding operation’. - a container freight station;

- bee-keeping and production of honey and beeswax;

- setting up and operating a warehousing facility for storage of sugar.

• Exemption is provided to foreign companies in respect of any income received by it in India in Indian currency on account of sale of crude oil to any person in India subject to specified conditions.

- FMV as may be substantiated by the issuing company

Following provisions will apply to a service provider, who is not a 'manufacturer' -

Inputs becoming waste while providing output service - If some inputs become waste while providing output services, they are 'used in provision of output services'. In such case, no 'amount' or 'duty' is payable when he sells them as scrap, as it cannot be said that he has 'manufactured' them.

The word "manufacture" or "produce articles" used in the provision to Section 80HH have not been defined in the Act. The word "manufacture" has been considered by the Supreme Court and the High Courts on numerous occasions, and the common thread which runs in all the decisions is that it is only when a new and distinct commodity commercially accepted as such comes into existence as a result of the processing, that a commodity can be said to have been manufactured.Having regard to the fact that the word "article" used in the section is an article which is manufactured or produced and the word "produce" having been used in juxtaposition with the word "manufacture" it connotes the bringing into existence of new goods. The result of production should be the coming into existence of a new article. The terms "production" and "produce" would also take in by-products, intermediate products and residual products. All of them should be products or articles which are capable of being regarded as new articles. By holding that a "new" article should emerge from manufacture or production, new words are not being added to Section 80HH. The term new has been employed in the decisions of the courts only to indicate the end result of the process of production or manufacture. It is only when that result can be said to have been achieved that the industrial undertaking which brings about such a result by its process of production or manufacture would qualify for the benefits conferred under the section. In view of the aforesaid, it could not be said that retreading of tyres resulted in the production of an article[CIT v. Madurai Pandian Engineering Corpn. Ltd. It must, therefore, be understood in its normal connotation, the sense in which it is understood in the commercial world. The word "articles" in Section 80HH is preceded by the words "it has begun or begins to manufacture or produce". The word "articles" occurring in Section 80HH(2)(i) does not comprehend and take within its ambit a dam, a bridge and so on. If a dam is an article, so would be a bridge, a road, an underground canal and a multi-storeyed building. To say that all of them fall within the meaning of the word "articles" is to overstrain the language beyond its normal and ordinary meaning. It is equally difficult to say that the process of constructing a dam is a process of manufacture or a process of production. The definition of 'scrap' as given in Explanation (b) is not limited to scrap from the manufacture or mechanical working of materials alone but extends to cover 'waste' also. Therefore, the scope of the term 'scrap' as defined in Explanation (b) cannot be interpreted so as to restrict its application to scrap from the manufacture or mechanical working of materials alone. The first part of the definition of 'scrap' in Explanation (b) refers not only to scrap from the 'manufacture' but also to 'mechanical working of materials'. Both the phrases, namely, manufacture and mechanical working of materials differ in their meaning and content. 'Mechanical working of materials' refers to physical operations on materials. It signifies physical operations to bring about physical change to which the material is subjected in order to change its shape, properties or structure. In order to fall in the definition of 'scrap', it is not necessary that the same should occur in the course of manufacture; it can also occur in the course of mechanical working of materials, i.e., in the course of physical operations on materials. Thus, both the operations/processes, namely, the manufacture and mechanical working of materials, can give rise to scrap. Any article or thing arising from the physical operations on materials which is not usable as such would therefore fall in the category of 'scrap'. As stated earlier, the second part of the definition, i.e., 'which is definitely not usable as such because of breakage, cutting up, wear and other reasons' also throws light on the scope of the term 'scrap' inasmuch as it seeks to define the characteristics of scrap. In order to constitute 'scrap', the article or thing must not be usable as such because of breakage, cutting up, wear and other reasons. The use of the words 'other reasons' in the second part of the definition of 'scrap' is significant. In order to constitute 'scrap', what is contemplated by Explanation (b) is the non-usability of materials as such, which could even be for a reason other than breakage, cutting up and wear. The phraseology employed in Explanation (b) shows that the term 'scrap' has been defined in wide terms so as to include both (i) waste, and (ii) scrap from the manufacture or mechanical working of materials. However, both of them have been used as one phrase, i.e., as 'waste and scrap from the manufacture or mechanical working of materials', for the second part of the definition and, therefore, both of them should definitely be not usable as such because of breakage, cutting up, wear or other reasons.

Old Aluminium Utensils/Vessels purchased for converting them into new aluminium utensils

There were three entries under consideration –

Entry 5 read "Aluminium household utensils whether made of aluminium and aluminium alloys".

Entry 6 read "Aluminium products (including aluminium extrusion) and products, aluminium alloys not elsewhere mentioned in this Schedule."

Entry 83 read "Metal scraps other than those specified in the second Schedule."

The question for consideration is as to under which entry the old aluminum vessels purchased for conversion thereof into new aluminum utensils fall. The Tribunal held that prior to amendment of entry 5, the word 'and" was there between "aluminum" and "household" and it appears to have been left inadvertently to be mentioned in the revised entry. The Tribunal held the word "and" should still be read there and finally held that "old aluminum vessel" fell in entry 5 and not in entry 83.

Held by the Supreme Court- A finding of fact has been arrived at by the Tribunal that the appellant used to purchase the old aluminium vessels and scrap which were used for conversion to new household utensils. Old aluminium vessels are pressed to convert the same into scrap. Appellant, thus, is a scrap dealer and not a dealer in aluminium vessels within the meaning of Entry 5.

The dictionary meaning of scrap is "a small piece or amount of something especially one that is left over after the greater part has been used or material, especially metal, discarded for reprocessing".

The Entries contained in the First Schedule appended to the Act are in three parts. Entry 5 deals with aluminium household utensils. Entry 6 deals with aluminium products and aluminium alloys and entry 83 deals with metal scraps. Indisputably, aluminium metal scraps would also come within the purview of Entry 83. As the appellant deals in metal scrap, its case will come within the purview of Entry 83. All aluminium products do not come within the purview of Entry 5. It deals with only domestic utensils. For other aluminium products a different rate of tax has been provided in Entry 6. If there exists an entry which covers the goods in question, by necessary implication the same would be considered to have been excluded from another entry.

We will assume that the Entry 5 is capable of two interpretations. It may be read in the manner in which the Tribunal did, but it can also be read as "household utensils made up of aluminium or aluminium alloy." Use of the word "Aluminium" at the beginning may be superfluous. In any event the dealer cannot be said to be dealing with aluminium household utensils or household utensils made up of aluminium and aluminium alloys. We, therefore, are of the opinion that it was entry 83 which is attracted to the facts of the present case. [Baby Varghese v. State of Kerala, VSTI 2008 …B-436; VSTI 2008 (Delhi, Punjab, Haryana)...B-607; 2008 NTN (Vol. 38) – 123; (2008) 32 PHT 185 (SC); (2008) 16 VST 448 (SC); (2010) 56 S.T.A. 73, decided on 1.8.2008 by the Supreme Court]

Empty Drums

Empty drums sold by the dealer which are usable as containers shall be taxable as "containers made of tin, iron or steel". [Shorta Drum Retreading Works, Kanpur, decided on 17.9.1984 u/s. 35 by Commissioner of Sales Tax, U.P., Lucknow]

Looking to the judgment of Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Rainbow Steel Limited v. Commissioner of Sales Tax, 1981 UPTC 400, to tax the old drums as "old, discarded, unserviceable, obsolete" item, it must be old in the sense that it has become non functional or non usable. As there is no finding by the S.T.O. that the drums purchased by the Assessee were absolutely non usable, the Tribunal was right in holding that the sale of old drums, though purchased against the issuance of Form 3-A were not taxable. Before the decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case 1981 UPTC 400 a belief was entertained that the turnover of old drums was taxable and therefore, Form 3-A was used. In these circumstances mere use of Form 3-A is not sufficient to hold that the turnover of the old drums was liable to tax under the law and nor was the S.T.O. justified in drawing the inference from this fact that the old drums were non usable. MANUFACTURE OR PRODUCE - CLAUSE (i) OF SUB-SECTION (2)

626. CIT v. N.C. Budharaja & Co. [1993] 204 ITR 412 (SC)

The words 'manufacture' and 'production' have received extensive judicial attention both under this Act as well as the Central Excise Act and the various sales tax laws. The word 'production' has a wider connotation than the word 'manufacture'. While every manufacture can be characterised as production, every production need not amount to manufacture.

The word 'production' or 'produce' when used in juxtaposition with the word 'manufacture' takes in bringing into existence new goods by a process which may or may not amount to manufacture. It also takes in all the by-products, intermediate products and residual products which emerge in the course of manufacture of goods.

The expressions 'manufacture' and 'produce' are normally associated with movables, articles and goods, big and small—but they are never employed to denote the construction activity of the nature involved in the construction of a dam or for that matter a bridge, a road or a building.

♦♦

CIT v. Sterling Foods (Goa) [1995] 79 Taxman 381/213 ITR 851 (Bom.)

Section 80HH was not intended to be applied to industrial undertakings engaged in 'processing of goods' not amounting to manufacture or production of articles.

On a careful reading of the expression 'manufacture or produce articles' used in section 80HH of the Act in the light of the expressions 'in the manufacture or processing of goods' appearing in section 33B of the Act and section 2(8)(c) of the Finance Act, 1975, it is clear that the Legislature has specifically used the expression 'processing' in juxtaposition to 'manufacture' wherever it intended to extend the benefit to an industrial undertaking which is engaged in the processing of goods or articles and avoided using that expression in cases where it intended to confine the benefit only to industrial undertakings engaged in the 'manufacture or production' of goods or articles. Evidently, the Legislature has used a narrower expression in section 80HH than the one used in section 33B of the Act and section 2(8)(c) of the Finance Act, 1975. This is a clear indication of the legislative intention behind using the expression 'manufacture or produce articles' in section 80HH in contradistinction to 'manufacture or processing of goods' used in section 33B of the very Act and in the Finance Act.

On a careful reading of section 80HH of the Act in the light of scheme thereof and other provisions of the Act, it is clear that the Legislature intended to extend the benefit of deduction under section 80HH only to the industrial undertakings which manufacture or produce articles.

This section was not intended to be applied to industrial undertakings which are engaged in 'processing of goods' not amounting to manufacture or production of articles. There may be processes undertaken by an industrial undertaking which may result in conversion of the article into a new commercial commodity or may change the nature and character of the article in such a manner that it may lose its original identity and get transformed into an entirely new commo-dity. In such cases, 'manufacture' can be said to have taken place. But in cases where no such transformation takes place, each and every process supplied to an article cannot tantamount to 'manufacture or production' of goods or articles.

Thus, the benefit of section 80HH is available to industrial undertakings which 'manufacture or produce articles'. Industrial undertakings engaged in 'processing of goods or articles' not amounting to 'manufacture or production' are not entitled to the benefit of this section.

♦♦

CIT v. Lucky Mineral (P.) Ltd. [1996] 87 Taxman 215 (Raj.)

The meaning of the word 'manufacture' in the context of the language of section 80HH is required to be construed in the popular sense in which it is commonly understood by the people.

'Manufacture' implies a change, but every change is not 'manufacture' although every change in the article is the result of the treatment, labour and manipulation. To bring about the change qualifying as manufacture, something more is necessary and that something is transformation, i.e., a new and different article, having a distinct name, character or use, must emerge.

♦♦

ARTICLE - CLAUSE (i) OF SUB-SECTION (2)

628. CIT v. N.C. Budharaja & Co. [1993] 70 Taxman 312/204 ITR 412 (SC)

The word 'article' is not defined in the Act or the Rules. It must, therefore, be understood in its normal connotation, the sense in which it is understood in commercial world. The word 'articles' in section 80HH is preceded by words 'it has begun or begins to manufacture or produce'. The word 'articles' occurring in section 80HH(2)(i) does not comprehend and take within its ambit, a dam, a bridge and so on. If a dam is an article, so would be a bridge, a road, or underground canal and a multi-storeyed building. To say that all of them fall within the meaning of word 'articles' is to over-strain the language beyond its normal and ordinary meaning. It is equally difficult to say that the process of constructing a dam is a process of manufacture or a process of production. It is true that a dam is composed of several articles, viz., stones, concretes, cement, etc. But to say that the end product, the dam, is an article is to be unfaithful to the normal connotation of the word. A dam is constructed, it is not manufactured or produced.

The expressions 'manufacture' and 'produce' are normally associated with movables, articles and goods, big and small, but they are never employed to denote the construction activity of the nature involved in the construction of a dam or for that matter a bridge, a road or a building.

Therefore, the activity of construction of a dam could not be characterised as manufacture or producing of article or articles, as the case may be, within the meaning of section 80HH(2)(i).

2.14-12 Toolings, used for production of refractories, is tangible fixed asset and not consumables and hence should be ac-counted as per AS 10/ICDS-V and not as per AS 2/ICDS-II

Toolings, used for production of refractories, is fixed asset and not consumables and hence the treatment of toolings should be as per AS 10/ICDS-V and not as per AS 2/ICDS-II.

Case Study 2.14.12.1: A company is in the business of manufacturing refractories (a material which retains its strength at high temperatures). The manufacturing process requires that to give shape to refractories, it is required to be filled into 'tooling' (comprised of an outer jacket made by a special metal). These toolings are imported in India. Toolings have a limited useful life of 3 years. As per the present accounting policy, the company treats toolings as consumables having a life of 3 years and accordingly the cost of tooling is amortised over a period of 3 years. Hence, toolings are disclosed under 'inventories'. Whether the present treatment done by company is correct ?

Answer: No. Toolings cannot be treated as inventory (consumables) because consumables are generally consumed in the production process whereas toolings do not get consumed but facilitate production process. Toolings are used in the production of refractories (finished goods) and have a limited useful life. [EAC opinion Query 26 Volume 29 Opinion finalised on 15 Dec 2009] Accordingly, toolings are fixed assets which should be depreciated in accordance with the Act and the Rules.

A company is in the business of manufacturing of tea. The company, to follow existing rules, is required to distribute foodstuff to its employees at concessional rates. The company purchases foodstuff in bulk quantity. The distribution of foodstuff to employees is at subsidized rates (lesser that the bulk cost). Whether ICDs-II applies to stock of such foodstuff?

In accordance with AS 2/ICDS-II, foodstuff cannot be treated as 'inventory'. Rather it is a short term employee benefit as explained by Para 8(d) of AS 15. Valuation of foodstuff should be as follows:-

Foodstuff at the period end should be valued at cost. [Follow AS 2/ICDS-II principles while arriving at the cost]

For the damaged stock, valuation should be lesser of cost or net realizable value. [Follow AS 2/ICDS-II principles]

Since foodstuff is provided at subsidized rates only once the employee renders services, foodstuff for which employees have already rendered services but distribution is pending on the part of the company; such foodstuff should be valued at amount receivable from employee's i.e. subsidized rates. [Because certain portion, i.e. cost (-) subsidized rate, would have already been recognized under AS 15 when the services were rendered by employees].

2.14-14 Empty beer bottles left behind by customer at bar or liquor vend is inventory?

Empty beer bottles left behind by customers at bar or liquor vend are clearly assets of the bar/liquor vend entity as customer has relinquished title by leaving it behind. As these are held for sale in ordinary course of business till they are disposed off, they are clearly 'inventories'.

Case Study 2.14.14.1: A company is in the business of running bars and retail sale of beer bottles. In the case of bars the customer leaves empty bottles at the bars itself which the company acquires, keeps account of the empty bottles and calls tenders for disposal of the empty beer bottles. At the end of the year the company accounted for empty bottles as the closing stock.

(A)

Whether the empty bottles can be considered as an asset of the company (keeping in view the fact that while selling beer at the bars, the company does not have any right on the empty bottles because bottles are also sold to the customers) ?

(B)

Whether the empty bottles can be shown as inventory ?

(C)

If yes, how the company should value such inventory ?

Scraps and CRC cuttings left over in the course of manufacturing of Stampings from Iron and Steel sheets and sheet scraps: Whether covered within the Entry 28 of Third Schedule "Ferrous and non-ferrous metals"?

Relying upon the judgments of M.P. High Court in the case of Chhaganlal M. Mittal v. Commissioner of Sales Tax reported in 74 STC 290 and of Kerala High Court in Jacob Phillips v. State of Kerala reported 116 STC 23, in which, following the ruling of Supreme Court in the case of State of Tamilnadu v. Pyare Lal Malhotra, 37 STC 319, it has been held respectively that G.I. barbed wire made from G.I. wire and G.P. sheets turned into different sizes and shapes did not remain G.I. wire and G.P. sheets, as defined in section 14(iv) of the Central Sales Tax Act, it is held that carving out and manufacturing of "stampings" out of G.P. and B.P. Sheets, a special manufacturing process having been involved, the "stampings" emerging therefrom are different from G.P. and B.P. sheets and "stampings" are not covered within entry 28 of Third Schedule. Rather they are electrical goods and accordingly taxable @12.5% under the DVAT Act. However, the left over and the scrap of G.P. and B.P. sheets obtained after manufacturing/carving out "stampings" from them are, in the light of provisions of section 14(iv) of the Central Sales Tax Act, the "iron and steel" and fall under the entry aforesaid and taxable @4%. [Clarification dated 14.2.2006 issued u/s 84 of the Delhi Value Added Tax Act, 2004 by the Commissioner of Trade Taxes, Delhi on the application of M/s Surya Industries, Delhi, STI 2006 (Delhi, Punjab, Haryana)(Delhi Commissioner' Decisions) 25]

Old Aluminium Vessels purchased for metal value

Old aluminium vessels purchased for metal value and used for reprocessing is aluminium scrap. [Prabhat Rolling Metal Works v. Commissioner of Commercial Taxes, (1988) 69 STC 359 (Kar.)]

where it was held that slag/dross of copper alloys is not excisable and hence not dutiable - also followed in Tata Iron v. CCE (2001) 135 ELT 1142 (CEGAT) [Departmental appeal against decision in Tata Iron admitted by SC, but no stay - (2002) 139 ELT A306] - also followed in Apollo Tyre Tubes v. CCE (2012) 275 ELT 85 (CESTAT). In CC v. Universal Cables 149 ELT 968 (CEGAT 3 member bench), it was held that dross and skimming of Aluminium obtained in manufacture of Aluminium rods is not excisable. - Departmental appeal dismissed by SC on 19-7-1996 - 151 ELT A175.

Dross and ash are not 'manufactured products' - Bajaj Auto v. CCE (2015) 322 ELT 419 (SC).

Zinc dross is not manufactured product. Hence, excise duty is not payable even if it is marketable - Aster P Ltd. v. CCE (2013) 42 GST 311 = 40 taxmann.com 66 (CESTAT).

Slag emerging as waste during manufacture of zinc and lead ingots is neither marketable nor a manufactured commodity. Hence, it is not an excisable commodity - Hindustan Zinc v. CCE 2004 (173) ELT 131 (CESTAT).

In National Steel Industries v. CCE 2003 (154) ELT 696 (CEGAT), it was held that zinc dross and skimming is not 'excisable goods'. Merely selling does not mean dross and skimming are marketable commodity as even rubbish can be sold - Departmental appeal admitted by SC - 2003 (158) ELT A185.

In Tata Iron Steel Co. Ltd. v. CCE 1997(94) ELT 258 (CEGAT), it has been held that molten slag and granulated slag is not 'goods' though it is possible to sell it.

In Tata Metaliks v. CCE 2003(155) ELT 117 = 54 RLT 807 (CEGAT), it was held that slag generated during the process of manufacture of pig iron is not excisable [departmental appeal dismissed by SC - 2003 (157) ELT A267] - quoted and followed in Jain Carbide v. CCE 2003 (158) ELT 850 (CESTAT) * Birla Corporation v. CCE (2008) 224 ELT 68 (CESTAT).

This view has been accepted vide CBEC circular No. 1027/15/2016-CX dated 25-4-2016.

Slag arising during manufacture of sponge iron does not amount to manufacture of slag. Excise duty is not payable even if it is saleable. Rule 6(3) of Cenvat Credit Rules is also not applicable - Hariyana Steel v. CCE (2015) 325 ELT 400 (CESTAT).

In a contrary view, in Adhunik Power Transmission v. UOI (2015) 51 GST 467 = 57 taxmann.com 379 (Jhar HC DB), it was held that zinc dross is a manufactured product.

Industrial dust - Industrial dust is not excisable - UOI v. Alcobex Metals (2016) 53 GST 81 = 64 taxmann.com 127 = 325 ELT 242 (SC) I [confirming decision in Alcobex Metals v. CCE 2004 taxmann.com 1516 = 168 ELT 455 (CESTAT), where it was held that 'industrial dust' arising during manufacture of brass or scrap is not excisable', since it is only waste, refuse. It is not manufactured goods.

Mud containing some metal - In Swastik Power Lines v. CCE 2005 (184) ELT 79 (CESTAT), it was held that mud containing small quantity of metal is not excisable.

Effluent waste is not 'goods' - Effluent waste is not 'goods' as it is not purchased by any one - Gujarat State Fertilizers v. CCE (2015) 51 GST 173 = 56 taxmann.com 448 (CESTAT).

Bagasse generated in manufacture of sugar - Bagasse is waste generated during manufacture of sugar. It is not excisable goods - CCE v. Basti Sugar Mills (2008) 224 ELT 572 (CESTAT SMB) - relying on CCE v. Skhakumbari Sugar (2004) 176 ELT 819 (CESTAT) where appeal filed by revenue was rejected by SC - 189 ELT A62 - same view in Kisan Sahkari Chini Mills v. CCE (2012) 37 STT 578 = 27 taxmann.com 56 (CESTAT) - confirmed in CCE v. Kisan Sahakari Chini Mills (2014) 302 ELT 346 (All HC DB).

followed in Swastik Power Lines v. CCE 2005 (184) ELT 79 (CESTAT), where it was held that mud containing small quantity of metal is not excisable.

Mixed sweepings of cigarette paper, filter rod, aluminium foil, ribbon etc. arising during manufacture of cigarettes and sold at low prices, is not a manufactured product and not dutiable - CCE v. ITC Ltd. (2008) 221 ELT 543 (CESTAT). Waste lubricating oil - In Vikrant Tyres v. CCE (2004) 171 ELT 23 (CESTAT), it was held that waste oil does not emerge from process of manufacture and hence is not dutiable - followed in Spic Pharmaceuticals v. CCE (2007) 213 ELT 679 (CESTAT) - ROM application of department dismissed by Tribunal in CCE v. Spic Pharmaceuticals (2007) 213 ELT 301 (CESTAT).

In Nahar Spinning Mills v. CCE (2010) 256 ELT 92 (CESTAT), lubricating oil was used in machine over a period time, getting burnt up and was drained out when no longer usable. It was held that this is not 'manufacture' - same view in Yamaha Motors v. CCE (2010) 259 ELT 400 (CESTAT)

Waste transformer oil is not excisable goods - Lucas Indian Services v. CCE (2008) 232 ELT 472 (CESTAT).

Waste oil is mixture of various used oils and dirt. It cannot be classified in any particular heading of CETA. Therefore, no duty is payable on its clearance - CCE v. Ashok Leyland (2008) 230 ELT 470 (CESTAT).

In contrary view, in CCE v. Empire Industries (2008) 232 ELT 161 (CESTAT), it was held that burnt/used lubricating oil collected from different machines is excisable product.

Floor sweepings - Mixed sweepings of cigarette paper, filter rod, aluminium foil, ribbon etc. arising during manufacture of cigarettes and sold at low prices, is not a manufactured product and not dutiable - CCE v. ITC Ltd. (2008) 221 ELT 543 (CESTAT).

Floor sweepings arising in process of manufacture of soap is waste material including mud, rubbish etc. It is disposed off at nominal value. The goods are not excisable - Kailash Soap v. CCE (2008) 231 ELT 176 (CESTAT).

Floor sweeping during manufacture of biscuits is not 'manufactured' although it has some value - Harinagar Sugar Mills v. CCE (2014) 310 ELT 775 (CESTAT SMB).

Waste of base metal generated by way of sweeping of floor cannot be considered as having been manufactured - Tempo Instruments v. CCE (2008) 225 ELT 444 (CESTAT).

Gas which escapes in atmosphere is not 'manufactured product' - Refinery gas generated in factory which escapes in atmosphere is not 'manufactured' product - CBEC circular No. 246/80/96-CX dated 1-10-1996 - quoted and followed in Bongaigaon Refinery v. CCE (2008) 227 ELT 273 (CESTAT) - relying on Indian Oil Corporation v. CCE (2007) 217 ELT 359 (CESTAT). Also followed in CCE v. Deepak Fertilisers (2009) 243 ELT 408 (CESTAT).

Oxygen gas which escapes in atmosphere during manufacture of Nitrogen is not 'manufactured product'. Hence, rule 6 of Cenvat Credit Rules does not apply - CCE v. Air Liquid India Holding (2009) 238 ELT 122 (CESTAT SMB).

Cotton waste during manufacture of cotton yarn - Cotton waste arising during manufacture of cotton yarn is not manufacture - Gem Spinners v. CCE (2008) 226 ELT 233 (CESTAT).

Spent sulphuric acid is not 'goods' - In Indian Tube Co. Ltd. v. CCE - 1988 (37) ELT 418 (CEGAT), the Tribunal had held that diluted Sulphuric acid which remains after use has no marketability or saleability. Hence, it is not liable to duty. Appeal of revenue against the order was dismissed by Supreme Court - CCE v. Indian Tube Co. Ltd. - 1995 (77) ELT 21 (SC). In Markfed Vanaspati v. CCE 2000(116) ELT 204 = 36 RLT 170 (CEGAT 3 member bench), in para 18, it was observed that Supreme Court has decided that spent sulphuric acid which remains after use, cannot be said to have been manufactured. - the view confirmed CCE v. Markfed Vanaspati 2003 AIR SCW 2158 = (2003) 4 SCC 184 = AIR 2003 SC 3534 = 153 ELT 491 (SC) - in respect of similar issue in case of spent earth.

Scrap obtained from something else metal scrap—Difference between them

Scrap (core stampings), obtained from the burnt or used transformer on its dismantling, is not taxable under the entry relating to the taxability of "all kinds of minerals, ores, metals, alloys," because what is taxable under this entry is the scrap of the metal, i.e., metal as such (and not the scraps obtained from other commodities). Such scrap (such as the bunches of tin plates kept inside the transformer) is taxable under the entry relating to the taxability of "old, discarded, unserviceable, obsolete machinery, vehicle, and stores. …including waste products" [Executive Engineer, Electricity Stores Division v. Commissioner of Sales Tax, 1999 UPTC 1010, decided on 6.8.1998 by the Hon'ble Supreme Court].

does not become excisable. Sludge is not result of any manufacturing process - Larsen Toubro Ltd. v. CCE 2004 (173) ELT 515 (CESTAT).

DES (Diethyl Sulphate) sludge is not a by-product arising out of manufacture of chemicals and is not marketable. It is not liable to duty - CCE v. Dharamsi Morarji Chem (2007) 210 ELT 679 (CESTAT). In Ahmedabad Electricity Co v. UOI 2001(131) ELT 535 = 39 RLT 902 (Guj HC DB), it was held that coal ash (cinder) which is a residue or waste of coal burnt in boiler is not a manufactured product and is not excisable - quoted and followed in Smithkline Beecham v. CCE 2001(132) ELT 108 (CEGAT) * CCE v. Perfect Stoneware Pipes 2002(146) ELT 222 (CEGAT) * Ballarpur Industries v. CCE 2002(146) ELT 623 (CEGAT) - confirmed in UOI v. Ahmedabad Electricity Co. Ltd. 2003 AIR SCW 5529 = 134 STC 24 = 158 ELT 3 (SC) - followed in KCP Sugar v. CCE 2004 (167) ELT 222 (CESTAT), where it was held that boiler ash and cinder are one and the same - accepted by department and earlier circular withdrawn - CBEC circular No. 822/19/2005-CX dated 18-11-2005.

Boiler ash is not excisable goods - Shri Vithal SSK v. CCE (2014) 300 ELT 516 (CESTAT).

Fly ash i.e. ash of burnt coal is not manufactured, and hence not excisable goods even if it is marketable - Mettur Thermal Power Station v. CBEC (2015) 52 GST 481 = 61 taxmann.com 402 (Mad HC).

In UOI v. Ahmedabad Electricity Co. Ltd. 2003 AIR SCW 5529 = 134 STC 24 = 158 ELT 3 (SC) (para 29), it was observed, 'Manufacturing process involved treatment, labour or manipulation by the manufacturer resulting in a new and different article. It requires a deliberate skilful manipulation of the inputs or the raw materials. This was not so in case of scrap'.

Waste/scrap generated from sources other than raw materials is not excisable - Indian Petrochemical Corporation Ltd. v. CCE 2006 (198) ELT 193 (CESTAT).

In Kusum Products v. CCE 2003 (156) ELT 900 (CEGAT) also, it was held that burning of coal in boiler is not a process of manufacture and cinder is not dutiable even if it may be sold at a price - same view in Khandesh Extraction v. CCE 2003 (156) ELT 928 (CEGAT).

Waste transformer oil is not excisable goods - Lucas Indian Services v. CCE (2008) 232 ELT 472 (CESTAT).

A manufacturer of beverages cannot be held to be manufacturer of glass and have no intention to manufacture broken glass bottles. No duty is payable on broken glass cleared - Pepsico (I) Holding v. CCE (2008) 231 ELT 487 (CESTAT).

In CCE v. Dhillon Kool Drinks 2001(130) ELT 475 (CEGAT), it was held that waste and scrap arising out of broken bottles through the process of filling, handling etc. is neither generated during the course of manufacture of glass bottles nor it could be considered as a manufactured product. - Departmental appeal dismissed by SC - (2002) 144 ELT A210.

In Gujarat Ambuja Cements v. CCE 2004 (163) ELT 399 (CESTAT), assessee was manufacture of cement. Steel scrap was generated during construction work in the factory (and not in manufacture of cement). Cenvat credit was not taken on steel. It was held that scrap is not liable to duty - followed in Larsen Toubro Ltd. v. CCE 2004 (173) ELT 515 (CESTAT) * Zuari Cement v. CCE 2007 (210) ELT 219 (CESTAT).

In Alcobex Metals v. CCE (2004) 168 ELT 455 (CESTAT), it was held that 'industrial dust' arising during manufacture of brass or scrap is not excisable', since it is only waste, refuse. It is not manufactured goods - followed in Swastik Power Lines v. CCE 2005 (184) ELT 79 (CESTAT), where it was held that mud containing small quantity of metal is not excisable.

Mixed sweepings of cigarette paper, filter rod, aluminium foil, ribbon etc. arising during manufacture of cigarettes and sold at low prices, is not a manufactured product and not dutiable - CCE v. ITC Ltd. (2008) 221 ELT 543 (CESTAT).

Brass Coils

Learned standing counsel is justified in pointing out that Entry 39 of Schedule includes ores, metals, scraps and alloys including sheets and circles, as are used in the manufacture of brass wares and copper wares. He submits that it was not the case of the assessee that the brass coils were to be used in manufacture of brass ware or copper wares. On the contrary his case was that he was to perform the job work qua manufacturer of shaving blades and other shaving goods/equipments. In any case, not for manufacture of brass wares and copper wares. In view of the aforesaid, this court finds no good ground to interfere with the order of the Tribunal. [Sherwani Industrial Syndicate Ltd. v. Commissioner of Trade Tax, 2011 (53) STJ 39, decided on 3.8.2011 by the Allahabad High Court]

SECTION 41(2) OF THE INCOME-TAX ACT, 1961-BALANCING CHARGE-
WHETHER IN VIEW OF FACTS MENTIONED UNDER CAPTION 'DEDUCTIONS - IN 
RESPECT OF PROFITS AND GAINS OF INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKING, ETC., IN 
BACKWARD AREAS', SECTION 41(2) WAS NOT ATTRACTED TO PROFITS FROM 
SALE OF SCRAP BUT WAS APPLICABLE TO PROFITS FROM SALE OF DRUMS-
HELD, YES

FACT: The assessee was engaged in the manufacture and sale of different varieties of metallic wires and in the course of such manufacturing activity, waste material, viz., scrap metal, was obtained. The assessee's claim for deduction under section 80HH in respect of profits attributable to sale proceeds of scrap and drums and value of scrap at close of the accounting year was rejected by the ITO on the ground that the impugned profits could not be said to have been derived from the industrial undertakings. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the assessee's claim on the ground that scrap metal was a direct offshoot of the manufacturing activity of the assessee and eventually it could not be put into a different category other than the one from which the main product was derived. On appeal, the revenue contended, inter alia, that sections 41(1) and 41(2) were applicable to profits derived from sale of scrap metal and drums.

HELD: Section 41(1 ) brings to tax certain amounts by a fiction of law. Therefore, the operation of such fiction should be limited to the language of the section. Where the assessee has incurred a loss or expenditure or trading liability and this trading liability has been allowed as deduction in an earlier year and something has later on been recovered in respect of such liability or such liability has either been remitted or has ceased to exist, section 41( 1) comes into operation. But according to the facts in the present case, nothing happened as contemplated by section 41(1) . Sale proceeds derived were for the sale of the particular product and not recoupment of earlier purchase. Accordingly, section 41(1) had no application to the facts of the instant case.

Further, the particular receipt under consideration is, insofar as scrap was concerned, realisation from the sale of waste material from manufacturing activity of the assessee-company and it was not a receipt from the sale of some of its old machinery, plant or building resulting in balancing charge as contemplated under section 41(2) . Therefore, section 41( 2) also had no application to the facts of the instant case as far as scrap was concerned. The section could be attracted insofar as the sale price of drums was concerned.

In fact, the assessee was entitled to deduction in respect of profits and gains from newly established industrial undertaking as contemplated under section 80HH in relation to profits from sale of scrap since this scrap, being a waste product which had a commercial value, was directly derived from the industrial undertaking which the assessee was carrying on and was sold in the normal course of running the industrial undertaking.

HEADNOTE: I. Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from hotels or industrial undertakings etc., in backward areas - Assessment year 1979-80 - Whether income from sale of scrap not being relatable to industrial activities of assessee-company, could not be allowed for deduction under section 80HH - Held, yes

FACT: For the assessment year 1979-80, the assessee-company claimed deduction under section 80HH on income from sale of scrap. The Tribunal disallowed the claim of the assessee on ground that income from sale of scrap was not relatable to the industrial activities of the assessee.

On reference :

HELD: This Court in a case concerning the same assessee in Pandian Chemicals Ltd. v. CIT [2002] 254 ITR 562, had held, inter alia, that scrap not being a necessary by product in the process of manufacturer, the income from the sale of scrap could not be regarded as income derived from the industrial undertaking.

Therefore, the Tribunal was right in law in holding that the income from the sale of scrap was not relatable to the industrial activities of the assessee for the purpose of section 80HH.

as far as scrap was concerned. The section could be attracted insofar as the sale price of drums was concerned.

In fact, the assessee was entitled to deduction in respect of profits and gains from newly established industrial undertaking as contemplated under section 80HH in relation to profits from sale of scrap since this scrap, being a waste product which had a commercial value, was directly derived from the industrial undertaking which the assessee was carrying on and was sold in the normal course of running the industrial undertaking. While giving the relief under section 80HH, value of closing stock of scrap would also have to be included. The sale proceeds of drums used for storing water and which had become useless could not, however, be said to be directly derived from the industrial undertaking considering the manufactur-ing activity in which the assessee was involved. This surplus was also of the nature falling under section 41(2 ). Therefore, the assessee was not entitled to relief in respect of profits attributable to sale of drums.

HEADNOTE: II. Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from hotels or industrial undertakings, etc., in backward areas (Computation of deduction) - Assessment years 1993-94 and 1994-95 - Whether scrap generated from manufacturing process has direct and immediate nexus with industrial undertaking and any income from sale of such scrap has to be included for purpose of benefit of section 80HH - Held, yes [Para 15] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: While computing deduction under section 80HH, the Assessing Officer excluded income from the sale of scrap by xerographic equipment unit and toner, developer, photocopier unit holding that income from the scrap could not be said to be income derived from the industrial undertaking.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) directed the Assessing Officer to take income from sale of scrap as income derived from industrial undertaking.

The Tribunal confirmed the order of the Commissioner (Appeals).

On revenue's appeal:

HELD: The word "derived from" under section 80-HH has to be understood as something which has immediate nexus with the industrial undertaking. In the instant case, the scrap generated from the concerned units has direct and immediate nexus with the industrial undertaking since the said scrap has been generated from the manufacturing process itself. Thus, the Commissioner (Appeals) as well as the Tribunal have committed no error in allowing the benefit of section 80-HH to the assessee on the aforesaid income. [Para 15]

HEADNOTE: I. Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from hotels and industrial undertakings, etc., in backward areas - Assessment year 1992-93 - Whether deduction under section 80HH is allowable on profit from sale of scrap in case of an industrial undertaking - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company, an industrial undertaking, had claimed deduction under section 80HH on sale of scrap. The Assessing Officer held that the deduction could be available only on the profits and gains derived from industrial undertaking and not from income incidental to the activity of industrial undertaking. Therefore, for the purpose of determining the deduction, the income shown from sale of scrap should be excluded. In appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that the generation of scrap was independent to manufacturing activity and, therefore, the assessee was not entitled to claim of deduction under section 80HH and the action of the Assessing Officer was confirmed.

On second appeal :

HELD: In Fenner (India) Ltd. v. CIT (No. 2) [2000] 241 ITR 803, the Madras High Court expressed the view that the scrap materials has direct link or nexus with the industrial undertaking and, therefore, profit from the sale of the scrap materials should be eligible for deduction under section 80HH. Following that decision, it was to be held in the instant case that the relief under section 80HH was allowable to the assessee on profit on sale of scrap. [Para 13]

HEADNOTE: Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from hotels or industrial undertaking, etc., in backward areas - Assessment year 1994-95 - Assessee, engaged in running of steel and iron re-rolling mill, derived income from sale of brass scrap which he obtained from dismantling certain guns purchased in auction and which could not be used for re-rolling - He claimed deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I on such income which was denied as it was not considered as income arising from industrial undertaking - Assessee had stated that he dealt in steel scrap and was not aware that inside guns, there was brass scrap which was removed - Thus, it was only a fortuitous circumstance that, in relevant assessment year, assessee had purchased guns without knowledge that brass scrap was inside them which was separated and it could not be said to be a by-product obtained in process of manufacture - Whether since brass was not an essential raw material of industrial unit, in question and brass was not at all connected with steel re-rolling, there was no nexus between brass scrap obtained on dismantling of guns and main activity of assessee of steel re-rolling and, therefore, separation of brass could not be said to be in process of manufacture or a product or by-product of activity of assessee’s industrial undertaking - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, profit on sale of brass scrap could not be said to be profit and gain derived from industrial undertaking so as to be entitled to deduction under sections 80HHC and 80-I - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee, engaged in the manufacture of re-rolled products of iron and steel in his re-rolling mill, filed his return of income which was accepted as such. In the course of the survey conducted under section 133A, the assessee had offered to pay tax on Rs. 10 lakhs. When required to explain the surrender, the assessee submitted that he had purchased certain guns in auction and certain quantity of brass scrap was obtained from breaking and dismantling those guns and the balance was iron scrap. It was contended that the said activity tantamounted to production of goods and, hence, income from industrial undertaking. The Assessing Officer, however, did not consider the income from sale of brass scrap as arising from industrial undertaking for purposes of allowing deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I and allowed the claim only in respect of other income. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) accepted the assessee’s submission. On revenue’s appeal, the Tribunal reversed the impugned order and allowed the revenue’s appeal. It accepted the plea that the assessee had purchased guns and the income from brass scrap which could not be used for re-rolling, thus, was not entitled to deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I.

On appeal to the High Court :

HELD: The assessee in his explanation had stated that he dealt in steel scrap and was not aware of the fact that inside the guns, there was brass scrap which was removed. Thus, it was clear from the reply that brass was not an ingredient used in the process of manufacture in industrial undertaking of the assessee. The brass scrap had no direct nexus with the appellant’s industrial undertaking. It could not be said that brass scrap was a profit or gain which directly flowed, neither it had close connection with undertaking of the assessee. By removal of brass scrap which was not useful for steel rerolling work no different and distinct article came into existence, it was only incidental as was apparent from the assessee’s reply. [Paras 13 and 14]

Further, composition of brass scrap was not at all changed, that was only removed as that was not useful to the assessee for the activity of manufacturing which he was carrying on. It was only a fortuitous circumstance that in the relevant assessment year, the assessee had purchased the guns without the knowledge that brass scrap was inside them which was separated and it could not be said to be a by-product obtained in the process of manufacture. There was no nexus between brass and activity of steel rerolling. Brass was not at all an input in the process of manufacture of steel rerolling. It was not a raw material at all for the process of rerolling in which the assessee was involved. It was purely incidental that brass was found inside guns which were purchased in that year. Guns might have several components, sometimes brass or some other articles which may not be connected at all with the manufacturing process of the industrial undertaking. [Paras 22, 23, 24 and 25]

HEADNOTE: Section 147 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Income escaping assessment - Non-disclosure of primary facts - Assessment years 1979-80 to 1984-85 - Petitioner’s claim for deduction under section 80HH was allowed for some years by Assessing Officer, for other years by Commissioner (Appeals) and Tribunal - Subsequently, Assessing Officer issued notices for reassessment alleging that entire manufacturing activity was not carried on in backward area and petitioner had failed to disclose fully and truly all material facts for making assessment - Petitioner contended that all facts had been disclosed before assessment was made and Assessing Officer was not able to specify exact information which was required and which was not disclosed - Whether, therefore, revenue could claim that there was no true and full disclosure of facts - Held, no

FACT: The petitioner-company, which was carrying on the business of manufacturing and sale of beedies, set up a factory in a backward area. Some of the raw beedies were entrusted to contractors for being manufactured and with that along with raw beedies manufactured by the assessee itself in the industrial undertaking, the further processes of heating, ringing, belleying, wrapping and packing were carried on with the consequence that the finished product was made in the factory which was in the backward area. The petitioner claimed deduction under section 80HH. Deduction was allowed for some years by the ITO, for some years by the Commissioner (Appeals) and for some years by the Tribunal. On the ground that a part of the manufacturing activity was carried on outside the backward area, notices were issued alleging that the petitioner had failed to disclose fully and truly all the material facts for making the assessment. Petitioner questioned the issue of notices contending that they lacked jurisdiction inasmuch as the facts had been disclosed before the assessments were made.

On petition :

HELD: Sub-section (2) of section 80HH lays down certain conditions, one of which is that the industrial undertaking should manufacture or produce articles in any backward area and another condition is that it should employ 10 or more workers in the manufacturing process carried on with the aid of power. It was not the case of the revenue that any of these conditions were not fulfilled. Their only case was that the entire manufacturing activity from beginning to end was not carried on in the backward area and an initial part of it had been entrusted to the contractors who carried on that part of the activity outside the backward area. The contention, therefore, was that the profit shown as the profit of the industrial undertaking in the backward area might actually include a small part of the profit derived from activity outside the backward area and, therefore, there was inflation of the profit and consequentially inflation of the deduction claimed by the assessee, that could be withdrawn by reopening the assessment. [Para 5]

The revenue rejected the assessee’s clam for investment allowance by resorting to the Schedule XI on the ground that all items that were installed in the factory premises, with the exception of tools, jigs, dies and tools were to be aggregated and. consequently, since the value of machinery and plant exceeded Rs. 20 lakhs, the assessee could not be categorised as a small scale Industrial unit.

On second appeal: HELD: The policy of the Government to promote the small scale units by providing various concessions through the Ministry of Industry, considering their contribution to the overall growth and economic development of the country, was echoed in the memorandum explaining the provisions of the Finance Bill, 1986. The benefits as were extended to the small scale units by the Industry Ministry were considered under the Act for the first time in 1976. which was the grant of investment allowance to such units and this continued over the years. In 1986, through the Finance Bill, 1986, it was observed that the upward revision of the value of the machinery and plant was being made in the light of the upward revision made by the Department of industrial Development through the notification dated 17-3-1985, to be effective from 1-4-1985. From the time small scale units were given concessions under the Act, there was never any Explanation or provision added to the Act, as to manner of determination of the aggregate value of the machinery and plant, that was contrary to the. one laid by the Ministry of Industry. Unlike the provisions of sections 80-I, 80HH etc., where the pre-requisites for a new industrial undertaking has been defined, there are no conditions specified in section 32A for grant of recognition as a small- scale unit, other than borrowal of the definition from the one recognised by the Ministry of Industries. This, suggests that the only authority which has the power to grant recognition to a unit as a small-scale unit being the Industry Ministry or the concerned department under that Ministry, so long as a unit ‘is recognised by that authority, for purposes of harmonious construction of the term small-scale unit, the same should be adopted for the purposes of this Act as well. In the absence of any specified Explanation or provision for the determination of the aggregate value of machinery and plant under the Act, it would be only proper that the manner of computation of the aggregate value of the machinery and plant as recognised by that Ministry is also adopted, so that uniformity for the same class or category under different Acts can be maintained. Such uniformity of view is what is intended by the Legislature and will only be proper for achieving the objective of the growth of these units and their contribution to the overall economic development of the country and, last but not the least, to reducing avoidable litigation. Therefore, the assessee’s plea that the aggregate value of machinery and plant should be determined in the like manner as done by the Directorate of Industries was to be accepted. Since the Directorate of Industries had accorded recognition to the assessee as a small scale industrial unit, the assessee’s claim of investment allowance on such items as were installed in the factory premises was upheld.

On second appeal:

HEADNOTE: Section 80HHC of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from industrial undertakings in backward area - Assessee-company had set up an industrial undertaking in a backward area and was carrying on business of manufacture and sale of V-belts, oil seals, O-rings, rubber moulded products, etc. - Whether profits and gains from sale of scrap material resulting in manufacturing process were eligible for deduction in an amount equal to 20 per cent under section 80HH, since scrap materials came within manufacturing process of industrial undertaking set-up by assessee - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company, carrying on the business of manufacture and sale of V-belts, oil seals, O-rings, rubber moulded products, etc., set-up an industrial undertaking in a backward area. It claimed deduction of 20 per cent of net profits allowable under section 80HH in respect of profit on sale of scrap which resulted in the manufacturing process. The ITO disallowed that claim. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the assessee's claim. On further appeal, the Tribunal reversed the Commissioner (Appeals)'s order.

On reference :

HELD: Section 80HH is meant to give a tax rebate to certain categories of assessees and one, who wants to claim such a relief, must strictly satisfy the requirements prescribed therein. He must establish that his profits and gains are derived from his industrial undertaking or the business of hotel. Axiomatic proposition of law is that it is not sufficient if a commercial connection is established between the profits earned and the industrial undertaking and the law requires that such profits must have been derived from the industrial undertaking. The industrial undertaking itself must be the source of that profit. The business of the industrial undertaking must strictly yield that profit. It must be the direct source of profit and not a means to earn any other profit.

In the instant case, in the industrial undertaking for the manufacture of V-belts, oil seals, O-rings and rubber moulded products, certain scrap materials resulted, which had a saleable value. To say that the scrap materials had no direct link or nexus with the industrial undertaking, could not at all be expected to commend acceptance, especially, on the facts and in the circumstances of the instant case. The scrap materials came within the manufacturing process of the industrial undertaking in the manufacture of certain products such as V-belts, oil seals, O-rings and certain rubber moulded products, etc. In that view of the matter, profits and gains from the sale of scrap materials were eligible for deduction in an amount equal to 20 per cent under section 80HH, inasmuch as such gains or profits were derived from the industrial undertaking and includible in the gross total income of the assessee and the question relatable to the profit on the sale of scrap was answered in favour of the assessee.

venth Schedule’, appearing in section 80-I(2)(iii) in the context of the fact that the deduction under section 80HH is meant to encourage establishment of new industrial undertakings in backward areas when such industrial undertaking ‘has begun or begins to manufacture or produce articles’ and in context of the fact that section 80-I is designed to encourage industrial undertakings to manufacture or produce ‘any articles or thing not being article or thing specified in the list in the Eleventh Schedule’. Provisions of section 80HH or 80-I are meant for the benefit of industrial undertakings that carry out the activity of manufacture or production of articles or things and not for the scrap merchants who trade in buying old articles or things and take out their parts to sell them separately. All large scale junk dealers in discarded old and scrapped vehicles who might fish out a horn in working condition from such vehicle or pull out its steering wheel or part of its engine that may have a demand in the market of second hand spares will proclaim themselves to be manufacturers or producers of articles or things. No such startling result is intended by the provisions of sections 80HH and 80-I, having regard to their underlying purpose of encouraging industries for being set up for manufacturing or production of new articles or things. In fact, industrial undertaking formed by transfer of machinery or plant previously used for any purpose is disentitled to such benefits both under sections 80HH(2)(iii) and 80-I(2)(iii). [Para 23]

The ships imported for breaking up are obviously old ships, purchased to retrieve the material, particularly steel plates, for disposal in the market for re-rolling or re-cycling purposes which is the activity done by these ship breakers in the process of ship breaking.

Thus, there is nothing whatsoever in the process of ship breaking activity which can be termed as manufacture or production of any article or thing. The dismantled material is already existing as a component of the old ship. The process of extracting steel plates from it while dismantling the ship will not make such extraction of existing material an activity of manufacture or production of such material nor will the process of cutting extracted steel plates for convenient disposal be manufacture or production of such steel plates. Merely because the ship breaking is considered as an industry, it would not be an industry engaged in manufacture or production of any article or thing. Benefit of the provisions of sections 80HH and 80-I is clearly not intended for such ship breaking activities which do not result in bringing into existence any new article or thing. The word ‘manufacture’ in the context of sections 80HH and 80-I would mean making of articles or things. While dismantling, the ship steel plates are not made but only removed which is not the same thing as making of steel plates. The word ‘production’ in context of these provisions would mean the action of making or manufacturing from components or raw materials an article or thing and not just removing of an existing article or cutting it.

In the instant case, application of mechanical methods only removed the steel plates and other objects which were existing on the ships, which would not mean that the assessee produced those existing articles or things by the process of removing and cutting them. [Para 27]

The word ‘production’ or ‘produce’ when used in juxtaposition with word ‘manufacture’ takes in bringing into existence new goods by a process which may or may not amount to manufacture. The principle of adopting a liberal interpretation which advances the purpose and object of beneficial provisions cannot be carried out to the extent of doing violence to the plain and simple language of the enactment. [Para 27.1]

Therefore, ship breaking is not an activity which gives rise to manufacture and production of altogether new commercial articles or things. The assessees were not entitled to claim deductions under sections 80HH and 80-I and the Tribunal committed an error in upholding such deductions. [Para 27.2]

It was purely incidental that brass was found inside guns which were purchased in that year. Guns might have several components, sometimes brass or some other articles which may not be connected at all with the manufacturing process of the industrial undertaking. HEADNOTE: SECTION 80HH OF THE INCOME-TAX ACT, 1961-DEDUCTIONS-IN RESPECT OF PROFITS OF INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKING, ETC., IN BACKWARD. AREAS-WHETHER AN ASSESSEE-FIRM ENGAGED IN BUSINESS OF CONSTRUCTING DAMS, ETC., IS ENTITLED TO DEDUCTION UNDER SECTION 80HH-HELD, NO

FACT: The assessee-firm was engaged in the business of constructing dams, etc. The ITO held that the assessee was not entitled to deduction under section 80HH The Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the deduction.

On appeal, the revenue, relied on the order of the Full Bench in the case of ITO v. Hydle Constructions (P.) Ltd. [1983] 6 ITD .575 (Delhi) and contended that the assessee was not entitled to deduction under section 80HH because the end product of the assessee was a dam, which could not be considered to be an article within the meaning of section 80HH(2)(i).

HELD: In view of the Bombay High Court decision in CIT v. Shah Construction Co. Ltd. [1983] 142 ITR 696 and the ruling of the Full Bench for the Tribunal in Hydle Constructions (P.) Ltd. (supra) it could not be said that the assessee-company was engaged in the manufacture or processing of goods.

Thus, the Commissioner ( Appeals) was in error in holding that the company was entitled to section 80HH deduction.

HEADNOTE: Section 80HH, read with section 250/251, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from industrial undertakings, etc., in backward areas - Assessment year 1980-81 - Tribunal upheld order of AAC who accepted assessee’s submission that it had not made a claim before ITO for deduction under section 80HH on assumption that income was not sufficient to absorb said deduction, but in view of disallowance made by ITO, there was scope for that deduction to be absorbed and, therefore, assessee should be permitted to make its claim for that deduction - Whether by AAC’s order directing ITO to consider claim and allow it to extent permissible under law, interest of revenue was not prejudiced and assessee was merely enabled to obtain a benefit which law conferred - Held, yes

Section 251, read with section 80HH, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Commissioner (Appeals) - Powers of - Assessment year 1980-81 - Whether on facts stated under ‘Deductions - Profits and gains from industrial undertakings, etc., in backward areas’, amplitude of power of AAC being as extensive as that of ITO, it was well within his powers to have allowed assessee to raise its claim for deduction under section 80HH and further directing ITO to examine case and allow that claim to extent admissible under law - Held, yes

FACT: The AAC accepted the assessee’s submission that it had not made a claim before the ITO for deduction under section 80HH as, according to the computation made by the assessee in its return, the income was not sufficient to absorb the deduction, but in view of the disallowance made by the ITO, there was scope for that deduction to be absorbed and, therefore, the assessee should be permitted to make its claim for that deduction. The ITO was directed to consider that claim and allow the claim to the extent admissible in law. The Tribunal upheld the AAC’s order.

On reference :

HELD: By the order of the AAC, the interest of the revenue was not in anyway prejudiced. The assessee was not conferred any undue benefit. The assessee was merely enabled to obtain a benefit which the law conferred. The reason for not making the claim for deduction in the original return had been found to be bona fide and for an acceptable reason.

The amplitude of the power of the AAC is as extensive as that of the ITO. It was, therefore, well within his powers to have allowed the assessee to raise its claim for deduction under section 80HH and further directing the ITO to examine the case and allow that claim to the extent admissible in law.

SECTION 139(8)  OF THE INCOME-TAX ACT, 1961-RETURN OF INCOME- 
INTEREST FOR LATE FILING OF-WHETHER, BEFORE LEVYING INTEREST, ASSESSEE MUST BE PROVIDED OPPORTUNITY OF BEING HEARD-HELD, NO

FACT: The assessee-company was an industrial undertaking set up in a backward area, for the purpose of repairs of barges. It was following the financial year as its accounting year. For the assessment year 1976-77, its claim for deduction under section 80HH was disallowed by the ITO on the ground that its activities commenced prior to 31-12-1970 as was evident from the facts that it was allowed deduction under section 80J for the assessment year 1971-72 and that it had receipts from repairing charges during that year. The Commissioner (Appeals), however, held that the only receipt dur-ing that year being from repairing activity, no manufacturing activity commenced during that year but only in the next year and, hence, the assessee was entitled to the impugned relief.

On second appeal:

HELD: It was an admitted position that the repairing work and manufacturing activity were an integral part of one activity, and hence the activity taken as a whole had been in existence before the crucial date of 31-12-1970. The Commis-sioner (Appeals) was not correct in considering the individual items in the bill for repairing charges to find out whether those items reflected any manufactur-ing activity. The assessee was ineligible for the deduction, and the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) was to be reversed.

HEADNOTE: Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from industrial undertaking in backward areas - Assessment year 1991-92 - Whether business of receiving from clients untreated crank shafts, forgings, castings, etc., and subjecting them to heat treatment, in order to toughen them to requisite standards, so that they could be sold in market, is a manufacturing activity, entitling it to claim deduction as contemplated under sections 80HH and 80-I - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company claimed deductions in respect of profits and gains under sections 80HH and 80-I. The Assessing Officer rejected same on the ground that the assessee had not done any manufacturing activity. However, on appeal, the first appellate authority allowed the assessee’s claim. On the revenue’s appeal, the Tribunal following its earlier order relatable to the same assessee for the assessment years 1984-85 to 1986-87, held that the assessee was engaged in the manufacturing activity and, therefore, affirmed the order of the first appellate authority. The revenue’s application for reference was rejected by the Tribunal.

On application for reference :

HELD: The pivotal point, underlying the questions was as to whether the activity carried on by the assessee, namely, the business of receiving from its clients untreated crank shafts, forgings, castings, etc., and subjecting them to heat treatment, in order to toughen them to the requisite standards, so that they could be sold in market was a manufacturing activity, entitling it to claim the deductions, as contemplated under sections 80HH and 80-I. In the assessee’s own case in Tax Case Petition Nos. 592 to 594 of 1997 for the assessment years 1984-85 to 1986-87 it was held that the activity carried on by the assessee was one of manufacturing activity. The rationale or reasoning projected therein would hold goods here also, and the assessee’s activity could not be anyone other than the one relatable to manufacturing activity entitling it to claim necessary deductions under the original provisions administrated under sections 80HH and 80-I.

Thus, the activity of the assessee was the manufacturing activity entitling it to claim deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I.

HEADNOTE: Section 32A of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Investment allowance - Assessment year 1985-86 - Assessee-company engaged in manufacture of electronic typewriters and other office appliances, claimed that being registered as a small scale industrial unit by Directorate of Industries, it was entitled to investment allowance even though it manufactured articles specified in Schedule XI - It further submitted that aggregate value of machinery and plant, as defined in clause (2) of Explanation to section 32A(2) had to be determined with reference to only those items of machinery and plant which were actually involved in production or manufacturing process - Assessing Officer rejected assessee’s claim by resorting to Schedule XI on ground that all items installed in factory premises with exception of tools, etc., were to be aggregated and since value of such machinery and plant exceeded Rs. 20 lakhs, assessee could not be categorised as a small scale industrial unit - Whether aggregate value of machinery and plant should be determined in like manner as done by Directorate of Industries, and since that Directorate had recognised assessee as a small scale industrial unit, assessee’s claim of investment allowance on such items as were installed in factory premises was to be upheld - Held, yes.

Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction - New industrial undertaking in backward areas - Assessment year 1985-86 - Whether assessee’s claim, that technical service charges representing cost of the ‘brain’ - Component of electric typewriter manufactured by it, though billed separately for purposes of excise duty, was to be included as part of profit of undertaking for deduction under section 80HH, had to be allowed -Held, yes.

FACT: For the assessment year 1985-86, the assessee-company claimed that the profit derived from the undertaking for purposes of deduction under section 80HH should be determined on the basis that the Income shown under the head "Services" was from the industrial undertaking. The assessee, while selling the electronic typewriters, had charged for the price of the typewriters separately from the technical service charge that represented the value of the software provided as part of the typewriters, because, according to the assessee, no excise duty was leviable on such software. The excise authorities, however, had levied excise duty on the entire cost, including the cost of the software which represented the ‘brain’ or the central processing unit (CPU) of the typewriter. The Commissioner (Appeals) rejected the assessee’s claim by observing that since the assessee itself had treated the technical service charge separately, It could not be included as part of the profit of the undertaking for deduction under section 80HH.

On second appeal:

HELD: The "brain" or the CPU is the main driving force behind the electronic typewriters and the sale of the typewriters would be incomplete without the "brain" or the CPU. The treatment of the CPU or the "brain" as software services does not in any way change its true nature, which is that it is part of the machine and both of them need each other to form one complete composite unit. The maintaining of separate account for the value of the "brain" as technical service charges does not affect its true classification as the main strength of the electronic typewriters. Therefore, the profit derived from the industrial undertaking had to be worked out including the income from the sale of technical services and on that profit, assessee should be allowed deduction under section 80HH.

EDITOR’S NOTE

The Tribunal also allowed/disallowed certain other claims of the assessee by following the decision dated 28-1-1994 of the Special Bench of the Tribunal in the case of the assessee itself for the assessment year 1984- 85 in IT Appeal No. 3483 (Delhi) of 1983.

On further appeal:

Following the said decision, with regard to the order of the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal on the scrap sales inclusion for the purpose of deduction under section 80HHC, the assessee's plea is accepted and accordingly, the order of the Income tax Appellate Tribunal is set aside in this regard.
