manufacture. The associated words are indicative of the mind of Legislature. Where a word is doubtful or ambiguous in nature, the meaning has to be ascertained by considering the company in which it is found and the meaning of the word associated with it. The words 'manufacture' and 'production' have received extensive judicial attention both under the Act as well as the Central Excise Act and the various sales tax laws. The word 'production' has wider connotation than the word 'manufacture'. Applying the principles spelt out by the Apex Court in CIT v. N.C. Budharaja & Co. [1993] 204 ITR 412/ 70 Taxman 312 and the ordinary meaning of the word 'produce' as disclosed by the dictionary and by its ordinary connotation, it could be held that when the word 'manufacture' appears in the company of the word 'production', which has wider connotation than the word 'manufacture', then in that event the word 'manufacture' would have to be interpreted in a wider sense and would have to be understood at par with meaning assigned to the word 'production' and if such approach contemplated by the Legislature is adopted, then in that event it is not difficult to reach the conclusion that the assessees were the industrial undertakings, engaged in manufacture and production of articles and things. Further, the Apex Court in the aforementioned case observed that the word 'production' or 'produce' takes into account all the by-products, intermediate products and residual products which emerge in the course of manufacture of goods. The Apex Court while considering the next word 'articles' occurring in the said clause has noticed that the word 'articles' is preceded by the words 'it has begun or begins to manufacture or produce' and reached to the conclusion that the expressions 'manufacture' and 'produce' are normally associated with movables, i.e., articles and goods, big and small.

Applying the said yardstick adopted by the Apex Court and considering the peculiar nature of the ship-breaking activity, it could be viewed that the ship-breaking activity gave rise to manufacture and production of altogether a new commercial article or thing which is commercially identifiable in the commercial world other than the ship and, therefore, the assessees should be held entitled to claim deductions under sections 80HHA and 80-I.

HEADNOTE: Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - In respect of certain income of hotels or industries in backward areas - Assessment year 1979-80 - Whether industrial undertakings engaged in processing of goods or articles not amounting to manufacture or production are entitled to benefit of section 80HH - Held, no - Whether processing of prawns amounts to manufacture or production of articles within meaning of section 80HH, so as to entitle an assessee, engaged in such processing and sale of prawns, to deduction under section 80HH - Held, no

FACT: The assessee derived income from sale of prawns. The nature of activity carried on by the assessee was purchase of raw prawns, subjecting the same to the process of cutting the heads and tails, cleaning, etc., and thereafter selling the same. In the assessment for the assessment year 1979-80, the assessee claimed deduction under section 80HH from the income from sale of prawns on the ground that the activity of processing of prawns before putting them for sale amounted to 'manufacture' and 'production' of articles within the meaning of section 80HH. The ITO rejected the claim, observing that the activity of processing prawns for the purpose of sale did not amount to manufacture or production of goods or articles within the meaning of section 80HH. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the deduction to the assessee and the Tribunal confirmed the order of Commissioner (Appeals).

On reference :

HELD: Section 80HH applies to those industrial undertakings only which 'manufacture or produce articles'. The manufacturing process mentioned in clause (iv) of sub-section (2) refers to the process undertaken to achieve the above object, i.e., to 'manufacture or produce articles'. Sub-section (4) also uses the same expression 'begins to manufacture or produce articles'. This section nowhere uses the expression 'processes goods or articles'.

On a careful reading of section 80HH in the light of scheme thereof and other provisions of the Act referred to above, it is clear that the Legislature intended to extend the benefit of deduction under section 80HH only to the industrial undertakings which manufacture or produce articles. Manufacture, as observed by the Supreme Court in Dy. CST v. Pio Food Packers [1980] 46 STC 63, is the end result of one or more processes through which the original commodity is made to pass. The nature and extent of processing may vary from one case to another, and indeed there may be several stages of processing and perhaps different kinds of processing at each stage and with each process suffered, the original commodity experiences a change. But it is only when the change, or a series of changes, take the commodity to the point where commercially it can no longer be regarded as the original commodity but instead is recognised as a new and distinct article that a manufacture can be said to take place. Where the commodity retains a continuing substantial identity through the processing stage, it cannot be said that there has been manufacture. Similarly, the word 'production' has a wider connotation than the word 'manufacture'. While every manufacture can be characterised as production, every production need not amount to manufacture. As observed by the Supreme Court in CIT v. B. C. Budharaja Co. [1993] 204 ITR 412, the word 'production' or 'produce' when used in juxtaposition with the word 'manufacture' takes in bringing into existence new goods by a process which may or may not amount to manufacture. It also takes in all the by-products, intermediate products and residual products, which emerge in the course of manufacture of goods. This section was not intended to beapplied to industrial undertakings which are engaged in 'processing of goods' not amounting to manufacture or production of articles. 'Processing' means subjecting a commodity to a process or treatment so as to develop it or make it fit for market. Processing is, thus, an operation on an article so that it undergoes a change. There may be processes undertaken by an industrial undertaking which may result in conversion of the article into a new commercial commodity or may change the nature and character of the article in such a manner that it may lose its original identity and get transformed into an entirely new commodity. In such cases 'manufacture' can be said to have taken place.

HEADNOTE: Sections 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction - Profits and gains from newly established industrial undertakings, etc. in backward areas - Three units belonging to assessee were crushing barytes into powder for hire and receiving crushing charges - Further, assessee had not prepared separate profit and loss accounts and balance sheets for each unit - Whether barytes are distinct not only in form and name but also in use from barytes powder and barytes powder is distinct and separate article produced from barytes and, therefore, barytes powder is an article produced from barytes - Held, yes - Whether sections 80HH and 80-I do not contemplate division of profits and gains in respect of a unit and Assessing Officer may compute such profits and gains under section 80HH on such reasonable basis as he may deem fit - Held, yes - Whether when industrial units satisfied other critiera laid down under sections 80HH and 80-I, assessee was entitled to deduction - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee established three industrial units in backward areas. The units were crushing barytes into powder for hire and receiving crushing charges. The Assessing Officer held that mere crushing of barytes was not a manufacturing activity nor the powder produced could be called a new article. He further found that the assessee had not prepared separate profit and loss accounts and balance sheets in respect of each unit. He, therefore, disallowed the assessee’s claim for deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I. The Commissioner (Appeals) affirmed the order of the Assessing Officer. However, the Tribunal found that the barytes powder so produced got its marketability for its use for the purposes totally different from that of barytes. It further held that irrespective of the fact that there was no division of account, still they were entitled for the benefit of sections 80HH and 80-I as having satisfied the conditions laid down thereunder.

On reference :

HELD: Sections 80HH and 80-I do not contemplate the division of profits and gains in respect of a unit, provided the industrial undertaking satisfies the criteria laid down under section 80HH. The proviso of section 80HH(c ) itself provides that if in the opinion of the Assessing Officer, the computation of the profits and gains of industrial undertaking presents exceptional difficulties, the officer may compute such profits and gains on such reasonable basis as he may deem fit. In other words, it empowers the Assessing Officer to ascertain the profits and gains of a particular unit and make assessment. Therefore, the assessee was entitled to the benefit of sections 80HH and 80-I, provided the criteria laid down were satisfied.

It is not disputed that the barytes were made into powder by using power and the powder is a distinct and separate article from barytes and the use of barytes powder is in the manufacturing of paints while the barytes are used in a different form for different purposes.

Further, the barytes powder is marketed as such. Therefore, barytes are distinct not only in form and name but also in use from barytes powder and barytes powder is distinct and separate article produced from barytes. Therefore, it cannot be said that barytes powder is not an article produced from barytes. As a result, the assessee was entitled to deductions under sections 80HH and 80-I.

J.V. Prasad for the Applicant.

Sections 80HH and 80-I of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - The assessee’s contention was that the Commissioner (Appeals) was not correct in holding that deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I was not allowable on the profits on the processing charges received in respect of raw nuts belonging to other processed in the assessee’s factory located in the backward area
Where the assessee’s contention was that the Commissioner (Appeals) was not correct in holding that deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I was not allowable on the profits on the processing charges received in respect of raw nuts belonging to other processed in the assessee’s factory located in the backward area.

The assessee will furnish necessary details before the Assessing Officer to show that he was doing all the activities relating to the processing of raw nuts, starting from drying to packing before export, in which case the charges should be includible in the assessee’s profit for the purpose of sections 80HH and 80-I.

Section 80HH of Income-tax Act, 1961
Where part of business activity is carried out in backward area assessee would be entitled only to a proportionate deduction
ITO v. Echel Mehra Forest Ind. (P.) Ltd. [1983] 16 TTJ (Chd.) 324
The assessee company was based in backward areas declared in Schedule VIII. The forests where it fell trees and brought them to its company were situated in non-backward areas. From forests to the depots situated in backward areas, the wood floated through river and floating of the wood in the river to the depot was a mixed process of transport and it passed through backward and non-backward areas. While the  assessee claimed 100 per cent deduction the Income-tax Officer held that no deduction was to be allowed as the assessee was situated in non-backward area. The Commissioner, on appeal, after taking into consideration the length of backward areas the wood travelled through granted 2.5  per cent of the total relief admissible under section 80HH.
Held that the assessee was not entitled to 100 per cent relief but on facts on basis of length of backward area through which the wood travelled  assessee could be allowed 1.5  per cent of relief contemplated in section 80HH.

facts.text: The assessee was engaged in the manufacture and sale of different varieties of metallic wires and in the course of such manufacturing activity, waste material, viz., scrap metal, was obtained. The assessee's claim for deduction under section 80HH in respect of profits attributable to sale proceeds of scrap and drums and value of scrap at close of the accounting year was rejected by the ITO on the ground that the impugned profits could not be said to have been derived from the industrial undertakings. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the assessee's claim on the ground that scrap metal was a direct offshoot of the manufacturing activity of the assessee and eventually it could not be put into a different category other than the one from which the main product was derived. On appeal, the revenue contended, inter alia, that sections 41(1) and 41(2) were applicable to profits derived from sale of scrap metal and drums.

The assessee-company, carrying on the business of manufacture and sale of V-belts, oil seals, O-rings, rubber moulded products, etc., set-up an industrial undertaking in a backward area. It claimed deduction of 20 per cent of net profits allowable under section 80HH in respect of profit on sale of scrap which resulted in the manufacturing process. The ITO disallowed that claim. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the assessee's claim. On further appeal, the Tribunal reversed the Commissioner (Appeals)'s order.

On reference :

For the assessment year 1979-80, the assessee-company claimed deduction under section 80HH on income from sale of scrap. The Tribunal disallowed the claim of the assessee on ground that income from sale of scrap was not relatable to the industrial activities of the assessee.

On reference :

The assessee, being an owner of a cold storage situated in a backward area wherein potatoes were kept in the relevant assessment year, claimed investment allowance under section 32A on machinery and plant installed in the cold storage on the ground that the cold storage involved ‘manufac-turing’. The ITO disallowed the assessee’s claim, holding that a cold storage involved only processing and not manufacture or production of an article or thing. He also disallowed the assessee’s claim for deduction under section 80HH, On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order of the ITO.

On second appeal;

While computing deduction under section 80HH, the Assessing Officer excluded income from the sale of scrap by xerographic equipment unit and toner, developer, photocopier unit holding that income from the scrap could not be said to be income derived from the industrial undertaking.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) directed the Assessing Officer to take income from sale of scrap as income derived from industrial undertaking.

The Tribunal confirmed the order of the Commissioner (Appeals).

On revenue's appeal:

The assessee, engaged in the manufacture of re-rolled products of iron and steel in his re-rolling mill, filed his return of income which was accepted as such. In the course of the survey conducted under section 133A, the assessee had offered to pay tax on Rs. 10 lakhs. When required to explain the surrender, the assessee submitted that he had purchased certain guns in auction and certain quantity of brass scrap was obtained from breaking and dismantling those guns and the balance was iron scrap. It was contended that the said activity tantamounted to production of goods and, hence, income from industrial undertaking. The Assessing Officer, however, did not consider the income from sale of brass scrap as arising from industrial undertaking for purposes of allowing deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I and allowed the claim only in respect of other income. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) accepted the assessee’s submission. On revenue’s appeal, the Tribunal reversed the impugned order and allowed the revenue’s appeal. It accepted the plea that the assessee had purchased guns and the income from brass scrap which could not be used for re-rolling, thus, was not entitled to deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I.

On appeal to the High Court :

The assessee-company, an industrial undertaking, had claimed deduction under section 80HH on sale of scrap. The Assessing Officer held that the deduction could be available only on the profits and gains derived from industrial undertaking and not from income incidental to the activity of industrial undertaking. Therefore, for the purpose of determining the deduction, the income shown from sale of scrap should be excluded. In appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that the generation of scrap was independent to manufacturing activity and, therefore, the assessee was not entitled to claim of deduction under section 80HH and the action of the Assessing Officer was confirmed.

On second appeal :

The assessee dealt in marine products for the purpose of exports. It processed these products, and froze and packed the same as per export specifications. It also bought meat in the market and subjected the same to several processes such as cleaning, removing bones and fat through chemical and scientific methods, bifurcating chunks, trimming and finally packing the same in a fit condition for the export market. For this purpose the assessee used several types of machinery. The assessee claimed deduction under section 80HH which was allowed by the ITO but was later on negatived by the Commissioner under section 263. On appeal, the Tribunal allowed the assessee's claim.

On reference :

The assessee-firm was engaged in the business of constructing dams, etc. The ITO held that the assessee was not entitled to deduction under section 80HH The Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the deduction.

On appeal, the revenue, relied on the order of the Full Bench in the case of ITO v. Hydle Constructions (P.) Ltd. [1983] 6 ITD .575 (Delhi) and contended that the assessee was not entitled to deduction under section 80HH because the end product of the assessee was a dam, which could not be considered to be an article within the meaning of section 80HH(2)(i).

The Assessing Officer included the scrap sales in the total turnover of the assessee for computing deduction under section 80HHC.

The assessee submitted that the scrap sales did not represent the turnover manufactured by the appellant and the said amount would reduce the cost of raw materials consumed.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) as well as the Tribunal upheld the order of the Assessing Officer.

On further appeal:

The assessee-company was engaged in manufacture and sale of high tensile fasteners, cold extruded parts, etc., in Padi. It had a unit at 'k', a notified backward area, which manufactured fasteners and sockets. The assessee claimed deduction under section 80HH in respect of forging work done in 'k' unit on products manufactured in Padi, which it called as 'sub-contract receipts'. The Assessing Officer rejected the claim for deduction in respect of 'k' unit. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) directed the Assessing Officer to allow relief in accordance with law. Aggrieved, the revenue went in appeal before the Tribunal, which was allowed by a common order holding that the receipt on sub-contract could not be treated as income derived from the industrial undertaking for the purpose of granting relief under section 80HH.

On assessee's appeal :

The assessee-company was a manufacturer and exporter of stainless steel utensils.

In the process of manufacturing stainless steel utensils, some portion of the steel, which cannot be used or reused for manufacturing utensils, remains unused, which was treated as scrap and the same was disposed of in the local market.

For the purpose of availing deduction under section 80HHC, assessee was not including sale proceeds of scrap in the 'total turnover' but was showing the same in the profit and loss account.

According to revenue, the sale proceeds from scraps must be included in the 'total turnover' as the assessee was selling scrap and forms part of sales.

On appeal, High Court passed the order in favour of assessee.

On further appeal to the Supreme Court:

The assessee had installed an industrial unit at a notified backward area. During the year in appeal the assessee received a sum on account of job charges for twisting of yarn during the year. The claim of the assessee under sections 80HH and 80-I was rejected by the assessing officer on the ground that separate balance sheet in respect of the unit had not been filed; that the assessee had done job work and was not manufacturing goods on his own account and that, the twisting of year did not amount to manufacturing of goods for the purposes of sections 80HH and 80-I claims. The Commissioner (Appeals) held that the assessee was entitled to a deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I.

On appeal:

The assessee was engaged in manufacture of Iron & Steel products. Credit on Modvat on the duty paid on inputs and capital goods was availed by the assessee. They had availed credit of duty paid on conveyor belts as well which after repeated use were worn-out and became unfit for further use for intended purpose. These belts were sold out as waste and scrap and removed on receipt of consideration.

A show-cause notice was issued by the revenue demanding duty on the clearance of waste of conveyor belts.

The Commissioner confirmed the duty on the assessee along with interest and also a penalty of equal amount was imposed under section 11AC.

On appeal, the Tribunal set aside the Commissioner's order.

On second appeal, the High Court remanded back the matter to the Tribunal for fresh consideration.

Before the Tribunal:

The petitioner-company, which was carrying on the business of manufacturing and sale of beedies, set up a factory in a backward area. Some of the raw beedies were entrusted to contractors for being manufactured and with that along with raw beedies manufactured by the assessee itself in the industrial undertaking, the further processes of heating, ringing, belleying, wrapping and packing were carried on with the consequence that the finished product was made in the factory which was in the backward area. The petitioner claimed deduction under section 80HH. Deduction was allowed for some years by the ITO, for some years by the Commissioner (Appeals) and for some years by the Tribunal. On the ground that a part of the manufacturing activity was carried on outside the backward area, notices were issued alleging that the petitioner had failed to disclose fully and truly all the material facts for making the assessment. Petitioner questioned the issue of notices contending that they lacked jurisdiction inasmuch as the facts had been disclosed before the assessments were made.

On petition :

The assessee, a private trust, carried on the business of purchasing forests, felling the trees and converting them into logs and, subsequently, sawing them into timber of various sizes and varieties fit to be used in construction of buildings and also for being put to other uses inclusive Of manufacture of furniture. The business operations of the assessee were carried on in a backward area. The ITO allowed the assessee’s claim for deduction under section 80HH in respect of the profits and gains derived from the said industrial undertaking. However, the Commissioner held that all the activities of the assessee did not represent manufacturing activities. Accor-dingly, he set aside the assessment under section 263 and directed the ITO to examine each activity and allow deduction under section 80HH only in respect of those activities, which actually represented manufacturing of commodities.

On appeal to the Tribunal:

The assessee was a manufacturer of commutators. It also manufactured certain goods on sub-contract basis for others and received services/job charges and besides receipts from sale of copper scrap. They claimed deduction under section 80HHC including the said receipts. The assessing authority held that the receipts from the sub-contract receipts and scrap fell within the Explanation ( baa) to section 80HHC and, therefore, the same could not be included. Aggrieved by the said order, the assessee preferred an appeal. The appellate authority held that as there was a direct nexus between the receipts from special contract as well as sale of scrap material, it did not fall within the Explanation ( baa) and the assessee was entitled to include the said receipts in the income from the business and profits. The revenues appeal to the Tribunal came to be dismissed.

The assessee established three industrial units in backward areas. The units were crushing barytes into powder for hire and receiving crushing charges. The Assessing Officer held that mere crushing of barytes was not a manufacturing activity nor the powder produced could be called a new article. He further found that the assessee had not prepared separate profit and loss accounts and balance sheets in respect of each unit. He, therefore, disallowed the assessee’s claim for deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I. The Commissioner (Appeals) affirmed the order of the Assessing Officer. However, the Tribunal found that the barytes powder so produced got its marketability for its use for the purposes totally different from that of barytes. It further held that irrespective of the fact that there was no division of account, still they were entitled for the benefit of sections 80HH and 80-I as having satisfied the conditions laid down thereunder.

On reference :

The assessee ran a cold storage and had claimed that it was an industrial undertaking in a backward area and since it had satisfied all the conditions laid down in section 80HH(2), it was entitled to the benefit of the aforesaid section. The ITO rejected its claim as according to him the assessee was not engaged in the manufacture of articles and hence the necessary conditions were not satisfied and, therefore, the claim could not be allowed. On appeal, the Commissioner upheld the order of the assessing authority, which order had been confirmed in further appeal by the Tribunal.

On reference :

The assessee-company was an industrial undertaking set up in a backward area, for the purpose of repairs of barges. It was following the financial year as its accounting year. For the assessment year 1976-77, its claim for deduction under section 80HH was disallowed by the ITO on the ground that its activities commenced prior to 31-12-1970 as was evident from the facts that it was allowed deduction under section 80J for the assessment year 1971-72 and that it had receipts from repairing charges during that year. The Commissioner (Appeals), however, held that the only receipt dur-ing that year being from repairing activity, no manufacturing activity commenced during that year but only in the next year and, hence, the assessee was entitled to the impugned relief.

On second appeal:

The assessee-company was engaged in business of excavating and breaking boulder stones from stone quarries and supplying the same to a construction company for their work. The assessee claimed investment allowance and deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I which were denied by the Assessing Officer on the ground that the assessee was not engaged in any industrial activity. The Commissioner (Appeals) held that the assessee was entitled to investment allowance in respect of dumpers used in the business and directed the Assessing Officer to allow the same as well as to entertain the claim of the assessee under sections 80HH and 80-I.

On revenue’s appeal :

The assessee-company was engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling soyabean oil. For the relevant assessment year, it claimed deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I on the amount realized by it from sale of the old gunny bags (packing material). The Assessing Officer disallowed the assessee's claim holding that the said income could not be treated as an income derived from an industrial undertaking. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) granted deduction as claimed by the assessee. On the revenue's appeal, the Tribunal upheld the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) holding that the amount earned by the assessee from the sale of old gunny bags was an income derived from industrial undertaking within the meaning of section 80HH/80-I and was eligible for deduction.

The assessee was a jeweller engaged in the business of manufacture and sale of ornaments. He claimed deduction under section 80HH for the assessment year 1983-84. The ITO declined the assessee's claim. One of the grounds on which the ITO disallowed the assessee's claim was that the assessee had not employed any worker in the manufacturing process to fulfil the condition prescribed in section 80HH(2)(iv). On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the finding of ITO.

On second appeal, it was contended that the assessee was giving job work to artisans to prepare jewellery as per assessee's requirement for which money was paid to them and as such it was entitled to the deduction.

For the assessment years 1979-80 and 1980-81, the assessee, a private limited company, claimed relief under section 80HH on the gross income in respect of its liquid section which had been newly set up in a backward area. The contention of the assessee was that the relief should be allowed on the gross income and not on the net income. The ITO held that relief could be granted only on the net income of the liquid section. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) affirmed the order of the ITO. On second appeal, the Tribunal also upheld the order of the ITO.

On reference:

The assessee-company, which was retreader and established its plant in a backward area, claimed deductions under sections 80HH and 80J. The Assessing Officer disallowed the assessee's claim. On second appeal, the Tribunal held that the business of tyre retreading amounted to the production of a new article and that, therefore, the assessee was entitled to the relief under sections 80J and 80HH.

On reference:

The assessee company was engaged in the activities of manufacturing of articles and also in the construction activity. The profit and loss account of the assessee included profit and loss from the construction activity also. The ITO did not grant relief under section 80HH to the assessee on ground that the ascertainment of income from the manufacturing and other activities was not possible as the assessee being also engaged in the construction activity and that the profit and loss being one for both the activities the Tribunal held that the relief under section 80HH was not for manufacturing activity but on the products made by the industrial undertaking, and division of activities like manufacturing and other activities was uncalled for.

On reference:

The assessee-firm started an industrial undertaking in 1977. The claim of deduction under section 80J for the assessment years 1975-76 and 1976-77 was disallowed by the ITO on the ground that the cost of old machinery used in the undertaking exceeded 20 per cent of the total cost of machinery and plant. Again for the assessment year 1977-78 the assessee claimed deduction under sections 80J and 80HH. The ITO disallowed the assessee's claim on the ground that since in the earlier assessment years the assessee was not allowed these deductions, it was not entitled to claim these deductions for the assessment year in question even if the total cost of the old machinery was less than 20 per cent of the total value of the machinery and plant used in the business. On second appeal, the Tribunal held that the assessee was entitled to deductions claimed under sections 80HH and 80J for the assessment year in question, even if it was not so entitled in the earlier years.

On reference:

The business of the assessee-company was centrifuging rubber latex. It claimed that the business involved manufacture or production of articles and things and so, the company was entitled to deduction under section 80J as well as under section 80HH for the relevant assessment year in respect of a unit working in a backward area. The ITO rejected the said plea. He held that the assessee did not carry on manufacturing operations nor did it produce any article. In his view, the assessee only made the latex more concentrated. The reliefs claimed under sections 80J and 80HH were denied. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the said decision. On second appeal, the Tribunal observed that the notification dated 8-7-1983 (No. 189 of 1983), considered the latex concentrate, preserved latex, etc., as manufactured goods. After adverting to the said notification it held that the Government had proclaimed that the assessee was a manufacturer and that the said notification had to be applied with equal force to the Act also and accordingly, held that the assessee was entitled to deductions under sections 80J and 80HH.

On reference :

The assessee, a private limited company, was repairing and manufacturing transformers. It claimed deduction under section 80-IA in respect of transformer oil, scrap and labour charges for sale of scrap.

The Assessing Officer noticed that company had been engaged in repairing of old transformer and it did not manufacture new transformer.

The assessee submitted that company had been manufacturing aluminium HT/LT Leg Coils which were used in old burnt transformers and on the basis of the said manufacturing, the assessee had claimed 100 per cent deduction under section 80-IA(2)(iv)(c).

The Assessing Officer had held that assessee had not manufactured or produced transformer oil and scrap, rather had purchased the T/oil from market and only centrifuging i.e., processing had been done, but no new article or thing had been produced/manufactured. Finally, the Assessing Officer had turned down the plea of the assessee of 100 per cent deduction under section 80-IA.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that the assessee was entitled for the benefits under section 80-IA.

On second appeal, the Tribunal allowed deduction under section 80-IA on transformer oil, which was not sold, but was a part of assembly of transformer, and disallowed deduction under section 80-IA on scrap and the labour charges for the sale of scrap.

On further appeal:

The assessee claimed deduction under section 80HHC stating that it was engaged in the manufacture and sale of harvester combines and its spare parts and components. The Assessing Officer while computing deduction under section 80HHC included warranty claims received by the assessee and the amount realized on sale of scrap as part of total turnover. He, further excluded 90 per cent of the provision written back and 90 per cent of the interest income being received from customers on delayed payments from the profits of business for the purpose of computing deduction under section 80HHC.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the action of the Assessing Officer.

On second appeal :

The assessee had set a cement unit in a backward area. For the assessment year 1976-77, the assessee claimed deduction under section 80HH stating, inter alia, that since there was no taxable income in the said unit in that year, the said relief under section 80HH should be carried forward. The ITO worked out deduction under section 80HH at Rs. 24,21,501 and held that as there was no taxable profit during the year, the amount of Rs. 24,21,501 would be carried forward and adjusted in the subsequent year when the assessee’s unit would go into profit. For the assessment you 1977-78, the ITO worked out deduction under section. 80HH at Rs. 54,95,585 and allowed the same alongwith carried forward relief of Rs. 24,21,501 for the assessment year 1976-77. Subsequently, the ITO realising that there was no provision for carry forward and set off of earlier year’s ‘deficiency’ under section

80HH, took the view that in the assessment framed for the assessment year 1977- 78 there was a mistake apparent from the record inasmuch as ‘deficiency’ of Rs. 24,21,501 was not only carried forward but also set off, which should be corrected. He, therefore, rectified the assessment order for the assessment year 1977- 78 under section 154 and withdrew the deduction of Rs. 24,21,501 allowed in the assessment order. On appeal, the assessee contended, inter alia, that rectification under section 154 could not be made in respect of the assessment year 1977-78 without first rectifying the assessment for the assessment year 1976-77. The Commissioner (Appeals) rejected the contention of the assessee and upheld the order of the ITO passed under section 154.

On second appeal:

The assessee-company was engaged in the business of centrifug- ing rubber latex. It had employed more than then ten persons

in its concern. For the relevant assessment year, it claimed deduction under sections 80J and 80HH. The ITO rejected the assessee’s claim on the ground that it was not an industrial undertaking which manufactured or produced any article or thing. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the action of the ITO.

On second appeal:

The adjudicating authority picked up certain items and held that they were scrap arising out of mechanical working of metal done by the assessee. He rejected the assessee’s contention that those items were mostly structural items used for construction purposes and were not in the range of production. He further noted that the assessee had removed said scrap clandestinely without payment of duty. He, therefore, demanded duty and levied penalty on the assessee.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the impugned order.

On second appeal :

The assessee was a registered firm engaged in the business of construction of overhead water tanks. It claimed deduction under section 80HH for the assessment year 1985-86 and under sections 80HH and 80-I for the assessment year 1986-87. The Tribunal, allowed the assessee's claim on the ground that the assessee was an industrial undertaking engaged in the manufacture or production of articles or thing.

On reference:

For the assessment year 1981-82, the assessee had made a claim of deduction under section 80HH against its profits and loss without setting off of earlier years’ losses which included brought forward business losses and unabsorbed depreciation. The ITO, however, took the view that after allowing deduction under sections 32,32A, 71 and 72, there was no positive income of the assessee for the relevant assessment year and, therefore, no deduction was available to the assessee under section 80HH. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) reversed the ITO’s order and upheld the assessee’s claim.

On appeal by the revenue:

The assessee-firm carrying on business of ship breaking, pleaded that it was an industrial undertaking and as such deduction under section 80HH and 80-I should be allowed. The assessee had explained that more than 20 workers had been employed and other conditions were fulfilled. The ITO, however, held that the assessee was not an industrial undertaking and, thus, rejected its claim, but the Commissioner (Appeals) accepted it.

On second appeal by the revenue :

For the assessment years 1987-88 and 1989-90, the assessee claimed deduction under sections 80HHA and 80-I which was denied on the ground that shipbreaking activity did not involve any manufacturing activity within the meaning of these sections. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) decided the issue in favour of the assessee by relying on the decision of the Bombay High Court in the case of CST v. Indian Metal Traders [1978] 41 STC 169.

On revenue’s appeal :

The appellants manufacture steel ingots. The appellants contend that the scrapped cast iron moulds continue to fall under TI 68 and therefore set off of duty paid is claimable on the finished goods under Notification 201/79. The department, on the other hand, contend that after having been scrapped they no longer fall under TI 68 but under TI 26.

The assessee was engaged in the manufacture of wiring harness. For manufacture of wiring harness, the inputs were insulated electrical wires and terminals. During the process, small cut pieces and rejected pieces of insulated wires were generated as scrap which were not usable.

The Adjudicating Authority opined that the waste and scrap of insulated electrical wires was classifiable under Tariff Item No. 85489000 and, therefore, issued on the assessee three show cause notices demanding a certain excise duty.

The Adjudicating Authority further decided the said show cause notices and held that in view of insertion of Explanation to section 2(d) of the Central Excise Act, 1944 the scrap became marketable and, therefore, it became classifiable under Tariff Item No. 85489000.

The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order of the Adjudicating Authority.

On second appeal:

For the assessment year 1985-86, the assessee-company claimed that the profit derived from the undertaking for purposes of deduction under section 80HH should be determined on the basis that the Income shown under the head "Services" was from the industrial undertaking. The assessee, while selling the electronic typewriters, had charged for the price of the typewriters separately from the technical service charge that represented the value of the software provided as part of the typewriters, because, according to the assessee, no excise duty was leviable on such software. The excise authorities, however, had levied excise duty on the entire cost, including the cost of the software which represented the ‘brain’ or the central processing unit (CPU) of the typewriter. The Commissioner (Appeals) rejected the assessee’s claim by observing that since the assessee itself had treated the technical service charge separately, It could not be included as part of the profit of the undertaking for deduction under section 80HH.

On second appeal:

The AAC accepted the assessee’s submission that it had not made a claim before the ITO for deduction under section 80HH as, according to the computation made by the assessee in its return, the income was not sufficient to absorb the deduction, but in view of the disallowance made by the ITO, there was scope for that deduction to be absorbed and, therefore, the assessee should be permitted to make its claim for that deduction. The ITO was directed to consider that claim and allow the claim to the extent admissible in law. The Tribunal upheld the AAC’s order.

On reference :

The assessee claimed deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I on the ground that the assessee was an industrial undertaking, engaged in the activity of manufacturing. The Assessing Officer holding that ship breaking would not constitute any manufacturing activity, rejected the assessee’s claim. The Commissioner (Appeals), upheld the order passed by the Assessing Officer. On second appeal, the Tribunal, however, held that ship breaking resulted in production of articles and amounted to manufacturing, and that deduction should be allowed to the assessee under sections 80HH and 80-I.

On reference :

The assessee's business was extraction of slates from quarries. The ITO took the view that the assessee was engaged in mining, and, hence, was not eligible to deduction under section 80HH. The Commissioner (Appeals), however, held that the business carried on by the assessee would not amount to mining business and, hence, deduction under section 80HH was admissible.

On second appeal:

• The assessee had acquired a large extent of land in a backward area as per industry policy for setting up an undertaking for manufacture of polimerisation initiators. It had complied with all legal obligations and started production in December 1986.

• Meanwhile, the Taxation Laws (Amendment and Miscellaneous provisions) Act, 1986 came into effect on 10-9-1986 which gave Government a power to make a retrospective notification subject to a condition that such retrospectivity did not date prior to 1-4-1983. Thereafter Government issued notification with effect from 1-4-1983 and removed the abovementioned area from the list of backward area.

• The assessee, in its revised return filed for the relevant assessment year, claimed deduction under section 80HH for specified amount.

• The same was rejected by the Assessing Officer.

• On appeal, Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the deduction but subsequently relying on Circular No.484 of CBDT modified his order and denied the deduction allowed by him earlier.

• On cross-appeals:

For the assessment years 1978-79 and 1979-80, the assessee- company claimed deduction under section 80HHA in respect of its business of toddy contracts. The ITO disallowed the assessee's claim. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that the assessee could not claim to have manufactured any article and, therefore, was, not entitled to deduction under section 80HHA.

On second appeal:

The assessee-company was engaged in the activity of processing tobacco for others known as thrashing. In its return of income, the assessee claimed deduction under section 80HH on the ground that its activity of thrashing and redrying of tobacco leaves amounted to manufacture or production. The Assessing Officer disallowed the above claim. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the assessee's claim. On revenue's appeal, Tribunal confirmed the order of the Commissioner (Appeals).

On appeal:

The Assessing Officer, having found that in the miscellaneous income sale of scrap was also included by the assessee, excluded 90 per cent of the scrap sales treating it as miscellaneous income in terms of Explanation (baa) to section 80HHC from the deduction allowable under section 80HHC. The Assessing Officer also excluded scrap sales from the export turnover of the assessee.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) directed the Assessing Officer not to exclude 90 per cent of the scrap sales from the deduction allowable under section 80HHC.

On revenue’s appeal :

While completing the assessment for the assessment year 1982-83, the ITO allowed relief under section 80HH to the assessee-company. The Commissioner exercising his powers under section 263 noted that sales of waste material, export incentive duty drawback and import licence premium were credited to the profit and loss account of the industrial unit for the year ended on 31-3-1982. He held that the above incomes credited to the profit and loss account did not arise out of the industrial activity of the assessee-firm and consequently, they should have been excluded in computing the profits of the concerned unit. As in the assessment order this aspect had been completely overlooked by the ITO, the Commissioner directed the ITO to withdraw the deduction under section 80HH already granted by him and modify the assessment accordingly.

On appeal:

A partnership firm KB carried on business of selling diesel engines at a backward area in the State of Maharashtra. The business was carried on in the trade name of 'CD' up to 30-9-1976. The business assets of 'CD' were valued at Rs. 35,066. The assessee-firm was formed by a deed of partnership dated 1-10-1976. It took over the said business and assets and carried on the business of selling diesel engines. It subsequently purchased machinery worth Rs. 79,726 for manufacturing fuel injection pipes for diesel engines by making nipples and giving shapes at both the ends of the tubes which were used as raw material in the process. For the assessment year 1978-79, the assessee-firm claimed deductions under (i) section 32A and (ii) section 80HH. The ITO disallowed both the deductions. On appeal, the AAC affirmed the order of the ITO. On second appeal, the Tribunal, however, allowed the deduction on both the counts.

On reference, the revenue contended that section 80HH was not attracted because (i) there existed no industrial undertaking, (ii) the industrial undertaking did not either manufacture or produce any article, (iii) it was formed by splitting up or reconstruction of a business already in existence and/or by the transfer to a new business of machinery previously used.

The assessee-firm’s business consisted of tannery and export of hides and skins. It commenced its business on 1-5-1976. On account of death of a partner a fresh partnership was constituted which continued upto the assessment year 1979-80. The assessee-firm claimed relief under section 80J which was denied by the ITO on the ground that two partners of the assessee-firm were previously partners of another firm and on dissolution of said firm they were allotted land, buildings, machinery and plant and the assessee-firm with the aid of said assets established new industrial undertaking. For this purpose, the sophisticated and imported machinery which were mostly in Madras, allotted to the share of the two partners were transferred to, another place where the industrial undertaking was set up. The AAC confirmed the order of the ITO. On further appeal, the Tribunal held that the previous user contemplated under section 80J(4) should be by the assessee and not by any other person and the assessee was entitled to the relief under section 80J.

The assessee had also claimed deduction under section 80HH which too was denied by the ITO and AAC. On further appeal, the Tribunal held that the assessee would be entitled to the relief. It also held that in any event, the plant and machinery previously used, were not in any backward area, as it was common ground that such plant and machinery were in Madras, which was not a backward area and, therefore, the assessee was entitled to relief under section 80HH.

On reference :

held.text:
Section 41(1 ) brings to tax certain amounts by a fiction of law. Therefore, the operation of such fiction should be limited to the language of the section. Where the assessee has incurred a loss or expenditure or trading liability and this trading liability has been allowed as deduction in an earlier year and something has later on been recovered in respect of such liability or such liability has either been remitted or has ceased to exist, section 41( 1) comes into operation. But according to the facts in the present case, nothing happened as contemplated by section 41(1) . Sale proceeds derived were for the sale of the particular product and not recoupment of earlier purchase. Accordingly, section 41(1) had no application to the facts of the instant case.

Further, the particular receipt under consideration is, insofar as scrap was concerned, realisation from the sale of waste material from manufacturing activity of the assessee-company and it was not a receipt from the sale of some of its old machinery, plant or building resulting in balancing charge as contemplated under section 41(2) . Therefore, section 41( 2) also had no application to the facts of the instant case as far as scrap was concerned. The section could be attracted insofar as the sale price of drums was concerned.

In fact, the assessee was entitled to deduction in respect of profits and gains from newly established industrial undertaking as contemplated under section 80HH in relation to profits from sale of scrap since this scrap, being a waste product which had a commercial value, was directly derived from the industrial undertaking which the assessee was carrying on and was sold in the normal course of running the industrial undertaking.

While giving the relief under section 80HH, value of closing stock of scrap would also have to be included. The sale proceeds of drums used for storing water and which had become useless could not, however, be said to be directly derived from the industrial undertaking considering the manufactur-ing activity in which the assessee was involved. This surplus was also of the nature falling under section 41(2 ). Therefore, the assessee was not entitled to relief in respect of profits attributable to sale of drums.

In Fenner (India) Ltd. v. CIT (No. 2) [2000] 241 ITR 803, the Madras High Court expressed the view that the scrap materials has direct link or nexus with the industrial undertaking and, therefore, profit from the sale of the scrap materials should be eligible for deduction under section 80HH. Following that decision, it was to be held in the instant case that the relief under section 80HH was allowable to the assessee on profit on sale of scrap. [Para 13]

The word "derived from" under section 80-HH has to be understood as something which has immediate nexus with the industrial undertaking. In the instant case, the scrap generated from the concerned units has direct and immediate nexus with the industrial undertaking since the said scrap has been generated from the manufacturing process itself. Thus, the Commissioner (Appeals) as well as the Tribunal have committed no error in allowing the benefit of section 80-HH to the assessee on the aforesaid income. [Para 15]

This Court in a case concerning the same assessee in Pandian Chemicals Ltd. v. CIT [2002] 254 ITR 562, had held, inter alia, that scrap not being a necessary by product in the process of manufacturer, the income from the sale of scrap could not be regarded as income derived from the industrial undertaking.

Therefore, the Tribunal was right in law in holding that the income from the sale of scrap was not relatable to the industrial activities of the assessee for the purpose of section 80HH.

The assessee in his explanation had stated that he dealt in steel scrap and was not aware of the fact that inside the guns, there was brass scrap which was removed. Thus, it was clear from the reply that brass was not an ingredient used in the process of manufacture in industrial undertaking of the assessee. The brass scrap had no direct nexus with the appellant’s industrial undertaking. It could not be said that brass scrap was a profit or gain which directly flowed, neither it had close connection with undertaking of the assessee. By removal of brass scrap which was not useful for steel rerolling work no different and distinct article came into existence, it was only incidental as was apparent from the assessee’s reply. [Paras 13 and 14]

Further, composition of brass scrap was not at all changed, that was only removed as that was not useful to the assessee for the activity of manufacturing which he was carrying on. It was only a fortuitous circumstance that in the relevant assessment year, the assessee had purchased the guns without the knowledge that brass scrap was inside them which was separated and it could not be said to be a by-product obtained in the process of manufacture. There was no nexus between brass and activity of steel rerolling. Brass was not at all an input in the process of manufacture of steel rerolling. It was not a raw material at all for the process of rerolling in which the assessee was involved. It was purely incidental that brass was found inside guns which were purchased in that year. Guns might have several components, sometimes brass or some other articles which may not be connected at all with the manufacturing process of the industrial undertaking. [Paras 22, 23, 24 and 25]

Thus, there was no nexus between the brass scrap obtained on dismantling of the guns and the main activity of the assessee of steel rerolling. Gun was not an essential raw material of appellants’ industrial unit, in any case, brass was not at all connected with steel re-rolling. Thus, separation of brass could not be said to be in the process of manufacture or a product or a by-product of the activity of the assessee’s industrial undertaking. There was no direct nexus between the separation of the brass from the guns and the main activity. Thus, considering the provisions of sections 80HH and 80-I, it could not be said to be profit and gain derived from industrial undertaking. Thus, deductions on profits and gains under sections 80HH and 80-I were not admissible and had been rightly disallowed by the Tribunal. [Para 28]

Resultantly, the instant appeal was to be dismissed. [Para 29]

The Legislature intended to extend the benefit of deduction under section 80HH only to the industrial undertakings which manufacture or produce articles. This section is not intended to be applied to industrial undertakings which are engaged in ‘processing of goods’ not amounting to manufacture or production of articles. The ship-breaking activity involves buying of damaged and unserviceable ships which are otherwise uneconomic to run, for the purpose of breaking and scrapping and sale of various goods and scrap obtained from such breaking and dismantling of old and used ships. Process is employed for breaking ship for dismantling and selling the scrap and substantial part of the items fitted in the ship and the oil contained in the tankers are sold in the same from without carrying out any further act, except removal of same from the ship and the remaining ship, made mainly of iron and steel, is then broken into different pieces of different sizes and shapes and sold by weight. Therefore, at the end of the process employed by the assessee, what is acquired are iron bars, plating rods, bronze, gunmetal copper and non-ferrous metal which, though marketable and commercial commodities, cannot be said to be manufactured or produced articles or things. For all practical purposes it is scrap. The scrap cannot be called a manufacture product or produced article because they are no new commodities but parts of the old and discarded ship as held by the Bombay High Court in the case of CST v. Delhi Iron & Steel Co. (P.) Ltd. [1995] 98 STC 202 the condemned and unserviceable ship purchased by the dealer is not a ship but re-rollable scrap in the form of an old ship for dismantling, in effect, the dealer acquires only the old materials and articles contained therein which are sold by it in the form in which they are acquired. No process whatsoever is applied to the goods, much less any process of manufacture. The issue stood squarely covered in favour of the revenue by the decision of the Bombay Bench of the Tribunal in the case of Asst. CIT v. Virendra & Co. [1995] 55 ITD 309 which held that ‘the meaning of manufacture and production of articles and things’ would have to be considered in their ordinary plain and natural meaning. Breaking or dismantling a ship would perhaps be just the opposite of manufacturing or production of an article or an thing. When a ship is dismantled or broken, what is obtained by the persons who are engaged in that process are the components by which the ship is constructed or manufactured and if it is possible to reassemble those pieces or parts, the ship may be manufactured or constructed. Hence, it would be doing violence to the language of the section if it is said that while a ship is being dismantled or broken or destroyed, in effect an article or thing is being manufactured or produced. Hence, the activity of breaking or dismantling of a ship cannot be considered to be an industrial undertaking which manufactured or produced articles or things and, therefore, the assessee was not entitled to deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I.

Regarding the contention of the assessee that the Government of India had recognised ship breaking as industry and, hence, the assessee was entitled to deduction claimed, there was no presumption that every industry is engaged in ‘manufacture’ or ‘production of articles or things’. Even if ship breaking is considered as an industry in the light of the definition of section 2(f) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, it will not mean that it would amount to manufacture or production so as to entitle the assessee to claim deductions under the respective sections. The assessee being governed by the Factories Act also would not change the matter in any way because that is broadly meant for welfare of labourers employed. The argument that a ship-breaking industry is labour intensive and that in the process heavy machinery like cranes and winches are employed is not relevant in absence of any manufacturing process involved. Mere application of systematic and sophisticated machines in the process would not treat an activity into manufacture. Thus, ship breaking activity amounts to carrying out the manufacturing process in a reverse order, as originally the ship is built from iron sheets and iron bars and other materials and by process of breaking the same, ship was reconverted into iron scrap and other materials. In view of the above, the findings of the Commissioner (Appeals) were to be reversed.
