Glass Industries Ltd. 1998 (97) ELT 5 (SC). Subsequent processing of refining/finishing has no relevance merely because of adding the value, but ultimately subject to the concerned Chapter Notes/Section Notes of the Tariff Heading.

Since a plant and machinery (being an immovable property) cannot be treated as marketable, it is not treated as an excisable goods because it is attached to the earth - Triveni Engg. & Industries Ltd. v. CCE 2000 (120) ELT 273 (SC) [in the same case, the Supreme Court has admitted the assembly operation as amounting to manufacture] but in light of the marketability concept, it was held that the plant and machinery assembled at site is not excisable good - CCE v. Virdi Bros. 2007 (207) ELT 321 (SC).

Since the definition of the term ‘manufacture’ given in section 2(f) of the Central Excise Act, 1944 has been replaced by section 4 of the Central Excise Tariff Act, the existing Chapters of Central Excise Tariff Act have been governed by relevant Chapter Notes and Section Notes. The term ‘removal’ in terms of rules 4 and 5 of the Central Excise Rules, 2002 is a legal fiction. Section Note of section XVI read with section notes 3 and 4 and heading No. 84.19 assumes ‘plant’ as an excisable commodity in terms of section 2(d ) and 2(f) of the 1944 Act. But because of the test of marketability, the CBEC Circular No. 53/2/98-CX, dated April 2, 1998 - 100 ELT T10 issued under section 27B, provides a great degree of relief to the assessee. While applying the order No. 58/1/2002-CX, dated January 15, 2002 (139) ELT - T34 of Triveni Engg. & Industries Ltd. (supra), it could be concluded that :—

u In case of piece-by-piece assembly/installation, involving equipments, pipes, tubes, insulation, ducting, etc. if the goods have been converted into an immovable property which could not be moved to the market as such, then assembly shall not amount to manufacture (for Chapters 84 and 85).

u Several goods like storage tanks, etc., having the height, could not be removed as such to the market and their dismantling creates waste and scrap, such storage tanks and other goods shall not be subject to levy.

u Assembly/fabrication of complete system creating a new commodity which is specified in the tariff and which is capable of being bought to the market for sale or purchase but temporarily installed for effective use shall be dutiable as per respective tariff headings as prescribed.

Duty on waste and scrap

3. For the same, there are 3 points :

u Whether it is an excisable good in terms of the relevant Chapter Notes or Section Notes;

u Whether it arises during the course of manufacturing process;

u Whether it is marketable, if not, then it is not called as an excisable commodity. Mere fetching a nominal value has no relevance.

Any waste and scrap arising from manufacture or mechanical working of input/raw materials (i.e., due to manufacturing process) is only liable to duty - Hindalco Industries Ltd. v. CCE 2002 (144) ELT 339 (Trib. - Delhi) provided that the same shall be marketable. Scrap arising through dismantling of buildings, repair of machinery, etc., is not liable to duty - Hindustan Petroleum Corpn. Ltd. v. CCE 2002 (144) ELT 555 (Trib. - Bang.), National Winder v. CCE 2002 (147) ELT 463 (Trib. - Delhi). However, scrap generated in workshop used for maintenance of plant other than old part or scrap generated by dismantling of used machinery shall be liable to pay duty - Budhewal Co-op. Sugar Mills Ltd. v. CCE 2002 (141) ELT 490 (Trib. - Delhi) but subject to fulfilment of other conditions. However, packing materials of inputs/raw materials could not be treated to be waste arising out of processing of the input for which credit has been taken - CCE v. West Coast Industrial Gases Ltd. 2003 (155) ELT 11 (SC).

The notice was opposed on the sole ground that the order-in-original had already merged with the order dated 13-10-2004, hence, on the date of issuance of show-cause notice there was no order-in-original, which could be reviewed by the Commissioner. That contention of the assessee was negatived, and the Commissioner enhanced the penalty. However, the Tribunal allowed the appeal of the assessee. The High Court held that the penalty whole hog was a subject-matter of the challenge before the Commissioner (Appeals), and was also capable of being challenged before the Commissioner (Appeals). Likewise, the Commissioner (Appeals) had jurisdiction to, and was capable of reversing, modifying or affirming the order of penalty also, which was in issue before it. It might be noticed in the instant case, that the order in original imposed a penalty lesser than the one which according to the department was required to be imposed, and the penalty as imposed was challenged. It was well-nigh possible that in appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) could have set aside the order altogether, or could have reduced it as well, while maintaining imposition of penalty, might be rightly, or wrongly. Therefore, on the parameters laid down by the Supreme Court, the superior jurisdiction was capable of reversing, modifying, or affirming the order which was in issue before it, and in the instant case the Commissioner (Appeals) declined to modify, and simply affirmed it. Thus, in the facts and circumstances, the Commissioner could not exercise his power of revision under section 84 to the extent the order of adjudicating authority was found to be erroneous by him and about which no appeal lay at the instance of the revenue, notwithstanding that to the extent the assessee was aggrieved, he had preferred the appeal and the order in appeal had been passed.

In order to set over this controversy in the above definition of ‘input’, the Legislature has clarified that even if an item is not contained in the final product still it would be classifiable as an ‘input’ under the above definition. In other words, it has been clarified by the definition of ‘input’ that the following considerations will not be relevant :

(a)Use of input in the manufacturing process be it direct or indirect; and (b)even if the input is not contained in the ‘final product’ it would still be covered by the definition.

These considerations have been made irrelevant by the use of expression ‘goods used in or in relation to the manufacture of final products’ which, as stated above, is the crucial requirement of the definition of ‘input’. In this regard, some case laws are cited hereunder :

In J.K. Cement Works v. CCE 2010 (252) ELT 249 (Trib. - Delhi), it was held that only those goods which form part of the process carried out by a manufacturer for converting raw material into finished goods can be considered as inputs and the goods which are not integrally connected with the process of manufacture resulting in utilization of such product directly or indirectly in the manufacture of finished product cannot be said to be input. Therefore, oxygen, helium and acetylene gases used for repair and maintenance of plant and machinery are not covered by the definition of ‘input’.

In Reva Electric Car Co. (P.) Ltd. v. CCE 2010 (250) ELT 149 (Trib. - Bang.), the Tribunal held that it is unambiguously clear that the rejection was at the pre-manufacturing stage and for no reasons attributable to the appellant. Rejection at the pre-manufacturing stage is also indispensable for quality control. It can be said that any rejection of input without ulterior motive or oblique purpose may not disentitle an assessee from the benefit of law relating to CENVAT credit.

It did not appear that the car manufacturer had escaped duty. The revenue should, therefore, allow entitlement of CENVAT credit in the absence of any violation of law. Accordingly, the demand of Rs. 6,90,150 on the count of using of inputs for R&D was unsustainable in the absence of any finding to show that the R&D had not resulted in finished goods and that finished goods had escaped duty. Exercise of Research having resulted in the finished goods and that had suffered duty, CENVAT credit was admissible for which demand of Rs. 6,90,150 was set aside.

In HIM Technoforge Ltd.’s case (supra), the respondent was a manufacturer of rough forgings and forging articles of steel falling under Chapter 7326 of the CETA, 1985. They also availed CENVAT credit of inputs and capital goods. The dispute related to ‘metal band saw blades’ and ‘steel shots’ as to whether they could be considered as capital goods as contended by the department or could be treated as inputs as claimed by the respondent. The original authority after taking note of the duration of use of these items and the purpose for which they were used held that they were capital goods.

The Commissioner (Appeals) treated the above products as ‘inputs’. He held that under the CENVAT Credit Rules, the term ‘input’ has been defined to mean all goods, except HSD oil, LSD and motor spirit used in or in relation to the manufacture of final products whether directly or indirectly and whether contained in the final product or not. In view of this above definition of the ‘input’ under the CENVAT Credit Rules, both the items, namely, ‘metal saw blade’ and ‘steel shots’ used by the appellants in connection with the production of goods on consumable would merit classification under inputs only and, therefore, the credit taken by them was in order.

The Tribunal held that if the role and period of usage as recorded by the original authority was taken into account, the decision of Commissioner (Appeals) had clearly held that the same were in the nature of consumables used in relation to manufacture of final products and, therefore, appropriately to be treated as inputs.

4.2 Waste and Scrap - In Tera Cables India (P.) Ltd. v. CCE 2010 (258) ELT 111 (Trib. - Ahd.), a small amount of Rs. 9,456 stood denied to the appellant on the ground that the credit had been availed on the waste and scrap, which could not be considered as an input for the appellant’s final product. The lower authorities had nowhere discussed as to how the waste and scrap could not be considered as an input. The cable waste of cut length was being utilized and consumed by the appellant in its own factory in the manufacture of finished goods. The duty paid cable waste received in the factory had been accounted for in the input register and its consumption had been shown in the manufacture of the final product. The final product manufactured out of the same was accounted for in the RG-1 Part I Register, which stood cleared on payment of duty. As such to deny the benefit of waste and scrap on the ground that the same was not an input was not justified.

Other queries

We are manufacturers of Aluminium and we sell Aluminium Dross. Supreme Court had held that ‘dross is not goods’. However, now, Central Excise Tariff has specific headings for dross and slag with effect from February 28, 2005. These are sold and have market value. Should it be held as ‘goods’ with effect from February 28, 2005? It is true that in Union of India v. Indian Aluminium Co. Ltd. - 1995 (77) ELT 268 (SC) = AIR 1995 SC 1580 = 1995 Supp (2) SCC 465 = 1995 AIR SCW 2436 = 1995 (58) ECR 612 (SC 3-member Bench judgment), it was held that ‘dross and skimmings’ arising during manufacture of Aluminium is not ‘excisable goods’. They are merely refuse or ashes given out in process of removing impurities from raw material. Hence they are not ‘excisable goods’ as understood in commercial parlance, even if they are sold and they fetch some price. This was followed in CCE v. Tata Iron & Steel Co. Ltd. 2004 AIR SCW 1948 = 165 ELT 386 = 61 RLT 239 (SC 3-member Bench), where it was held that zinc dross and skimmings are merely refuse, scum or rubbish. It is not result of treatment, labour or manipulation, even if it fetches some price in market. Everything which is sold is not necessarily a marketable commodity known to commerce and worthwhile to trade in.

In CC v. Universal Cables 149 ELT 968 (CEGAT 3- member Bench), it was held that dross and skimming of Aluminium obtained in manufacture of Aluminium rods is not excisable. - Departmental appeal dismissed by the Supreme Court on July 9, 1996 - 151 ELT A 175.

However, now CETA has following specific entries with effect from February 28, 2005 - ‘Brass Dross’ (2620 30 10), ‘Aluminium Dross’ (2620 40 10) and slag/dross from manufacture of iron or steel (2619).

In Balaji Enterprises v. CCE 1997 AIR SCW 2026 = 92 ELT 3 (SC) = AIR 1997 SC 2170, it has been observed and noted that whenever things like waste and scrap have been sought to be taxed in the Central Excise Act, specific entries have been made for this purpose. Supreme Court has noted various specific examples from the old tariff in this regard.

Waste is not obtained by any process of manufacturing but in the course of manufacturing and processing to produce the end product. The intention of legislature to cover waste or scrap in relation to manufacture is required to be specifically mentioned in tariff item before liability to pay duty on waste or scrap arises - Plastics Packaging (P.) Ltd. v. CCE - 1991 (51) ELT 271 (Bom HC). In Shree Synthetic Ltd. v. CCE - 1991 (52) ELT 238 (CEGAT), it was held - "Waste is normally not considered as ‘goods’ except where it is deemed to be ‘goods’ by way of legal fiction and specific mention in any provision, rule or the tariff."

‘Waste or scrap’ will be ‘goods’ and hence taxable only if specifically mentioned in CETA (Tariff) - Kamath Packaging (P.) Ltd. v. CCE - 1992 (60) ELT 666 (CEGAT).

Hence, in my view, these may get covered as dutiable with effect from February 28, 2005.

Act. The High Court held that the assessee was entitled to avail credit of service tax on the service. Even earlier, various services, like insurance, advertising, air travel agent, courier etc., have been judicially held to be eligible input services for purposes of availment of input tax credit. During the year 2010, the eligibility to tax credit in respect of certain other services was considered in the judicial forums. Brief details of these cases are given in the succeeding sub-paragraphs. 6.1 Business auxiliary service - A manufacturer and exporter of hand tools deployed agents in foreign countries for the purpose of canvassing and processing orders on its behalf, and paid commission to them. The department took the stand that service tax credit could not be allowed since the payments were connected with a post-removal activity. The Tribunal however held that, since such activities fell within the domain of sales promotion, credit was allowable - CCE v. Ambika Overseas 2010 (20) STR 514 (New Delhi - CESTAT).

6.2 Cargo handling service - In one case, the adjudicating authority denied tax credit in respect of cargo handling service on the ground that the service was used outside the factory premises, i.e., from the place of removal to the customers’ premises. The Tribunal relied upon the Larger Bench decision in ABB Ltd. v. CCE&ST [2009] 21 STT 77 (Bang. - CESTAT) and held that credit was allowable - CCE v. H.E.G. Ltd. [2010] 28 STT 277 (New Delhi - CESTAT).

6.3 Construction service - Where the assessee constructed a compound wall around its factory by utilising construction service, and it was found that the site plan indicated that the compound wall was an integral part of the factory, the Tribunal held that tax credit was admissible - CCE v. Raymond Zambaiti (P.) Ltd. 2010 (18) STR 734 (Mum. - CESTAT). On the contrary, construction service used in the residential colony for employees of the assessee was held as not eligible for credit, since such an activity might be a welfare activity but not an activity which was integrally related to the business activities carried on by the assessee - CCE v. Manikgarh Cement [2010] 29 STT 230 (Mum.).

6.4 Consulting engineer’s service - An assessee availed credit of service tax on consultancy services for environmental evaluation work including onsite evaluation and report submission. The department disallowed the credit on the ground that there was nothing on record to link the services with the factory premises of the assessee. However, the Tribunal noticed that the purchase order had been raised at the address of the factory premises, and for this reason, the Tribunal held that the credit availed was in order - Cabot Sanmar Ltd. v. CCE 2010 (19) STR 681 (Chennai - CESTAT).

6.5 Courier service - An assessee had used courier services for placing orders, filing quotations for procurement as well as marketing, dispatch instructions, issuing cheques for procurement, sending stock transfer documents to depots/head office etc. The Tribunal confirmed the order of the first appellate authority allowing credit by placing reliance on the Larger Bench decision in ABB Ltd. case (supra) - CCE v. Apar Industries Ltd. 2010 (20) STR 624 (Ahd. - CESTAT).

6.6 Customs house agent’s service - An assessee used customs house agent’s service for clearance of imported goods at the port and their transport to the assessee’s factory. The Tribunal held that the assessee was eligible to avail service tax credit - Nelsun Paper Mills Ltd. v. CCE 2010 (18) STR 648 (Chennai - CESTAT).

6.7 Dry cleaning service - A manufacturer of medicaments and drugs availed service tax credit on dry cleaning services in respect of uniforms/clothings of its workers. The Tribunal held that credit taken was in order, since wearing of clean uniforms/clothings in the drug industry was a mandatory requirement under the Drugs & Cosmetics Act - CCE v. Fourtts (I) Laboratories (P.) Ltd. 2010 24 STT 153 (Chennai - CESTAT).

6.8 Event management service - In connection with the celebrations connected with the expansion of its plant, an assessee used Event Management service and availed service tax credit. The credit was disallowed by the adjudicating authority. The Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the disallowance, by observing that the celebrations were mainly an ‘entertainment’ which could not be treated as ‘activities relating to business’. The Tribunal confirmed the appellate order - Hindustan Zinc Ltd. v. CCE [2010] 28 STT 139 (New Delhi - CESTAT).

In other words, the waste and scrap arising out of capital goods on which no credit has been availed, shall not be dutiable - Southern Agrifurane Industries Ltd. v. CCE 2003 (158) ELT 323 (Trib. - Chennai), provided that no Cenvat credit on such capital goods was taken - Kesoram Rayon v. CCE 2003 (162) ELT 620 (Trib. - Kol.).

If any waste is not marketable, the same shall not be dutiable - CCE v. Indian Tube Co. Ltd. 1995 (77) ELT 21 (SC); Union of India v. Indian Aluminium Co. Ltd.’s case (supra). For example, refuse, rubbish and ashes thrown up in the course of manufacture are not goods even if they may fetch some prices - CCE v. Tata Iron & Steels Co. Ltd. 2004 (165) ELT 386 (SC). If the resultant waste (after process of a waste) is same having almost identical chemical and physical properties, resultant waste could not be said as manufactured waste - Indian Organic Chemicals Ltd. v. CCE 1996 (88) ELT 644 (SC).

Waste and scrap is dutiable only when it is a manufactured product and not otherwise - Elphinstone Metal Rolling Mills v. CCE 2004 (167) ELT 481 (SC)

A by-product is something of value, which is produced in making main product or it is a substance obtained in the course of a specific process, but it is not the primary product. If it is not marketable (although sold in market in few occasions), the same will not be dutiable - Gujarat State Fertilizers Co. Ltd. v. CCE 1997 (90) ELT 149 (Trib. - New Delhi). For example, by-product obtained during the course of processing of rice in the rice mill, not fit for human consumption, does not fall within the ambit of definition of ‘vegetable oil’ contained in section 3(h) of the National Oil Seeds and Vegetable Oil Development Board Act - A.P. Rice Bran Solvent Extractors Association v. Union of India 1998 (103) ELT 481 (SC).

And waste and scrap arising out of manufacture of exempted goods are exempt from the whole of the duty of excise vide Notification No. 89/95-CE, dated May 18, 1995, provided that in such factory, any other excisable goods (other than exempted goods) shall not be manufactured - see also E.P. Inclusive Part

5. The expression viz., ‘used in or in relation to the manufacture of final products’ in the specific/substantive part of the definition is so wide that it would cover innumerable items as ‘input’ and to avoid such contingency the Legislature has incorporated the inclusive part after the substantive part qualified by the place of use. For example, one of the categories mentioned in the inclusive part is ‘used as packing material’. Packing material by itself would not suffice till it is proved that the term is used in the course of manufacture of final product. Mere fact that the item is a packing material whose value is included in the accessible value of final product will not entitle the manufacturer to take credit. Oils and lubricants mentioned in the definition are required for smooth running of machines and, hence, they are included as they are used in relation to manufacture of final product. The intention of the Legislature is that inputs falling in the inclusive part must have nexus with the manufacture of the final product.

In Indo Rama Synthetics (India) Ltd. v. CCE 2007 (219) ELT 122 (Bom.), the High Court held that the credit of duty paid on the goods or fuel used in the generation of electricity is available, provided the electricity is used for the manufacture of final product. The use of electricity must have nexus with goods manufactured in the factory.

5.1 Primary packing material - In Wrigley India (P.) Ltd. v. CCE 2010 (255) ELT 201 (Punj. & Har.), it was held that it is not a matter of dispute that chewing gum/bubble gums manufactured by the assessees are directly or primarily packed with the printed aluminium foils without tattoos. It means, putting a ‘boomer-tattoo’ in the package material of bubble gum is an additional step in aid used for promotional material and it is not termed as a packing material, as such, especially when it is depicted on the packing that ‘free tattoo inside’. The primary function of putting the ‘tattoo’ in the wrapped bubble gum is to promote the trade and to attract the children rather than to be used for the purpose of packing ‘tattoo’.

Again it is not a matter of dispute that these printed ‘tattoos’ are not used for initial packing in the real sense, rather they are wrapped. Therefore, it cannot possibly be said that the ‘Boomer-tattoo’ is used as initial packing material, meaning thereby the wrapper of the ‘tattoo’ on the bubble gum is not at all required in the form of primary packing. There is no direct and indirect use of the ‘tattoo’ in or in relation to the manufacture of the product, rather it is separately known tattoo in the market, has a separate identity, specific purpose of promotion of the product and for the purpose of advertisement. Hence, it is not a packing material and cannot be considered as inputs within the meaning and definition considered as ‘inputs’ as contemplated under the relevant Rules.

In CCE v. International Tractors Ltd. - 2010 (255) ELT 203 (Punj. & Har.), the respondent was the manufacturer of traction and tractor components. The components manufactured by the respondent were duly packed in boxes and thereafter were sold. The Tribunal had allowed the credit on the goods of full packing of boxes. It had been observed by the Tribunal that duty was paid on the boxes.

The revenue contended that the respondent never received inputs in the packing of boxes and in fact the goods were delivered to the respondent in pallets and, hence, the respondent was not entitled to any credit.

It was held that CESTAT could allow availment of CENVAT credit in respect of duty paid on the packing material.

Place of use

6. The third part of the definition of ‘input’ is the ‘place of use’. Rule 2(k)( i) mandatorily requires that the goods meant for input should be used in the process of manufacture within the premises of the factory. It is a condition precedent to avail CENVAT credit on ‘inputs’ that the product should be manufactured within the premises of the factory. But, at the same time, it is not mandatory for the output service provider to utilize the inputs within the premises of the output service provider. Even if the input is used outside the premises of the service provider, CENVAT credit is allowed for such inputs.

On appeal, the Tribunal held as under :

u The definitions of ‘input’ in rule 2(k) and ‘input service’ in rule 2(l) are not at all comparable or pari materia and coverage of the ‘input service’ is definitely wider.

u The definition of ‘input’ is exhaustive and is restrictive in scope. It treats all goods used in or in relation to manufacture of final products or for any other purpose within the factory of production. But certain goods which would be eligible as per definition have been excluded and certain goods which could be interpreted as not includible have been specifically included, i.e., packing material, lubricating oil, accessories, etc. Therefore, all goods other than specified as includible have to be shown to be used in or in relation to manufacture of final product or for any other purpose within the factory of production. In fact, the Apex Court in Maruti Suzuki Ltd. v. CCE 2009 (240) ELT 641 has held that input and capital goods used in captive means are covered by the definition, expanding the scope of definition.

u The Legislature has not used the word in the inclusive part ‘that it is to be used in or in relation of the final product’.

u From the above, it is clear that the intention of the Legislature was that those activities should be in relation to the business.

u It cannot be viewed that a garden is not relating to manufacture. A good garden creates a better atmosphere and environment which increases the working efficiency and the consumer would feel good.

u In view of the above discussion, the assessee was entitled to Cenvat credit availed on the garden maintenance services which were used in or in relation to the manufacture of final products or used in relation to the business activity and, in the instant case, the services used by the assessee were in relation to the business activity and it was entitled to Cenvat credit. DSCL Sugar [2014] 41 taxmann.com 64/43 GST 151 (Allahabad) and also in CCE v. KCP Sugar & Industries Corporation Ltd. - 2015 (321) ELT A223 (A.P.) on ground that even though marketable, Bagasse was non-manufactured product and therefore, not excisable and even payment under rule 6 would not be required. The Department went in appeal before Supreme Court in UOI v. DSCL Sugar Ltd. 2015 (322) E.L.T. 769, wherein it was held as follows :

Facts : Assessee was manufacturing sugarcane and molasses. In the process of manufacture of sugar, sugarcane is crushed, its juice is extracted and Bagasse emerges as residue/waste of sugarcane. Since Bagasse was liable to Nil rate of duty, department argued that it was 'exempted goods' and demanded Cenvat reversal under rule 6(3) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004.

Held :

No manufacture/deemed manufacture : Bagasse is only an agriculture waste and residue and not result of any process; hence, it is not covered in definition of 'manufacture' under section 2(f) of Central Excise Act, 1944. Further, there is no Chapter note or Section note in Central Excise Tariff declaring process in respect of bagasse as amounting to manufacture.

Not excisable, even if deemed to be marketable : Hence, notwithstanding amendment in 2008 in section 2(d) ibid, creating a fiction of deemed marketability, bagasse is not excisable as it is not passing test of 'manufacture'.

Cenvat Rule 6 inapplicable [for period prior to 1-3-2015] : Since bagasse is not excisable, hence, even if NIL-rated, cenvat rule 6 is inapplicable thereto. Therefore, denial of credit on electricity on ground that bagasse is excisable exempted goods, was incorrect.

3.3 Zinc Dross also held to be non-manufactured by Bombay High Court : The Bombay High Court in Hindalco Industries Ltd. v. UOI [2015] 49 GST 429 opined that Aluminium dross and skimmings, etc. not 'manufactured' goods and not liable to duty, even if marketable/bought and sold. The facts and judgment are :

Facts : In course of manufacture of aluminium sheets/coils, aluminium dross/skimmings emerged as byproducts. Department demanded duty thereon arguing that in view of Explanation to section 2(d), said goods were marketable. Assessee argued that 'aluminium dross/skimmings' were not 'manufactured goods' and were not, therefore, liable to duty.

Held : Conditions contemplated under section 2(d) (excisable goods, movability and marketability) and section 2(f) (manufacture) have to be satisfied conjunctively in order to entail imposition of excise duty. Merely because goods satisfy test of being marketed and saleable and merely because goods are listed in tariff, it does not mean that they are 'manufactured goods'. In various judgments, Supreme Court held that 'aluminium dross/skimmings' are not manufactured goods and said view was followed in context of 'zinc dross and flux skimming'. Hence, impugned goods were not manufactured goods and could not, therefore, be charged to excise duty.

3. Section 115JB of the Act provides for levy of MAT on the 'Book Profits' of a company. In this regard, book profits are to be computed with reference to the profit and loss account prepared in accordance with the provisions of Part-II and Part-III of Schedule VI to the Companies Act and would be subject to adjustments provided for in the Explanation to section 115JB of the Act.

The Explanation 1 to section 115JB of the Act sets out the mechanism for computing the book profits. The Explanation stipulates certain additions and deletions to the net profit to arrive at the book profit. In the current context, clause (c) is relevant, which provides that book profit shall be increased by 'any provision made for meeting liabilities other than ascertained liabilities'.

The issue as to what is a provision made for ascertained liability has been decided in a number of cases. There are several judicial precedents, where the Courts have taken a view (in the context of tax deductibility under section 37 of the Act) that a liability created on the basis of reliable estimates and past experience is an ascertained liability. Reliance in this regard can be placed on the following rulings:

3.1 Rotork Controls India (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2009] 180 Taxman 422 (SC) - In this case in the context of provision for warranty, the Supreme Court held that in this case a contingent liability, for which reliable estimate can be made on the basis of scientific working, is allowable as deduction under section 37 of the Act.

3.2 CIT v. Vinitec Corpn. (P.) Ltd. [2005] 146 Taxman 313 (Delhi) - In this case again in the context of provision for warranty, the Delhi High Court held that provision for warranty created on an acceptable basis was to be allowed as deduction.

3.3 Metal Box Co. of India Ltd. v. Their Workmen [1969] 73 ITR 53 (SC) - In this case, the Supreme Court in the context of provision for gratuity observed that in case a liability is properly ascertained then the same is to be allowed. As mentioned above, this decision of the Supreme Court has been referred to in Jacob Engg. (India) (P.) Ltd.'s case (supra).

3.4 Bharat Earth Movers v. CIT [2000] 245 ITR 428 / 112 Taxman 61 (SC) - In this case, the Supreme Court, in the context of provision for leave encashment created on the basis of a scheme, held that it was eligible for deduction. The Court held that this liability was not a contingent liability as it was capable of being ascertained with a reasonable certainty.

3.5 CIT v. Echjay Forgings (P.) Ltd. [2001] 116 Taxman 322 (Bom.) - In this case, the Mumbai High Court held that the provision for gratuity created on the basis of actuarial valuation could not be regarded as unascertained liability, accordingly, had to be allowed as deduction in computing the book profit.

Further, in the context of MAT computation as well, various judicial precedents have held that provisions which are capable of estimation with a reasonable certainty are allowable, as they are ascertainable and, thus, no adjustment is required for the same while ascertaining 'Book Profit' for MAT computation purposes.

For the purpose of allowability of provision for foreseeable losses under the MAT provisions reference may also be made to the cases of Mazagon Docks Ltd. (supra) and Jacobs Engg. (India) (P.) Ltd. (supra).

CCE 2010 (249) ELT 394 (Trib. - Bang.), it is classified in the Explanation 2 to rule 2 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 that the inputs include the goods used in the manufacture of capital goods, which are further used in the factory of manufacturer. In this case, there was no dispute that pollution control equipments and storage tanks were categorized as capital goods in terms of definition in rule 2 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 and that the items in dispute, namely, cement and steel products were used in the construction of the said capital goods. In such circumstances, the said items, namely, cement and steel products were to be treated as inputs in the manufacture of the capital goods, which were, in turn, used within the factory of manufacturer in terms of Explanation to rule 2 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004. Thus, the assessees were entitled to the benefit of CENVAT credit on the said items as inputs and not as capital goods. Hence, the availment of credit on the quantum of cement and steel products used in the manufacture of storage tanks and pollution control equipments was proper and legal and the question of recovery of the credit did not arise.

The Commissioner (Appeals) rejected the appeal filed by the appellants. The Tribunal held on an analysis of the definition of ‘input’ that it includes goods, which are further used in the factory of the manufacturer. It was argued by the department that the appellants were not a manufacturer. It was undisputed that the appellant were not a manufacturer, but ‘a person’ who was providing output services under the category of ‘Storages and warehouse’ services. It is clear from the definition of the ‘capital goods’ that the credit on the duty paid on tubes and fittings, as well as storage tanks is eligible for availment of CENVAT credit. It was undisputed in this case that the inputs, viz., cement, TNT bars and steel tubes were used for the purpose of construction of storage tanks and for the pipelines for transfer of liquid cargo, and, therefore, the benefit of credit could not be denied to the appellants, as the appellants were using these inputs for manufacture of the capital goods, i.e., storage tanks and pipeline for delivery of the cargo from such storage tank to truck delivery station. The CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 clearly allowed the appellants to take CENVAT credit.

6. Rate of DDT should not exceed rate specified in Article 10 in India-Germany DTAA: ITAT

Giesecke & Devrient [India] Pvt Ltd. v. ACIT [2020] 120 taxmann.com 338 (Delhi - Trib.)

The issue before the Delhi Tribunal was:

"Whether Assessing Officer (AO) erred in not extending the benefit of applicable Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement between India and Germany (DTAA) qua the rate of tax on payment of dividend to the shareholder?"

The Delhi Tribunal held that there is no dispute that the liability is on the payer company to pay DDT, but, at the same time, we must not lose sight of the fact that dividend distribution tax (DDT) is part of tax as defined in Section 2(43) of the Act. It must be remembered that this additional Income-tax [DDT] levied u/s 115-0 is a tax on income and definition of "Income" includes dividend.

As per the Income-tax Rules, relevant details regarding payment of DDT have to be provided in the Income-tax return form and have to be disclosed in the Tax Audit Return [Form 3CD]. Further, the Income-tax assessment order read with the Income-tax computation form quantifies DDT liability.

It would not be out of place to mention that the Act does not provide for a separate adjudication/passing of separate order with regard to adjudication of liability of DDT.

Further, the generally accepted principles relating to interpretation of treaties in the light of object of eliminating double taxation does not bar the application of tax treaties to DDT. Thus, the DDT levied by the appellant should not exceed the rate specified in Article 10 in India Germany DTAA.

Assessee filed return of income for the Assessment Year 2006-07 by declaring the taxable income as 'NIL'. The case was selected for scrutiny and it was held that software supplied was chargeable to income tax from royalty and technical services.

The assessee contended that from the perusal of Article 4 of the Notification, it was evident that paragraph 12 of Article 12 of India-Singapore DTAA has been deleted and has been substituted by the paragraph which provides for levy of tax on the royalties or fees for technical services at the rate not exceeding 10%. Thus, the Tribunal had rightly held that new provision which was in existence shall apply for the entire fiscal year as defined in DTAA.

The Karnataka High Court held that paragraph 2 of Article 12, which provided for levy of tax on royalties or fees for technical services at the rate not exceeding 12% had been deleted and in its place, the provision which provides for levy of tax on the royalties or fees for technical services at the rate not exceeding 10% had been substituted.

Thus, the substitution had the effect of deleting the old rule and making the new rule operative. Therefore, the Tribunal had rightly determined the rate of tax as substituted in clause 2 of article 12 of DTAA for the entire fiscal year as defined in DTAA and was liable to be taxed at 10%.

Compliance with customs regulations is critical when importing second-hand machinery. The Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC) has issued Circular No. 25/2015-Cus., dated 15-10-2015, providing comprehensive guidelines for the import of used machinery:

The import must be accompanied by an inspection/appraisement report by an overseas chartered engineer or equivalent.

If an overseas report is not available, the importer may obtain a report from any of the DGFT-notified agencies in India, or from a locally empanelled chartered engineer at customs stations.

The value of the machinery will be examined in light of the chartered engineer's report, and any doubts regarding the declared value must be justified by the importer.

In cases where significant differences in value arise, customs officers may apply Rule 12 of the Customs Valuation Rules (CVR), 2007 to determine the correct value.

These stringent customs requirements help ensure that the valuation and condition of second-hand machinery are thoroughly assessed before entry into India.

Be prepared for higher compliance costs.

Evaluate if loss of RODTEP/Drawback is offset by duty deferment benefits.

4.8 The assessee, an aircraft operator, availed credit of service tax paid/reimbursed to Airport Authority of India for availing of the services of authority such as landing, parking, and x-ray in connection with the operation of the aircraft owned by it. The lower authorities denied said credit on the ground that the services were not connected, directly or indirectly, in or in relation to the manufacture of final products and clearance of final products. In the instant appeal, the assessee contended that the aircrafts were used by its officials as conveyance between its plants and were essential for the business purpose and those services were related to business only. On detailed examination of the definition of ‘input service’, it was found that the definition is in two parts.

Part-I includes the services used by the manufacturer whether directly or indirectly in or in relation to the manufacturing of final products and clearance of final products from the place of removal.

And Part-II includes services used in relation to setting up, modernization, renovation or repairs of a factory premises of provider of output services or an office relating to such factory or premises, advertisement or sales promotion, market research, storage up to the place of removal, procurement of inputs, activities relating to business.

The Tribunal held that the contention of the revenue that the definition of input service is to be read as a whole could not be accepted. Further, in the assessee’s own case in Force Motor Ltd. v. CCE [F.O. A/547/08, dated 11-7-2008], the Tribunal had held that the activities specified after the phrase ‘such as’ are only illustrations and examples and not exhaustive. Therefore, an activity other than those illustrated but related to business will also get covered under the definition of ‘input service’. The assessee was a manufacturing unit and according to the above definition, the use of the phrase ‘such as’ would mean inclusion of an activity which is of a kind as of the illustrations. The main issue to be decided in the case was as to whether the services provided by the authority could form a part of the business activities. It was clear that the aircraft which was stationed at airport was used by the assessee for the business activities and that stand was taken by the assessee before the lower authorities, which was not declined by them. Therefore, it was held that the services rendered by the authority and service tax charged by them would get covered under the definition of ‘input services’ as per the rule 2( l).

What if you could delay paying import duties—and sometimes avoid them completely?

That's the advantage offered by the MOOWR Scheme.

Re-introduced by the Government of India in 2019, the Manufacture and Other Operations in Warehouse Regulations (MOOWR) revamped the 1966 version to align with WTO norms.

Unlike the schemes Advance Authorization (AA), Export Promotion of Capital Goods (EPCG), Export Oriented Unit (EOU), or Special Economic Zone (SEZ), MOOWR does not involve export obligation.

It is suitable for any manufacturer or processor—large or small, domestic or global. There's no restriction on location or investment size.

WHAT MOOWR OFFERS

MOOWR lets manufacturers:

Import capital goods and raw materials without paying customs duty ('duty') upfront

Defer duty on raw materials until finished goods are sold in domestic market.

Save interest: No interest is charged on the deferred customs duty for raw materials component when finished goods are sold in domestic market.

Avoid duty

On raw materials used in finished goods exported

On capital goods re-exported after its lifetime

Defer and avoid duty on waste generated during the manufacture process when the finished goods are sold in domestic market and overseas market respectively.

MOOWR – Case Study

Let's understand MOOWR with a simple illustration before understanding the other nuances.

ABC Technologies obtained MOOWR license in the year 2023. They import sensors for manufacture of finished goods. With MOOWR, they deferred/avoided customs duty.

Machinery

ABC imported machinery worth Rs. 1 crore. Normally, customs duty payable would be Rs. 10 lakhs.

With MOOWR, they paid nothing upfront. They saved Rs. 60k /year in interest—6% of Rs. 10 lakhs.

Ten years later (i.e. after its lifetime), if they export or scrap the machinery, no duty is payable. If sold in India, duty is payable but no interest payable.

Raw material

ABC imported raw material worth Rs. 50 lakhs. No duty was paid at the time of import, though duty payable was Rs. 10 lakhs.

Assuming a timeline of 3 months for conversation of raw material into finished goods and its ultimate sale, interest saving would be at least Rs. 15K —6% * 3* Rs. 10 lakhs/12.

Packing material

ABC imported packaging materials worth Rs. 10 lakhs.

70% of it was used for exported products —no customs duty was paid at the time of import, and such duty shall be waived off upon export.

Customs Duty is payable only on 30% of the packing material used for domestic sales.

More importantly, no interest payable on the Customs Duty payable on the raw materials used manufacture of goods for domestic sales.

Assume a working capital cycle of 3 months, ABC can save interest on packing material worth Rs. 3 lakhs for a period of 3 months.

MOOWR –KEY COMPLIANCE REQUIREMENTS

1.

Import without customs duty- File a bill of entry for warehousing. No duty or IGST is payable upfront.

2.

Manufacture-Use imported and local inputs for manufacture. Pay GST on domestic purchases. Declare input-output norms.

3.

Job Work-Goods can be sent for job work after reaching the MOOWR unit, they must return within 1 year. Tools and molds also can be sent for job work.

4.

Export-Raise GST invoice, e-way bill, and seal goods. Submit export proof within 1 month to the bond officer at jurisdictional customs office.

5.

Sell in India-File bills of entry for home consumption for the raw material component of finished goods.

Example: If inputs consumed in manufacture of finished goods were imported through 5 Bills of Entry (BOE), separate bills of entry for home consumption for such 5 BOE must be filed at the time of sale. This is a huge compliance burden, especially when goods are sourced across multiple consignments.

6.

Records and Compliances

Maintain records for receipt, processing and removal of goods procured

Maintain separate inventory for domestic and imported goods.

Use FIFO method for tracking the goods procured.

Appoint a warehouse keeper who is responsible for day-to-day functioning of the warehouse.

File returns by the 10th of the following month.

Goods received from SEZs or FTWZs are treated as imports and must follow bonding formalities.

Getting clearance from Committee of Disputes involving inter-departmental litigation is a futile exercise decides the Supreme Court and recalls its earlier orders

In this article, the author has analyzed the Supreme Court’s decision wherein the Court has considered the role of the Committee on Disputes set up by the Government of India for approval of Court cases by this Committee in cases of Public Sector Undertakings and has observed that the objective sought to be achieved by this procedure has not been achieved and the same leads to delays. Hence, the Court has recalled its directions in various orders on this matter. It could be hoped that the Government of India would soon order scrapping of this procedure.

T.N. PANDEY*

Introduction

1. The Supreme Court of India has decided in the case of Electronics Corpn. of India v. UOI [2011] 30 STT 472 that in inter-departmental litigation getting clearance from Committee on Disputes (COD) has not served the objective for which it was introduced and has outlived its utility in the changed scenario and, hence, it has recalled its order in earlier cases requiring COD approval.

Historical background

2. It was decided by the Government of India (GOI) that public sector undertakings of the Central Government and Union of India should not fight their litigation in the Courts. Hence, the Cabinet Secretary, GOI was ‘called upon to handle the matter personally’. Initially, the Committee was called a ‘High Powered Committee’ (HPC).

This was followed by another Committee called ‘Committee of Secretaries’ (COS) and finally christened as ‘Committee on Disputes’ (COD). These Committees were constituted to ensure that resources of the State are not frittered away in intense litigations between the entities of the State which could be best resolved by an empowered Committee - COD. The Committee(s) constituted was/were intended to ensure that no litigation comes to the Court without the parties had an opportunity of conciliation before an in-house Committee. The principle outlined behind the constitution of the Committee was sound, laudatory and unexceptionable. However, over the years, the objective sought to be achieved failed to be realized and led to delays in finalization of disputes. Hence, the entire mechanism in this regard has been reviewed by the Apex Court.

2.1 Facts of the cases before the Supreme Court

(a) Case No. 1 - Electronics Corporation of India Ltd. (‘assessee’ for short) is a Central Government Public Sector Undertaking (‘PSU’). It is registered as a Government company under the Companies Act, 1956. It is under the control of Department of Atomic Energy, Government of India. A dispute had been raised by the Central Government (Ministry of Finance) by issuing show-cause notices to the assessee alleging that the corporation was not entitled to avail/utilize Modvat/Cenvat credit in respect of inputs whose values stood written off. Accordingly, it was proposed in the show-cause notices that the credit taken on inputs was liable to be reversed. Thus, the short point which arose for determination in the present case was whether the Central Government was right in insisting on reversal of credit taken by the assessee on inputs whose values stood written off.

The adjudicating authority held that there was no substance in the contention of the assessee that the write off was made in terms of AS-2. The case of the assessee before the CCE (adjudicating authority) was that it was a financial requirement as prescribed in AS-2; that an inventory more than three years old had to be written off/derated in value; that such derating in value did not mean that the inputs were unfunctionable; that the inputs were still lying in the factory and they were useful for production and, therefore, they were entitled to Modvat/Cenvat credit. As stated above, this argument was rejected by the adjudicating authority and the demand against the assessee stood confirmed. Against the order of the adjudicating authority, the assessee decided to challenge the same by filling an appeal before the CESTAT. Accordingly, the assessee applied before the Committee on Disputes (COD). However, the COD vide its decision dated 2nd Nov., 2006 refused to grant clearance though in an identical case, the COD granted clearance to Bharat Heavy Electricals Ltd. (‘BHEL’). Accordingly, the assessee filed a writ petition in the Andhra Pradesh High Court. The High Court dismissed the petition. Hence, an appeal was filed before the Supreme Court.

CARGO HANDLING SERVICES - SOME ISSUES

In this article, the author has taken up for discussion different issues in respect of cargo handling services with reference to relevant case-laws.

Definition

1. The Cargo handling services have been subjected to service tax by the Finance Act, 2002, with effect from August 16, 2002. Cargo handling service is defined (as substituted by the Finance Act, 2008 with effect from May 16, 2008) under section 65(23) of the Finance Act, 1994 as loading, unloading, and packing or unpacking of cargo and includes—

u Cargo handling services provided for freight in special containers or for non-containerized freight, services provided by a container freight terminal or any other freight terminal, for all modes of transport and cargo handling service incidental to freight; and

u Service of packing together with transportation of cargo or goods, with or without one or more of other services like loading, unloading, and unpacking

but does not include handling of export cargo or passenger baggage or mere transportation of goods.

The taxable service in relation to cargo handling has been defined under section 65(105)(zr ) as a service provided or to be provided to any person, by a cargo handling agency in relation to cargo handling services.

Exclusion

2. The CBEC Instruction lr. No. F. No. B11/1/2002-TRU, dated August 1, 2002 also indicated that the following services are excluded from the tax net—

u Services provided in relation to export cargo;

u Passenger baggage;

u Mere transportation of goods;

u Services provided in relation to storage of agriculture produce or for goods meant to be stored in cold storage;

u All the services in relation to handling of goods would be appropriately covered under port service and no separate levy will be attracted under cargo handling service;

u Marketing or canvassing for cargo for airlines;

u Ridhi Sidhi Transport v. CCE, Belgaum [2009] 18 STT 484 (Bang. - CESTAT) : The appellants had to provide cargo handling services in terms of the agreement entered into by them with Grasim Industries. The receipt for the services is given in the letter of Grasim to the appellants. In terms of the said agreement, the amount to be paid was split up into three categories, viz., rake handling (consisting of loading and unloading expenses) at Rs. 20 per M.T., local transportation charges (from yard to godown) at Rs. 53 per MT and service charges of Rs. 4 per MT. It was the contention of the appellants that the rake handling charges of Rs. 20 per MT were not liable for service tax. The Tribunal held that the contention did not appear to be correct because in terms of the Finance Act, Cargo handling means loading, unloading, packing or unpacking cargo, etc., for all modes of transport. When loading and unloading are integral parts of cargo handling services and when the gross receipt includes the said charges, there is no question of claiming any abatement or arguing that the same is not taxable under the category of ‘Cargo handling service’. The Tribunal held that the appellants did not have a case on merit.

u In re, Bharat Haribhau Salunke [Orders-in-Appeal Nos. PII/PAP/83-88 (Pn.) of 2008, dated 18-6-2008] : The appellant was transporting sugar from sugar house to godown within the factory. It was held that mere transportation of goods is excluded from cargo handling service. Transportation inside the factory is not considered as cargo handling service.

Activity of stitching of sugar bags is not related to loading, unloading, packing or unpacking of goods. Sugar bags cannot be considered as cargo. Impugned activity is not covered under ‘Cargo handling service’. Show-cause notice was issued and confirmed mechanically.

(supra) has expressed that marketability is a decisive test for durability. It only means ‘saleable’ or ‘suitable for sale’. It need not be, in fact, marketed. The article should be capable of being sold or being sold to consumers in the market, as it is without anything more. In the absence of a finding, that the goods are ‘marketable’, i.e., saleable or suitable for sale, it could not be said to be a good, which may be subject to excisability.

The Apex Court in the case of Union of India v. Indian Aluminium Co. Ltd. 1995 (58) ECR 612 has reiterated that marketability is a question of fact to be decided on the facts of each case. It was held that it may be possible to recover something from a particular thing, they can, therefore, be sold but that does not make them a marketable commodity. In other words, everything, which is sold, is not necessarily a marketable commodity as known to the commercial world and, it may be worthwhile to trade in. Since marketability test is essentially a question of fact - Hindustan Zinc Ltd. v. CCE 2005 (181) ELT 170 (SC), there must be some serious attempts to go to market and collect proper evidences, but it cannot be established on basis of mere stability. Sufficient proof that product is commercially known is required - Gujarat Nermada Valley Fert. Co. Ltd. v. CCE 2005 (184) ELT 128 (SC) which could not be viewed through a hawker’s eye - Mahindra & Mahindra Ltd. v. CCE 2005 (190) ELT 301 (Trib. - LB) unless the product is capable of being marketed and is known to those who are in the market, as having an identity as a distinct identifiable commodity, that the article is subject to excise duty. Fact that articles fall within Schedule, not make them marketable. Actual sale is not necessary but article must be capable of being sold in market or known in market as good - Gujarat Nermada Valley Fert. Co. Ltd.’s case (supra ). Actual purchase and sale, or fact of their being marketed or their general availability in market is not required to be proved- Mahindra & Mahindra Ltd.’s case (supra).

Article is not eligible to be taxed only because it is having saleable value. CCE v. Indian Aluminium Co. Ltd. 2006 (203) ELT 3 (SC). Mention of an item in an exemption notification is not determinative of its excisability. New Shorrock Mills v. CCE 2006 (202) ELT 192 (Trib. - LB); Indore Wire Co. Ltd. v. Union of India 2006 (203) ELT 179 (SC). Mere listing of an item in the Schedule to the Act is not sufficient to make it excisable - Ahmedabad Electricity Co. Ltd.’s case (supra). Mere mention of item in ISI is also not sufficient - Tata Iron & Steel Co. Ltd. v. Union of India 2004 (164) ELT 372 (SC).

Once marketability of an article is established, the fact that it is not actually sold but is entirely consumed captively or that it is sold only to one or two buyers has no relevance. However, mere manufacturing activity by itself, does not prove marketability. Inter-unit transfer of an item does not prove its marketability. Product produced must be a distinct commodity known in common parlance to commercial community for the purpose of buying and selling - Cipla Ltd. v. CCE 2008 (225) ELT 403 (SC).

Accordingly, articles like storage units, running counters, wall and kitchen units normally not capable to be removed without cannibalizing, are not furniture and not excisable goods - Craft Interiors (P.) Ltd. v. CCE 2006 (203) ELT 529 (SC). The goods, which are removed and used for mandatory quality control test and are destroyed during such test, cannot be considered as amounting to removal and as such do not fall under category of ‘excisable goods’ - CCE v. Tarco Cable Co. Ltd. 2001 (127) ELT A49 (SC). Intellectual property or information technology being an intangible asset if once put on a paper, cassette, diskettes or any other thing to supply the same, fall under the category of ‘excisable goods’ just like drawings, designs, manuals and technical materials - Associated Cement Companies Ltd. v. CCE 2001 (128) ELT 21 (SC).

Section 65(105)(j) - Clearing and forwarding agents’ services v. Consignment agent

4.3 The assessee had entered into contracts with two steel companies, the TISCO and TRL. As per the said contract the assessee was to take delivery of the steel materials on behalf of the TISCO and TRL from the railway siding. Thereafter, it was to transport said materials to its own premises/godown and sort and stock said materials after weighment in accordance with instructions of the company’s representative. The assessee was to further arrange for and to take all necessary steps for safe custody and protection of steel materials and was to nominate a hub manager in its premises. Further, it had to deliver materials to company’s customers on production of delivery orders and if the hub manager required, the materials would be loaded on the transport vehicles, etc., of the customer or as nominated by the company. The assessee was to bear all the expenses since time of receipt of materials at its premises till these were dispatched and in case of failing to account for the stock, it was liable for consequences. The assessee received consideration of certain sum which comprised of consignment agent service receipts, and receipts towards reimbursement of expenditure, bending and bundling charges and stock verification charges from the said companies in respect of services rendered. The revenue issued a show-cause notice (SCN) on 13-9-2004 and demanded service tax from the assessee for the period 1-9-1999 to 31-3-2004 by stating that services provided by the assessee to its clients fell under the category of ‘Clearing and forwarding agent’. On non-compliance of same the revenue confirmed service tax liability upon the assessee along with penalty and interest. In the instant appeal, the assessee contended that it had acted as a consignment agent which activity was not covered under ‘Clearing and forwarding agent’s service’ and, therefore, it was not liable to pay service tax.

The Tribunal held that according to the Finance Act, 1994, imposing service tax on certain taxable services, any service provided or to be provided by a ‘Clearing and forwarding agent’ to a ‘client’ in relation to ‘Clearing and forwarding operations’ ‘in any manner’ shall be taxable service under section 65(105)(j). Incidence of levy is on the service of ‘Clearing and forwarding operations’, provided measure of tax is ‘value’ of such service. Thus, service provided by a ‘Clearing and forwarding agent’ to his client directly or indirectly in any manner gives rise to a taxable event, provided the service so rendered is ‘Clearing and forwarding operation’. Levy is attracted when there is provision of service: (a) of clearing and forwarding operations; (b) by a ‘Clearing and forwarding agent’; (c) to a client; (d) directly or indirectly; and (e) in any manner.

4.2-5 Clearance of waste by service provider

Following provisions will apply to a service provider, who is not a 'manufacturer' -

Inputs becoming waste while providing output service - If some inputs become waste while providing output services, they are 'used in provision of output services'. In such case, no 'amount' or 'duty' is payable when he sells them as scrap, as it cannot be said that he has 'manufactured' them.

Input becoming waste/scrap before putting to use - If the inputs become waste even before taking them out of stores, an 'amount' equal to Cenvat taken will be payable. The reason is that in such case, it cannot be said that the inputs were used 'for providing output services'.

Sale of empty packing material - A service provider availing Cenvat on inputs is not required to pay any 'amount' on packing material/empty drums sold by him, even if he had availed Cenvat on such inputs.

Sale of goods on which no Cenvat was availed - A service provider is not required to pay any 'amount' if he sells/disposes of inputs or goods on which he has not availed Cenvat credit.

Inputs becoming waste while providing output service - If some inputs become waste while providing output services, they are 'used in provision of output services'. In such case, no 'amount' or 'duty' is payable when he sells them as scrap, as it cannot be said that he has 'manufactured' them.

Input becoming waste/scrap before putting to use - If the inputs become waste even before taking them out of stores, an 'amount' equal to Cenvat taken will be payable. The reason is that in such case, it cannot be said that the inputs were used 'for providing output services'.

The word "manufacture" or "produce articles" used in the provision to Section 80HH have not been defined in the Act. The word "manufacture" has been considered by the Supreme Court and the High Courts on numerous occasions, and the common thread which runs in all the decisions is that it is only when a new and distinct commodity commercially accepted as such comes into existence as a result of the processing, that a commodity can be said to have been manufactured.Having regard to the fact that the word "article" used in the section is an article which is manufactured or produced and the word "produce" having been used in juxtaposition with the word "manufacture" it connotes the bringing into existence of new goods. The result of production should be the coming into existence of a new article. The terms "production" and "produce" would also take in by-products, intermediate products and residual products. All of them should be products or articles which are capable of being regarded as new articles. By holding that a "new" article should emerge from manufacture or production, new words are not being added to Section 80HH. The term new has been employed in the decisions of the courts only to indicate the end result of the process of production or manufacture. It is only when that result can be said to have been achieved that the industrial undertaking which brings about such a result by its process of production or manufacture would qualify for the benefits conferred under the section. 9.4-4c Article or thing - The word "article" is not defined in the Act or the Rules. The word "articles" occurring in Section 80HH(2)(i) does not comprehend and take within its ambit a dam, a bridge and so on. If a dam is an article, so would be a bridge, a road, an underground canal and a multi-storeyed building. To say that all of them fall within the meaning of the word "articles" is to overstrain the language beyond its normal and ordinary meaning. The definition of 'scrap' as given in Explanation (b) is not limited to scrap from the manufacture or mechanical working of materials alone but extends to cover 'waste' also. Therefore, the scope of the term 'scrap' as defined in Explanation (b) cannot be interpreted so as to restrict its application to scrap from the manufacture or mechanical working of materials alone. The first part of the definition of 'scrap' in Explanation (b) refers not only to scrap from the 'manufacture' but also to 'mechanical working of materials'. Both the phrases, namely, manufacture and mechanical working of materials differ in their meaning and content. 'Mechanical working of materials' refers to physical operations on materials. It signifies physical operations to bring about physical change to which the material is subjected in order to change its shape, properties or structure. In order to fall in the definition of 'scrap', it is not necessary that the same should occur in the course of manufacture; it can also occur in the course of mechanical working of materials, i.e., in the course of physical operations on materials. Thus, both the operations/processes, namely, the manufacture and mechanical working of materials, can give rise to scrap. Any article or thing arising from the physical operations on materials which is not usable as such would therefore fall in the category of 'scrap'. As stated earlier, the second part of the definition, i.e., 'which is definitely not usable as such because of breakage, cutting up, wear and other reasons' also throws light on the scope of the term 'scrap' inasmuch as it seeks to define the characteristics of scrap. In order to constitute 'scrap', the article or thing must not be usable as such because of breakage, cutting up, wear and other reasons. The use of the words 'other reasons' in the second part of the definition of 'scrap' is significant. In order to constitute 'scrap', what is contemplated by Explanation (b) is the non-usability of materials as such, which could even be for a reason other than breakage, cutting up and wear. The phraseology employed in Explanation (b) shows that the term 'scrap' has been defined in wide terms so as to include both (i) waste, and (ii) scrap from the manufacture or mechanical working of materials. However, both of them have been used as one phrase, i.e., as 'waste and scrap from the manufacture or mechanical working of materials', for the second part of the definition and, therefore, both of them should definitely be not usable as such because of breakage, cutting up, wear or other reasons.

Old Aluminium Utensils/Vessels purchased for converting them into new aluminium utensils

There were three entries under consideration –

Entry 5 read "Aluminium household utensils whether made of aluminium and aluminium alloys".

Entry 6 read "Aluminium products (including aluminium extrusion) and products, aluminium alloys not elsewhere mentioned in this Schedule."

Entry 83 read "Metal scraps other than those specified in the second Schedule."

The question for consideration is as to under which entry the old aluminum vessels purchased for conversion thereof into new aluminum utensils fall. The Tribunal held that prior to amendment of entry 5, the word 'and" was there between "aluminum" and "household" and it appears to have been left inadvertently to be mentioned in the revised entry. The Tribunal held the word "and" should still be read there and finally held that "old aluminum vessel" fell in entry 5 and not in entry 83.

Held by the Supreme Court- A finding of fact has been arrived at by the Tribunal that the appellant used to purchase the old aluminium vessels and scrap which were used for conversion to new household utensils. Old aluminium vessels are pressed to convert the same into scrap. Appellant, thus, is a scrap dealer and not a dealer in aluminium vessels within the meaning of Entry 5.

The dictionary meaning of scrap is "a small piece or amount of something especially one that is left over after the greater part has been used or material, especially metal, discarded for reprocessing".

The Entries contained in the First Schedule appended to the Act are in three parts. Entry 5 deals with aluminium household utensils. Entry 6 deals with aluminium products and aluminium alloys and entry 83 deals with metal scraps. Indisputably, aluminium metal scraps would also come within the purview of Entry 83. As the appellant deals in metal scrap, its case will come within the purview of Entry 83. All aluminium products do not come within the purview of Entry 5. It deals with only domestic utensils. For other aluminium products a different rate of tax has been provided in Entry 6. If there exists an entry which covers the goods in question, by necessary implication the same would be considered to have been excluded from another entry.

We will assume that the Entry 5 is capable of two interpretations. It may be read in the manner in which the Tribunal did, but it can also be read as "household utensils made up of aluminium or aluminium alloy." Use of the word "Aluminium" at the beginning may be superfluous. In any event the dealer cannot be said to be dealing with aluminium household utensils or household utensils made up of aluminium and aluminium alloys. We, therefore, are of the opinion that it was entry 83 which is attracted to the facts of the present case. [Baby Varghese v. State of Kerala, VSTI 2008 …B-436; VSTI 2008 (Delhi, Punjab, Haryana)...B-607; 2008 NTN (Vol. 38) – 123; (2008) 32 PHT 185 (SC); (2008) 16 VST 448 (SC); (2010) 56 S.T.A. 73, decided on 1.8.2008 by the Supreme Court]

MANUFACTURE OR PRODUCE - CLAUSE (i) OF SUB-SECTION (2)

626. CIT v. N.C. Budharaja & Co. [1993] 204 ITR 412 (SC)

The words 'manufacture' and 'production' have received extensive judicial attention both under this Act as well as the Central Excise Act and the various sales tax laws. The word 'production' has a wider connotation than the word 'manufacture'. While every manufacture can be characterised as production, every production need not amount to manufacture.

The word 'production' or 'produce' when used in juxtaposition with the word 'manufacture' takes in bringing into existence new goods by a process which may or may not amount to manufacture. It also takes in all the by-products, intermediate products and residual products which emerge in the course of manufacture of goods.

The expressions 'manufacture' and 'produce' are normally associated with movables, articles and goods, big and small—but they are never employed to denote the construction activity of the nature involved in the construction of a dam or for that matter a bridge, a road or a building.

♦♦

CIT v. Sterling Foods (Goa) [1995] 79 Taxman 381/213 ITR 851 (Bom.)

Section 80HH was not intended to be applied to industrial undertakings engaged in 'processing of goods' not amounting to manufacture or production of articles.

On a careful reading of the expression 'manufacture or produce articles' used in section 80HH of the Act in the light of the expressions 'in the manufacture or processing of goods' appearing in section 33B of the Act and section 2(8)(c) of the Finance Act, 1975, it is clear that the Legislature has specifically used the expression 'processing' in juxtaposition to 'manufacture' wherever it intended to extend the benefit to an industrial undertaking which is engaged in the processing of goods or articles and avoided using that expression in cases where it intended to confine the benefit only to industrial undertakings engaged in the 'manufacture or production' of goods or articles. Evidently, the Legislature has used a narrower expression in section 80HH than the one used in section 33B of the Act and section 2(8)(c) of the Finance Act, 1975. This is a clear indication of the legislative intention behind using the expression 'manufacture or produce articles' in section 80HH in contradistinction to 'manufacture or processing of goods' used in section 33B of the very Act and in the Finance Act.

On a careful reading of section 80HH of the Act in the light of scheme thereof and other provisions of the Act, it is clear that the Legislature intended to extend the benefit of deduction under section 80HH only to the industrial undertakings which manufacture or produce articles.

This section was not intended to be applied to industrial undertakings which are engaged in 'processing of goods' not amounting to manufacture or production of articles. There may be processes undertaken by an industrial undertaking which may result in conversion of the article into a new commercial commodity or may change the nature and character of the article in such a manner that it may lose its original identity and get transformed into an entirely new commo-dity. In such cases, 'manufacture' can be said to have taken place. But in cases where no such transformation takes place, each and every process supplied to an article cannot tantamount to 'manufacture or production' of goods or articles.

Thus, the benefit of section 80HH is available to industrial undertakings which 'manufacture or produce articles'. Industrial undertakings engaged in 'processing of goods or articles' not amounting to 'manufacture or production' are not entitled to the benefit of this section.

♦♦

CIT v. Lucky Mineral (P.) Ltd. [1996] 87 Taxman 215 (Raj.)

The meaning of the word 'manufacture' in the context of the language of section 80HH is required to be construed in the popular sense in which it is commonly understood by the people.

'Manufacture' implies a change, but every change is not 'manufacture' although every change in the article is the result of the treatment, labour and manipulation. To bring about the change qualifying as manufacture, something more is necessary and that something is transformation, i.e., a new and different article, having a distinct name, character or use, must emerge.

ARTICLE - CLAUSE (i) OF SUB-SECTION (2)

628. CIT v. N.C. Budharaja & Co. [1993] 70 Taxman 312/204 ITR 412 (SC)

The word 'article' is not defined in the Act or the Rules. It must, therefore, be understood in its normal connotation, the sense in which it is understood in commercial world. The word 'articles' in section 80HH is preceded by words 'it has begun or begins to manufacture or produce'. The word 'articles' occurring in section 80HH(2)(i) does not comprehend and take within its ambit, a dam, a bridge and so on. If a dam is an article, so would be a bridge, a road, or underground canal and a multi-storeyed building. To say that all of them fall within the meaning of word 'articles' is to over-strain the language beyond its normal and ordinary meaning. It is equally difficult to say that the process of constructing a dam is a process of manufacture or a process of production. It is true that a dam is composed of several articles, viz., stones, concretes, cement, etc. But to say that the end product, the dam, is an article is to be unfaithful to the normal connotation of the word. A dam is constructed, it is not manufactured or produced.

The expressions 'manufacture' and 'produce' are normally associated with movables, articles and goods, big and small, but they are never employed to denote the construction activity of the nature involved in the construction of a dam or for that matter a bridge, a road or a building.

Therefore, the activity of construction of a dam could not be characterised as manufacture or producing of article or articles, as the case may be, within the meaning of section 80HH(2)(i).

2.14-12 Toolings, used for production of refractories, is tangible fixed asset and not consumables and hence should be ac-counted as per AS 10/ICDS-V and not as per AS 2/ICDS-II

Toolings, used for production of refractories, is fixed asset and not consumables and hence the treatment of toolings should be as per AS 10/ICDS-V and not as per AS 2/ICDS-II.

Case Study 2.14.12.1: A company is in the business of manufacturing refractories (a material which retains its strength at high temperatures). The manufacturing process requires that to give shape to refractories, it is required to be filled into 'tooling' (comprised of an outer jacket made by a special metal). These toolings are imported in India. Toolings have a limited useful life of 3 years. As per the present accounting policy, the company treats toolings as consumables having a life of 3 years and accordingly the cost of tooling is amortised over a period of 3 years. Hence, toolings are disclosed under 'inventories'. Whether the present treatment done by company is correct ?

Answer: No. Toolings cannot be treated as inventory (consumables) because consumables are generally consumed in the production process whereas toolings do not get consumed but facilitate production process. Toolings are used in the production of refractories (finished goods) and have a limited useful life. [EAC opinion Query 26 Volume 29 Opinion finalised on 15 Dec 2009] Accordingly, toolings are fixed assets which should be depreciated in accordance with the Act and the Rules.

2.14-13 Whether foodstuffs purchased by company for supply to staff at subsidised rates should be treated as inventory and valued as per ICDS-II?

A company is in the business of manufacturing of tea. The company, to follow existing rules, is required to distribute foodstuff to its employees at concessional rates. The company purchases foodstuff in bulk quantity. The distribution of foodstuff to employees is at subsidized rates (lesser that the bulk cost). Whether ICDs-II applies to stock of such foodstuff?

In accordance with AS 2/ICDS-II, foodstuff cannot be treated as 'inventory'. Rather it is a short term employee benefit as explained by Para 8(d) of AS 15. Valuation of foodstuff should be as follows:-

Foodstuff at the period end should be valued at cost. [Follow AS 2/ICDS-II principles while arriving at the cost]

For the damaged stock, valuation should be lesser of cost or net realizable value. [Follow AS 2/ICDS-II principles]

Since foodstuff is provided at subsidized rates only once the employee renders services, foodstuff for which employees have already rendered services but distribution is pending on the part of the company; such foodstuff should be valued at amount receivable from employee's i.e. subsidized rates. [Because certain portion, i.e. cost (-) subsidized rate, would have already been recognized under AS 15 when the services were rendered by employees].
