manufacture. The associated words are indicative of the mind of Legislature. Where a word is doubtful or ambiguous in nature, the meaning has to be ascertained by considering the company in which it is found and the meaning of the word associated with it. The words 'manufacture' and 'production' have received extensive judicial attention both under the Act as well as the Central Excise Act and the various sales tax laws. The word 'production' has wider connotation than the word 'manufacture'. Applying the principles spelt out by the Apex Court in CIT v. N.C. Budharaja & Co. [1993] 204 ITR 412/ 70 Taxman 312 and the ordinary meaning of the word 'produce' as disclosed by the dictionary and by its ordinary connotation, it could be held that when the word 'manufacture' appears in the company of the word 'production', which has wider connotation than the word 'manufacture', then in that event the word 'manufacture' would have to be interpreted in a wider sense and would have to be understood at par with meaning assigned to the word 'production' and if such approach contemplated by the Legislature is adopted, then in that event it is not difficult to reach the conclusion that the assessees were the industrial undertakings, engaged in manufacture and production of articles and things. Further, the Apex Court in the aforementioned case observed that the word 'production' or 'produce' takes into account all the by-products, intermediate products and residual products which emerge in the course of manufacture of goods. The Apex Court while considering the next word 'articles' occurring in the said clause has noticed that the word 'articles' is preceded by the words 'it has begun or begins to manufacture or produce' and reached to the conclusion that the expressions 'manufacture' and 'produce' are normally associated with movables, i.e., articles and goods, big and small.

Applying the said yardstick adopted by the Apex Court and considering the peculiar nature of the ship-breaking activity, it could be viewed that the ship-breaking activity gave rise to manufacture and production of altogether a new commercial article or thing which is commercially identifiable in the commercial world other than the ship and, therefore, the assessees should be held entitled to claim deductions under sections 80HHA and 80-I.

HEADNOTE: Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - In respect of certain income of hotels or industries in backward areas - Assessment year 1979-80 - Whether industrial undertakings engaged in processing of goods or articles not amounting to manufacture or production are entitled to benefit of section 80HH - Held, no - Whether processing of prawns amounts to manufacture or production of articles within meaning of section 80HH, so as to entitle an assessee, engaged in such processing and sale of prawns, to deduction under section 80HH - Held, no

FACT: The assessee derived income from sale of prawns. The nature of activity carried on by the assessee was purchase of raw prawns, subjecting the same to the process of cutting the heads and tails, cleaning, etc., and thereafter selling the same. In the assessment for the assessment year 1979-80, the assessee claimed deduction under section 80HH from the income from sale of prawns on the ground that the activity of processing of prawns before putting them for sale amounted to 'manufacture' and 'production' of articles within the meaning of section 80HH. The ITO rejected the claim, observing that the activity of processing prawns for the purpose of sale did not amount to manufacture or production of goods or articles within the meaning of section 80HH. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the deduction to the assessee and the Tribunal confirmed the order of Commissioner (Appeals).

On reference :

HELD: Section 80HH applies to those industrial undertakings only which 'manufacture or produce articles'. The manufacturing process mentioned in clause (iv) of sub-section (2) refers to the process undertaken to achieve the above object, i.e., to 'manufacture or produce articles'. Sub-section (4) also uses the same expression 'begins to manufacture or produce articles'. This section nowhere uses the expression 'processes goods or articles'.

On a careful reading of section 80HH in the light of scheme thereof and other provisions of the Act referred to above, it is clear that the Legislature intended to extend the benefit of deduction under section 80HH only to the industrial undertakings which manufacture or produce articles. Manufacture, as observed by the Supreme Court in Dy. CST v. Pio Food Packers [1980] 46 STC 63, is the end result of one or more processes through which the original commodity is made to pass. The nature and extent of processing may vary from one case to another, and indeed there may be several stages of processing and perhaps different kinds of processing at each stage and with each process suffered, the original commodity experiences a change. But it is only when the change, or a series of changes, take the commodity to the point where commercially it can no longer be regarded as the original commodity but instead is recognised as a new and distinct article that a manufacture can be said to take place. Where the commodity retains a continuing substantial identity through the processing stage, it cannot be said that there has been manufacture. Similarly, the word 'production' has a wider connotation than the word 'manufacture'. While every manufacture can be characterised as production, every production need not amount to manufacture. As observed by the Supreme Court in CIT v. B. C. Budharaja Co. [1993] 204 ITR 412, the word 'production' or 'produce' when used in juxtaposition with the word 'manufacture' takes in bringing into existence new goods by a process which may or may not amount to manufacture. It also takes in all the by-products, intermediate products and residual products, which emerge in the course of manufacture of goods. This section was not intended to beapplied to industrial undertakings which are engaged in 'processing of goods' not amounting to manufacture or production of articles. 'Processing' means subjecting a commodity to a process or treatment so as to develop it or make it fit for market. Processing is, thus, an operation on an article so that it undergoes a change. There may be processes undertaken by an industrial undertaking which may result in conversion of the article into a new commercial commodity or may change the nature and character of the article in such a manner that it may lose its original identity and get transformed into an entirely new commodity. In such cases 'manufacture' can be said to have taken place.

TTJ 1/27 ITR (Trib.) 611 (Rajkot) (SB)

The definition of 'scrap' as given in Explanation (b) is not limited to scrap from the manufacture or mechanical working of materials alone but extends to cover 'waste' also. Therefore, the scope of the term 'scrap' as defined in Explanation (b) cannot be interpreted so as to restrict its application to scrap from the manufacture or mechanical working of materials alone. The first part of the definition of 'scrap' in Explanation (b) refers not only to scrap from the 'manufacture' but also to 'mechanical working of materials'. Both the phrases, namely, manufacture and mechanical working of materials differ in their meaning and content. 'Mechanical working of materials' refers to physical operations on materials. It signifies physical operations to bring about physical change to which the material is subjected in order to change its shape, properties or structure. In order to fall in the definition of 'scrap', it is not necessary that the same should occur in the course of manufacture; it can also occur in the course of mechanical working of materials, i.e., in the course of physical operations on materials. Thus, both the operations/processes, namely, the manufacture and mechanical working of materials, can give rise to scrap. Any article or thing arising from the physical operations on materials which is not usable as such would therefore fall in the category of 'scrap'. As stated earlier, the second part of the definition, i.e., 'which is definitely not usable as such because of breakage, cutting up, wear and other reasons' also throws light on the scope of the term 'scrap' inasmuch as it seeks to define the characteristics of scrap. In order to constitute 'scrap', the article or thing must not be usable as such because of breakage, cutting up, wear and other reasons. The use of the words 'other reasons' in the second part of the definition of 'scrap' is significant. In order to constitute 'scrap', what is contemplated by Explanation (b) is the non-usability of materials as such, which could even be for a reason other than breakage, cutting up and wear. The phraseology employed in Explanation (b) shows that the term 'scrap' has been defined in wide terms so as to include both (i) waste, and (ii) scrap from the manufacture or mechanical working of materials. However, both of them have been used as one phrase, i.e., as 'waste and scrap from the manufacture or mechanical working of materials', for the second part of the definition and, therefore, both of them should definitely be not usable as such because of breakage, cutting up, wear or other reasons.

HEADNOTE: Sections 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction - Profits and gains from newly established industrial undertakings, etc. in backward areas - Three units belonging to assessee were crushing barytes into powder for hire and receiving crushing charges - Further, assessee had not prepared separate profit and loss accounts and balance sheets for each unit - Whether barytes are distinct not only in form and name but also in use from barytes powder and barytes powder is distinct and separate article produced from barytes and, therefore, barytes powder is an article produced from barytes - Held, yes - Whether sections 80HH and 80-I do not contemplate division of profits and gains in respect of a unit and Assessing Officer may compute such profits and gains under section 80HH on such reasonable basis as he may deem fit - Held, yes - Whether when industrial units satisfied other critiera laid down under sections 80HH and 80-I, assessee was entitled to deduction - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee established three industrial units in backward areas. The units were crushing barytes into powder for hire and receiving crushing charges. The Assessing Officer held that mere crushing of barytes was not a manufacturing activity nor the powder produced could be called a new article. He further found that the assessee had not prepared separate profit and loss accounts and balance sheets in respect of each unit. He, therefore, disallowed the assessee’s claim for deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I. The Commissioner (Appeals) affirmed the order of the Assessing Officer. However, the Tribunal found that the barytes powder so produced got its marketability for its use for the purposes totally different from that of barytes. It further held that irrespective of the fact that there was no division of account, still they were entitled for the benefit of sections 80HH and 80-I as having satisfied the conditions laid down thereunder.

On reference :

HELD: Sections 80HH and 80-I do not contemplate the division of profits and gains in respect of a unit, provided the industrial undertaking satisfies the criteria laid down under section 80HH. The proviso of section 80HH(c ) itself provides that if in the opinion of the Assessing Officer, the computation of the profits and gains of industrial undertaking presents exceptional difficulties, the officer may compute such profits and gains on such reasonable basis as he may deem fit. In other words, it empowers the Assessing Officer to ascertain the profits and gains of a particular unit and make assessment. Therefore, the assessee was entitled to the benefit of sections 80HH and 80-I, provided the criteria laid down were satisfied.

It is not disputed that the barytes were made into powder by using power and the powder is a distinct and separate article from barytes and the use of barytes powder is in the manufacturing of paints while the barytes are used in a different form for different purposes.

Further, the barytes powder is marketed as such. Therefore, barytes are distinct not only in form and name but also in use from barytes powder and barytes powder is distinct and separate article produced from barytes. Therefore, it cannot be said that barytes powder is not an article produced from barytes. As a result, the assessee was entitled to deductions under sections 80HH and 80-I.

Dutiability of waste and scrap

3.3 Waste and scrap is practically treated as 'final product' for excise purposes. As discussed above earlier, there was view that dross, skimmings, remnants, bagasse etc. arising during manufacture are not 'goods' even if they fetch some price. Now, this view may not be valid after 10-5-2008.

Thus, waste and scrap can be 'goods' but dutiable only if 'manufactured' and are mentioned in Tariff.

Following discussions and case law is relevant even after 10-5-2008.

Meaning of scrap - The dictionary meaning of 'scrap' is 'a small piece or amount of something especially one that is left over after the greater part had been used or material, especially metal, discarded after processing' - Baby Varghese v. State of Kerala (2008) 16 VST 448 (SC).

Waste and scrap is 'final product' under Cenvat - Board has clarified that waste and scrap is treated as 'final product' under rule 2(e) of Cenvat Credit Rules [that time rule 57AA(c)] and its clearance is as if it is a final product. - MFDR TRU No. 345/2/2000-TRU dated 29-8-2000 (However, this is so if waste is 'manufactured'. Further, waste is not 'final product' if not mentioned in Central Excise Tariff. In any case, this view has not been fully endorsed by Tribunal).

Scrap can be 'goods' - In Khandelwal Metal and Engg. Works v. UOI - 1985 (Supp) 1 SCR 750 = 1985 (20) ELT 222 (SC) = AIR 1985 SC 1211 = (1985) 3 SCC 620, Apex Court held that scrap would be liable to duty, if it is known in commercial parlance by that name and has an established market - followed in Dhrunal Chhotalal Patel v. UOI - 1993 (63) ELT 27 (Bom HC).

In Greysham v. CCE 2000(117) ELT 350 (CEGAT), it was held that waste and scrap of steel arising during manufacture is dutiable as it is marketable and specifically mentioned in tariff.

Iron scrap recovered from slag arising out of manufacture of iron in blast furnace is excisable commodity - Steel Authority of India v. CCE 2006 (197) ELT 113 (CESTAT).

Cotton waste arising in the course of manufacture of cotton yarn and acid sludge arising in the course of refining of crude oil into kerosene can be treated as 'intended manufacture' as they arise regularly and also sold regularly from time to time. - CST v. Bharat Petroleum 1995(77) ELT 790 = 85 STC 220 (SC).

[Earlier, a view was held waste and scrap is not 'manufactured' but arises during the course of manufacture. It is not obtained by any process of manufacture but is obtained in course of manufacture of end product. Waste or scrap is in nature of rubbish and has no distinguishing name character or use and hence it is not goods. However, in view of subsequent judgments of Supreme Court, these judgments are no more valid.]

In Windorz India v. CCE 2002(145) ELT 148 (CEGAT), it was held that cut pieces of Aluminium rods, bars etc. arising during manufacture of Aluminium windows is 'scrap' as defined in CETA and is dutiable.

Duty is payable on waste arising during manufacture of exempted product - CCE v. AG Flats (2012) 277 ELT 96 (CESTAT).

Old Aluminium Utensils/Vessels purchased for converting them into new aluminium utensils

There were three entries under consideration –

Entry 5 read "Aluminium household utensils whether made of aluminium and aluminium alloys".

Entry 6 read "Aluminium products (including aluminium extrusion) and products, aluminium alloys not elsewhere mentioned in this Schedule."

Entry 83 read "Metal scraps other than those specified in the second Schedule."

The question for consideration is as to under which entry the old aluminum vessels purchased for conversion thereof into new aluminum utensils fall. The Tribunal held that prior to amendment of entry 5, the word 'and" was there between "aluminum" and "household" and it appears to have been left inadvertently to be mentioned in the revised entry. The Tribunal held the word "and" should still be read there and finally held that "old aluminum vessel" fell in entry 5 and not in entry 83.

Held by the Supreme Court- A finding of fact has been arrived at by the Tribunal that the appellant used to purchase the old aluminium vessels and scrap which were used for conversion to new household utensils. Old aluminium vessels are pressed to convert the same into scrap. Appellant, thus, is a scrap dealer and not a dealer in aluminium vessels within the meaning of Entry 5.

The dictionary meaning of scrap is "a small piece or amount of something especially one that is left over after the greater part has been used or material, especially metal, discarded for reprocessing".

The Entries contained in the First Schedule appended to the Act are in three parts. Entry 5 deals with aluminium household utensils. Entry 6 deals with aluminium products and aluminium alloys and entry 83 deals with metal scraps. Indisputably, aluminium metal scraps would also come within the purview of Entry 83. As the appellant deals in metal scrap, its case will come within the purview of Entry 83. All aluminium products do not come within the purview of Entry 5. It deals with only domestic utensils. For other aluminium products a different rate of tax has been provided in Entry 6. If there exists an entry which covers the goods in question, by necessary implication the same would be considered to have been excluded from another entry.

We will assume that the Entry 5 is capable of two interpretations. It may be read in the manner in which the Tribunal did, but it can also be read as "household utensils made up of aluminium or aluminium alloy." Use of the word "Aluminium" at the beginning may be superfluous. In any event the dealer cannot be said to be dealing with aluminium household utensils or household utensils made up of aluminium and aluminium alloys. We, therefore, are of the opinion that it was entry 83 which is attracted to the facts of the present case. [Baby Varghese v. State of Kerala, VSTI 2008 …B-436; VSTI 2008 (Delhi, Punjab, Haryana)...B-607; 2008 NTN (Vol. 38) – 123; (2008) 32 PHT 185 (SC); (2008) 16 VST 448 (SC); (2010) 56 S.T.A. 73, decided on 1.8.2008 by the Supreme Court]

MANUFACTURE OR PRODUCE - CLAUSE (i) OF SUB-SECTION (2)

626. CIT v. N.C. Budharaja & Co. [1993] 204 ITR 412 (SC)

The words 'manufacture' and 'production' have received extensive judicial attention both under this Act as well as the Central Excise Act and the various sales tax laws. The word 'production' has a wider connotation than the word 'manufacture'. While every manufacture can be characterised as production, every production need not amount to manufacture.

The word 'production' or 'produce' when used in juxtaposition with the word 'manufacture' takes in bringing into existence new goods by a process which may or may not amount to manufacture. It also takes in all the by-products, intermediate products and residual products which emerge in the course of manufacture of goods.

The expressions 'manufacture' and 'produce' are normally associated with movables, articles and goods, big and small—but they are never employed to denote the construction activity of the nature involved in the construction of a dam or for that matter a bridge, a road or a building.

♦♦

CIT v. Sterling Foods (Goa) [1995] 79 Taxman 381/213 ITR 851 (Bom.)

Section 80HH was not intended to be applied to industrial undertakings engaged in 'processing of goods' not amounting to manufacture or production of articles.

On a careful reading of the expression 'manufacture or produce articles' used in section 80HH of the Act in the light of the expressions 'in the manufacture or processing of goods' appearing in section 33B of the Act and section 2(8)(c) of the Finance Act, 1975, it is clear that the Legislature has specifically used the expression 'processing' in juxtaposition to 'manufacture' wherever it intended to extend the benefit to an industrial undertaking which is engaged in the processing of goods or articles and avoided using that expression in cases where it intended to confine the benefit only to industrial undertakings engaged in the 'manufacture or production' of goods or articles. Evidently, the Legislature has used a narrower expression in section 80HH than the one used in section 33B of the Act and section 2(8)(c) of the Finance Act, 1975. This is a clear indication of the legislative intention behind using the expression 'manufacture or produce articles' in section 80HH in contradistinction to 'manufacture or processing of goods' used in section 33B of the very Act and in the Finance Act.

On a careful reading of section 80HH of the Act in the light of scheme thereof and other provisions of the Act, it is clear that the Legislature intended to extend the benefit of deduction under section 80HH only to the industrial undertakings which manufacture or produce articles.

This section was not intended to be applied to industrial undertakings which are engaged in 'processing of goods' not amounting to manufacture or production of articles. There may be processes undertaken by an industrial undertaking which may result in conversion of the article into a new commercial commodity or may change the nature and character of the article in such a manner that it may lose its original identity and get transformed into an entirely new commo-dity. In such cases, 'manufacture' can be said to have taken place. But in cases where no such transformation takes place, each and every process supplied to an article cannot tantamount to 'manufacture or production' of goods or articles.

Thus, the benefit of section 80HH is available to industrial undertakings which 'manufacture or produce articles'. Industrial undertakings engaged in 'processing of goods or articles' not amounting to 'manufacture or production' are not entitled to the benefit of this section.

♦♦

CIT v. Lucky Mineral (P.) Ltd. [1996] 87 Taxman 215 (Raj.)

The meaning of the word 'manufacture' in the context of the language of section 80HH is required to be construed in the popular sense in which it is commonly understood by the people.

'Manufacture' implies a change, but every change is not 'manufacture' although every change in the article is the result of the treatment, labour and manipulation. To bring about the change qualifying as manufacture, something more is necessary and that something is transformation, i.e., a new and different article, having a distinct name, character or use, must emerge.

♦♦

B.S. Bajaj & Sons v. CIT [1996] 135 CTR (Punj. & Har.) 491

ARTICLE - CLAUSE (i) OF SUB-SECTION (2)

628. CIT v. N.C. Budharaja & Co. [1993] 70 Taxman 312/204 ITR 412 (SC)

The word 'article' is not defined in the Act or the Rules. It must, therefore, be understood in its normal connotation, the sense in which it is understood in commercial world. The word 'articles' in section 80HH is preceded by words 'it has begun or begins to manufacture or produce'. The word 'articles' occurring in section 80HH(2)(i) does not comprehend and take within its ambit, a dam, a bridge and so on. If a dam is an article, so would be a bridge, a road, or underground canal and a multi-storeyed building. To say that all of them fall within the meaning of word 'articles' is to over-strain the language beyond its normal and ordinary meaning. It is equally difficult to say that the process of constructing a dam is a process of manufacture or a process of production. It is true that a dam is composed of several articles, viz., stones, concretes, cement, etc. But to say that the end product, the dam, is an article is to be unfaithful to the normal connotation of the word. A dam is constructed, it is not manufactured or produced.

The expressions 'manufacture' and 'produce' are normally associated with movables, articles and goods, big and small, but they are never employed to denote the construction activity of the nature involved in the construction of a dam or for that matter a bridge, a road or a building.

Therefore, the activity of construction of a dam could not be characterised as manufacture or producing of article or articles, as the case may be, within the meaning of section 80HH(2)(i).

2.14-12 Toolings, used for production of refractories, is tangible fixed asset and not consumables and hence should be ac-counted as per AS 10/ICDS-V and not as per AS 2/ICDS-II

Toolings, used for production of refractories, is fixed asset and not consumables and hence the treatment of toolings should be as per AS 10/ICDS-V and not as per AS 2/ICDS-II.

Case Study 2.14.12.1: A company is in the business of manufacturing refractories (a material which retains its strength at high temperatures). The manufacturing process requires that to give shape to refractories, it is required to be filled into 'tooling' (comprised of an outer jacket made by a special metal). These toolings are imported in India. Toolings have a limited useful life of 3 years. As per the present accounting policy, the company treats toolings as consumables having a life of 3 years and accordingly the cost of tooling is amortised over a period of 3 years. Hence, toolings are disclosed under 'inventories'. Whether the present treatment done by company is correct ?

Answer: No. Toolings cannot be treated as inventory (consumables) because consumables are generally consumed in the production process whereas toolings do not get consumed but facilitate production process. Toolings are used in the production of refractories (finished goods) and have a limited useful life. [EAC opinion Query 26 Volume 29 Opinion finalised on 15 Dec 2009] Accordingly, toolings are fixed assets which should be depreciated in accordance with the Act and the Rules.

2.14-13 Whether foodstuffs purchased by company for supply to staff at subsidised rates should be treated as inventory and valued as per ICDS-II?

A company is in the business of manufacturing of tea. The company, to follow existing rules, is required to distribute foodstuff to its employees at concessional rates. The company purchases foodstuff in bulk quantity. The distribution of foodstuff to employees is at subsidized rates (lesser that the bulk cost). Whether ICDs-II applies to stock of such foodstuff?

In accordance with AS 2/ICDS-II, foodstuff cannot be treated as 'inventory'. Rather it is a short term employee benefit as explained by Para 8(d) of AS 15. Valuation of foodstuff should be as follows:-

Foodstuff at the period end should be valued at cost. [Follow AS 2/ICDS-II principles while arriving at the cost]

For the damaged stock, valuation should be lesser of cost or net realizable value. [Follow AS 2/ICDS-II principles]

Since foodstuff is provided at subsidized rates only once the employee renders services, foodstuff for which employees have already rendered services but distribution is pending on the part of the company; such foodstuff should be valued at amount receivable from employee's i.e. subsidized rates. [Because certain portion, i.e. cost (-) subsidized rate, would have already been recognized under AS 15 when the services were rendered by employees].

on 12-8-2005 to review the imposition of penalty. The notice was opposed on the sole ground that the order-in-original had already merged with the order dated 13-10-2004, hence, on the date of issuance of show-cause notice there was no order-in-original, which could be reviewed by the Commissioner. That contention of the assessee was negatived, and the Commissioner enhanced the penalty. However, the Tribunal allowed the appeal of the assessee. The High Court held that the penalty whole hog was a subject-matter of the challenge before the Commissioner (Appeals), and was also capable of being challenged before the Commissioner (Appeals). Likewise, the Commissioner (Appeals) had jurisdiction to, and was capable of reversing, modifying or affirming the order of penalty also, which was in issue before it. It might be noticed in the instant case, that the order in original imposed a penalty lesser than the one which according to the department was required to be imposed, and the penalty as imposed was challenged. It was well-nigh possible that in appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) could have set aside the order altogether, or could have reduced it as well, while maintaining imposition of penalty, might be rightly, or wrongly. Therefore, on the parameters laid down by the Supreme Court, the superior jurisdiction was capable of reversing, modifying, or affirming the order which was in issue before it, and in the instant case the Commissioner (Appeals) declined to modify, and simply affirmed it. Thus, in the facts and circumstances, the Commissioner could not exercise his power of revision under section 84 to the extent the order of adjudicating authority was found to be erroneous by him and about which no appeal lay at the instance of the revenue, notwithstanding that to the extent the assessee was aggrieved, he had preferred the appeal and the order in appeal had been passed.

In order to set over this controversy in the above definition of ‘input’, the Legislature has clarified that even if an item is not contained in the final product still it would be classifiable as an ‘input’ under the above definition. In other words, it has been clarified by the definition of ‘input’ that the following considerations will not be relevant :

(a)Use of input in the manufacturing process be it direct or indirect; and (b)even if the input is not contained in the ‘final product’ it would still be covered by the definition.

These considerations have been made irrelevant by the use of expression ‘goods used in or in relation to the manufacture of final products’ which, as stated above, is the crucial requirement of the definition of ‘input’. In this regard, some case laws are cited hereunder :

In J.K. Cement Works v. CCE 2010 (252) ELT 249 (Trib. - Delhi), it was held that only those goods which form part of the process carried out by a manufacturer for converting raw material into finished goods can be considered as inputs and the goods which are not integrally connected with the process of manufacture resulting in utilization of such product directly or indirectly in the manufacture of finished product cannot be said to be input. Therefore, oxygen, helium and acetylene gases used for repair and maintenance of plant and machinery are not covered by the definition of ‘input’.

In Reva Electric Car Co. (P.) Ltd. v. CCE 2010 (250) ELT 149 (Trib. - Bang.), the Tribunal held that it is unambiguously clear that the rejection was at the pre-manufacturing stage and for no reasons attributable to the appellant. Rejection at the pre-manufacturing stage is also indispensable for quality control. It can be said that any rejection of input without ulterior motive or oblique purpose may not disentitle an assessee from the benefit of law relating to CENVAT credit.

It did not appear that the car manufacturer had escaped duty. The revenue should, therefore, allow entitlement of CENVAT credit in the absence of any violation of law. Accordingly, the demand of Rs. 6,90,150 on the count of using of inputs for R&D was unsustainable in the absence of any finding to show that the R&D had not resulted in finished goods and that finished goods had escaped duty. Exercise of Research having resulted in the finished goods and that had suffered duty, CENVAT credit was admissible for which demand of Rs. 6,90,150 was set aside.

In HIM Technoforge Ltd.’s case (supra), the respondent was a manufacturer of rough forgings and forging articles of steel falling under Chapter 7326 of the CETA, 1985. They also availed CENVAT credit of inputs and capital goods. The dispute related to ‘metal band saw blades’ and ‘steel shots’ as to whether they could be considered as capital goods as contended by the department or could be treated as inputs as claimed by the respondent. The original authority after taking note of the duration of use of these items and the purpose for which they were used held that they were capital goods.

The Commissioner (Appeals) treated the above products as ‘inputs’. He held that under the CENVAT Credit Rules, the term ‘input’ has been defined to mean all goods, except HSD oil, LSD and motor spirit used in or in relation to the manufacture of final products whether directly or indirectly and whether contained in the final product or not. In view of this above definition of the ‘input’ under the CENVAT Credit Rules, both the items, namely, ‘metal saw blade’ and ‘steel shots’ used by the appellants in connection with the production of goods on consumable would merit classification under inputs only and, therefore, the credit taken by them was in order.

The Tribunal held that if the role and period of usage as recorded by the original authority was taken into account, the decision of Commissioner (Appeals) had clearly held that the same were in the nature of consumables used in relation to manufacture of final products and, therefore, appropriately to be treated as inputs.

4.2 Waste and Scrap - In Tera Cables India (P.) Ltd. v. CCE 2010 (258) ELT 111 (Trib. - Ahd.), a small amount of Rs. 9,456 stood denied to the appellant on the ground that the credit had been availed on the waste and scrap, which could not be considered as an input for the appellant’s final product. The lower authorities had nowhere discussed as to how the waste and scrap could not be considered as an input. The cable waste of cut length was being utilized and consumed by the appellant in its own factory in the manufacture of finished goods. The duty paid cable waste received in the factory had been accounted for in the input register and its consumption had been shown in the manufacture of the final product. The final product manufactured out of the same was accounted for in the RG-1 Part I Register, which stood cleared on payment of duty. As such to deny the benefit of waste and scrap on the ground that the same was not an input was not justified.

Conclusion

17. In this discussion we have tried to bring home the attitude of the assessing authorities which is not commensurate with the avowed policy of the Government or of the advice of various commissions. They still continue to have a superiority complex and to treat the taxpayers only as taxevaders. Such an obsession should be shed if the assessees have to go to the department without any fear. It is true that some assessees are not all honest in their returning the true incomes, but then it is not obligatory on the part of the assessing authority to start scrutiny with suspicion.

Handling of tetraethyl lead compound

.

80. (1) Tetraethyl lead compound shall not be unloaded from a ship unless—

(a)

it is packed in specially constructed steel drums of substantial construction, sealed with an inner and outer bung, and fitted with rolling roofs on to the shell as an added precaution;

(b)

all receptacles containing tetraethyl lead compound are distinctively and durably marked with the words "Tetraethyl Lead Compound Poison"; and

(c)

two sets of protective equipment comprising the following are provided and kept readily available for use in the event of any leakage of tetraethyl lead compound—

(i)

rubber gloves,

(ii)

rubber boots,

(iii)

rubber apron or oilskin suit, and

(iv)

suitable respirator, which should be either of canister type containing minimum of 50cc. of activated charcoal or an airline respirator with an independent fresh air supply.

(2) Following measures shall be taken while unloading tetraethyl lead compound:—

(a)

no receptacle containing tetraethyl lead compound shall be opened within the limits of the port;

(b)

before commencement of the unloading operations, the consignment of tetraethyl lead compound shall be inspected on board the vessel by a responsible person. No tetraethyl lead compound drums showing any sign of leakage shall be unloaded until suitably repaired or placed in a larger receptacle or container offering sufficient precautions from leakage;

(c)

drums containing tetraethyl lead compound shall be discharged under the supervision of a responsible person;

(d)

drums containing tetraethyl lead compound shall be loaded discharged in rope slings with a maximum of two drums at a separate sling for each drum. Hooks shall on no account be used;

(e)

dock workers handling drums containing tetraethyl lead compound shall be provided with heavy gloves of canvas or leather and shall use such gloves; and

(f)

adequate quantities of non-inflammable solvent or kerosene and soap and water to deal with any leakages of tetraethyl lead compound shall be kept readily available where the work of handling of the tetraethyl lead compound is carried on.

(3) Following measures shall be taken in the event of leakage of tetraethyl lead compound:—

(a)

the area on which the leakage of tetraethyl lead compound has occurred (including the outside of a drum) shall be treated as follows:—

(i)

flush with kerosene or some other light oil solvent followed by water. If the surface permits, wash thoroughly with soap working up as much lather as possible, and again flush with water;

(ii)

if it is possible to obtain quickly a supply of common bleaching lime (Ca O Cl2) the area should first be treated generously with a mixture of bleaching lime and water in the form of thin slurry (NEVER use the dry powder) alternatively a five per cent solution of sulphury! chloride (SO2 Cl2) in kerosene may be used;

(b)

if contamination of absorbent material such as wooden flooring, dunnage, or other packing material has taken place, then such material shall, after treatment as above, be removed from the place where tetraethyl lead compound is being handled;

(c)

any clothing which becomes contaminated by tetraethyl lead compound shall be removed immediately and cleaned by repeated rinsing in a non-inflammable dry cleaning fluid;

(d)

if tetraethyl lead compound can be smelled, dock workers not assigned to deal with the leakage of tetraethyl lead compound shall be removed from that place; and

(e)

dock workers assigned to deal with leakage of tetraethyl lead compound shall wear the protective equipment described under sub-regulation 1(c).

(4) Suitable protective clothing shall be provided for handling of tetraethyl lead compound in refrigerated spaces.

Other queries

We are manufacturers of Aluminium and we sell Aluminium Dross. Supreme Court had held that ‘dross is not goods’. However, now, Central Excise Tariff has specific headings for dross and slag with effect from February 28, 2005. These are sold and have market value. Should it be held as ‘goods’ with effect from February 28, 2005? It is true that in Union of India v. Indian Aluminium Co. Ltd. - 1995 (77) ELT 268 (SC) = AIR 1995 SC 1580 = 1995 Supp (2) SCC 465 = 1995 AIR SCW 2436 = 1995 (58) ECR 612 (SC 3-member Bench judgment), it was held that ‘dross and skimmings’ arising during manufacture of Aluminium is not ‘excisable goods’. They are merely refuse or ashes given out in process of removing impurities from raw material. Hence they are not ‘excisable goods’ as understood in commercial parlance, even if they are sold and they fetch some price. This was followed in CCE v. Tata Iron & Steel Co. Ltd. 2004 AIR SCW 1948 = 165 ELT 386 = 61 RLT 239 (SC 3-member Bench), where it was held that zinc dross and skimmings are merely refuse, scum or rubbish. It is not result of treatment, labour or manipulation, even if it fetches some price in market. Everything which is sold is not necessarily a marketable commodity known to commerce and worthwhile to trade in.

In CC v. Universal Cables 149 ELT 968 (CEGAT 3- member Bench), it was held that dross and skimming of Aluminium obtained in manufacture of Aluminium rods is not excisable. - Departmental appeal dismissed by the Supreme Court on July 9, 1996 - 151 ELT A 175.

However, now CETA has following specific entries with effect from February 28, 2005 - ‘Brass Dross’ (2620 30 10), ‘Aluminium Dross’ (2620 40 10) and slag/dross from manufacture of iron or steel (2619).

In Balaji Enterprises v. CCE 1997 AIR SCW 2026 = 92 ELT 3 (SC) = AIR 1997 SC 2170, it has been observed and noted that whenever things like waste and scrap have been sought to be taxed in the Central Excise Act, specific entries have been made for this purpose. Supreme Court has noted various specific examples from the old tariff in this regard.

Waste is not obtained by any process of manufacturing but in the course of manufacturing and processing to produce the end product. The intention of legislature to cover waste or scrap in relation to manufacture is required to be specifically mentioned in tariff item before liability to pay duty on waste or scrap arises - Plastics Packaging (P.) Ltd. v. CCE - 1991 (51) ELT 271 (Bom HC). In Shree Synthetic Ltd. v. CCE - 1991 (52) ELT 238 (CEGAT), it was held - "Waste is normally not considered as ‘goods’ except where it is deemed to be ‘goods’ by way of legal fiction and specific mention in any provision, rule or the tariff."

‘Waste or scrap’ will be ‘goods’ and hence taxable only if specifically mentioned in CETA (Tariff) - Kamath Packaging (P.) Ltd. v. CCE - 1992 (60) ELT 666 (CEGAT).

Hence, in my view, these may get covered as dutiable with effect from February 28, 2005.

Remelting scrap ingots of iron and steel:

Products roughly cast in the form of ingots without feeder-heads or hot tops, or of pigs, having obvious surface faults and not complying with the chemical composition of pig iron, spiegeleisen or ferro-alloys.

Products of which less than 90% by weight passes through a sieve with a mesh aperture of 1 mm and of which 90% or more by weight passes through a sieve with a mesh aperture of 5 mm.

(ij)

Semi-finished products :

Continuous cast products of solid, section, whether or not subjected to primary hot-rolling; and other products of solid sections, which have not been further worked than subjected to primary hot-rolling or roughly shaped by forging, including blanks for angles, shapes or sections.

These products are not presented in coils.

(k)

Flat-rolled products:

Rolled products of solid rectangular (other than square) cross-section, which do not conform to the definition at (ij) above in the form of:

–

coils of successively superimposed layers, or

–

straight lengths, which if of a thickness less than 4.75 mm, are of width measuring at least ten times the thickness or if of a thickness of 4.75 mm or more are of a width which exceeds 150 mm and measures at least twice the thickness.

Flat-rolled products include those with patterns in relief derived directly from rolling (for example, grooves, ribs, chequers, tears, buttons and lozenges) and those, which have been perforated, corrugated or polished, provided that they do not thereby assume the character of articles or products of other headings.

Flat-rolled products of a shape other than rectangular or square, of any size, are to be classified as products of a width of 600 mm or more, provided that they do not assume the character of articles or products of other headings.

(l)

Bars and rods, hot-rolled, in irregularly wound coils :

Hot-rolled products in irregularly wound coils, which have a solid cross-section in the shape of circles, segments of circles, ovals, rectangles (including squares), triangles, or other convex polygons (including "flattened circles" and "modified rectangles", of which two opposite sides are convex arcs, the other two sides being straight, of equal length and parallel). These products may have indentations, ribs, grooves or other deformations produced during the rolling process (reinforcing bars and rods).

(m)

Other bars and rods :

Products which do not conform to any of the definitions at (ij), (k) or (l) above or to the definition of wire, which have a uniform solid cross-section along their whole length in the shape of circles, segments of circles, ovals, rectangles (including squares), triangles or other convex polygons (including "flattened circles" and "modified rectangles", of which two opposite sides are convex arcs, the other two sides being straight, of equal length and parallel). The products may :

–

have indentations, ribs, grooves or other deformations produced during the rolling process (reinforcing bars and rods)

–

be twisted after rolling.

(n)

Angles, shapes and sections :

Products having a uniform solid cross-section along their whole length which do not conform to any of the definitions at (ij), (k), (l) or (m) above or to the definition of wire.

Chapter 72 does not include products of heading 7301 or 7302.

(o)

Wire :

Cold-formed products in coils, of any uniform solid cross-section along their whole length, which do not conform to the definition of flat-rolled products.

(p)

Hollow drill bars and rods :

Hollow bars and rods of any cross-section, suitable for drills, of which the greatest external dimension of the cross-section exceeds 15 mm but does not exceed 52 mm, and of which the greatest internal dimension does not exceed one half of the greatest external dimension. Scrapping Yard and Collection Centre

.

13. (1) The Scrapping Yard shall be set up in an adequate area having space for vehicular movement, storing the vehicles or items received and recyclable material recovered, commensurate to the size and voluminous nature of the scraps to be handled by the facility.

(2) The Scrapping Yard shall be a gated area to handle, depollute and dismantle End-of-Life Vehicles, white goods and other scraps along with facility for measuring radiation as is followed for import of scrap.

(3) Material handling machines shall be utilised to minimise human intervention and create safe work places.

(4) All Scrapping Yards shall engage competent and trained manpower to process the End-of-Life vehicles, goods and other scraps.

(5) The Scrapping Yard shall have dry areas (free from water logging), impermeable surfaces like asphalt or concrete flooring, asphalt or concrete roads, adequate workshop facilities for in-house maintenance, fire protection systems etc. to maintain safe work places and all other required measures for keeping pollution under control.

(6) Scrapping Yard shall be equipped with a depollution system, preferably with zero discharge system and dismantling work shall be done using technology for processing the End-of-Life vehicles, goods and other scraps.

(7) The Scrapping Yard shall comply with relevant health and safety legislation or regulation and environmental norms.

(8) The Scrapping yard shall have,-

(a)

Suitable earmarked area for parking of waste vehicles on non-permeable asphalt or concrete or epoxy coated flooring with adequate drainage facility and no waste or potentially waste vehicle shall be parked on roads or public spaces even during processing of applications for deposit and shall be accommodated within the premises of the Registered Vehicle Scrapping Facility only.

(b)

Certified de-polluting equipment to ensure zero leakage of pollutants during draining of fuels or fluids or gases and liquids, certified de-risking equipment for safe neutralization or removal of airbags, pre-tensioner etc., appropriate dismantling equipment for the activities defined (such as de-risking, de-polluting, dismantling, shredding, shearing, bailing etc.), designated areas for storing the segregated scrap, adequate space for storage and handling of segregated spares, designated space for temporary storage of automotive hazardous waste such as tyres, batteries, fuel, oils, liquids and gases, suitable safety and occupational health equipment, material handling equipment for the safe transportation of spares, scrap etc.

(c)

Appropriate Industrial grade lighting and ventilation systems, conformity to noise pollution norms and appropriate effluent treatment plants or water recycling plants.

(9) Scrapping Yards shall accredit themselves with the latest version of quality standards viz. ISO 9001 (Quality management system), ISO14001 (Environmental Management System) and ISO 45001 (Occupational health and safety) within twelve months of commencement of operations.

(10) In case Scrapping Yards do not have adequate capability or provisions for responsible recycling of hazardous waste (like e-waste, lead acid batteries, lithium-ion components, or for recovery of rare earth metals, etc.), or for recycling of scrap material which is outside its scope, then such materials shall be sold to duly authorised recyclers or agencies, who have adequate capability and licence.

(11) Records of the transactions shall be maintained, clearly stating the volumes off-loaded and the name, authorisation number, Permanent Account Number, Goods and Services Tax and other commercial details of the authorized recycler/agency. Such records shall be subjected to periodical audit.

Every case of tacit acceptance shall be informed to National Authority, immediately upon its occurrence, by the competent authority and ship recycling facility. 7. Procedure for obtaining entry permission to recycling facility from Port Authority/State Maritime Board.—

(1)

Entry permission shall be given by the Port Authority or State Maritime Board within one working day after receipt of clearances granted by all the concerned departments/agencies and permission to recycle by Competent Authority.

(2)

Entry permission shall be granted by the Port Authority only to the authorized ship recycling facility subject to fulfilment of following specific requirements like—

(a)

In case of beaching, all the double bottoms should be free from substances that may cause environmental damage. Ship or ships shall be allowed to beach one at a time, provided that all around there is at least five meters space.

(b)

In the case of petroleum oil cargo tanks and petroleum slop tanks; on production of gas-free for hot work certificate along with gas free certificate given by the Petroleum and Explosives Safety Organization/PESO.

(c)

In case of ships of special concern, on production of No Objection Certificate/NOC from Atomic Energy Regulatory Board; and

(d)

In the case of war ships and naval vessels on production of No Objection Certificate/NOC from the Naval Department, the Atomic Energy Regulatory Board/AERB and the Customs Department.

(3)

Petroleum tankers which have not obtained "fit for hot work" certificate for all cargo tanks, slop tanks, forward deep fuel oil tanks and forward coffer dams shall not be allowed to beach.

(4)

On beaching of ship or ships entering recycling facility, the Ship Recycler shall take necessary actions—

(a)

ensure that the vessel is secured properly;

(b)

leftovers in bunkers are removed with proper precautions, including sufficient ventilation in engine room;

(c)

bunker and bunker contents are disposed of to a registered dealer for petroleum products;

(d)

used oil and sludge are disposed of to registered recyclers/refinery only.

(5)

The ship recyclers shall be liable to penalty and fines, including cancellation of license for ship recycling in the event they are found to have not complied with the aforesaid provisions during examination of their records or during inspections of their plots/yards by concerned agencies after observing Principle of Natural Justice.

8. Permission from the State Pollution Control Board/SPCB and Directorate of Industrial Safety and Health/DISH prior to Cutting operation.—

(1)

The activities of ship recycling are identified as a hazardous process under section 2 (cb) of the Factories Act, 1948 (63 of 1948) and the provisions of Chapter-IVA, sections 41A to 41H of the Factories Act, 1948 (63 of 1948) shall be applicable.

(2)

Directorate of Industrial Safety and Health shall inspect the ship recycling operation whenever felt necessary to check and ensure compliance with the provisions under the Factories Act,1948(63 of 1948).

(3)

After beaching the ships, the Ship Recycler, shall remove all the loose and hazardous wastes including oil and petroleum hydrocarbon from, tanks, stop tanks etc.

(4)

The State Pollution Control Board/SPCB shall issue decontamination certificate to ship recycler after inspection which will be done with proper lighting in the engine room. Simultaneously, Gas free and hot work permit as per section 68 H of the Factories Act 1948 (63 of 1948) shall be issued by competent authority/agency after ensuring safe and complete removal oils/used oil/hydrocarbon.

(5)

Removal of hazardous material and other wastes prior commencement of cutting. —

(a)

All the hazardous materials and wastes listed in ship recycling plan is to be removed as far as practicable.

(b)

All the loose and hazardous wastes including those oils and petroleum hydrocarbons from pipe lines, tanks, slop tanks etc. shall be removed and decontamination certificate shall be issued by State Pollution Control Board/SPCB to the ship recycler after satisfactory completion of physical inspection. Simultaneously, gas free and hot work permit as per section 68 H of the Factories Act 1948 (63 of 1948) shall be issued by competent authority/agency after ensuring removal of oils/used oil/hydrocarbon from bunkers/pipe lines etc.

(c)

Any leftover oils, used oils, sludge are handled with safely taking due precautions for possible damage to environment due to leakage and disposed of for further recycling/disposal.

(d)

Any sweepings of cargo (left over of last cargo) shall be permitted to be cleared upon completion of proper import processes thereto where the sweeping/left out cargo has no commercial value or not fit for consumption/use. Such cargo shall be disposed of by the ship recycling facility as per appropriate rules and regulations applicable for that cargo.

9. Procedure for Cutting permission.—

(1)

The competent authority may grant permission for cutting operations within a maximum period of two working days upon satisfactory verification of following items, namely: —

(a)

A certificate from the State Pollution Control Board that all kinds of oils, cargo residues and other loose hazardous wastes are completely removed and respective holds and tanks are decontaminated.

(b)

"Safe for entry and safe for hot work" certificate has to be issued by the Petroleum and Explosives Safety Organization/PESO for cargo and slop tanks of petroleum tankers, or by any competent agency authorized by the Directorate of Industrial Safety and Health/DISH under the Factories Act, 1948 (63 of 1948);

(c)

Inspection shall be carried out by the Safety officer of Directorate of Industrial Safety and Health/DISH or authorized person of Directorate of Industrial Safety and Health/DISH to ensure -

(i)

ignitable materials are completely removed from confined spaces that need to be certified for hot work;

(ii)

areas in engine room are practically gas free with proper venting and well within explosive limits by use of calibrated multi-gas monitoring meter. On satisfactory compliance of this inspection, Safe for entry and safe for hot work permission shall be issued for engine room;

(iii)

bunker area and those common areas of ships where there is likelihood of ignitable gases generations need to be properly ventilated and ensure that spaces are well within explosive limits by use of calibrated portable gas meters.

(2)

In case any short coming is noted then the same shall be communicated in writing within two working days to enable the recycler to re-submit the request upon necessary corrections.

10. Monitoring of worker safety and hazardous material during dismantling activity.—

(1)

Worker safety:

(a)

A Safety officer/Safety Officer as per the Factories Act 1948 (63 of 1948) shall be engaged by ship recycling facility.

(b)

A competent person shall be engaged for issuance and continuous monitoring of conditions based on which safe for entry and safe for hot work permits issued as per the Factories Act 1948 (63 of 1948).

(c)

All the equipment such as crane, winch, chain rope and shackles, generator set and any other safety equipment installed in the ship recycling facility or hired for the purpose of recycling shall be installed and maintained in accordance with the provisions of the Factories Act, 1948 (63 of 1948) and rules made thereunder and any other relevant Acts and rules.

(d)

A safety officer/Safety Supervisor is responsible for conducting meetings prior to starting any activity, briefing the risks involved in the activity and control measures taken to minimize such risks.

(e)

A placard displaying important precautions (do's and don'ts) to be followed during ship recycling activity is installed at prominent places within the premises and that such display is made in English and other language(s) as understood by the workers involved in recycling.

(f)

A calibrated explosive gas detector, a multi gas monitor including hydrogen sulphide (H2S) gas monitor, portable gas meters and an oxygen percentage analyzer are available on the site in working condition.

(g)

Adequate lighting arrangement is made in the common areas of yard and in the spaces where activity is carried out. The SRF should conspicuously mark and maintain an emergency exit route and such route should always be free from any obstructions.

(h)

The emergency response plan drill should be conducted once in 6 months. Further, an off-site emergency plan for the whole district should be prepared and to be conducted once in a year.

(2)

Handling, storage and disposal of hazardous material:

(a)

One Safety Officer/One Safety supervisor as per section 41C(b) of the Factories Act 1948 (63 of 1948) shall be engaged by ship recycling facility.

(b)

Supervisor shall ensure that hazardous materials are handled, stored, transported and disposed as per the approved ship recycling plan and in accordance with local legislations.

Even earlier, various services, like insurance, advertising, air travel agent, courier etc., have been judicially held to be eligible input services for purposes of availment of input tax credit. During the year 2010, the eligibility to tax credit in respect of certain other services was considered in the judicial forums. Brief details of these cases are given in the succeeding sub-paragraphs. 6.1 Business auxiliary service - A manufacturer and exporter of hand tools deployed agents in foreign countries for the purpose of canvassing and processing orders on its behalf, and paid commission to them. The department took the stand that service tax credit could not be allowed since the payments were connected with a post-removal activity. The Tribunal however held that, since such activities fell within the domain of sales promotion, credit was allowable - CCE v. Ambika Overseas 2010 (20) STR 514 (New Delhi - CESTAT).

6.2 Cargo handling service - In one case, the adjudicating authority denied tax credit in respect of cargo handling service on the ground that the service was used outside the factory premises, i.e., from the place of removal to the customers’ premises. The Tribunal relied upon the Larger Bench decision in ABB Ltd. v. CCE&ST [2009] 21 STT 77 (Bang. - CESTAT) and held that credit was allowable - CCE v. H.E.G. Ltd. [2010] 28 STT 277 (New Delhi - CESTAT).

6.3 Construction service - Where the assessee constructed a compound wall around its factory by utilising construction service, and it was found that the site plan indicated that the compound wall was an integral part of the factory, the Tribunal held that tax credit was admissible - CCE v. Raymond Zambaiti (P.) Ltd. 2010 (18) STR 734 (Mum. - CESTAT). On the contrary, construction service used in the residential colony for employees of the assessee was held as not eligible for credit, since such an activity might be a welfare activity but not an activity which was integrally related to the business activities carried on by the assessee - CCE v. Manikgarh Cement [2010] 29 STT 230 (Mum.).

6.4 Consulting engineer’s service - An assessee availed credit of service tax on consultancy services for environmental evaluation work including onsite evaluation and report submission. The department disallowed the credit on the ground that there was nothing on record to link the services with the factory premises of the assessee. However, the Tribunal noticed that the purchase order had been raised at the address of the factory premises, and for this reason, the Tribunal held that the credit availed was in order - Cabot Sanmar Ltd. v. CCE 2010 (19) STR 681 (Chennai - CESTAT).

6.5 Courier service - An assessee had used courier services for placing orders, filing quotations for procurement as well as marketing, dispatch instructions, issuing cheques for procurement, sending stock transfer documents to depots/head office etc. The Tribunal confirmed the order of the first appellate authority allowing credit by placing reliance on the Larger Bench decision in ABB Ltd. case (supra) - CCE v. Apar Industries Ltd. 2010 (20) STR 624 (Ahd. - CESTAT).

6.6 Customs house agent’s service - An assessee used customs house agent’s service for clearance of imported goods at the port and their transport to the assessee’s factory. The Tribunal held that the assessee was eligible to avail service tax credit - Nelsun Paper Mills Ltd. v. CCE 2010 (18) STR 648 (Chennai - CESTAT).

6.7 Dry cleaning service - A manufacturer of medicaments and drugs availed service tax credit on dry cleaning services in respect of uniforms/clothings of its workers. The Tribunal held that credit taken was in order, since wearing of clean uniforms/clothings in the drug industry was a mandatory requirement under the Drugs & Cosmetics Act - CCE v. Fourtts (I) Laboratories (P.) Ltd. 2010 24 STT 153 (Chennai - CESTAT).

6.8 Event management service - In connection with the celebrations connected with the expansion of its plant, an assessee used Event Management service and availed service tax credit. The credit was disallowed by the adjudicating authority. The Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the disallowance, by observing that the celebrations were mainly an ‘entertainment’ which could not be treated as ‘activities relating to business’. The Tribunal confirmed the appellate order - Hindustan Zinc Ltd. v. CCE [2010] 28 STT 139 (New Delhi - CESTAT).

However, packing materials of inputs/raw materials could not be treated to be waste arising out of processing of the input for which credit has been taken - CCE v. West Coast Industrial Gases Ltd. 2003 (155) ELT 11 (SC). In other words, the waste and scrap arising out of capital goods on which no credit has been availed, shall not be dutiable - Southern Agrifurane Industries Ltd. v. CCE 2003 (158) ELT 323 (Trib. - Chennai), provided that no Cenvat credit on such capital goods was taken - Kesoram Rayon v. CCE 2003 (162) ELT 620 (Trib. - Kol.).

If any waste is not marketable, the same shall not be dutiable - CCE v. Indian Tube Co. Ltd. 1995 (77) ELT 21 (SC); Union of India v. Indian Aluminium Co. Ltd.’s case (supra). For example, refuse, rubbish and ashes thrown up in the course of manufacture are not goods even if they may fetch some prices - CCE v. Tata Iron & Steels Co. Ltd. 2004 (165) ELT 386 (SC). If the resultant waste (after process of a waste) is same having almost identical chemical and physical properties, resultant waste could not be said as manufactured waste - Indian Organic Chemicals Ltd. v. CCE 1996 (88) ELT 644 (SC).

Waste and scrap is dutiable only when it is a manufactured product and not otherwise - Elphinstone Metal Rolling Mills v. CCE 2004 (167) ELT 481 (SC)

A by-product is something of value, which is produced in making main product or it is a substance obtained in the course of a specific process, but it is not the primary product. If it is not marketable (although sold in market in few occasions), the same will not be dutiable - Gujarat State Fertilizers Co. Ltd. v. CCE 1997 (90) ELT 149 (Trib. - New Delhi). For example, by-product obtained during the course of processing of rice in the rice mill, not fit for human consumption, does not fall within the ambit of definition of ‘vegetable oil’ contained in section 3(h) of the National Oil Seeds and Vegetable Oil Development Board Act - A.P. Rice Bran Solvent Extractors Association v. Union of India 1998 (103) ELT 481 (SC).

And waste and scrap arising out of manufacture of exempted goods are exempt from the whole of the duty of excise vide Notification No. 89/95-CE, dated May 18, 1995, provided that in such factory, any other excisable goods (other than exempted goods) shall not be manufactured - see also E.P. Electropressings (P.) Ltd. v. CCE 2002 (140) ELT 230 (Trib. - Delhi).

Inclusive Part

5. The expression viz., ‘used in or in relation to the manufacture of final products’ in the specific/substantive part of the definition is so wide that it would cover innumerable items as ‘input’ and to avoid such contingency the Legislature has incorporated the inclusive part after the substantive part qualified by the place of use. For example, one of the categories mentioned in the inclusive part is ‘used as packing material’. Packing material by itself would not suffice till it is proved that the term is used in the course of manufacture of final product. Mere fact that the item is a packing material whose value is included in the accessible value of final product will not entitle the manufacturer to take credit. Oils and lubricants mentioned in the definition are required for smooth running of machines and, hence, they are included as they are used in relation to manufacture of final product. The intention of the Legislature is that inputs falling in the inclusive part must have nexus with the manufacture of the final product.

In Indo Rama Synthetics (India) Ltd. v. CCE 2007 (219) ELT 122 (Bom.), the High Court held that the credit of duty paid on the goods or fuel used in the generation of electricity is available, provided the electricity is used for the manufacture of final product. The use of electricity must have nexus with goods manufactured in the factory.

5.1 Primary packing material - In Wrigley India (P.) Ltd. v. CCE 2010 (255) ELT 201 (Punj. & Har.), it was held that it is not a matter of dispute that chewing gum/bubble gums manufactured by the assessees are directly or primarily packed with the printed aluminium foils without tattoos. It means, putting a ‘boomer-tattoo’ in the package material of bubble gum is an additional step in aid used for promotional material and it is not termed as a packing material, as such, especially when it is depicted on the packing that ‘free tattoo inside’. The primary function of putting the ‘tattoo’ in the wrapped bubble gum is to promote the trade and to attract the children rather than to be used for the purpose of packing ‘tattoo’.

Again it is not a matter of dispute that these printed ‘tattoos’ are not used for initial packing in the real sense, rather they are wrapped. Therefore, it cannot possibly be said that the ‘Boomer-tattoo’ is used as initial packing material, meaning thereby the wrapper of the ‘tattoo’ on the bubble gum is not at all required in the form of primary packing. There is no direct and indirect use of the ‘tattoo’ in or in relation to the manufacture of the product, rather it is separately known tattoo in the market, has a separate identity, specific purpose of promotion of the product and for the purpose of advertisement. Hence, it is not a packing material and cannot be considered as inputs within the meaning and definition considered as ‘inputs’ as contemplated under the relevant Rules.

In CCE v. International Tractors Ltd. - 2010 (255) ELT 203 (Punj. & Har.), the respondent was the manufacturer of traction and tractor components. The components manufactured by the respondent were duly packed in boxes and thereafter were sold. The Tribunal had allowed the credit on the goods of full packing of boxes. It had been observed by the Tribunal that duty was paid on the boxes.

The revenue contended that the respondent never received inputs in the packing of boxes and in fact the goods were delivered to the respondent in pallets and, hence, the respondent was not entitled to any credit.

It was held that CESTAT could allow availment of CENVAT credit in respect of duty paid on the packing material.

Place of use

6. The third part of the definition of ‘input’ is the ‘place of use’. Rule 2(k)( i) mandatorily requires that the goods meant for input should be used in the process of manufacture within the premises of the factory. It is a condition precedent to avail CENVAT credit on ‘inputs’ that the product should be manufactured within the premises of the factory. But, at the same time, it is not mandatory for the output service provider to utilize the inputs within the premises of the output service provider. Even if the input is used outside the premises of the service provider, CENVAT credit is allowed for such inputs.

5. We send scrap (say, 100 kg.) to the job worker for further processing. Job-worker returns 80 kg. scrap after processing under job work agreement issued under delivery challan. The job worker does not receive any service charges for this, but, in lieu thereof, takes 20 kg. as the service charge. No financial transaction takes place. Whether these type of transactions are allowed under excise law ? Will there be any liability on our (principal manufacturer's) part ? Kindly clarify

Assuming that process amounts to manufacture, liability to pay duty is of the manufacturer : in this case, job-worker. Hence, in case of 80 kg. manufactured on job-work basis and returned to principal manufacturer, the value will be determined as per rule 10A(iii) of the Central Excise Valuation (Determination of Price of Excisable Goods) Rules, 2000 read with Ujagar Prints (SC)'s case.

The job-work charges would form part of the value and since, in this case, the job-work charges are in kind in form of retention of 20 kg. scrap, the value would be determined based on value of scrap retained by the job-worker.

When job-worker sells 20 kg. (after processing), duty thereon would be payable separately at the time of removal.

CENVAT CREDIT - REVERSAL ON EXEMPTED SERVICE AND SERVICES COVERED UNDER FULL REVERSE CHARGE ?

6. We are manufacturing goods which are 100% excisable and are also providing Goods Transport Agency's Services, which are exempt as per mega exemption notification (transport of defence and military equipments). When taking and availing cenvat, is it necessary to reverse cenvat on exempted service as per rule 6 of CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 ? Is it necessary to reverse credit, even if service is provided on reverse charge mechanism ? Kindly clarify.

Reversal under rule 6 would apply to exempted services provided by service provider. Hence, it would equally apply to exempt Goods Transport Agency's Services.

However, where services are covered under reverse charge, they cease to be 'output service' and hence, no credit can be availed in respect thereof. Hence, any wrongly taken credit has to be reversed.

SERVICE TAX - SUPPLY OF BEDS IN TRAINS v. ABATEMENT

7. Whether supply of bed rolls in the trains attracts Service tax before 1-10-2012 and whether there is any abatement of 30% after 1-10-2012 on the same service ? If yes, under which notification ?

Supply of bed rolls in trains is a taxable service and is not eligible for any exemption or abatement. The abatement relates only to 'transport of passengers by railways' and the service in question is altogether different.

SERVICE TAX - OUTDOOR CATERING v. FACTORY CANTEEN

8. If outdoor caterer is providing catering service in a mess within the factory premises : Is the service exempt as per the mega exemption notification ?

Entries 19 and 19A of the Mega Exemption Notification No. 25/2012-ST, dated 20-6-2012 read as follows :

"19. Services provided in relation to serving of food or beverages by a restaurant, eating joint or a mess, other than those having the facility of air-conditioning or central air-heating in any part of the establishment, at any time during the year;";

19A. Services provided in relation to serving of food or beverages by a canteen maintained in a factory covered under the Factories Act, 1948 (63 of 1948), having the facility of air-conditioning or central air-heating at any time during the year."

It appears that mess would be covered by Entry 19A (if maintained as per Factories Act and having AC) or Entry 19 (if non-AC).

Some experts would suggest that mess services are provided by company to employees and not by outdoor caterer and hence, exemption cannot be availed. However, the most important fact to be noted is that 'company has hired outdoor caterer to run mess' in compliance with law and therefore, mess is run/operated by caterer and mess services would thus, be exempt as aforesaid. Employer-company is not the service provider; in fact, it is duty bound to arrange for canteen and canteen/mess services are provided only by the caterer.

Cenvat credit relating to garden maintenance services 5.5 In the case of ISMT Ltd. v. CCE&C [2010] 24 STT 326 (Mum. - CESTAT), the assessee had availed Cenvat credit of service tax paid on garden maintenance service. Same was denied on the ground that said service was not used in or in relation to the manufacture, directly or indirectly in the manufacture of the final products and clearance of final products from the place of removal. On appeal, the Tribunal held as under :

u The definitions of ‘input’ in rule 2(k) and ‘input service’ in rule 2(l) are not at all comparable or pari materia and coverage of the ‘input service’ is definitely wider.

u The definition of ‘input’ is exhaustive and is restrictive in scope. It treats all goods used in or in relation to manufacture of final products or for any other purpose within the factory of production. But certain goods which would be eligible as per definition have been excluded and certain goods which could be interpreted as not includible have been specifically included, i.e., packing material, lubricating oil, accessories, etc. Therefore, all goods other than specified as includible have to be shown to be used in or in relation to manufacture of final product or for any other purpose within the factory of production. In fact, the Apex Court in Maruti Suzuki Ltd. v. CCE 2009 (240) ELT 641 has held that input and capital goods used in captive means are covered by the definition, expanding the scope of definition.

u The Legislature has not used the word in the inclusive part ‘that it is to be used in or in relation of the final product’.

u From the above, it is clear that the intention of the Legislature was that those activities should be in relation to the business.

u It cannot be viewed that a garden is not relating to manufacture. A good garden creates a better atmosphere and environment which increases the working efficiency and the consumer would feel good.

u In view of the above discussion, the assessee was entitled to Cenvat credit availed on the garden maintenance services which were used in or in relation to the manufacture of final products or used in relation to the business activity and, in the instant case, the services used by the assessee were in relation to the business activity and it was entitled to Cenvat credit. Accordingly, the appeal was to be allowed.

3.2 Bagasse held non-manufactured by Supreme Court : The Circular aforesaid was challenged successfully in Balrampur Chini Mills Ltd. v. UOI [2013] 30 taxmann.com 175 (Allahabad) and CCE v. DSCL Sugar [2014] 41 taxmann.com 64/43 GST 151 (Allahabad) and also in CCE v. KCP Sugar & Industries Corporation Ltd. - 2015 (321) ELT A223 (A.P.) on ground that even though marketable, Bagasse was non-manufactured product and therefore, not excisable and even payment under rule 6 would not be required. The Department went in appeal before Supreme Court in UOI v. DSCL Sugar Ltd. 2015 (322) E.L.T. 769, wherein it was held as follows :

Facts : Assessee was manufacturing sugarcane and molasses. In the process of manufacture of sugar, sugarcane is crushed, its juice is extracted and Bagasse emerges as residue/waste of sugarcane. Since Bagasse was liable to Nil rate of duty, department argued that it was 'exempted goods' and demanded Cenvat reversal under rule 6(3) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004.

Held :

No manufacture/deemed manufacture : Bagasse is only an agriculture waste and residue and not result of any process; hence, it is not covered in definition of 'manufacture' under section 2(f) of Central Excise Act, 1944. Further, there is no Chapter note or Section note in Central Excise Tariff declaring process in respect of bagasse as amounting to manufacture.

Not excisable, even if deemed to be marketable : Hence, notwithstanding amendment in 2008 in section 2(d) ibid, creating a fiction of deemed marketability, bagasse is not excisable as it is not passing test of 'manufacture'.

Cenvat Rule 6 inapplicable [for period prior to 1-3-2015] : Since bagasse is not excisable, hence, even if NIL-rated, cenvat rule 6 is inapplicable thereto. Therefore, denial of credit on electricity on ground that bagasse is excisable exempted goods, was incorrect.

3.3 Zinc Dross also held to be non-manufactured by Bombay High Court : The Bombay High Court in Hindalco Industries Ltd. v. UOI [2015] 49 GST 429 opined that Aluminium dross and skimmings, etc. not 'manufactured' goods and not liable to duty, even if marketable/bought and sold. The facts and judgment are :

Facts : In course of manufacture of aluminium sheets/coils, aluminium dross/skimmings emerged as byproducts. Department demanded duty thereon arguing that in view of Explanation to section 2(d), said goods were marketable. Assessee argued that 'aluminium dross/skimmings' were not 'manufactured goods' and were not, therefore, liable to duty.

Held : Conditions contemplated under section 2(d) (excisable goods, movability and marketability) and section 2(f) (manufacture) have to be satisfied conjunctively in order to entail imposition of excise duty. Merely because goods satisfy test of being marketed and saleable and merely because goods are listed in tariff, it does not mean that they are 'manufactured goods'. In various judgments, Supreme Court held that 'aluminium dross/skimmings' are not manufactured goods and said view was followed in context of 'zinc dross and flux skimming'. Hence, impugned goods were not manufactured goods and could not, therefore, be charged to excise duty.
