12. (1) The owner of different types of ships intended to be recycled within India shall fulfill the following conditions for safe-for- entry or safe-for-hot work, as the case may be, namely:—

(a)

In case of Oil tankers and Chemical tankers, safe for entry and safe for hot work permits are to be obtained for every compartment before actual entry and cutting operations are initiated by ship recyclers.

(b)

The compartment-wise permits as specified under clause (a), shall be required to be obtained in addition to the permission for recycling issued by the competent authority.

(c)

For petroleum oil cargo tankers and petroleum slop tanks, the Petroleum and Explosives Safety Organization/PESO or an authority approved by it shall issue gas free and fit for hot work certificate.

(2) For the purpose of issuing the safe-for-entry and safe-for-hot work permits, inspection shall be carried out by the Safety officer of the Directorate of Industrial Safety and Health/DISH or authorized person of the Directorate of Industrial Safety and Health to ensure the conditions specified under the Fifth Schedule.

(3) In the case of ship recycling process of non - tanker ships, petroleum tankers and slop tankers, the Ship Recyclers shall fulfill the following conditions for safe-for-hot work, namely: —

(a)

Provide portable water hoses with a dedicated water pump with adequate take-off points for attaching additional hoses, for working on the recycling vessel, for immediate water supply in the event of fire, and for wetting the asbestos etc., before its removal from the vessel.

(b)

No naked light or flame or hot work shall be permitted inside a confined space or area, unless it has been made completely free of the flammable material, tested and found safe by a competent person.

(c)

Obtain Naked Light Certificate (Hot Work Permit) as per the rule 68-H of the model rules made under the Factories Act, 1948 (63 of 1948), issued by the relevant authority.

(d)

Keep the area assigned for hot work free from any explosive mixture such that the explosive meter reading is below explosive limit.

(e)

Use only non-sparking tools and flameproof hand lamps protected with guard and safety torches inside such confined space or area for initial inspection, cleaning or other work required to be done for making the area safe.

(f)

Undertake welding, flame cutting and other hot work only on the orders of a competent person after appropriate precautions, as required, are taken to reduce the risk of fire and explosion.

(4) The explosive meter reading of the recycling facility shall be recorded in the work permit by the relevant issuing authority.

(5) Any safe-for-entry or safe-for-hot work certificate or permit shall only be issued by the relevant authorities only after conducting the necessary inspections and satisfying themselves of due compliance of the same, as specified under the Fifth Schedule.

1.The assessee availed Cenvat credit of service tax paid on mobile phone services in respect of the phones used by its own employees and officers. The department sought to deny the benefit on the ground that the phones were not installed in the factory premises and, therefore, could not be treated as input service in terms of the Board’s Circular No. 59/8/2003 dated 20-6-2003. 2.The assessee was exporting some portion of its goods and was availing services of Cargo Handling Agency (CHA). Its claim of Cenvat credit of service tax paid for use of such services was rejected by the department on the ground that services of CHA were engaged in relation to the activity after removal from the factory and in the port area. In the instant appeal, the assessee contended that the definition of ‘input service’ under rule 2(1) is extended one and it includes activities relating to business; that the service of CHA availed by them should be treated as relating to their business activity and, therefore, credit should be extended.

3.The assessee had got certain circles/gardens prepared and put-up signboards for advertising its products. For this purpose, it had availed the services of construction service providers. The assessee claimed construction service as input service and sought credit of service tax paid on such services. The department denied the assessee’s claim on the ground that availing of construction services for the aforesaid purpose could not be treated as part of activity relating to advertising services.

The Tribunal held :

1.In view of decision of the Tribunal in the case of Indian Rayon & Industries Ltd. v. CCE [2007] 6 STT 328 (Mum. - CESTAT), the assessee was eligible to input credit on mobile services.

2.The CHA services availed in respect of export did not have any nexus with the manufacture and clearance of the product from the factory. The business activities, which were sought to be included in the extended definition, could not include the services rendered in the port area. Therefore, the appeal on this aspect was to be rejected.

3.Setting up of circles/gardens away from the factory for the purpose of putting signboards cannot be considered as relating to activity in relation to advertisement. This can lead to a situation where any massive building built away from the factory premises where signboards were also put up can be treated in relation to advertisement of the product. While putting up a signboard is definitely a part of advertisement services, the same cannot be, unrealistically, extended to various activities like setting up circles/gardens with the help of construction service providers. Thus, the Tribunal rejected the assessee’s appeal.

ALLOWABILITY OF PROVISION FOR FORESEEABLE LOSSES UNDER THE MINIMUM ALTERNATE TAX (MAT)

3. Section 115JB of the Act provides for levy of MAT on the 'Book Profits' of a company. In this regard, book profits are to be computed with reference to the profit and loss account prepared in accordance with the provisions of Part-II and Part-III of Schedule VI to the Companies Act and would be subject to adjustments provided for in the Explanation to section 115JB of the Act.

The Explanation 1 to section 115JB of the Act sets out the mechanism for computing the book profits. The Explanation stipulates certain additions and deletions to the net profit to arrive at the book profit. In the current context, clause (c) is relevant, which provides that book profit shall be increased by 'any provision made for meeting liabilities other than ascertained liabilities'.

The issue as to what is a provision made for ascertained liability has been decided in a number of cases. There are several judicial precedents, where the Courts have taken a view (in the context of tax deductibility under section 37 of the Act) that a liability created on the basis of reliable estimates and past experience is an ascertained liability. Reliance in this regard can be placed on the following rulings:

3.1 Rotork Controls India (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2009] 180 Taxman 422 (SC) - In this case in the context of provision for warranty, the Supreme Court held that in this case a contingent liability, for which reliable estimate can be made on the basis of scientific working, is allowable as deduction under section 37 of the Act.

3.2 CIT v. Vinitec Corpn. (P.) Ltd. [2005] 146 Taxman 313 (Delhi) - In this case again in the context of provision for warranty, the Delhi High Court held that provision for warranty created on an acceptable basis was to be allowed as deduction.

3.3 Metal Box Co. of India Ltd. v. Their Workmen [1969] 73 ITR 53 (SC) - In this case, the Supreme Court in the context of provision for gratuity observed that in case a liability is properly ascertained then the same is to be allowed. As mentioned above, this decision of the Supreme Court has been referred to in Jacob Engg. (India) (P.) Ltd.'s case (supra).

3.4 Bharat Earth Movers v. CIT [2000] 245 ITR 428 / 112 Taxman 61 (SC) - In this case, the Supreme Court, in the context of provision for leave encashment created on the basis of a scheme, held that it was eligible for deduction. The Court held that this liability was not a contingent liability as it was capable of being ascertained with a reasonable certainty.

3.5 CIT v. Echjay Forgings (P.) Ltd. [2001] 116 Taxman 322 (Bom.) - In this case, the Mumbai High Court held that the provision for gratuity created on the basis of actuarial valuation could not be regarded as unascertained liability, accordingly, had to be allowed as deduction in computing the book profit.

Further, in the context of MAT computation as well, various judicial precedents have held that provisions which are capable of estimation with a reasonable certainty are allowable, as they are ascertainable and, thus, no adjustment is required for the same while ascertaining 'Book Profit' for MAT computation purposes.

For the purpose of allowability of provision for foreseeable losses under the MAT provisions reference may also be made to the cases of Mazagon Docks Ltd. (supra) and Jacobs Engg. (India) (P.) Ltd. (supra).

In Vedanta Global Ltd. v. CCE 2010 (253) ELT 440 (Trib. - New Delhi) (LB), the Tribunal held that goods like cement and steel items are used for laying ‘foundation’ and for building. ‘Supporting structures’ cannot be treated as either inputs for capital goods or as inputs in relation to the final for capital goods or as inputs in relation to the final products and, therefore, no credit of duty paid on the same can be allowed under the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004.

In Tata Motors Ltd. v. CCE 2010 (252) ELT 265 (Trib. - Kol.), it was held that castable refractory is used for fining of furnace, which gets consumed while melting during the process of manufacture of castings. It is settled that such lining material used in the furnace is clearly an input and credit is available.

In SLR Steels Ltd. v. CCE 2010 (249) ELT 394 (Trib. - Bang.), it is classified in the Explanation 2 to rule 2 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 that the inputs include the goods used in the manufacture of capital goods, which are further used in the factory of manufacturer. In this case, there was no dispute that pollution control equipments and storage tanks were categorized as capital goods in terms of definition in rule 2 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 and that the items in dispute, namely, cement and steel products were used in the construction of the said capital goods. In such circumstances, the said items, namely, cement and steel products were to be treated as inputs in the manufacture of the capital goods, which were, in turn, used within the factory of manufacturer in terms of Explanation to rule 2 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004. Thus, the assessees were entitled to the benefit of CENVAT credit on the said items as inputs and not as capital goods. Hence, the availment of credit on the quantum of cement and steel products used in the manufacture of storage tanks and pollution control equipments was proper and legal and the question of recovery of the credit did not arise.

In Sai Samhita Storages (P.) Ltd. v. CC&CE 2010 (255) ELT 91 (Trib. - Bang.), the appellants were service providers under the category of ‘storage and warehousing services’. They availed CENVAT credit on cement and TMT bars. The department found that the appellants were not eligible to avail CENVAT credit. They issued a show-cause notice for reversal of the amount taken as credit. The appellants contested the same. The lower authority confirmed the demand with interest and also imposed penalties.

The Commissioner (Appeals) rejected the appeal filed by the appellants. The Tribunal held on an analysis of the definition of ‘input’ that it includes goods, which are further used in the factory of the manufacturer. It was argued by the department that the appellants were not a manufacturer. It was undisputed that the appellant were not a manufacturer, but ‘a person’ who was providing output services under the category of ‘Storages and warehouse’ services. It is clear from the definition of the ‘capital goods’ that the credit on the duty paid on tubes and fittings, as well as storage tanks is eligible for availment of CENVAT credit. It was undisputed in this case that the inputs, viz., cement, TNT bars and steel tubes were used for the purpose of construction of storage tanks and for the pipelines for transfer of liquid cargo, and, therefore, the benefit of credit could not be denied to the appellants, as the appellants were using these inputs for manufacture of the capital goods, i.e., storage tanks and pipeline for delivery of the cargo from such storage tank to truck delivery station. The CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 clearly allowed the appellants to take CENVAT credit.

In Vikram Cement v. CCE 2009 (242) ELT 545 (Trib. - Delhi), the Tribunal held that credit on welding electrodes used for repair and maintenance is not available as input.

6. Rate of DDT should not exceed rate specified in Article 10 in India-Germany DTAA: ITAT

Giesecke & Devrient [India] Pvt Ltd. v. ACIT [2020] 120 taxmann.com 338 (Delhi - Trib.)

The issue before the Delhi Tribunal was:

"Whether Assessing Officer (AO) erred in not extending the benefit of applicable Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement between India and Germany (DTAA) qua the rate of tax on payment of dividend to the shareholder?"

The Delhi Tribunal held that there is no dispute that the liability is on the payer company to pay DDT, but, at the same time, we must not lose sight of the fact that dividend distribution tax (DDT) is part of tax as defined in Section 2(43) of the Act. It must be remembered that this additional Income-tax [DDT] levied u/s 115-0 is a tax on income and definition of "Income" includes dividend.

As per the Income-tax Rules, relevant details regarding payment of DDT have to be provided in the Income-tax return form and have to be disclosed in the Tax Audit Return [Form 3CD]. Further, the Income-tax assessment order read with the Income-tax computation form quantifies DDT liability.

It would not be out of place to mention that the Act does not provide for a separate adjudication/passing of separate order with regard to adjudication of liability of DDT.

Further, the generally accepted principles relating to interpretation of treaties in the light of object of eliminating double taxation does not bar the application of tax treaties to DDT. Thus, the DDT levied by the appellant should not exceed the rate specified in Article 10 in India Germany DTAA.

7. Paragraph substituted in a tax treaty is applicable for entire fiscal year & not from date of its notification

Director of Income Tax (International Taxation) v. Autodesk Asia (P.) Ltd. [2020] 120 taxmann.com 324 (Karnataka)

Assessee filed return of income for the Assessment Year 2006-07 by declaring the taxable income as 'NIL'. The case was selected for scrutiny and it was held that software supplied was chargeable to income tax from royalty and technical services.

The instant appeal was filed by the revenue with regard to the rate of tax under the DTAA for Assessment Year 2006-07.

The revenue submitted that the Notification dated 18-7-2005 issued under section 90 came into force with effect from 1-8-2005. With reference to Section 195(1), the rates in force mean the dates on which credit take place in the account and therefore, AO had rightly applied the rate of tax under the Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement (DTAA).

The assessee contended that from the perusal of Article 4 of the Notification, it was evident that paragraph 12 of Article 12 of India-Singapore DTAA has been deleted and has been substituted by the paragraph which provides for levy of tax on the royalties or fees for technical services at the rate not exceeding 10%. Thus, the Tribunal had rightly held that new provision which was in existence shall apply for the entire fiscal year as defined in DTAA.

The Karnataka High Court held that paragraph 2 of Article 12, which provided for levy of tax on royalties or fees for technical services at the rate not exceeding 12% had been deleted and in its place, the provision which provides for levy of tax on the royalties or fees for technical services at the rate not exceeding 10% had been substituted.

Thus, the substitution had the effect of deleting the old rule and making the new rule operative. Therefore, the Tribunal had rightly determined the rate of tax as substituted in clause 2 of article 12 of DTAA for the entire fiscal year as defined in DTAA and was liable to be taxed at 10%.

6.5-1 In Hero Motocorp Ltd. v. CCE 2012 (285) ELT 218 (Tri. - Delhi) - The Tribunal held that on bare reading of Rule 2(k) it was clear that 'input' meant and included accessories of final product cleared along with final product. Rule 138(4)(b) of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1989 made it incumbent on driver of every vehicle to carry the tool kit prescribed by the manufacturer. Since carrying of the tool kit in the vehicle was obligatory for the driver, it could be safely inferred that tool kit was necessary accessory of the motor vehicle because driving of the vehicle without those accessories would be violative of Rule 138(4)(b) of the Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989. Thus, the Tribunal was of the view that the appellants had supplied the tool kit as per the statutory requirements under the Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989 as accessories to be used in relation to the manufacture of vehicle. Thus 'tool kit' was squarely covered by the definition of 'input' under Rule 2(k)(i) of the CENVAT credit Rules and that the appellants had rightly availed of the CENVAT credit in relation to tool kit.

Second-Hand Goods – Import Policy: Second-hand goods are broadly classified based on the type of machinery or equipment and whether they require authorization for import. The DGFT categorizes these goods as follows: 3. Compliance under Customs Law:

Compliance with customs regulations is critical when importing second-hand machinery. The Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC) has issued Circular No. 25/2015-Cus., dated 15-10-2015, providing comprehensive guidelines for the import of used machinery:

The import must be accompanied by an inspection/appraisement report by an overseas chartered engineer or equivalent.

If an overseas report is not available, the importer may obtain a report from any of the DGFT-notified agencies in India, or from a locally empanelled chartered engineer at customs stations.

The value of the machinery will be examined in light of the chartered engineer's report, and any doubts regarding the declared value must be justified by the importer.

In cases where significant differences in value arise, customs officers may apply Rule 12 of the Customs Valuation Rules (CVR), 2007 to determine the correct value.

These stringent customs requirements help ensure that the valuation and condition of second-hand machinery are thoroughly assessed before entry into India.

4. Judicial Pronouncements:

Recent judicial rulings provide clarity on the legal treatment of second-hand machinery imports. Some important cases include:

Ratnamani Metal & Tubes Ltd. v. Commissioner of Customs[2022] 143 taxmann.com 180 (Ahd. - CESTAT): The case concerned the confiscation of second-hand office furniture and equipment imported as part of a manufacturing plant. The customs authority denied clearance, arguing that these items did not qualify as capital goods under the Foreign Trade Policy, 2015-2020. The Tribunal ruled in favor of the appellant, stating that the goods met the definition of capital goods and were eligible for import, setting aside the confiscation order.

Warburg Pincus India (P.) Ltd. v. Commissioner of Customs (Imports), Mumbai [Order No. A/86120/2017-WZB/SMB, dated 28-2-2017] : In this case, the appellant imported second-hand furniture and faced confiscation under Section 111(d) of the Customs Act. The tribunal ruled that the furniture qualified as capital goods, allowing the appellant to import them freely under the EXIM policy, thereby overturning the earlier decision of the Commissioner (Appeals).

5. Conclusion:

The import of second-hand machinery presents a practical and cost-efficient solution for Indian startups. However, it is imperative to comply with the relevant provisions of the Customs Act and DGFT guidelines to avoid potential legal hurdles. 7. In the case of Pratibha Processors v. Union of India AIR 1997 SC 138, in paragraph 13, the Supreme Court has observed : "In fiscal statutes, the import of the words—’tax’, ‘interest’, ‘penalty’, etc., is well known. They are different concepts. ‘Tax’ is the amount payable as a result of the charging provision. It is a compulsory exaction of ‘money by a public authority for public purposes, the payment of which is enforced by law. Penalty is ordinarily levied on an assessee for some contumacious conduct or for a deliberate violation of the provision of the particular statute. Interest is compensatory in character and is imposed on an assessee, who has withheld payment of any tax as and when it is due and payable, the levy of interest is geared to actual amount of tax withheld and the extent of the delay in paying the tax on the due date. Essentially it is compensatory and different from penalty—which is penal in character. Generally levy of interest is automatic, even if the default is due to reasonable cause. While levy of interest is generally automatic, in case of penalty the right of being heard has to be given. Also where penalty is also provided separately for the same default in addition to interest, then generally interest will be compensatory and mandatory.

Similarly, in the case of CCE v. International Auto Ltd. [2010] 24 STT 586 (SC), it was held that when differential duty is paid after date of clearance, it indicates short-payment/short-levy on date of removal and, hence, interest which is for loss of revenue, becomes leviable under section 11AB. In this case the assessee was a supplier of auto parts to manufacturers of motor vehicles. Since price difference arose between price on date of removal and enhanced price at which goods were ultimately sold, department sought to recover interest on differential duty paid by the assessee under section 11AB. It was held that the assessee was liable to pay interest on such differential duty.

SPECIAL SCENARIOS TO WATCH

Inter-Unit Transfers Allowed- Goods can be transferred from one MOOWR unit to another.

Scrap/waste disposal in the domestic market attracts duty; it's waived if exported.

Goods received from SEZs or FTWZs are treated as imports and must follow bonding formalities. Inputs received free of cost must be declared at nominal value and properly recorded.

Goods returning from testing or repairs should be handled as fresh imports or DTA inputs.

CHALLENGES AND FUTURE UNCERTAINTY

While MOOWR is a beneficial scheme, these challenges are hindering its performance.

Complex compliance: Filing multiple BOEs for each DTA sale is time-consuming and complex.

No depreciation is allowed when capital goods are sold in the domestic market—duty is on full import value.

No RODTEP or Drawback: MOOWR-based exports are less competitive given they are not eligible for RODTEP scrips or Drawback. Typically benefits RODTEP and Drawback would be in the range of 4-5% of the value of exported good, which is significant for a lot of exporters.

New concern: The Finance Act 2024 empowered the Government of India to exclude certain goods or operations from the applicability of MOOWR scheme. This adds unpredictability, making long-term planning difficult for businesses relying on this scheme and creating an unease in doing business.

Takeaways

If you are importing raw materials or machinery regularly, consider obtaining a MOOWR license.

Be prepared for higher compliance costs.

Evaluate if loss of RODTEP/Drawback is offset by duty deferment benefits.

MOOWR is one of the most flexible and cash-flow-friendly customs schemes available in India. It's ideal for businesses that import raw material or machinery and sell their finished goods either in domestic market or export market.

Small and Mid-sized manufacturers initially hesitate to register under MOOWR because of compliance worries. But once they set up the systems, the cash flow benefits are too significant to ignore.

4.8 The assessee, an aircraft operator, availed credit of service tax paid/reimbursed to Airport Authority of India for availing of the services of authority such as landing, parking, and x-ray in connection with the operation of the aircraft owned by it. The lower authorities denied said credit on the ground that the services were not connected, directly or indirectly, in or in relation to the manufacture of final products and clearance of final products. In the instant appeal, the assessee contended that the aircrafts were used by its officials as conveyance between its plants and were essential for the business purpose and those services were related to business only. On detailed examination of the definition of ‘input service’, it was found that the definition is in two parts.

Part-I includes the services used by the manufacturer whether directly or indirectly in or in relation to the manufacturing of final products and clearance of final products from the place of removal.

And Part-II includes services used in relation to setting up, modernization, renovation or repairs of a factory premises of provider of output services or an office relating to such factory or premises, advertisement or sales promotion, market research, storage up to the place of removal, procurement of inputs, activities relating to business.

The Tribunal held that the contention of the revenue that the definition of input service is to be read as a whole could not be accepted. Further, in the assessee’s own case in Force Motor Ltd. v. CCE [F.O. A/547/08, dated 11-7-2008], the Tribunal had held that the activities specified after the phrase ‘such as’ are only illustrations and examples and not exhaustive. Therefore, an activity other than those illustrated but related to business will also get covered under the definition of ‘input service’. The assessee was a manufacturing unit and according to the above definition, the use of the phrase ‘such as’ would mean inclusion of an activity which is of a kind as of the illustrations. The main issue to be decided in the case was as to whether the services provided by the authority could form a part of the business activities. It was clear that the aircraft which was stationed at airport was used by the assessee for the business activities and that stand was taken by the assessee before the lower authorities, which was not declined by them. Therefore, it was held that the services rendered by the authority and service tax charged by them would get covered under the definition of ‘input services’ as per the rule 2( l).

What if you could delay paying import duties—and sometimes avoid them completely?

That's the advantage offered by the MOOWR Scheme.

Re-introduced by the Government of India in 2019, the Manufacture and Other Operations in Warehouse Regulations (MOOWR) revamped the 1966 version to align with WTO norms.

Unlike the schemes Advance Authorization (AA), Export Promotion of Capital Goods (EPCG), Export Oriented Unit (EOU), or Special Economic Zone (SEZ), MOOWR does not involve export obligation.

It is suitable for any manufacturer or processor—large or small, domestic or global. There's no restriction on location or investment size.

WHAT MOOWR OFFERS

MOOWR lets manufacturers:

Import capital goods and raw materials without paying customs duty ('duty') upfront

Defer duty on raw materials until finished goods are sold in domestic market.

Save interest: No interest is charged on the deferred customs duty for raw materials component when finished goods are sold in domestic market.

Avoid duty

On raw materials used in finished goods exported

On capital goods re-exported after its lifetime

Defer and avoid duty on waste generated during the manufacture process when the finished goods are sold in domestic market and overseas market respectively.

MOOWR – Case Study

Let's understand MOOWR with a simple illustration before understanding the other nuances.

ABC Technologies obtained MOOWR license in the year 2023. They import sensors for manufacture of finished goods. With MOOWR, they deferred/avoided customs duty.

Machinery

ABC imported machinery worth Rs. 1 crore. Normally, customs duty payable would be Rs. 10 lakhs.

With MOOWR, they paid nothing upfront. They saved Rs. 60k /year in interest—6% of Rs. 10 lakhs.

Ten years later (i.e. after its lifetime), if they export or scrap the machinery, no duty is payable. If sold in India, duty is payable but no interest payable.

Raw material

ABC imported raw material worth Rs. 50 lakhs. No duty was paid at the time of import, though duty payable was Rs. 10 lakhs.

Assuming a timeline of 3 months for conversation of raw material into finished goods and its ultimate sale, interest saving would be at least Rs. 15K —6% * 3* Rs. 10 lakhs/12.

Packing material

ABC imported packaging materials worth Rs. 10 lakhs.

70% of it was used for exported products —no customs duty was paid at the time of import, and such duty shall be waived off upon export.

Customs Duty is payable only on 30% of the packing material used for domestic sales.

More importantly, no interest payable on the Customs Duty payable on the raw materials used manufacture of goods for domestic sales.

Assume a working capital cycle of 3 months, ABC can save interest on packing material worth Rs. 3 lakhs for a period of 3 months.

MOOWR –KEY COMPLIANCE REQUIREMENTS

1.

Import without customs duty- File a bill of entry for warehousing. No duty or IGST is payable upfront.

2.

Manufacture-Use imported and local inputs for manufacture. Pay GST on domestic purchases. Declare input-output norms.

3.

Job Work-Goods can be sent for job work after reaching the MOOWR unit, they must return within 1 year. Tools and molds also can be sent for job work.

4.

Export-Raise GST invoice, e-way bill, and seal goods. Submit export proof within 1 month to the bond officer at jurisdictional customs office.

5.

Sell in India-File bills of entry for home consumption for the raw material component of finished goods.

Example: If inputs consumed in manufacture of finished goods were imported through 5 Bills of Entry (BOE), separate bills of entry for home consumption for such 5 BOE must be filed at the time of sale. This is a huge compliance burden, especially when goods are sourced across multiple consignments.

6.

Records and Compliances

Maintain records for receipt, processing and removal of goods procured

Maintain separate inventory for domestic and imported goods.

Use FIFO method for tracking the goods procured.

Appoint a warehouse keeper who is responsible for day-to-day functioning of the warehouse.

File returns by the 10th of the following month.

SPECIAL SCENARIOS TO WATCH

Inter-Unit Transfers Allowed- Goods can be transferred from one MOOWR unit to another.

Scrap/waste disposal in the domestic market attracts duty; it's waived if exported.

Goods received from SEZs or FTWZs are treated as imports and must follow bonding formalities.

Getting clearance from Committee of Disputes involving inter-departmental litigation is a futile exercise decides the Supreme Court and recalls its earlier orders

In this article, the author has analyzed the Supreme Court’s decision wherein the Court has considered the role of the Committee on Disputes set up by the Government of India for approval of Court cases by this Committee in cases of Public Sector Undertakings and has observed that the objective sought to be achieved by this procedure has not been achieved and the same leads to delays. Hence, the Court has recalled its directions in various orders on this matter. It could be hoped that the Government of India would soon order scrapping of this procedure.

T.N. PANDEY*

Introduction

1. The Supreme Court of India has decided in the case of Electronics Corpn. of India v. UOI [2011] 30 STT 472 that in inter-departmental litigation getting clearance from Committee on Disputes (COD) has not served the objective for which it was introduced and has outlived its utility in the changed scenario and, hence, it has recalled its order in earlier cases requiring COD approval.

Historical background

2. It was decided by the Government of India (GOI) that public sector undertakings of the Central Government and Union of India should not fight their litigation in the Courts. Hence, the Cabinet Secretary, GOI was ‘called upon to handle the matter personally’. Initially, the Committee was called a ‘High Powered Committee’ (HPC).

This was followed by another Committee called ‘Committee of Secretaries’ (COS) and finally christened as ‘Committee on Disputes’ (COD). These Committees were constituted to ensure that resources of the State are not frittered away in intense litigations between the entities of the State which could be best resolved by an empowered Committee - COD. The Committee(s) constituted was/were intended to ensure that no litigation comes to the Court without the parties had an opportunity of conciliation before an in-house Committee. The principle outlined behind the constitution of the Committee was sound, laudatory and unexceptionable. However, over the years, the objective sought to be achieved failed to be realized and led to delays in finalization of disputes. Hence, the entire mechanism in this regard has been reviewed by the Apex Court.

2.1 Facts of the cases before the Supreme Court

(a) Case No. 1 - Electronics Corporation of India Ltd. (‘assessee’ for short) is a Central Government Public Sector Undertaking (‘PSU’). It is registered as a Government company under the Companies Act, 1956. It is under the control of Department of Atomic Energy, Government of India. A dispute had been raised by the Central Government (Ministry of Finance) by issuing show-cause notices to the assessee alleging that the corporation was not entitled to avail/utilize Modvat/Cenvat credit in respect of inputs whose values stood written off. Accordingly, it was proposed in the show-cause notices that the credit taken on inputs was liable to be reversed. Thus, the short point which arose for determination in the present case was whether the Central Government was right in insisting on reversal of credit taken by the assessee on inputs whose values stood written off.

The adjudicating authority held that there was no substance in the contention of the assessee that the write off was made in terms of AS-2. The case of the assessee before the CCE (adjudicating authority) was that it was a financial requirement as prescribed in AS-2; that an inventory more than three years old had to be written off/derated in value; that such derating in value did not mean that the inputs were unfunctionable; that the inputs were still lying in the factory and they were useful for production and, therefore, they were entitled to Modvat/Cenvat credit. As stated above, this argument was rejected by the adjudicating authority and the demand against the assessee stood confirmed. Against the order of the adjudicating authority, the assessee decided to challenge the same by filling an appeal before the CESTAT. Accordingly, the assessee applied before the Committee on Disputes (COD). However, the COD vide its decision dated 2nd Nov., 2006 refused to grant clearance though in an identical case, the COD granted clearance to Bharat Heavy Electricals Ltd. (‘BHEL’). Accordingly, the assessee filed a writ petition in the Andhra Pradesh High Court. The High Court dismissed the petition. Hence, an appeal was filed before the Supreme Court.

CARGO HANDLING SERVICES - SOME ISSUES

In this article, the author has taken up for discussion different issues in respect of cargo handling services with reference to relevant case-laws.

Definition

1. The Cargo handling services have been subjected to service tax by the Finance Act, 2002, with effect from August 16, 2002. Cargo handling service is defined (as substituted by the Finance Act, 2008 with effect from May 16, 2008) under section 65(23) of the Finance Act, 1994 as loading, unloading, and packing or unpacking of cargo and includes—

u Cargo handling services provided for freight in special containers or for non-containerized freight, services provided by a container freight terminal or any other freight terminal, for all modes of transport and cargo handling service incidental to freight; and

u Service of packing together with transportation of cargo or goods, with or without one or more of other services like loading, unloading, and unpacking

but does not include handling of export cargo or passenger baggage or mere transportation of goods.

The taxable service in relation to cargo handling has been defined under section 65(105)(zr ) as a service provided or to be provided to any person, by a cargo handling agency in relation to cargo handling services.

Exclusion

2. The CBEC Instruction lr. No. F. No. B11/1/2002-TRU, dated August 1, 2002 also indicated that the following services are excluded from the tax net—

u Services provided in relation to export cargo;

u Passenger baggage;

u Mere transportation of goods;

u Services provided in relation to storage of agriculture produce or for goods meant to be stored in cold storage;

u All the services in relation to handling of goods would be appropriately covered under port service and no separate levy will be attracted under cargo handling service;

u Marketing or canvassing for cargo for airlines;

u Service or auction of abandoned cargo;

u Handling of empty containers.

Issues

3. Nearly nine case-laws with different points are covered under the cargo handling services. Those are discussed as under:

u Ridhi Sidhi Transport v. CCE, Belgaum [2009] 18 STT 484 (Bang. - CESTAT) : The appellants had to provide cargo handling services in terms of the agreement entered into by them with Grasim Industries. The receipt for the services is given in the letter of Grasim to the appellants. In terms of the said agreement, the amount to be paid was split up into three categories, viz., rake handling (consisting of loading and unloading expenses) at Rs. 20 per M.T., local transportation charges (from yard to godown) at Rs. 53 per MT and service charges of Rs. 4 per MT. It was the contention of the appellants that the rake handling charges of Rs. 20 per MT were not liable for service tax. The Tribunal held that the contention did not appear to be correct because in terms of the Finance Act, Cargo handling means loading, unloading, packing or unpacking cargo, etc., for all modes of transport. When loading and unloading are integral parts of cargo handling services and when the gross receipt includes the said charges, there is no question of claiming any abatement or arguing that the same is not taxable under the category of ‘Cargo handling service’. The Tribunal held that the appellants did not have a case on merit.

u In re, Bharat Haribhau Salunke [Orders-in-Appeal Nos. PII/PAP/83-88 (Pn.) of 2008, dated 18-6-2008] : The appellant was transporting sugar from sugar house to godown within the factory. It was held that mere transportation of goods is excluded from cargo handling service. Transportation inside the factory is not considered as cargo handling service.

Activity of stitching of sugar bags is not related to loading, unloading, packing or unpacking of goods. Sugar bags cannot be considered as cargo. Impugned activity is not covered under ‘Cargo handling service’. Show-cause notice was issued and confirmed mechanically.

Cargo means goods carried by sea, road or air. Bagasee being residual waste of sugarcane and used as fuel for stream generation cannot be considered as cargo.

Press mud is held as not marketable and non-excisable by the Supreme Court in CCE v. Titawi Sugar Complex 2003 (152) ELT 21. Press mud cannot be considered as goods. Activity of handling press mud is not falling under cargo handling service.

(supra) has expressed that marketability is a decisive test for durability. It only means ‘saleable’ or ‘suitable for sale’. It need not be, in fact, marketed. The article should be capable of being sold or being sold to consumers in the market, as it is without anything more. In the absence of a finding, that the goods are ‘marketable’, i.e., saleable or suitable for sale, it could not be said to be a good, which may be subject to excisability.

The Apex Court in the case of Union of India v. Indian Aluminium Co. Ltd. 1995 (58) ECR 612 has reiterated that marketability is a question of fact to be decided on the facts of each case. It was held that it may be possible to recover something from a particular thing, they can, therefore, be sold but that does not make them a marketable commodity. In other words, everything, which is sold, is not necessarily a marketable commodity as known to the commercial world and, it may be worthwhile to trade in. Since marketability test is essentially a question of fact - Hindustan Zinc Ltd. v. CCE 2005 (181) ELT 170 (SC), there must be some serious attempts to go to market and collect proper evidences, but it cannot be established on basis of mere stability. Sufficient proof that product is commercially known is required - Gujarat Nermada Valley Fert. Co. Ltd. v. CCE 2005 (184) ELT 128 (SC) which could not be viewed through a hawker’s eye - Mahindra & Mahindra Ltd. v. CCE 2005 (190) ELT 301 (Trib. - LB) unless the product is capable of being marketed and is known to those who are in the market, as having an identity as a distinct identifiable commodity, that the article is subject to excise duty. Fact that articles fall within Schedule, not make them marketable. Actual sale is not necessary but article must be capable of being sold in market or known in market as good - Gujarat Nermada Valley Fert. Co. Ltd.’s case (supra ). Actual purchase and sale, or fact of their being marketed or their general availability in market is not required to be proved- Mahindra & Mahindra Ltd.’s case (supra).

Article is not eligible to be taxed only because it is having saleable value. CCE v. Indian Aluminium Co. Ltd. 2006 (203) ELT 3 (SC). Mention of an item in an exemption notification is not determinative of its excisability. New Shorrock Mills v. CCE 2006 (202) ELT 192 (Trib. - LB); Indore Wire Co. Ltd. v. Union of India 2006 (203) ELT 179 (SC). Mere listing of an item in the Schedule to the Act is not sufficient to make it excisable - Ahmedabad Electricity Co. Ltd.’s case (supra). Mere mention of item in ISI is also not sufficient - Tata Iron & Steel Co. Ltd. v. Union of India 2004 (164) ELT 372 (SC).

Once marketability of an article is established, the fact that it is not actually sold but is entirely consumed captively or that it is sold only to one or two buyers has no relevance. However, mere manufacturing activity by itself, does not prove marketability. Inter-unit transfer of an item does not prove its marketability. Product produced must be a distinct commodity known in common parlance to commercial community for the purpose of buying and selling - Cipla Ltd. v. CCE 2008 (225) ELT 403 (SC).

Accordingly, articles like storage units, running counters, wall and kitchen units normally not capable to be removed without cannibalizing, are not furniture and not excisable goods - Craft Interiors (P.) Ltd. v. CCE 2006 (203) ELT 529 (SC). The goods, which are removed and used for mandatory quality control test and are destroyed during such test, cannot be considered as amounting to removal and as such do not fall under category of ‘excisable goods’ - CCE v. Tarco Cable Co. Ltd. 2001 (127) ELT A49 (SC). Intellectual property or information technology being an intangible asset if once put on a paper, cassette, diskettes or any other thing to supply the same, fall under the category of ‘excisable goods’ just like drawings, designs, manuals and technical materials - Associated Cement Companies Ltd. v. CCE 2001 (128) ELT 21 (SC).

(6) If the head room in the hold of a ship for the purpose of stacking and unstaking is less than 1.5 metres, suitable measures shall be taken to guard against accidents.

(7) Loads shall be safely slung before being hoisted. Loose dunnage or debris hanging or protruding from loads shall be removed and suitable means shall be adopted to prevent cargo from falling out.

(8) Cargo-handling bridles, such as pallet bridles, which are to remain attached to the lifting appliance while hoisting successive sling loads, shall be attached by shackles, or other positive means shall be taken to prevent them from becoming accidentally disengaged from the hook of the lifting appliance.

(9) When lifting appliance is operating without a load on the slings—

(a)

slings or chains shall be hooked securely to the appliances before the operators are given signal to move;

(b)

sharp hooks, multiple hooks and claws shall not hang at one end but shall be reeved through slings; and

(c)

the operators shall raise the appliance sufficiently to keep clear off dock workers and objects.

(10) Effective measures shall be taken, by the use of suitable packing or otherwise, to prevent edges of any load from coming into contact with any rope or chain sling which is likely to cause any damage to the rope or chain sling.

(11) Buckets, tubs and similar appliances shall not be loaded above their rims.

(12) No loads shall be lifted at strappings unless such strappings are approved as proper and safe slinging points. Movement of such loads is allowed only if everybody has left the danger zone.

(13) When working with lifting appliances, slopepulling, horizontal dragging and intentional swing of loads and lifting devices are prohibited.

Conclusion

3. From the above-mentioned cases, it is clear that lower authorities and Tribunals are still puzzled with the issue at hand. The problem that has persisted is that lower authorities have decided similar cases by assuming wrong grounds14. They have decided the cases holding that since there is no mens rea, such people cannot be held liable for payment of duty under section 11AB the issue which is still res integra, but actually they should have held that since there is no short payment, hence, there is no liability under section 11AB. The recent decision of Hon’ble High Court of Mumbai has given timely relief and has shown path to be followed by lower authorities. But let’s see how long the decision still holds good.

Section 65(105)(j) - Clearing and forwarding agents’ services v. Consignment agent

4.3 The assessee had entered into contracts with two steel companies, the TISCO and TRL. As per the said contract the assessee was to take delivery of the steel materials on behalf of the TISCO and TRL from the railway siding. Thereafter, it was to transport said materials to its own premises/godown and sort and stock said materials after weighment in accordance with instructions of the company’s representative. The assessee was to further arrange for and to take all necessary steps for safe custody and protection of steel materials and was to nominate a hub manager in its premises. Further, it had to deliver materials to company’s customers on production of delivery orders and if the hub manager required, the materials would be loaded on the transport vehicles, etc., of the customer or as nominated by the company. The assessee was to bear all the expenses since time of receipt of materials at its premises till these were dispatched and in case of failing to account for the stock, it was liable for consequences. The assessee received consideration of certain sum which comprised of consignment agent service receipts, and receipts towards reimbursement of expenditure, bending and bundling charges and stock verification charges from the said companies in respect of services rendered. The revenue issued a show-cause notice (SCN) on 13-9-2004 and demanded service tax from the assessee for the period 1-9-1999 to 31-3-2004 by stating that services provided by the assessee to its clients fell under the category of ‘Clearing and forwarding agent’. On non-compliance of same the revenue confirmed service tax liability upon the assessee along with penalty and interest. In the instant appeal, the assessee contended that it had acted as a consignment agent which activity was not covered under ‘Clearing and forwarding agent’s service’ and, therefore, it was not liable to pay service tax.

The Tribunal held that according to the Finance Act, 1994, imposing service tax on certain taxable services, any service provided or to be provided by a ‘Clearing and forwarding agent’ to a ‘client’ in relation to ‘Clearing and forwarding operations’ ‘in any manner’ shall be taxable service under section 65(105)(j). Incidence of levy is on the service of ‘Clearing and forwarding operations’, provided measure of tax is ‘value’ of such service. Thus, service provided by a ‘Clearing and forwarding agent’ to his client directly or indirectly in any manner gives rise to a taxable event, provided the service so rendered is ‘Clearing and forwarding operation’. Levy is attracted when there is provision of service: (a) of clearing and forwarding operations; (b) by a ‘Clearing and forwarding agent’; (c) to a client; (d) directly or indirectly; and (e) in any manner.

• Even where a subsidiary company amalgamates with its holding company, in order to obtain a tax neutral treatment of the amalgamation in the hands of such shareholder (i.e. holding company), there was a requirement to issues of shares to shareholders of the amalgamating company (i.e. the subsidiary), which was impossible to achieve as the holding company could not issue shares to itself. • Sectorial restrictions on business of Venture Capital Undertaking ('VCU') to claim exemption from income by VCF or VCC have been done away with i.e. 'pass through' status is accorded for all investments by VCF or VCC;

Share premium in excess of Fair Market Value ('FMV') to be treated as income

• It is proposed that if any consideration received for issue of shares is in excess of face value of shares, then the consideration exceeding FMV of the shares shall be chargeable to income tax under the head 'Income from other sources'.

• The FMV shall be higher of the following:

- FMV as per the prescribed guidelines; or

- FMV as may be substantiated by the issuing company

• This provision is proposed to be applicable only for companies in which public are not substantially interested (i.e. closely held companies). Further, this provision is not applicable to venture capital undertaking, with respect to shares issued to Venture Capital Company / fund.

Jindal Steel & Power Ltd. 2014 (300) ELT 401 (Tri. Delhi) the assessee was engaged in the manufacture of iron and steel. They filed a refund claim on the ground that they had paid excess duty at the time of clearances and that they were required to pay duty on such structural materials issued for captive consumption at 110% of the cost of the goods as per rule 8 of the Central Excise Valuation (Determination of Rules). They also submitted CAS-4 cost certificate issued by the Cost Accountant certifying the cost of goods. The Adjudicating Authority reflected the claim on the grounds including infirmities in the cost certificate and doctrine of unjust enrichment. The Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the appeal before the Tribunal. The Tribunal held that Revenue was not disputing the CAS-4 Certificate adopted by the assessee for the payment of duty. However, certain minor discrepancies were being pointed out by the Revenue at the time of grant of refund. The assessee was adopting the price of Rs.18,811.29 per metric ton for payment of duty on their final product. Same cost had to be adopted for the refund purpose also. The Tribunal upheld the findings of the Commissioner. 5.4 In CCE v. Balaji Cylinders (P.) Ltd. 2014 (304) ELT 84 (Mad.) the High Court held that section 11B of the Central Excise Act, 1944 provided that any person claiming refund of any duty of excise and interest, if any, paid on such duty was required to make an application for refund of such duty and interest, if any, paid on such duty, before expiry of one year from the relevant date in such form and manner as prescribed. However, stipulation of one year would not apply where any duty and interest, if any, had been paid under protest. In the instant case, at the request of the assessee, the assessment was final and not provisional. Thus, the period of limitation would be one year from the relevant assessment year to be counted from the date of final assessment year. The final assessment was made in 1998, claim for refund was filed in May, 2001 and held to be wholly barred by limitation.

Madura Coats Ltd. 2014 (301) ELT 161 (SC)the controversy in the present appeal pertained to the refund of the excess differential amount recovered by the respondent-assessee from the excise department to the consumers. The issue that arose for consideration was, whether the respondent-assessee had indeed recovered the excess amount from the consumers. Insofar as the instant aspect of the matter was concerned, the Supreme Court was satisfied that there was no question of assessee having recovered the excess amount from the consumers. This was because the assessee throughout asserted that so far as the Tyre Cord Fabrics were concerned, the duty payable was under Heading 59.02 of the classification effective from 01.08.1986 whereunder only basic excise duty was payable. In view of the above, it was obvious that the assessee did not recover any duty from the consumers under the Heading No. 59.09 at least till the show cause notice was issued on 25.02.1983. Accordingly, whatever amount was recovered from the assessee by the appellants could not be refunded to the consumers. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal filed by the Department.

5.6 In Union of India v. N.G. Thakkar & Sons 2014 (301) ELT 229 (Bom.) the issue to be considered by the Court was whether the incidence of duty was borne by customers. The auditors of the assessee certified that the sale price as recorded in commercial invoices did not include the Central Excise duty element. There was no fault found by Revenue in that certificate. The claim of the assessee that upward revision was the price of compounded asafetida cleared during the relevant period was not on account of inclusion of excise duty element but on account of increase in the price of raw materials used in the production of compounded asafetida had been verified by Commissioner of Central Excise (Appeals). The Tribunal's decision that the central duty had not been passed on to the customers was upheld by the High Court.

FACT: The assessee was engaged in the manufacture and sale of different varieties of metallic wires and in the course of such manufacturing activity, waste material, viz., scrap metal, was obtained. The assessee's claim for deduction under section 80HH in respect of profits attributable to sale proceeds of scrap and drums and value of scrap at close of the accounting year was rejected by the ITO on the ground that the impugned profits could not be said to have been derived from the industrial undertakings. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the assessee's claim on the ground that scrap metal was a direct offshoot of the manufacturing activity of the assessee and eventually it could not be put into a different category other than the one from which the main product was derived. On appeal, the revenue contended, inter alia, that sections 41(1) and 41(2) were applicable to profits derived from sale of scrap metal and drums.

HELD: Section 41(1 ) brings to tax certain amounts by a fiction of law. Therefore, the operation of such fiction should be limited to the language of the section. Where the assessee has incurred a loss or expenditure or trading liability and this trading liability has been allowed as deduction in an earlier year and something has later on been recovered in respect of such liability or such liability has either been remitted or has ceased to exist, section 41( 1) comes into operation. But according to the facts in the present case, nothing happened as contemplated by section 41(1) . Sale proceeds derived were for the sale of the particular product and not recoupment of earlier purchase. Accordingly, section 41(1) had no application to the facts of the instant case.

Further, the particular receipt under consideration is, insofar as scrap was concerned, realisation from the sale of waste material from manufacturing activity of the assessee-company and it was not a receipt from the sale of some of its old machinery, plant or building resulting in balancing charge as contemplated under section 41(2) . Therefore, section 41( 2) also had no application to the facts of the instant case as far as scrap was concerned. The section could be attracted insofar as the sale price of drums was concerned.

In fact, the assessee was entitled to deduction in respect of profits and gains from newly established industrial undertaking as contemplated under section 80HH in relation to profits from sale of scrap since this scrap, being a waste product which had a commercial value, was directly derived from the industrial undertaking which the assessee was carrying on and was sold in the normal course of running the industrial undertaking.

7. The next point in this appeal relates to deduction allowable under section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 ('the Act'), in respect of, profits attributable to sale proceeds of scrap and drums. The learned departmental representative submitted that the Commissioner (Appeals) erred in holding that the assessee is entitled to deduction under section 80HH in respect of profits attributable to sale proceeds of scrap and drums and value of stock at close of the accounting year.

8. The assessee is a domestic company in which the public are not substantially interested. Its main activity was manufacture and sale of super-enamelled aluminium, copper wire and DPC wires. The assessee claimed a deduction of Rs. 46,393 under section 80HH, being 20 per cent of Rs. 2,31,963 in the revised return filed. This deduction was claimed as allowable on the profits and gains derived from the industrial under- taking. According to the ITO, it was seen from the profit and loss account that the profits and gains include a sum of Rs. 93,948 (Rs. 92,367—sale of scrap and drums, and Rs. 1,581—value of scrap at close), which, according to the ITO, cannot be said to have been derived from the industrial undertaking. The ITO, in arriving at this conclusion, drew support from the decision of the Supreme Court in Cambay Electric Supply Industrial Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1978] 113 ITR 84 and the decision in the case of CIT v. Cochin Refineries Ltd. [1982] 135 ITR 278 (Ker.). Accordingly, he came to the conclusion that the sum of Rs. 28,410 alone is allowable as deduc-tion on the profits and gains of Rs. 1,47,051 being 20 per cent thereof.

9. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals), considering the nature of the business carried on by the assessee, came to the conclusion that the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of Cambay Electric Supply Industrial Co. Ltd. (supra) and that of the Kerala High Court in the case of Cochin Refineries Ltd. ( supra), will not stand in the way in arriving at the conclusion that the scrap metal is a direct offshoot of the manufactur-ing, activity of the assessee and, eventually, it cannot be put into a different category other than the one from which the main product is derived. Accordingly, he held as under:

"I am, therefore, of the considered opinion that in the appellant's case, the realisations from the waste material like scrap metal and empty drums, etc., will have to be construed as income derived from the industrial under- taking and the Income-tax Officer is, accordingly, directed to take that also into account for the purpose of allowing relief under section 80HH. In passing, however, I may mention that in any event, the Income-tax Officer is certainly not right in excluding the entire sale proceeds from the purview of relief under section 80HH as if it represented net profits. If At all the receipts under this category are to be held as not eligible for the said relief, then the Income-tax Officer should ascertain the net profit relatable to these receipts and not the gross receipts to deny the claim."

Aggrieved, the department is in appeal before us challenging the order passed by the Commissioner (Appeals).

10. The fact remains that the ITO, while admitting that the assessee is entitled to allowance under section 80HH, has excluded a sum of Rs. 93,948, being the sale proceeds of scrap metal and some empty drums credited to the profit and loss account on the ground that this cannot be said to be income derived from the industrial undertaking. The contention of the learned counsel appearing for the assessee was that profit from the sale of scrap metal and empty drums also was derived from the activity carried on by the assessee-company and formed part of the overall profit, and, therefore, it should also be considered as eligible for relief under section 80HH.

FACT: The petitioner-company, which was carrying on the business of manufacturing and sale of beedies, set up a factory in a backward area. Petitioner questioned the issue of notices contending that they lacked jurisdiction inasmuch as the facts had been disclosed before the assessments were made.

On petition :

HELD: Sub-section (2) of section 80HH lays down certain conditions, one of which is that the industrial undertaking should manufacture or produce articles in any backward area and another condition is that it should employ 10 or more workers in the manufacturing process carried on with the aid of power. It was not the case of the revenue that any of these conditions were not fulfilled. Their only case was that the entire manufacturing activity from beginning to end was not carried on in the backward area and an initial part of it had been entrusted to the contractors who carried on that part of the activity outside the backward area. The contention, therefore, was that the profit shown as the profit of the industrial undertaking in the backward area might actually include a small part of the profit derived from activity outside the backward area and, therefore, there was inflation of the profit and consequentially inflation of the deduction claimed by the assessee, that could be withdrawn by reopening the assessment. [Para 5]

HEADNOTE: Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from hotels or industrial undertaking, etc., in backward areas - Assessment year 1994-95 - Assessee, engaged in running of steel and iron re-rolling mill, derived income from sale of brass scrap which he obtained from dismantling certain guns purchased in auction and which could not be used for re-rolling - He claimed deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I on such income which was denied as it was not considered as income arising from industrial undertaking - Assessee had stated that he dealt in steel scrap and was not aware that inside guns, there was brass scrap which was removed - Thus, it was only a fortuitous circumstance that, in relevant assessment year, assessee had purchased guns without knowledge that brass scrap was inside them which was separated and it could not be said to be a by-product obtained in process of manufacture - Whether since brass was not an essential raw material of industrial unit, in question and brass was not at all connected with steel re-rolling, there was no nexus between brass scrap obtained on dismantling of guns and main activity of assessee of steel re-rolling and, therefore, separation of brass could not be said to be in process of manufacture or a product or by-product of activity of assessee’s industrial undertaking - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, profit on sale of brass scrap could not be said to be profit and gain derived from industrial undertaking so as to be entitled to deduction under sections 80HHC and 80-I - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee, engaged in the manufacture of re-rolled products of iron and steel in his re-rolling mill, filed his return of income which was accepted as such. In the course of the survey conducted under section 133A, the assessee had offered to pay tax on Rs. 10 lakhs. When required to explain the surrender, the assessee submitted that he had purchased certain guns in auction and certain quantity of brass scrap was obtained from breaking and dismantling those guns and the balance was iron scrap. It was contended that the said activity tantamounted to production of goods and, hence, income from industrial undertaking. The Assessing Officer, however, did not consider the income from sale of brass scrap as arising from industrial undertaking for purposes of allowing deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I and allowed the claim only in respect of other income. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) accepted the assessee’s submission. On revenue’s appeal, the Tribunal reversed the impugned order and allowed the revenue’s appeal. It accepted the plea that the assessee had purchased guns and the income from brass scrap which could not be used for re-rolling, thus, was not entitled to deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I.

On appeal to the High Court :

HELD: The assessee in his explanation had stated that he dealt in steel scrap and was not aware of the fact that inside the guns, there was brass scrap which was removed. Thus, it was clear from the reply that brass was not an ingredient used in the process of manufacture in industrial undertaking of the assessee. The brass scrap had no direct nexus with the appellant’s industrial undertaking. It could not be said that brass scrap was a profit or gain which directly flowed, neither it had close connection with undertaking of the assessee. By removal of brass scrap which was not useful for steel rerolling work no different and distinct article came into existence, it was only incidental as was apparent from the assessee’s reply. [Paras 13 and 14]

Further, composition of brass scrap was not at all changed, that was only removed as that was not useful to the assessee for the activity of manufacturing which he was carrying on. It was only a fortuitous circumstance that in the relevant assessment year, the assessee had purchased the guns without the knowledge that brass scrap was inside them which was separated and it could not be said to be a by-product obtained in the process of manufacture. There was no nexus between brass and activity of steel rerolling. Brass was not at all an input in the process of manufacture of steel rerolling. It was not a raw material at all for the process of rerolling in which the assessee was involved. It was purely incidental that brass was found inside guns which were purchased in that year. Guns might have several components, sometimes brass or some other articles which may not be connected at all with the manufacturing process of the industrial undertaking. [Paras 22, 23, 24 and 25]

FACT: The assessee firm was in the business of ship-breaking. The assessee’s business consisted of breaking ships and obtaining metal which was later on sold in the market. For the assessment year 1988-89 the assessee’s claims under sections 80HH and 80-I were rejected on the grounds that business of ship breaking did not amount to manufacture or production of an article or a thing and secondly that the assessee had succeeded to the business on retirement of one of the partners and, hence, it was a business formed by reconstruction of a business already in existence.

On second appeal :

HELD: In the light of the decision of the Bombay Court in the case of Ship Scrap Traders (supra) which was delivered after considering the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of CIT v. N.C. Budharaja & Co. [1993] 204 ITR 412/170 Taxman 312, the assessee was to be held as a manufacturer of an article or thing and deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I could not be denied on the ground that they did not manufacture new article or thing.

The contention of the learned counsel appearing for the assessee was that profit from the sale of scrap metal and empty drums also was derived from the activity carried on by the assessee-company and formed part of the overall profit, and, therefore, it should also be considered as eligible for relief under section 80HH. 11. The point for consideration in this appeal is whether the assessee is entitled to relief under section 80HH on profits attributable to sale value of scrap and drums. According to section 80HH, where the gross total income of an assessee includes any profits or gains 'derived from' an industrial undertaking, or the business of a hotel, to which the section applies, there shall, in accordance with and subject to the provisions of the section, be allowed, in computing the total income of the assessee, a deduction from such profits and gains of an amount equal to 20 per cent thereof. The assessee-company was manufacturing super- enamelled aluminium, copper wires and DPC wires in respect of which the turnover of Rs. 56.68 lakhs was accounted and under miscellaneous receipts was registered sale of scrap of Rs. 75,665 and drums of Rs. 16,702, aggregating to Rs. 92,367. The value of stock of scrap was Rs. 1,581. According to the learned counsel appearing for the assessee, the main activity of the assessee being manufacture and sale of different varieties of metallic wires, it is in the course of the manufacturing activity that scrap metal was obtained. The scrap metal, he stated, is the direct outcome from the materials used in the manufacture of different varieties of metallic wires. Therefore, this amounts, if nothing else, to a by-product of the main product manufactured. Therefore, the scrap metals being directly derived from the industrial undertaking which was earned on by the assessee, profit derived from the sale therefrom would qualify for relief under section 80HH. Adverting to the drums, it was stated they were purchased for storing water and were sold when they became useless.

12. There is the judgment of the Supreme Court in the case of Cambay Electric Supply Industrial Co. Ltd. (supra ). In the said judgment, there was an observation to the effect that the expression 'attributable to' occurring in section 80E of the Act is certainly wider in import than the expression ‘derived from’. It was also pointed out therein that had the expression ‘derived from’ been used, it could have, with some force, been contended that a balancing charge arising from the sale of old machinery and build-ings cannot be regarded as profits and gains derived from the conduct of the business of generation and distribution of electricity. Taking a clue from the abovesaid observation, the learned departmental representative pointed out that inasmuch as the words 'derived from' are used in section 80HH, it will mean only direct receipts from a business of specified nature but does not include receipts which have no direct link with the business. Accord-ingly, the expression 'derived from', as occurring in section 80HH, will have a restricted meaning, whereby profit from the sale proceeds of the scrap metal obtained by the assessee in manufacturing various metallic wires cannot be considered as 'derived from' the manufacturing activity of the assessee.

13. The learned departmental representative also drew support from the decision of the Kerala High Court in Cochin Refineries Ltd.'s case (supra), wherein the Kerala High Court followed the decision of the Supreme Court in Cambay Electric Supply Industrial Co. Ltd.'s case (supra). In Cochin Refineries Ltd.'s case (supra), the Kerala High Court held as under:

". . . the words 'derived from' in section 80J of the Act cannot have a wide import so as to include any income which can in some manner be attributed to the business. The derivation of the income must be directly connected with the business in the sense that the income is generated by the business. It would not be sufficient if it is generated by the exploita- tion of a business asset. . . ." (p. 279)

HEADNOTE: Section 80HHC of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from industrial undertakings in backward area - Assessee-company had set up an industrial undertaking in a backward area and was carrying on business of manufacture and sale of V-belts, oil seals, O-rings, rubber moulded products, etc. - Whether profits and gains from sale of scrap material resulting in manufacturing process were eligible for deduction in an amount equal to 20 per cent under section 80HH, since scrap materials came within manufacturing process of industrial undertaking set-up by assessee - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company, carrying on the business of manufacture and sale of V-belts, oil seals, O-rings, rubber moulded products, etc., set-up an industrial undertaking in a backward area. It claimed deduction of 20 per cent of net profits allowable under section 80HH in respect of profit on sale of scrap which resulted in the manufacturing process. The ITO disallowed that claim. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the assessee's claim. On further appeal, the Tribunal reversed the Commissioner (Appeals)'s order.

On reference :

HELD: Section 80HH is meant to give a tax rebate to certain categories of assessees and one, who wants to claim such a relief, must strictly satisfy the requirements prescribed therein. He must establish that his profits and gains are derived from his industrial undertaking or the business of hotel. Axiomatic proposition of law is that it is not sufficient if a commercial connection is established between the profits earned and the industrial undertaking and the law requires that such profits must have been derived from the industrial undertaking. The industrial undertaking itself must be the source of that profit. The business of the industrial undertaking must strictly yield that profit. It must be the direct source of profit and not a means to earn any other profit.

In the instant case, in the industrial undertaking for the manufacture of V-belts, oil seals, O-rings and rubber moulded products, certain scrap materials resulted, which had a saleable value. To say that the scrap materials had no direct link or nexus with the industrial undertaking, could not at all be expected to commend acceptance, especially, on the facts and in the circumstances of the instant case. The scrap materials came within the manufacturing process of the industrial undertaking in the manufacture of certain products such as V-belts, oil seals, O-rings and certain rubber moulded products, etc. In that view of the matter, profits and gains from the sale of scrap materials were eligible for deduction in an amount equal to 20 per cent under section 80HH, inasmuch as such gains or profits were derived from the industrial undertaking and includible in the gross total income of the assessee and the question relatable to the profit on the sale of scrap was answered in favour of the assessee.
