Section 251, read with section 80HH, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Commissioner (Appeals) - Powers of - Assessment year 1980-81 - Whether on facts stated under ‘Deductions - Profits and gains from industrial undertakings, etc., in backward areas’, amplitude of power of AAC being as extensive as that of ITO, it was well within his powers to have allowed assessee to raise its claim for deduction under section 80HH and further directing ITO to examine case and allow that claim to extent admissible under law - Held, yes

FACT: The AAC accepted the assessee’s submission that it had not made a claim before the ITO for deduction under section 80HH as, according to the computation made by the assessee in its return, the income was not sufficient to absorb the deduction, but in view of the disallowance made by the ITO, there was scope for that deduction to be absorbed and, therefore, the assessee should be permitted to make its claim for that deduction. The ITO was directed to consider that claim and allow the claim to the extent admissible in law. The Tribunal upheld the AAC’s order.

On reference :

HELD: By the order of the AAC, the interest of the revenue was not in anyway prejudiced. The assessee was not conferred any undue benefit. The assessee was merely enabled to obtain a benefit which the law conferred. The reason for not making the claim for deduction in the original return had been found to be bona fide and for an acceptable reason.

The amplitude of the power of the AAC is as extensive as that of the ITO. It was, therefore, well within his powers to have allowed the assessee to raise its claim for deduction under section 80HH and further directing the ITO to examine the case and allow that claim to the extent admissible in law.

The Assessing Officer was not justified in disregarding the assessee’s request for consideration of the claim by merely showing that it was not a mistake apparent from record. The cause for action for claiming the relief had resulted from the order passed by the Assessing Officer under section 154. The Apex Court in the case of Anchor Pressings (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1986] 161 ITR 159 had laid down the test for allowing relief whether claimed or not and that test is that there must be precise factual material and clear data on the record sufficient to enable the ITO to consider whether the relief should be granted or not. In the instant case, it had, therefore, to be seen whether there was precise factual material and clear data on record or not for allowing relief under section 80HH. There was no doubt that the assessee was an industrial undertaking. There was also no doubt that in the earlier assessment years it had been granted relief under section 80J which meant that all the conditions as laid down under section 80J(4) stood fulfilled. Those conditions are in pari materia with the conditions laid down in section 80HH(2). Even for the assessment year under consideration, the assessee had claimed relief under section 80J which was allowed by the Assessing Officer. The only distinguishing feature between sections 80HH and 80J appeared to be that the industrial undertaking in respect of relief under section 80HH should be located in a backward area. The assessee had demonstrated that it got central subsidy precisely because the industrial undertaking was located in a backward area. The amount of capital subsidy received was reflected in the balance sheet as on 31-8-1982 and in the balance sheet of the immediately preceding year. The Assessing Officer had allowed depreciation on the actual cost/WDV of assets after reducing the amount of capital subsidy from the cost of the assets. All this clearly showed that the assessee’s industrial undertaking was located in a backward area. All these indicia clearly showed that the assessee was entitled to relief under section 80HH and the precise factual material and clear data was, therefore, available on record.

Under the Income-tax Act, the Assessing Officer has to compute the income according to the provisions of law. Section 80HH is part of the Act. It is true that there is an obligation on the part of the assessee also to claim a particular relief or deduction, but the Assessing Officer has also a duty to see that if through inadvertence or otherwise a particular relief which is otherwise admissible to the assessee has been omitted to be claimed, it should be allowed to the assessee.

In the instant case, the claim for relief under section 80HH surfaced only when the Assessing Officer passed the consequential order on 24-11-1988. The assessee thereupon filed an application under section 154 and also an appeal against the said order. Under the circumstances, this was all what the assessee could do. Since the precise factual material and clear data for getting the necessary relief under section 80HH were available on record. the Assessing Officer could not throw away the assessees application for rectification. The revenue authorities were, therefore, not justified in rejecting the claim of the assessee. Accordingly. the assessee’s application under section 154 did lie in the instant case. The Assessing Officer was, therefore, directed to consider the assessee claim under section 80HH as per the provisions of law.

"Deduction u/s. 80HH:

The company has claimed relief under section 80HH on account of the situation of the Century Cement in backward area. Section 80HH provides for deduction in respect of profits and gains from newly established industrial undertakings in backward areas subject to fulfilment of the conditions specified therein. The authorities had not come to the conclusion that the assessee did not fulfil the said conditions, as in view of their decision, the said question did not arise for consideration. The Tribunal, proceeded on the basis that the end-product of the assessee would not be an article.

An article would, inter alia, mean a particular object or substance, a material, thing or a class of things, material or tangible object.

Nobody manufactures a dam or a tunnel. A dam or tunnel is constructed, but the question, which arose for consideration, was although a tunnel or a dam would not be an article, which is capable of being manufactured, but whether the intermediate products may be considered to come within the purview of manufacturing activity/industrial undertaking within the meaning thereof. The question, which had not been gone into by the Tribunal was, if at all the gross total income of assessee included any profits and gains derived from an industrial undertaking, by reason of manufacture of intermediate product and not necessarily end-product, whether the benefit under the aforementioned provisions could be derived by the assessee-company.

Section 80J provides for deduction in respect of profits and gains from newly established undertakings or ships or hotel business in certain cases. Sub-section (4) of the said section declares that the same would apply to any industrial undertaking, which fulfils the conditions laid down therein; clause (iii) whereof refers to manufacture or production of articles.

Section 32A refers to an investment allowance, inter alia, in respect of a plant specified in sub-section (2) thereof, which is owned by the assessee and is wholly used for the purpose of business carried on by him, whereas clause (a) of sub-section (2) lays down a qualification to the effect that the assessee should be engaged in the business of operation of ships or aircraft; no such qualification has been laid down in clause (b) thereof. Sub-clause (iii) of clause (b ) of section 32A refers to any other industrial undertaking for the purpose of business of construction, manufacture or production of any article or thing, not being an article or thing specified in the list in the Eleventh Schedule. The said provision refers to construction and not to a construction company. It categorically refers to manufacture or production.

The question as to whether the companies, which undertake such composite business of manufacturing and constructions are entitled to the benefits of the aforementioned provisions in the light of the decisions relied upon by assessee was essentially question of fact which had not been considered by the Tribunal. It mainly proceeded on the basis of the end-product doctrine.

In the instant case, the assessee had not claimed benefit in respect of the entire profit earned by it, but was only asking for the relief to the extent to which it would have otherwise been entitled to, had it been held to be an ‘industrial company’ for the purpose of manufacture of the intermediate products, which it was required to manufacture for the purpose of utilization thereof in construction of dams and tunnels, etc. Therefore, it was obligatory on the part of the department to go into the said question. Such question was specifically raised by the assessee before the Commissioner (Appeals) as also before the Tribunal, but the same had not been considered in its proper perspective.

Having regard to the fact that the question as to whether the assessee was an ‘industrial company’ or not itself had been directed to be determined by the Assessing Officer by the Tribunal, the matter required fresh consideration at the hands of the Tribunal.

The decision of the Apex Court as also the other High Courts must, therefore, be considered while taking into the account the fact situation obtaining in each case. The interest of justice would be sub-served if the contention of the parties, which was the crux of the matter, to the effect that whether in relation to the intermediate products, the assessee-company fulfilled the criteria of ‘an industrial undertaking or not’ should be determined by the Tribunal in the light of the observations made herein before and on the basis thereof necessary reliefs could be granted in terms thereof.

He came to this conclusion on finding that the rates charged by the assessee from its holding company for the aforementioned work were much higher than those charged by TMI for the same work during the same year, which meant that the holding company had diverted part of its profits to the assessee-subsidiary company. The Commissioner (Appeals), looking to the close connection between the assessee and the holding company, partly upheld the ITO's order on appeal.

On cross-appeals, the assessee, inter alia, contended (i) that on expansion of the holding company's business, TMI was not able to meet all its require-ments and that it was in the holding company's interest to set up the assessee-subsidiary company to reduce its dependence on an outsider, (ii) that higher rates were allowed to be charged by the assessee initially to overcome its teething troubles and that in subsequent years, it had been progressively reduced, even to a level lower than that of the TMI rates, and (iii) that the onus was on the department to prove a mala fide inten- tion on the part of the holding company.

venth Schedule’, appearing in section 80-I(2)(iii) in the context of the fact that the deduction under section 80HH is meant to encourage establishment of new industrial undertakings in backward areas when such industrial undertaking ‘has begun or begins to manufacture or produce articles’ and in context of the fact that section 80-I is designed to encourage industrial undertakings to manufacture or produce ‘any articles or thing not being article or thing specified in the list in the Eleventh Schedule’. Provisions of section 80HH or 80-I are meant for the benefit of industrial undertakings that carry out the activity of manufacture or production of articles or things and not for the scrap merchants who trade in buying old articles or things and take out their parts to sell them separately. All large scale junk dealers in discarded old and scrapped vehicles who might fish out a horn in working condition from such vehicle or pull out its steering wheel or part of its engine that may have a demand in the market of second hand spares will proclaim themselves to be manufacturers or producers of articles or things. No such startling result is intended by the provisions of sections 80HH and 80-I, having regard to their underlying purpose of encouraging industries for being set up for manufacturing or production of new articles or things. In fact, industrial undertaking formed by transfer of machinery or plant previously used for any purpose is disentitled to such benefits both under sections 80HH(2)(iii) and 80-I(2)(iii). [Para 23]

The ships imported for breaking up are obviously old ships, purchased to retrieve the material, particularly steel plates, for disposal in the market for re-rolling or re-cycling purposes which is the activity done by these ship breakers in the process of ship breaking.

Thus, there is nothing whatsoever in the process of ship breaking activity which can be termed as manufacture or production of any article or thing. The dismantled material is already existing as a component of the old ship. The process of extracting steel plates from it while dismantling the ship will not make such extraction of existing material an activity of manufacture or production of such material nor will the process of cutting extracted steel plates for convenient disposal be manufacture or production of such steel plates. Merely because the ship breaking is considered as an industry, it would not be an industry engaged in manufacture or production of any article or thing. Benefit of the provisions of sections 80HH and 80-I is clearly not intended for such ship breaking activities which do not result in bringing into existence any new article or thing. The word ‘manufacture’ in the context of sections 80HH and 80-I would mean making of articles or things. While dismantling, the ship steel plates are not made but only removed which is not the same thing as making of steel plates. The word ‘production’ in context of these provisions would mean the action of making or manufacturing from components or raw materials an article or thing and not just removing of an existing article or cutting it.

In the instant case, application of mechanical methods only removed the steel plates and other objects which were existing on the ships, which would not mean that the assessee produced those existing articles or things by the process of removing and cutting them. [Para 27]

The word ‘production’ or ‘produce’ when used in juxtaposition with word ‘manufacture’ takes in bringing into existence new goods by a process which may or may not amount to manufacture. The principle of adopting a liberal interpretation which advances the purpose and object of beneficial provisions cannot be carried out to the extent of doing violence to the plain and simple language of the enactment. [Para 27.1]

Therefore, ship breaking is not an activity which gives rise to manufacture and production of altogether new commercial articles or things. The assessees were not entitled to claim deductions under sections 80HH and 80-I and the Tribunal committed an error in upholding such deductions. [Para 27.2]

FACT: The assessee-company was engaged in manufacture and sale of high tensile fasteners, cold extruded parts, etc., in Padi. It had a unit at 'k', a notified backward area, which manufactured fasteners and sockets. The assessee claimed deduction under section 80HH in respect of forging work done in 'k' unit on products manufactured in Padi, which it called as 'sub-contract receipts'. The Assessing Officer rejected the claim for deduction in respect of 'k' unit. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) directed the Assessing Officer to allow relief in accordance with law. Aggrieved, the revenue went in appeal before the Tribunal, which was allowed by a common order holding that the receipt on sub-contract could not be treated as income derived from the industrial undertaking for the purpose of granting relief under section 80HH.

On assessee's appeal :

HELD: The decision in CIT v. Tamilnadu Heat Treatment & Fetting Services [1999] 238 ITR 540/104 Taxman 210 (Mad.) is a case falling under sections 80HH and 80-I wherein the Court upheld the claim of the assessee as a sub-contractor to have the relief granted under sections 80HH and 80-I. The law declared in the above-stated case had direct relevance to the facts of the instant case. [Para 12]

In the subsequent decision in CIT v. Taj Fire Works Industries [2007] 288 ITR 92/[2006] 154 Taxman 380 (Mad.), a case where the assessee doing job work claimed the benefit of sections 80HH and 80-I, the Court held that since the assessee was involved in a systematic activity organized by the employer for the production and distribution of goods, it was entitled to the benefit of sections 80HH and 80-I. [Para 13]

In the instant case, the assessee's unit at 'k' was stated to be the only unit having hot forging machine. It was stated that the assessee, based at 'k', received bolts and nuts from Padi, manufactured using cold forging. The 'k' unit completed hot forging and after the process the products came to Padi where there was further value addition and after assembling nuts and bolts, they were marketed. Thus, it was only after the process was carried on by the 'k' unit, that the commodities reached a stage of marketability. The process of hot forging involved heating of raw materials to 1100 : C cutting, forming and piercing. Those nuts were then cooled and tapped. The nuts were then subject to heat treatment and surface coating, depending on customer's requirement to withstand higher stress. Thus, given the nature of the processing done at 'k' unit, the deduction was rightly considered by the Commissioner (Appeals) in the assessee's favour. [Para 15]

Further, the assessee's unit at 'k' had its own account maintained separately as an independent unit and out of the production process, it had derived income therein. Thus, it satisfied the test as given under section 80HH, which qualified for deduction in respect of receipts on job work done at the 'k' unit. Following the decisions in Tamilnadu Heat Treatment & Fetting Services (P.) Ltd.'s case (supra ) and Taj Fire Works Industries (supra), the order of the Tribunal was to be set aside. Accordingly, the Assessing Officer was to be directed to give effect to the direction of the Commissioner (Appeals). [Para 16]

FACT: The assessee was a small-scale industrial unit manufacturing graded metal (granite rubble of various sizes). It claimed deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I on the ground that it was carrying on a manufac- turing activity. The Assessing Officer denied the deductions holding that conversion of granite boulders into granite rubble of various sizes did not amount to manufacturing, as the raw material and the final product were the same and the only difference was in sizes and, therefore, the activity carried on by the assessee could not be held as a manufacturing activity.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that the various processes employed by the assessee ultimately resulted in an end-product (granite aggregate), which had a distinct utilitarian value, which the primary material of boulders did not possess and, therefore, the activity carried on by the assessee was in the nature of manufacturing activity. He, therefore, allowed the assessee’s claim for deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I.

HELD: It is well settled by the Supreme Court in the case of Pio Food Packers 46 STC 632 that in the case of a manufacturing activity the inputs and outputs should be commercially different. This "commercial identity" is to be considered in the light of the respective trade practice, or if there is no such trade practice, in the light of common partanee meaning. In the instant case, the raw material extracted by the assessee was the granite boulders. What was sold by the assessee was granite aggregate (commonly known as metal) of different commercial sizes of 1.1/2", 1", ½", ¼", etc. These different sizes of granite aggregates were used for different purposes, even though used generally in construction activities. The granite aggregates of different sizes sold by the assessee were commercially different from granite boulders extracted by the assessee from the quarry. There was no doubt that they were commercially different. Therefore, the assessee was carrying on a manufacturing activity and, hence, it was entitled for the deductions available under sections 80HH and 80-I. [Para 11]

The Rajasthan High Court in the case of CIT v. Chokshi Contacts (P.) Ltd. has held that deductions under sections 80HH and 80-I operate independently and the assessee is entitled to deductions under both sections, which is to be simultaneously granted without any order of preference. Section 41(1 ) brings to tax certain amounts by a fiction of law. Therefore, the operation of such fiction should be limited to the language of the section. Where the assessee has incurred a loss or expenditure or trading liability and this trading liability has been allowed as deduction in an earlier year and something has later on been recovered in respect of such liability or such liability has either been remitted or has ceased to exist, section 41( 1) comes into operation. But according to the facts in the present case, nothing happened as contemplated by section 41(1) . Sale proceeds derived were for the sale of the particular product and not recoupment of earlier purchase. Accordingly, section 41(1) had no application to the facts of the instant case.

Further, the particular receipt under consideration is, insofar as scrap was concerned, realisation from the sale of waste material from manufacturing activity of the assessee-company and it was not a receipt from the sale of some of its old machinery, plant or building resulting in balancing charge as contemplated under section 41(2) . This surplus was also of the nature falling under section 41(2 ). Therefore, the assessee was not entitled to relief in respect of profits attributable to sale of drums.

FACT: The assessee derived income from sale of prawns. The nature of activity carried on by the assessee was purchase of raw prawns, subjecting the same to the process of cutting the heads and tails, cleaning, etc., and thereafter selling the same. In the assessment for the assessment year 1979-80, the assessee claimed deduction under section 80HH from the income from sale of prawns on the ground that the activity of processing of prawns before putting them for sale amounted to 'manufacture' and 'production' of articles within the meaning of section 80HH. The ITO rejected the claim, observing that the activity of processing prawns for the purpose of sale did not amount to manufacture or production of goods or articles within the meaning of section 80HH. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the deduction to the assessee and the Tribunal confirmed the order of Commissioner (Appeals).

On reference :

HELD: Section 80HH applies to those industrial undertakings only which 'manufacture or produce articles'. The manufacturing process mentioned in clause (iv) of sub-section (2) refers to the process undertaken to achieve the above object, i.e., to 'manufacture or produce articles'. Sub-section (4) also uses the same expression 'begins to manufacture or produce articles'. This section nowhere uses the expression 'processes goods or articles'.

On a careful reading of section 80HH in the light of scheme thereof and other provisions of the Act referred to above, it is clear that the Legislature intended to extend the benefit of deduction under section 80HH only to the industrial undertakings which manufacture or produce articles. Manufacture, as observed by the Supreme Court in Dy. CST v. Pio Food Packers [1980] 46 STC 63, is the end result of one or more processes through which the original commodity is made to pass. The nature and extent of processing may vary from one case to another, and indeed there may be several stages of processing and perhaps different kinds of processing at each stage and with each process suffered, the original commodity experiences a change. But it is only when the change, or a series of changes, take the commodity to the point where commercially it can no longer be regarded as the original commodity but instead is recognised as a new and distinct article that a manufacture can be said to take place. Where the commodity retains a continuing substantial identity through the processing stage, it cannot be said that there has been manufacture. Similarly, the word 'production' has a wider connotation than the word 'manufacture'. While every manufacture can be characterised as production, every production need not amount to manufacture. As observed by the Supreme Court in CIT v. B. C. Budharaja Co. [1993] 204 ITR 412, the word 'production' or 'produce' when used in juxtaposition with the word 'manufacture' takes in bringing into existence new goods by a process which may or may not amount to manufacture. It also takes in all the by-products, intermediate products and residual products, which emerge in the course of manufacture of goods. This section was not intended to beapplied to industrial undertakings which are engaged in 'processing of goods' not amounting to manufacture or production of articles. 'Processing' means subjecting a commodity to a process or treatment so as to develop it or make it fit for market. Processing is, thus, an operation on an article so that it undergoes a change. There may be processes undertaken by an industrial undertaking which may result in conversion of the article into a new commercial commodity or may change the nature and character of the article in such a manner that it may lose its original identity and get transformed into an entirely new commodity. In such cases 'manufacture' can be said to have taken place.

On a perusal of Sec. 80-IC of the Act, we find that the same therein contemplates deduction of any profit and gains derived by an undertaking or an enterprise from an eligible business, while computing the total income of the assessee. The controversy in hand hinges around the aspect as to whether or not the sale of scrap generated in the course of the manufacturing activity could be brought within the realm of the profits and gains derived by the industrial undertaking from its eligible business u/s 80-IC of the Act. In our considered view, as the generation of scrap i.e. drums, tins, plastics, paper, cleaning material etc. can safely or in fact inescapably be held to be arising from and forming a part and parcel of the manufacturing process of an eligible undertaking, thus, the income from sale of the same would safely fall within the realm of the profit and gains derived by the undertaking from its eligible business. Accordingly, we find no reason as to why the sale of scrap generated in the course of its manufacturing activity was not to be included in the amount of the eligible profits while quantifying the assessee's claim for deduction under Sec. 80-IC of the Act. Our aforesaid view is fortified by the judgment of the Hon'ble High Court of Allahabad in the case Modi Xerox Ltd. (supra). In the aforesaid case the question of law that was inter alia raised before the Hon'ble High Court in context of the pari materia provisions of sec. 80HH of the Act, read as under :

"11. Whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case, the Ld. ITAT was legally justified in holding that deduction under section 80HH is to be allowed on total income including the profit from sale of scrap being part of income of the Industrial Undertaking?"

Answering the aforesaid issue, the Hon'ble High Court in the backdrop of the judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Pandian Chemicals Ltd. v. CIT [2003] 129 Taxman 539/262 ITR 278, had observed, that as the scrap generated in the course of the manufacturing process of the assessee's eligible business had a direct and immediate nexus with its industrial undertaking, the same, thus, was eligible for deduction u/s 80-HH of the Act. Observations of the Hon'ble High Court for the sake of clarity are reproduced as under:

"Now we come to the Question No. 11 which relate to deduction under section 80-HH before the Assessing Officer. Under section 80- HH, the assessee was entitled to the deduction equal to 20% of the gross total income of the assessee, which includes any profit and gains derived from the industrial undertaking. The assessee's case is that income of Rs. 63,66,932/- was deducted treating to be income from other sources and deduction under section 80-HH was not given on the aforesaid amount of Rs. 63,66,932/-. The assessee filed appeal against the said order and the Appellate Authority in Paragraph No. 6.2 directed the Assessing Officer to take the income from the sale of Scrap by xerographic equipment unit and Toner, Developer, Photocopier unit as profit of the said unit. The said order has been confirmed by the Tribunal.

Learned counsel for the appellant submitted that the Assessing Officer has rightly not deducted the said income from the profits and gain from the industrial unit, since the said income from the Scrap could not be said to be income derived from the industrial undertaking. He submits that the word 'derived from' in Section 80-HH has to be understood as something which has direct and immediate nexus with the assessee's industrial undertaking.

Learned counsel for the assessee refuting the submission of the appellant submitted that the Scrap was generated from the manufacturing process itself by different units of the assessee's undertaking, hence, the CIT Appeal has rightly taken the said income which was from the sale of Scrap as income derived from industrial undertaking.

HEADNOTE: Sections 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction - Profits and gains from newly established industrial undertakings, etc. in backward areas - Three units belonging to assessee were crushing barytes into powder for hire and receiving crushing charges - Further, assessee had not prepared separate profit and loss accounts and balance sheets for each unit - Whether barytes are distinct not only in form and name but also in use from barytes powder and barytes powder is distinct and separate article produced from barytes and, therefore, barytes powder is an article produced from barytes - Held, yes - Whether sections 80HH and 80-I do not contemplate division of profits and gains in respect of a unit and Assessing Officer may compute such profits and gains under section 80HH on such reasonable basis as he may deem fit - Held, yes - Whether when industrial units satisfied other critiera laid down under sections 80HH and 80-I, assessee was entitled to deduction - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee established three industrial units in backward areas. The units were crushing barytes into powder for hire and receiving crushing charges. The Assessing Officer held that mere crushing of barytes was not a manufacturing activity nor the powder produced could be called a new article. He further found that the assessee had not prepared separate profit and loss accounts and balance sheets in respect of each unit. He, therefore, disallowed the assessee’s claim for deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I. The Commissioner (Appeals) affirmed the order of the Assessing Officer. However, the Tribunal found that the barytes powder so produced got its marketability for its use for the purposes totally different from that of barytes. It further held that irrespective of the fact that there was no division of account, still they were entitled for the benefit of sections 80HH and 80-I as having satisfied the conditions laid down thereunder.

On reference :

HELD: Sections 80HH and 80-I do not contemplate the division of profits and gains in respect of a unit, provided the industrial undertaking satisfies the criteria laid down under section 80HH. The proviso of section 80HH(c ) itself provides that if in the opinion of the Assessing Officer, the computation of the profits and gains of industrial undertaking presents exceptional difficulties, the officer may compute such profits and gains on such reasonable basis as he may deem fit. In other words, it empowers the Assessing Officer to ascertain the profits and gains of a particular unit and make assessment. Therefore, the assessee was entitled to the benefit of sections 80HH and 80-I, provided the criteria laid down were satisfied.

It is not disputed that the barytes were made into powder by using power and the powder is a distinct and separate article from barytes and the use of barytes powder is in the manufacturing of paints while the barytes are used in a different form for different purposes.

Further, the barytes powder is marketed as such. Therefore, barytes are distinct not only in form and name but also in use from barytes powder and barytes powder is distinct and separate article produced from barytes. Therefore, it cannot be said that barytes powder is not an article produced from barytes. As a result, the assessee was entitled to deductions under sections 80HH and 80-I.

J.V. Prasad for the Applicant.

The Assessing Officer found that in these concerns, the directors of the company and their close relatives had a substantial interest. He, therefore, made an addition on the assumption that the assessee diverted its profit to the concerns in which its directors and their close relatives had a substantial interest. The Commissioner (Appeals) deleted the addition. The Tribunal confirmed the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) holding that there was no material to conclude that the sales effected by the assessee-company to the aforesaid two concerns were sham or bogus. On application under section 256(2):

HELD: The Tribunal, following the decision in Highland Produce Co. Ltd. v. ITO [1993] 45 ITD 488 (Cochin) and the decision of the High Court of Bombay in CIT v. Chase Bright Steel Ltd. (No. 1) [1989] 177 ITR 124, held that the expenditure incurred on repairs of the car was to be excluded.

As regards the addition in respect of sales to two concerns, the Tribunal appreciated the facts correctly and passed the order. As regards the claim of allowance under section 80HH, the Tribunal applied the ratio in decision Chokshi Metal Refinery v. CIT [1977] 107 ITR 63 (Guj.).

It was, thus, clear that the decision was based on points concluded and also on proper appreciation of facts. The Tribunal declined to state the case holding that the finding of the Tribunal was based on facts as found on record and the finding based on appreciation of facts did not give rise to any question of law.

The questions sought to be referred were concluded questions and the findings of the Tribunal were based on a proper appreciation of the facts. The questions were, thus, not found to be referable questions of law.

HEADNOTE: I. Section 80HH, read with  section 80-I, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from hotels or industrial undertakings, etc., in backward areas - Whether ship breaking activity results in production of a distinct and different article and, therefore, assessee doing said activity would be entitled to deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company, engaged in the business of ship breaking, claimed deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I. The Assessing Officer disallowed the assessee's claim. On appeal, the Tribunal allowed the assessee's claim. On the revenue's appeal, the High Court held that when a ship breaking activity is undertaken, the articles, which emerge from the activity of ship breaking, continue to be the part of the ship and such parts do not constitute new goods and, consequently, the assessee was not entitled to claim the benefit under sections 80HH and 80-I as there was neither production nor manufacture of new goods by the process of ship breaking.

On appeal to the Supreme Court :

HELD: The important test, which distinguishes the word 'production' from 'manufacture', is that the word 'production' is wider than the word 'manufacture'. Further, the Legislature has used the words 'manufacture' or 'production'. Therefore, the word 'production' cannot derive its colour from the word 'manufacture'. Further, even according to the dictionary meaning of word 'production', the word 'produce' is defined as something which is brought forth or yielded either naturally or as a result of effort and work. It is important to note that the word 'new' is not used in the definition of the word 'produce'. [Para 8]

Therefore, the Tribunal was right in allowing the deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I to the assessee holding that the ship breaking activity gave rise to the production of a distinct and different article. [Para 10]

The assessee had set a cement unit in a backward area. For the assessment year 1976-77, the assessee claimed deduction under section 80HH stating, inter alia, that since there was no taxable income in the said unit in that year, the said relief under section 80HH should be carried forward. The ITO worked out deduction under section 80HH at Rs. 24,21,501 and held that as there was no taxable profit during the year, the amount of Rs. 24,21,501 would be carried forward and adjusted in the subsequent year when the assessee’s unit would go into profit. For the assessment you 1977-78, the ITO worked out deduction under section. 80HH at Rs. 54,95,585 and allowed the same alongwith carried forward relief of Rs. 24,21,501 for the assessment year 1976-77. Subsequently, the ITO realising that there was no provision for carry forward and set off of earlier year’s ‘deficiency’ under section

80HH, took the view that in the assessment framed for the assessment year 1977- 78 there was a mistake apparent from the record inasmuch as ‘deficiency’ of Rs. 24,21,501 was not only carried forward but also set off, which should be corrected. He, therefore, rectified the assessment order for the assessment year 1977- 78 under section 154 and withdrew the deduction of Rs. 24,21,501 allowed in the assessment order. On appeal, the assessee contended, inter alia, that rectification under section 154 could not be made in respect of the assessment year 1977-78 without first rectifying the assessment for the assessment year 1976-77. The Commissioner (Appeals) rejected the contention of the assessee and upheld the order of the ITO passed under section 154.

On second appeal:

For the assessment year 1981-82, the assessee had made a claim of deduction under section 80HH against its profits and loss without setting off of earlier years’ losses which included brought forward business losses and unabsorbed depreciation. The ITO, however, took the view that after allowing deduction under sections 32,32A, 71 and 72, there was no positive income of the assessee for the relevant assessment year and, therefore, no deduction was available to the assessee under section 80HH. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) reversed the ITO’s order and upheld the assessee’s claim.

On appeal by the revenue:

• The assessee had acquired a large extent of land in a backward area as per industry policy for setting up an undertaking for manufacture of polimerisation initiators. It had complied with all legal obligations and started production in December 1986.

• Meanwhile, the Taxation Laws (Amendment and Miscellaneous provisions) Act, 1986 came into effect on 10-9-1986 which gave Government a power to make a retrospective notification subject to a condition that such retrospectivity did not date prior to 1-4-1983. Thereafter Government issued notification with effect from 1-4-1983 and removed the abovementioned area from the list of backward area.

• The assessee, in its revised return filed for the relevant assessment year, claimed deduction under section 80HH for specified amount.

• The same was rejected by the Assessing Officer.

• On appeal, Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the deduction but subsequently relying on Circular No.484 of CBDT modified his order and denied the deduction allowed by him earlier.

• On cross-appeals:

Sub-section (2) of section 80HH lays down certain conditions, one of which is that the industrial undertaking should manufacture or produce articles in any backward area and another condition is that it should employ 10 or more workers in the manufacturing process carried on with the aid of power. It was not the case of the revenue that any of these conditions were not fulfilled. Their only case was that the entire manufacturing activity from beginning to end was not carried on in the backward area and an initial part of it had been entrusted to the contractors who carried on that part of the activity outside the backward area. The contention, therefore, was that the profit shown as the profit of the industrial undertaking in the backward area might actually include a small part of the profit derived from activity outside the backward area and, therefore, there was inflation of the profit and consequentially inflation of the deduction claimed by the assessee, that could be withdrawn by reopening the assessment. [Para 5]

Sub-section (7) of section 80HH provides for this contingency by stating that where it appears to the Assessing Officer that owing to the close connection between the assessee carrying on the business to which this section applies and any other person, the business between them is so arranged that it produces to the assessee more than the ordinary profit, the profits and gains of this industrial undertaking may be reasonably estimated. In the instant case also, if the Assessing Officer had carefully scrutinised the accounts of the assessee and drawn the inference that because of the entrustment of the initial part of the contract process to contractors, the income from the industrial undertaking was likely to be inflated, with reference to the profit derived from the backward area, he could have reasonably estimated the profit instead of accepting the profit as shown by the assessee. That estimate, he failed to do at the time of the assessment and he sought to do the same by reopening the assessment. The question was whether he could do it by stating that there was an omission on the part of the assessee to disclose fully and truly all material facts. In the case of Parashuram Pottery Works Co. Ltd. v. ITO [1977] 106 ITR 1, the Supreme Court stated that the duty of an assessee in any case does not extend beyond making a true and full disclosure of primary facts. Once he has done that, his duty ends. It is for the ITO to draw the correct inference from the primary facts. It is no responsibility of the assessee to advise the ITO with regard to the inference, which he should draw from the primary facts. If an ITO draws an inference which appears subsequently to be erroneous, mere change of opinion with regard to that inference would not justify initiation of action for reopening assessments. In the instant case, the ITO failed to draw an inference that because of the entrustment of the initial manufacturing activity to contractors, the income derived from the industrial undertaking with reference to the backward area could be inflated and to that extent the income had to be estimated for confining the deduction to that profit which could be said to have been derived only from the backward area. Failing to draw that inference, blame could not be put on the assessee, when at the time of assessment the list of contractors, the quantity of beedies manufactured and the amount paid had been disclosed by the assessee. That disclosure was admitted in the counter affidavit. The ITO was not able to specify what extra information was required by him to have applied his mind to draw that inference for reducing the deduction to which the assessee was entitled. As long as it was not possible for the ITO to specify the exact information which was required and which was not disclosed, it was not possible to accept the claim that there was no true and full disclosure in the case. When that jurisdictional fact was not established, the ITO could not issue a notice under section 147(a). In the circumstances, the impugned notices were quashed. [Paras 6 & 7]

The writ petition was allowed. [Para 7]

Whether, assessee was entitled to investment allowance under
section 32A in respect of machinery and plant installed in cold
storage-Held, no

Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961-Deductions-Profits and 
gains from newly established industrial undertaking in backward
areas-Whether, assessee was entitled to relief in respect of cold 
storage, which was situated in backward area, under section 80HH-
Held, no

FACT: The assessee, being an owner of a cold storage situated in a backward area wherein potatoes were kept in the relevant assessment year, claimed investment allowance under section 32A on machinery and plant installed in the cold storage on the ground that the cold storage involved ‘manufac-turing’. The ITO disallowed the assessee’s claim, holding that a cold storage involved only processing and not manufacture or production of an article or thing. He also disallowed the assessee’s claim for deduction under section 80HH, On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order of the ITO.

On second appeal;

HELD: Section 32 A uses the expression ‘business of manufacture or production of any article or thing’. The expression used in section 80HH is similar, namely, ‘to manufacture or produce articles’. There is no reference to ‘processing’ as used in the definition of ‘industrial company’ under section 2(7)(d) of the Finance Act, 1966, and the Finance (No. 2) Act, 1967. Again, unlike section 80J(4)(iii), reference is not made in section 32A or 80HH to the operation of a cold storage plant. This would show that mere processing (even if the potatoes were held to undergo processing in a cold storage) is not recognised under sections 32A and 80HH to amount to manufacture or production of any article or thing. The same expression is used in section 80HHA and 80-I(2)(iii). Again, section 35C, which deals with agricultural development allowance, refers to a company or a co-operative society being engaged in the manufacture or processing of a relevant article or thing There-fore, as neither section 32A nor section 80HH refers to processing of any article or thing, the lower authorities were justified in rejecting the claims of the assessee.

SECTION 80HH*

Deductions - New industrial undertakings/hotels in backward areas

DERIVED

622. CIT v. Cement Distributors Ltd. [1994] 208 ITR 355 (Delhi)

The word 'derived' has to be assigned a restricted meaning as compared to the words 'attributable to' or 'referable to' and, therefore, to avail of a rebate under section 80HH, an assessee must establish that he has derived profits or gains from an industrial undertaking.

♦♦

A.M. Moosa, Bharath Sea Food v. CIT [1996] 135 CTR (Ker.) 110

The law that the amount in regard to which exemption is sought must be relatable to an industrial undertaking, as the amount which would be understood to be 'derived from' is more than settled.

♦♦

CIT v. Pandian Chemicals Ltd. [1998] 233 ITR 497 (Mad.)

A restricted meaning is given when the Legislature uses the expression, 'derived from'. There is no justification to give the expression 'derived from' a wider meaning to cover every receipt connected with the industrial undertaking.

♦♦

Fenner (India) Ltd. v. CIT 1998 Tax LR 927 (Mad.)

The expression 'derived from' used in section 80HH implies that section 80-HH is confined only to profits and gains derived from industrial undertaking and cannot be attributed to the original source of product.

♦♦

Pandian Chemicals Ltd. v. CIT [2003] 129 Taxman 539/262 ITR 278 (SC)

It is clear that the words 'derived from' in section 80HH must be understood as something which has direct or immediate nexus with an industrial undertaking.

♦♦

Dy. CIT v. Vindhya Telelinks Ltd. [1997] 63 ITD 127 (Jab. - Trib.)

An income can be said to be derived from an industrial undertaking only if it is directly related to the running of the industrial undertaking itself. The scope of the expression 'derived from' is much narrower than the expression 'attributable to'.

♦♦

CIT v. Alpine Solvex Ltd. [2005] 144 Taxman 67/276 ITR 92 (MP)

The words 'derived from' as used in section 80HH/80-I have got to be given restricted meaning.

♦♦

BIO Pharma v. Dy. CIT [2003] 85 ITD 575/[2002] 75 TTJ 486 (Ahd. - Trib.)

The expression 'derived from' has a definite but narrow meaning and it cannot receive a flexible or wider concept. The phrase 'profits and gains derived from an industrial undertaking' has been judicially interpreted as meaning that direct and immediate source of receipt is the industrial undertaking and the nexus is of the first degree in the genealogical tree. The correct connotation of the expression 'derived from', as laid down and explained by the Supreme Court in various decisions does not leave any doubt or ambiguity that interest from fixed deposits does not directly flow from an industrial undertaking and cannot be treated as derived from the industrial undertaking.

♦♦

CIT v. Modi Xerox Ltd. [2014] 50 taxmann.com 201/226 Taxman 152 (Mag.)/365 ITR 200 (All.)

The word 'derived from' under section 80HH has to be understood as something which has immediate nexus with the industrial undertaking. When the scrap generated from the concerned units has direct and immediate nexus with the industrial undertaking since the said scrap has been generated from the manufacturing process itself, benefit under section 80HH is available.

♦♦

Deccan Cements Ltd. v. CIT [2014] 41 taxmann.com 536/223 Taxman 194 (Mag.)/360 ITR 444/268 CTR 212 (AP)

The words 'profit derived from' and not 'attributable to'. Therefore, what is the import of the words 'derived from' has been explained by the Supreme Court in the case of Liberty India v. CIT [2009] 317 ITR 218/183 Taxman 349. Therein the Supreme Court had made it clear that the connotation of the words 'derived from' is narrower as compared to that of the words 'attributable to'. Hence, while reading the provision of section 80HH, the profit derived from the cement manufacturing activity is deductible thereunder and not otherwise.

In Fenner (India) Ltd. v. CIT (No. 2) [2000] 241 ITR 803, the Madras High Court expressed the view that the scrap materials has direct link or nexus with the industrial undertaking and, therefore, profit from the sale of the scrap materials should be eligible for deduction under section 80HH. Following that decision, it was to be held in the instant case that the relief under section 80HH was allowable to the assessee on profit on sale of scrap. [Para 13]
IT: Income from sale of scrap generated from manufacturing process of industrial undertaking has to be included for purpose of benefit of section 80HH

HEADNOTE: Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction - In respect of incomes of industries or hotels in backward area - Assessee, an exporter of prawns, bought prawns which were processed and thereafter exported - There was a detailed process by which prawns were prepared for export and one of the vital stages of that process was beheading, peeling and deveining of the prawns - Whether assessee was entitled to deduction under section 80HH - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee, an exporter of prawns used to buy prawns which were processed and ultimately exported. The assessee claimed deduction under section 80HH. The ITO disallowed the assessee's claim on the ground that the aforesaid business of the assessee was not one in which either manufacture or production was involved so as to attract the provisions of section 80HH.

On appeal, the Tribunal observed that, there was a detailed process by which prawns were prepared for export and one of the vital stages of that process was beheading, peeling and deveining of the prawns and, thus, allowed the deduction under section 80HH.

On reference:

HELD: Like in section 33, so also in section 80HH, the word 'manufacture' or 'produce' appear. HEADNOTE: Section 80-I, read with section 80HH, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from new industrial undertakings after a certain date - Assessment years 1987-88 to 1992-93 - Assessees engaged in dismantling of damaged/unserviceable ships claimed deduction under section 80HH and 80-I - Whether legislature intended to extend benefit of deductions only to industrial undertakings manufacturing or producing articles - Held, yes - Whether as ship-breaking activity amounts to carrying out manufacturing process in reverse order, assessees were not entitled to deduction claimed - Held, yes

FACT: The assessees, engaged in the business of breaking and dismantling of damaged or unserviceable ships and selling the goods obtained therefrom to various parties, claimed deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I. The Assessing Officer rejected the claims on the grounds that the assessee were not industrial undertaking within the meaning of section 80HH and 80-I and they did not fulfil any of the conditions of those sections and that there was nothing like a process of manufacturing done by the assessees. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that ship breaking was an industrial undertaking and, accordingly, the assessees were eligible for the deductions claimed.

On revenue’s appeal :

HELD: The Legislature intended to extend the benefit of deduction under section 80HH only to the industrial undertakings which manufacture or produce articles. This section is not intended to be applied to industrial undertakings which are engaged in ‘processing of goods’ not amounting to manufacture or production of articles. The ship-breaking activity involves buying of damaged and unserviceable ships which are otherwise uneconomic to run, for the purpose of breaking and scrapping and sale of various goods and scrap obtained from such breaking and dismantling of old and used ships. Process is employed for breaking ship for dismantling and selling the scrap and substantial part of the items fitted in the ship and the oil contained in the tankers are sold in the same from without carrying out any further act, except removal of same from the ship and the remaining ship, made mainly of iron and steel, is then broken into different pieces of different sizes and shapes and sold by weight. Therefore, at the end of the process employed by the assessee, what is acquired are iron bars, plating rods, bronze, gunmetal copper and non-ferrous metal which, though marketable and commercial commodities, cannot be said to be manufactured or produced articles or things. For all practical purposes it is scrap. The scrap cannot be called a manufacture product or produced article because they are no new commodities but parts of the old and discarded ship as held by the Bombay High Court in the case of CST v. Delhi Iron & Steel Co. (P.) Ltd. [1995] 98 STC 202 the condemned and unserviceable ship purchased by the dealer is not a ship but re-rollable scrap in the form of an old ship for dismantling, in effect, the dealer acquires only the old materials and articles contained therein which are sold by it in the form in which they are acquired. No process whatsoever is applied to the goods, much less any process of manufacture. The issue stood squarely covered in favour of the revenue by the decision of the Bombay Bench of the Tribunal in the case of Asst. CIT v. Virendra & Co. [1995] 55 ITD 309 which held that ‘the meaning of manufacture and production of articles and things’ would have to be considered in their ordinary plain and natural meaning. Breaking or dismantling a ship would perhaps be just the opposite of manufacturing or production of an article or an thing. When a ship is dismantled or broken, what is obtained by the persons who are engaged in that process are the components by which the ship is constructed or manufactured and if it is possible to reassemble those pieces or parts, the ship may be manufactured or constructed. Hence, it would be doing violence to the language of the section if it is said that while a ship is being dismantled or broken or destroyed, in effect an article or thing is being manufactured or produced. Hence, the activity of breaking or dismantling of a ship cannot be considered to be an industrial undertaking which manufactured or produced articles or things and, therefore, the assessee was not entitled to deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I.

HEADNOTE: Section 80HH, read with  section 80J of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profit and gains from hotels or industrial undertakings etc., in backward areas - Assessment years 1979-80 and 1980-81 - Whether business of tyre retreading does not amount to production of new article entitling assessee to relief under sections 80HH and 80J - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company, which was retreader and established its plant in a backward area, claimed deductions under sections 80HH and 80J. The Assessing Officer disallowed the assessee's claim. On second appeal, the Tribunal held that the business of tyre retreading amounted to the production of a new article and that, therefore, the assessee was entitled to the relief under sections 80J and 80HH.

On reference:

HELD: The word "manufacture" or "produce articles" used in the provision to section 80HH have not been defined in the Act. The word "manufacture" has been considered by the Supreme Court and the High Courts on numerous occasions and the common thread which runs in all the decisions is that it is only when a new and distinct commodity commercially accepted as such, comes into existence as a result of the processing, that a commodity can be said to have been manufactured.

Having regard to the fact that the word "article" used in the section is an article which is manufactured or produced and the word "produce" having been used in juxtaposition with the word "manufacture" it connotes the bringing into existence of new goods. The result of production should be the coming into existence of a new article. The terms "production" and "produce" would also take in by-products, intermediate products and residual products. All of them should be products or articles, which are capable of being regarded as new articles. By holding that a "new" article should emerge from manufacture or production new words are not being added to section 80HH. The term new has been employed in the decisions of the courts only to indicate the end result of the process of production or manufacture. It is only when that result can be said to have been achieved, that the industrial undertaking which brings about such a result by its process of production or manufacture, would qualify for the benefits conferred under the section. In view of aforesaid, it could not be said that retreading of tyres resulted in the production of an article for the purpose of section 80HH.

Hence, the Tribunal was not right in holding that the business of tyre retreading amounted to the production of a new article entitling the assessee to the relief under sections 80J and 80HH.

Section 80HHC of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from industrial undertakings in backward area - Assessee-company had set up an industrial undertaking in a backward area and was carrying on business of manufacture and sale of V-belts, oil seals, O-rings, rubber moulded products, etc. - Whether profits and gains from sale of scrap material resulting in manufacturing process were eligible for deduction in an amount equal to 20 per cent under section 80HH, since scrap materials came within manufacturing process of industrial undertaking set-up by assessee - Held, yes

Section 80HH is meant to give a tax rebate to certain categories of assessees and one, who wants to claim such a relief, must strictly satisfy the requirements prescribed therein. He must establish that his profits and gains are derived from his industrial undertaking or the business of hotel. Axiomatic proposition of law is that it is not sufficient if a commercial connection is established between the profits earned and the industrial undertaking and the law requires that such profits must have been derived from the industrial undertaking. The industrial undertaking itself must be the source of that profit. The business of the industrial undertaking must strictly yield that profit. It must be the direct source of profit and not a means to earn any other profit.

In the instant case, in the industrial undertaking for the manufacture of V-belts, oil seals, O-rings and rubber moulded products, certain scrap materials resulted, which had a saleable value. To say that the scrap materials had no direct link or nexus with the industrial undertaking, could not at all be expected to commend acceptance, especially, on the facts and in the circumstances of the instant case. The scrap materials came within the manufacturing process of the industrial undertaking in the manufacture of certain products such as V-belts, oil seals, O-rings and certain rubber moulded products, etc. In that view of the matter, profits and gains from the sale of scrap materials were eligible for deduction in an amount equal to 20 per cent under section 80HH, inasmuch as such gains or profits were derived from the industrial undertaking and includible in the gross total income of the assessee and the question relatable to the profit on the sale of scrap was answered in favour of the assessee.

This section is not intended to be applied to industrial undertakings which are engaged in ‘processing of goods’ not amounting to manufacture or production of articles. The ship-breaking activity involves buying of damaged and unserviceable ships which are otherwise uneconomic to run, for the purpose of breaking and scrapping and sale of various goods and scrap obtained from such breaking and dismantling of old and used ships. Process is employed for breaking ship for dismantling and selling the scrap and substantial part of the items fitted in the ship and the oil contained in the tankers are sold in the same from without carrying out any further act, except removal of same from the ship and the remaining ship, made mainly of iron and steel, is then broken into different pieces of different sizes and shapes and sold by weight. Therefore, at the end of the process employed by the assessee, what is acquired are iron bars, plating rods, bronze, gunmetal copper and non-ferrous metal which, though marketable and commercial commodities, cannot be said to be manufactured or produced articles or things. For all practical purposes it is scrap. The scrap cannot be called a manufacture product or produced article because they are no new commodities but parts of the old and discarded ship as held by the Bombay High Court in the case of CST v. Delhi Iron & Steel Co. (P.) Ltd. [1995] 98 STC 202 the condemned and unserviceable ship purchased by the dealer is not a ship but re-rollable scrap in the form of an old ship for dismantling, in effect, the dealer acquires only the old materials and articles contained therein which are sold by it in the form in which they are acquired. No process whatsoever is applied to the goods, much less any process of manufacture. The issue stood squarely covered in favour of the revenue by the decision of the Bombay Bench of the Tribunal in the case of Asst. CIT v. Virendra & Co. [1995] 55 ITD 309 which held that ‘the meaning of manufacture and production of articles and things’ would have to be considered in their ordinary plain and natural meaning. Breaking or dismantling a ship would perhaps be just the opposite of manufacturing or production of an article or an thing. When a ship is dismantled or broken, what is obtained by the persons who are engaged in that process are the components by which the ship is constructed or manufactured and if it is possible to reassemble those pieces or parts, the ship may be manufactured or constructed. Hence, it would be doing violence to the language of the section if it is said that while a ship is being dismantled or broken or destroyed, in effect an article or thing is being manufactured or produced. Hence, the activity of breaking or dismantling of a ship cannot be considered to be an industrial undertaking which manufactured or produced articles or things and, therefore, the assessee was not entitled to deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I.

Regarding the contention of the assessee that the Government of India had recognised ship breaking as industry and, hence, the assessee was entitled to deduction claimed, there was no presumption that every industry is engaged in ‘manufacture’ or ‘production of articles or things’. Even if ship breaking is considered as an industry in the light of the definition of section 2(f) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, it will not mean that it would amount to manufacture or production so as to entitle the assessee to claim deductions under the respective sections. The assessee being governed by the Factories Act also would not change the matter in any way because that is broadly meant for welfare of labourers employed. The argument that a ship-breaking industry is labour intensive and that in the process heavy machinery like cranes and winches are employed is not relevant in absence of any manufacturing process involved. Mere application of systematic and sophisticated machines in the process would not treat an activity into manufacture. Thus, ship breaking activity amounts to carrying out the manufacturing process in a reverse order, as originally the ship is built from iron sheets and iron bars and other materials and by process of breaking the same, ship was reconverted into iron scrap and other materials. In view of the above, the findings of the Commissioner (Appeals) were to be reversed.

Section 80HH(2)(i) mandates that the assessee who claims benefit of this section should have begun ‘manufacture’ or ‘production’ of articles after 31-12-1970, in any backward area. Though the term ‘industrial undertaking’ is capable of wider definition, and the word ‘industry’ has a very large ambit, the term ‘industrial undertaking’ used in section 80HH(1) having regard to the requirements set out in section 80HH(2)(i ), is limited to industries which manufacture or produce articles. The construction activity could not be regarded as industrial undertaking; nor could it be taken into account on the ground that the same assessee was also carrying on manufacturing activity along with the construction activity. If the profit and loss account was capable of being separated and that part pertaining to the manufacturing activity, ascertained then to that extent, the assessee was entitled to claim benefit under section 80HH, on the ground that the account was one and the activities of the assessee, includes manufacture, it could not claim benefit under section 80HH in respect of an activity that did not involve manufacture or production of articles. Therefore, the Tribunal was not correct in holding that the assessee–company was entitled to the relief under section 80HH in respect of its business which also comprised of business activities other than manufacturing one.

The contention, therefore, was that the profit shown as the profit of the industrial undertaking in the backward area might actually include a small part of the profit derived from activity outside the backward area and, therefore, there was inflation of the profit and consequentially inflation of the deduction claimed by the assessee, that could be withdrawn by reopening the assessment. [Para 5] Sub-section (7) of section 80HH provides for this contingency by stating that where it appears to the Assessing Officer that owing to the close connection between the assessee carrying on the business to which this section applies and any other person, the business between them is so arranged that it produces to the assessee more than the ordinary profit, the profits and gains of this industrial undertaking may be reasonably estimated. In the instant case also, if the Assessing Officer had carefully scrutinised the accounts of the assessee and drawn the inference that because of the entrustment of the initial part of the contract process to contractors, the income from the industrial undertaking was likely to be inflated, with reference to the profit derived from the backward area, he could have reasonably estimated the profit instead of accepting the profit as shown by the assessee. That estimate, he failed to do at the time of the assessment and he sought to do the same by reopening the assessment. The question was whether he could do it by stating that there was an omission on the part of the assessee to disclose fully and truly all material facts. In the case of Parashuram Pottery Works Co. Ltd. v. ITO [1977] 106 ITR 1, the Supreme Court stated that the duty of an assessee in any case does not extend beyond making a true and full disclosure of primary facts. Once he has done that, his duty ends. It is for the ITO to draw the correct inference from the primary facts. It is no responsibility of the assessee to advise the ITO with regard to the inference, which he should draw from the primary facts. If an ITO draws an inference which appears subsequently to be erroneous, mere change of opinion with regard to that inference would not justify initiation of action for reopening assessments. In the instant case, the ITO failed to draw an inference that because of the entrustment of the initial manufacturing activity to contractors, the income derived from the industrial undertaking with reference to the backward area could be inflated and to that extent the income had to be estimated for confining the deduction to that profit which could be said to have been derived only from the backward area. Failing to draw that inference, blame could not be put on the assessee, when at the time of assessment the list of contractors, the quantity of beedies manufactured and the amount paid had been disclosed by the assessee. That disclosure was admitted in the counter affidavit. The ITO was not able to specify what extra information was required by him to have applied his mind to draw that inference for reducing the deduction to which the assessee was entitled. As long as it was not possible for the ITO to specify the exact information which was required and which was not disclosed, it was not possible to accept the claim that there was no true and full disclosure in the case. When that jurisdictional fact was not established, the ITO could not issue a notice under section 147(a). In the circumstances, the impugned notices were quashed. [Paras 6 & 7]

The writ petition was allowed. [Para 7]

Rajappa AIR 1978 SC 548, has laid down that where there is (i) systematic activity, (ii) organised by co-operation between employer and employees, (iii) for the production and/or distribution of goods and services calculated to satisfy human wants and wishes, prima facie, there is an industry. Absence of profit motive or gainful object is irrelevant. This view of the Supreme Court has been followed by the jurisdictional High Court in the case of CIT v. J.B. Kharwar & Sons [1987] 163 ITR 394 and by Karnataka High Court in the case of Shankar Construction Co. v. CIT [1991] 189 ITR 463. In the case before the Karnataka High Court, the business of constructing dams and channels was taken as that of ‘industrial undertaking’ entitled to investment allowance; while in the case of J.B. Kharwar & Sons (supra) before the Gujarat High Court, the business was that of printing and dyeing of cloths and the work was taken as manufacturing work for the entitlement of deduction under section 80J. On the basis of the above case law, the working of the assessee-firm which was involved in the work of designing, erection and commissioning of water and air pollution control plants, would certainly be falling in the category of an ‘industrial undertaking’, and the assessee-firm was an ‘industrial undertaking’ as used in sections 80HH and 80J.

In the instant case, the activities of the assessee-firm were that of manufacturing or that of producing an article as they were constructing water/air pollution plants. Thus, the assessee-firm was an ‘industrial undertaking’ and was engaged in manufacturing or producing an article in the shape of air/water pollution control. That the assessee was manufacturing or producing the plant in backward area, was one of the requirements of the claim under section 80HH. The contention of the assessee was that only 11.45 per cent of the total receipt had been taken for deduction under section 80HH as that work alone was done in backward area and it was not expected from the assessee to have its office or plant in backward area. The crux of the case laws is that if an industrial undertaking begins to manufacture or produce outside in any backward area, it is entitled to deduction under section 80HH. The assessee-firm set up its own industrial undertaking at the site of its customers for whom water/air pollution control plant was manufactured and of the places which were falling under the backward area declared under the Act, then, naturally the assessee should be getting benefit of the same and the computation made by the assessee-firm of the same was correct one.

Thus the assessee-firm had been able to make out a case in its favour on the guidelines referred to above for qualifying its claim under sections 80HH and 80J and the ITO was justified in allowing its claim from the assessment year 1982-83 onwards till the year under consideration and the Commissioner committed an error in concluding otherwise and the order of Commissioner was to be quashed on this point.

As per the law laid down by the Supreme Court in several decisions, the expression 'derived from' is to be given restricted meaning in section 80HH/80-I while interpreting the section in which this expression is used. [Para 15]

In the instant case, the main and only business of the assessee, for which the plant was set up in the backward area, was to manufacture and to sell soya oil. Hence, all incomes derived from sale of soya oil would be income derived from an industrial undertaking for the purpose of calculating deduction under section 80HH/80-I.

The income earned by the assessee out of sale of gunny bags could not be kept at par or alike the income derived from sale of soya bean oil due to following reasons - Sale of gunny bags was not the main or even ancillary business activity of the assessee; it was not regular or continuous business activity; no investment was made by the assessee for their sale. The gunny bags were never manufactured by the assessee in its plant and merely because some gunny bags were lying in the factory as surplus or unused or as waste material for any reason and such bags were sold to earn income, then it could not be a ground to hold that for the purpose of section 80HH/80-I, such income was the income actually derived from the assessee's industrial undertaking. [Para 16]

In order to derive income from industrial undertaking, the assessee must show that it was earned by sale of goods/commodity which were manufactured/produced in the said industrial undertakings as a part of its main and day-to-day business activity. Only then, the income earned by sale of such goods can be termed as income derived from industrial undertaking within the meaning of section 80HH/80-I. It is for this reason that it has a direct or immediate nexus with the assessee's industrial undertaking established in the backward area. This necessarily follows that income, which has a direct or immediate nexus with the industrial undertaking, alone will be taken into consideration for calculating the deduction under section 80HH/80-I, ibid. Such was not the case in the instant case, because the income earned from sale of gunny bags was not the result of direct or immediate nexus with the business of assessee carried on in the industrial undertaking. [Para 17]

Hence, the Tribunal fell in error in holding that the income earned by the assessee from sale of gunny bags was an income earned from industrial undertaking within the meaning of section 80HH/80-I and, accordingly, the assessee was entitled to claim deduction from total income. That view was to be reversed and order of the Tribunal was to be set aside. [Para 21]
