Computation of Section 80HHC deduction

The deduction under section 80HHC, subject to several other conditions, incorporated in the section, is determined as under: Thus, if the total turnover increases, the advantage which the assessee would get under section 80HHC would decrease because the amount deductible substantially depends upon the ratio between the export turnover and total turnover. If the export turnover is higher, comparatively the amount deductible under section 80HHC would be more; or in other words, if compared to total turnover, export turnover is less the amount deductible from the income under section 80HHC would be reduced. [Para 10]

Meaning of the term 'turnover'

The term 'turnover' had neither been defined in the Act nor has been explained by any of the CBDT circulars. [Para 17]

In the aforesaid circumstances, one has to look at the meaning of the term 'turnover' in ordinary accounting or commercial parlance. [Para 18]

Normally, the term 'turnover' would show the sale effected by a business unit. It may happen that in the course of the business, in addition to the normal sales, the business unit may also sell some other things. [Para 19]

In ordinary accounting parlance, as approved by all accountants and auditors, the term 'sales', when reflected in the profit and loss account, would indicate sale proceeds from sale of the articles or things in which the business unit is dealing. When some other things like old furniture or a capital asset, in which the business unit is not dealing are sold, the sale proceeds therefrom would not be included in 'sales' but it would be shown separately. [Para 20]

In simple words, the word 'turnover' would mean only the amount of sale proceeds received in respect of the goods in which an assessee is dealing in. [Para 21]

So far as the scrap is concerned, the sale proceeds from the scrap may either be shown separately in the profit and loss account or may be deducted from the amount spent by the manufacturing unit on the raw material, which is steel in the case of the respondent-assessee, as the respondent-assessee is using stainless steel as raw material, from which utensils are manufactured. The raw material, which is not capable of being used for manufacturing utensils will have to be either sold as scrap or might have to be re-cycled in the form of sheets of stainless steel, if the manufacturing unit is also having its re-rolling plant. If it is not having such a plant, the manufacturer would dispose of the scrap of steel to someone who would re-cycle the said scrap into steel so that the said steel can be re-used. [Para 22]

When such scrap is sold, the sale proceeds of the scrap cannot be included in the term 'turnover' for the reason that the respondent-unit is engaged primarily in the manufacturing and selling of steel utensils and not scrap of steel. Therefore, the proceeds of such scrap would not be included in 'sales' in the Profit and Loss Account of the respondent-assessee. [Para 23]

The situation would be different in the case of the buyer, who purchases scrap from the respondent-assessee and sells it to someone else. The sale proceeds for such a buyer would be treated as 'turnover' for a simple reason that the buyer of the scrap is a person who is primarily dealing in scrap. In the case on hand, as the respondent-assessee is not primarily dealing in scrap but is a manufacturer of stainless steel utensils, only sale proceeds from sale of utensils would be treated as his 'turnover'. [Para 24]

The Institute of Chartered Accountants of India ('ICAI') has published some material under the head 'Guidance Note on Tax Audit under section 44AB'. The said material has been published so as to guide the members of the ICAI. In our opinion, when a recognized body of Accountants, after due deliberation and consideration publishes certain material for its members, one can rely upon the same. Para 5 of the said Note deals with 'Sales', 'turnover' and 'gross receipts'. The meaning given by the ICAI clearly denotes that in normal accounting parlance the word 'turnover' would mean 'total sales' as explained hereinabove. The said sales would definitely not include the scrap material which is either to be deducted from the cost of raw material or is to be shown separately under a different head. There is no reason for not accepting the meaning of the term 'turnover' given by a body of Accountants, which is having a statutory recognition. [Para 25]

If all accountants, auditors, businessmen, manufacturers etc. are normally interpreting the term 'turnover' as sale proceeds of the commodity in which the business unit is dealing, there is no reason to take a different view than the view normally taken by the persons who are concerned with the said term. [Para 26]

Aluminium Utensils/Vessels (Old) purchased for converting them into scrap

There were three entries under consideration –

Entry 5 read "Aluminium household utensils whether made of aluminium

and aluminium alloys".

Entry 6 read "Aluminium products (including aluminium extrusion) and products, aluminium alloys not elsewhere mentioned in this Schedule."

Entry 83 read "Metal scraps other than those specified in the second Schedule."

The question for consideration is as to under which entry the old aluminum vessels purchased for conversion thereof into new aluminum utensils fall. The Tribunal held that prior to amendment of entry 5, the word 'and" was there between "aluminum" and "household" and it appears to have been left inadvertently to be mentioned in the revised entry. The Tribunal held the word "and" should still be read there and finally held that "old aluminum vessel" fell in entry 5 and not in entry 83.

Held by the Supreme Court- A finding of fact has been arrived at by the Tribunal that the appellant used to purchase the old aluminium vessels and scrap which were used for conversion to new household utensils. Old aluminium vessels are pressed to convert the same into scrap. Appellant, thus, is a scrap dealer and not a dealer in aluminium vessels within the meaning of Entry 5.

The dictionary meaning of scrap is "a small piece or amount of something especially one that is left over after the greater part has been used or material, especially metal, discarded for reprocessing".

The Entries contained in the First Schedule appended to the Act are in three parts. Entry 5 deals with aluminium household utensils. Entry 6 deals with aluminium products and aluminium alloys and 83 deals with metal scraps. Indisputably, aluminium metal scraps would also come within the purview of Entry 83. As the appellant deals in metal scrap, its case will come within the purview of Entry 83. All aluminium products do not come within the purview of Entry 5. It deals with only domestic utensils. For other aluminium products a different rate of tax has been provided in Entry 6. If there exists an entry which covers the goods in question, by necessary implication the same would be considered to have been excluded from another entry.

We will assume that the Entry 5 is capable of two interpretations. It may be read in the manner in which the Tribunal did, but it can also be read as "household utensils made up of aluminium or aluminium alloy." Use of the word "Aluminium" at the beginning may be superfluous. In any event the dealer cannot be said to be dealing with aluminium household utensils or household utensils made up of aluminium and aluminium alloys. We, therefore, are of the opinion that it was entry 83 which is attracted to the facts of the present case. [Baby Varghese v. Clearance of waste by service provider

28.6-2 Following provisions will apply to a service provider, who is not a 'manufacturer'-

Inputs becoming waste while providing output service - If some inputs become waste while providing output services, they are 'used in provision of output services'. In such case, no 'amount' or 'duty' is payable when he sells them as scrap, as it cannot be said that he has 'manufactured' them.

Input becoming waste/scrap before putting to use - If the inputs become waste even before taking them out of stores, an 'amount' equal to Cenvat taken will be payable. The reason is that in such case, it cannot be said that the inputs were used 'for providing output services'.

Sale of empty packing material - A service provider availing Cenvat on inputs is not required to pay any 'amount' on packing material/empty drums sold by him, even if he had availed Cenvat on such inputs.

Sale of goods on which no Cenvat was availed - A service provider is not required to pay any 'amount' if he sells/disposes of inputs or goods on which he has not availed Cenvat credit.

Certified de-polluting equipment to ensure zero leakage of pollutants during draining of fuels or fluids or gases and liquids, certified de-risking equipment for safe neutralization or removal of airbags, pre-tensioner etc., appropriate dismantling equipment for the activities defined (such as de-risking, de-polluting, dismantling, shredding, shearing, bailing etc.), designated areas for storing the segregated scrap, adequate space for storage and handling of segregated spares, designated space for temporary storage of automotive hazardous waste such as tyres, batteries, fuel, oils, liquids and gases, suitable safety and occupational health equipment, material handling equipment for the safe transportation of spares, scrap etc.

(c)

Appropriate Industrial grade lighting and ventilation systems, conformity to noise pollution norms and appropriate effluent treatment plants or water recycling plants.

(9) Scrapping Yards shall accredit themselves with the latest version of quality standards viz. ISO 9001 (Quality management system), ISO14001 (Environmental Management System) and ISO 45001 (Occupational health and safety) within twelve months of commencement of operations.

(10) In case Scrapping Yards do not have adequate capability or provisions for responsible recycling of hazardous waste (like e-waste, lead acid batteries, lithium-ion components, or for recovery of rare earth metals, etc.), or for recycling of scrap material which is outside its scope, then such materials shall be sold to duly authorised recyclers or agencies, who have adequate capability and licence.

borderline case].

Fitting socket to PVC pipe is not manufacture as pipe remains pipe - CCE v. Sabhyata Plastics 2002(145) ELT 166 (CEGAT).

Reeling and rewinding - Reeling and rewinding of sewing thread is not 'manufacture' - CCE v. Anand Threads 2003 (157) ELT 103 (CESTAT) [Now it is 'deemed manufacture' as per chapter note in CETA]. Emptying of contents of drum is not manufacture - In Castrol India Ltd. v. CCE 1998(99) ELT 234 (CEGAT), it was held that emptying of drums is not a process amounting to manufacture and hence no duty is payable on such drums and proportionate duty need not be reversed - followed in G D Saini v. CCE 2001(130) ELT 240 (CEGAT) * CCE v. Hindustan Lever (2001) 137 ELT 751 (CEGAT) * Southern Refineries v. CCE (2001) 136 ELT 134 (CEGAT) * Tata Iron Steel v. CCE (2001) 136 ELT 968 (CEGAT). - also followed in West Coast Industrial Gases Ltd. v. CCE - (1999) 108 ELT 383 (CEGAT) [confirmed in CCE v. West Coast Industrial Gases 2003(155) ELT 11 (SC)] * BASF India v. CCE 2002(146) ELT 404 (CEGAT) * Deepak Fertilisers v. CCE 468 (CESTAT) * Jai Shree Agro Indus v. CCE 2006 (202) ELT 74 (CESTAT) - same view in Wipro Ltd. v. CCE 2006 (196) ELT 226 (CESTAT).

Cleaning, washing and sieving - Cleaning, washing and sieving of brass dross/ash is not manufacture. - Rina Metal Syndicate v. CCE 2001(130) ELT 885 (CEGAT). Washing coal to reduce its ash content would not amount to production or manufacture of new item - CCE v. Tata Iron 2003 (154) ELT 343 (SC) - contrary view in Megha Assam Coal Mines v. State of Assam (2005) 140 STC 339 (Gau HC).

Crushing, grinding of ore - Mining iron ore and then subjecting to process of crushing, grinding, screening and washing to remove foreign materials and to concentrate the ore does not manufacture of different commercial commodity and no excise duty is leviable - CCE v. Steel Authority of India 2003 (154) ELT 65 (CEGAT).

Sieving and grinding of iron ore fine to get iron ore chips is not 'manufacture' - ACCE v. Hygrade Pallet (2010) 249 ELT 266 (CESTAT).

Roasting of ore - Roasting of ore to obtain 'Molybdenum Concentrate' is not 'manufacture' - CC v. Hindustan Gas 2006 (202) ELT 693 (CESTAT).

Re-engraving of rollers is not 'manufacture' - Making gravure printing cylinders out of MS sheet for the first time is 'manufacture'. However, while the same cylinder is worked upon for re-engraving to make it usable as gravure printing cylinder, it is not manufacture. - JSS Printing Industries P Ltd. v. CCE 2000(122) ELT 309 (CEGAT 5 member bench). [Contrary view - Engraving/re-engraving of copper rollers is 'manufacture' - Jupiter Engravers v. UOI 1993(68) ELT 60 (Bom) - followed in Swan Mills v. CCE 2000(115) ELT 442 (CEGAT). Probably the judgments needs a review].

Printing on bare foil/films/paper - Printing a name on film is not manufacture - CC v. Paper Products Ltd. 2000(115) ELT 277 = 119 STC 552 (SC). Printing on bare plastic films does not amount to manufacture (as plastic film continues to be film) - Ellora Mechanical v. CCE 1998(98) ELT 109 (CEGAT) * CCE v. Supreme Industries Ltd. 2000(116) ELT 465 (CEGAT). Printing on Aluminium foil is not manufacture as foil remains foil - Swastik Packaging v. CCE 1986(23) ELT 217 (CEGAT). Printing on coated paper board is not manufacture as no new commodity arises - ITC Ltd. v. CCE 2004 (166) ELT 426 (CESTAT).

Printing on PVC film is not 'manufacture', as new product does not come into existence after such printing - CCE v. Caprihans India 2005 (181) ELT 77 (CESTAT).

The assessee-company was engaged in the activity of processing tobacco for others known as thrashing. In its return of income, the assessee claimed deduction under section 80HH on the ground that its activity of thrashing and redrying of tobacco leaves amounted to manufacture or production. The Assessing Officer disallowed the above claim. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the assessee's claim. On revenue's appeal, Tribunal confirmed the order of the Commissioner (Appeals).

Indian Aluminium Co. reported in 1995 (8) RLT 421 (SC)=1995 (77) ELT 268 (SC) has held that refuse, ashes, rubbish emerging in the course of manufacture are not excisable. (g)

The department was aware of the clearance of scrap generated by the appellants as the appellants had clearly indicated in their letter that MS scrap, cast iron, etc. were cleared during the year 1991-94. Therefore, the allegation of the department that the appellants have suppressed material fact from the department is not correct. Consequently, longer period of limitation for demand of duty cannot be invoked. Demand of duty for the larger period is not in consonance with the law laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Tamil Nadu Housing Board Vs. CCE reported in 1994 (4) RLT 526 (SC)=1994 (55) ECR 7 (SC) wherein it was held that when the law requires that an intention to evade payment of duty, then it is not mere failure to pay duty. Similarly in the case of Padmini Products Vs. CCE reported in 1989 (43) ELT 195 (SC), it was held that in order to make a demand for a period beyond six months, and up to a period of five years, something other than mere inaction or failure on the part of the manufacturer or producer or conscious or deliberate withholding of information when the manufacturer knows otherwise, is required before it is saddled with any duty liability, before the period of six months.

In the present case the period of dispute is 1993-98. Section 11AC was introduced with effect from 28.9.96. But the Commissioner has chosen to impose penalty under Section 11AC with retrospective effect, holding that what is relevant is only the date of issue of show cause and not the time of offence. Dutiability of waste and scrap

3.3 Waste and scrap is practically treated as 'final product' for excise purposes. As discussed above earlier, there was view that dross, skimmings, remnants, bagasse etc. arising during manufacture are not 'goods' even if they fetch some price. Now, this view may not be valid after 10-5-2008.

Thus, waste and scrap can be 'goods' but dutiable only if 'manufactured' and are mentioned in Tariff.

Following discussions and case law is relevant even after 10-5-2008.

Meaning of scrap - The dictionary meaning of 'scrap' is 'a small piece or amount of something especially one that is left over after the greater part had been used or material, especially metal, discarded after processing' - Baby Varghese v. State of Kerala (2008) 16 VST 448 (SC).

Waste and scrap is 'final product' under Cenvat - Board has clarified that waste and scrap is treated as 'final product' under rule 2(e) of Cenvat Credit Rules [that time rule 57AA(c)] and its clearance is as if it is a final product. - MFDR TRU No. 345/2/2000-TRU dated 29-8-2000 (However, this is so if waste is 'manufactured'. Further, waste is not 'final product' if not mentioned in Central Excise Tariff. In any case, this view has not been fully endorsed by Tribunal).

Scrap can be 'goods' - In Khandelwal Metal and Engg. Works v. UOI - 1985 (Supp) 1 SCR 750 = 1985 (20) ELT 222 (SC) = AIR 1985 SC 1211 = (1985) 3 SCC 620, Apex Court held that scrap would be liable to duty, if it is known in commercial parlance by that name and has an established market - followed in Dhrunal Chhotalal Patel v. UOI - 1993 (63) ELT 27 (Bom HC).

In Greysham v. CCE 2000(117) ELT 350 (CEGAT), it was held that waste and scrap of steel arising during manufacture is dutiable as it is marketable and specifically mentioned in tariff.

Iron scrap recovered from slag arising out of manufacture of iron in blast furnace is excisable commodity - Steel Authority of India v. CCE 2006 (197) ELT 113 (CESTAT).

Cotton waste arising in the course of manufacture of cotton yarn and acid sludge arising in the course of refining of crude oil into kerosene can be treated as 'intended manufacture' as they arise regularly and also sold regularly from time to time. - CST v. Bharat Petroleum 1995(77) ELT 790 = 85 STC 220 (SC).

[Earlier, a view was held waste and scrap is not 'manufactured' but arises during the course of manufacture. It is not obtained by any process of manufacture but is obtained in course of manufacture of end product. Waste or scrap is in nature of rubbish and has no distinguishing name character or use and hence it is not goods. However, in view of subsequent judgments of Supreme Court, these judgments are no more valid.]

In Windorz India v. CCE 2002(145) ELT 148 (CEGAT), it was held that cut pieces of Aluminium rods, bars etc. arising during manufacture of Aluminium windows is 'scrap' as defined in CETA and is dutiable.

Duty is payable on waste arising during manufacture of exempted product - CCE v. AG Flats (2012) 277 ELT 96 (CESTAT).

Goods rejected during testing - If finished product is rejected at testing stage, it is to be classified as scrap. - Durgapur Steel Plant v. CCE 2001(132) ELT 784 (CEGAT).

Therefore, oxygen, helium and acetylene gases used for repair and maintenance of plant and machinery are not covered by the definition of ‘input’.

It can be said that any rejection of input without ulterior motive or oblique purpose may not disentitle an assessee from the benefit of law relating to CENVAT credit.

It did not appear that the car manufacturer had escaped duty. The revenue should, therefore, allow entitlement of CENVAT credit in the absence of any violation of law. Accordingly, the demand of Rs. 6,90,150 on the count of using of inputs for R&D was unsustainable in the absence of any finding to show that the R&D had not resulted in finished goods and that finished goods had escaped duty. Exercise of Research having resulted in the finished goods and that had suffered duty, CENVAT credit was admissible for which demand of Rs. 6,90,150 was set aside.

In HIM Technoforge Ltd.’s case (supra), the respondent was a manufacturer of rough forgings and forging articles of steel falling under Chapter 7326 of the CETA, 1985. They also availed CENVAT credit of inputs and capital goods. The dispute related to ‘metal band saw blades’ and ‘steel shots’ as to whether they could be considered as capital goods as contended by the department or could be treated as inputs as claimed by the respondent. The original authority after taking note of the duration of use of these items and the purpose for which they were used held that they were capital goods.

The Commissioner (Appeals) treated the above products as ‘inputs’. He held that under the CENVAT Credit Rules, the term ‘input’ has been defined to mean all goods, except HSD oil, LSD and motor spirit used in or in relation to the manufacture of final products whether directly or indirectly and whether contained in the final product or not. In view of this above definition of the ‘input’ under the CENVAT Credit Rules, both the items, namely, ‘metal saw blade’ and ‘steel shots’ used by the appellants in connection with the production of goods on consumable would merit classification under inputs only and, therefore, the credit taken by them was in order.

The Tribunal held that if the role and period of usage as recorded by the original authority was taken into account, the decision of Commissioner (Appeals) had clearly held that the same were in the nature of consumables used in relation to manufacture of final products and, therefore, appropriately to be treated as inputs.

The expression viz., ‘used in or in relation to the manufacture of final products’ in the specific/substantive part of the definition is so wide that it would cover innumerable items as ‘input’ and to avoid such contingency the Legislature has incorporated the inclusive part after the substantive part qualified by the place of use. For example, one of the categories mentioned in the inclusive part is ‘used as packing material’. Packing material by itself would not suffice till it is proved that the term is used in the course of manufacture of final product. Mere fact that the item is a packing material whose value is included in the accessible value of final product will not entitle the manufacturer to take credit. Oils and lubricants mentioned in the definition are required for smooth running of machines and, hence, they are included as they are used in relation to manufacture of final product. The intention of the Legislature is that inputs falling in the inclusive part must have nexus with the manufacture of the final product.

It means, putting a ‘boomer-tattoo’ in the package material of bubble gum is an additional step in aid used for promotional material and it is not termed as a packing material, as such, especially when it is depicted on the packing that ‘free tattoo inside’. The primary function of putting the ‘tattoo’ in the wrapped bubble gum is to promote the trade and to attract the children rather than to be used for the purpose of packing ‘tattoo’.

Again it is not a matter of dispute that these printed ‘tattoos’ are not used for initial packing in the real sense, rather they are wrapped. Therefore, it cannot possibly be said that the ‘Boomer-tattoo’ is used as initial packing material, meaning thereby the wrapper of the ‘tattoo’ on the bubble gum is not at all required in the form of primary packing. There is no direct and indirect use of the ‘tattoo’ in or in relation to the manufacture of the product, rather it is separately known tattoo in the market, has a separate identity, specific purpose of promotion of the product and for the purpose of advertisement. Hence, it is not a packing material and cannot be considered as inputs within the meaning and definition considered as ‘inputs’ as contemplated under the relevant Rules.

In CCE v. International Tractors Ltd. - 2010 (255) ELT 203 (Punj. & Har.), the respondent was the manufacturer of traction and tractor components. The components manufactured by the respondent were duly packed in boxes and thereafter were sold. The Tribunal had allowed the credit on the goods of full packing of boxes. It had been observed by the Tribunal that duty was paid on the boxes.

The revenue contended that the respondent never received inputs in the packing of boxes and in fact the goods were delivered to the respondent in pallets and, hence, the respondent was not entitled to any credit.

It was held that CESTAT could allow availment of CENVAT credit in respect of duty paid on the packing material.

Place of use

6. The third part of the definition of ‘input’ is the ‘place of use’. Rule 2(k)( i) mandatorily requires that the goods meant for input should be used in the process of manufacture within the premises of the factory. It is a condition precedent to avail CENVAT credit on ‘inputs’ that the product should be manufactured within the premises of the factory. But, at the same time, it is not mandatory for the output service provider to utilize the inputs within the premises of the output service provider. Even if the input is used outside the premises of the service provider, CENVAT credit is allowed for such inputs.

We are manufacturers of Aluminium and we sell Aluminium Dross. Supreme Court had held that ‘dross is not goods’. However, now, Central Excise Tariff has specific headings for dross and slag with effect from February 28, 2005. These are sold and have market value. Should it be held as ‘goods’ with effect from February 28, 2005? It is true that in Union of India v. Indian Aluminium Co. Ltd. - 1995 (77) ELT 268 (SC) = AIR 1995 SC 1580 = 1995 Supp (2) SCC 465 = 1995 AIR SCW 2436 = 1995 (58) ECR 612 (SC 3-member Bench judgment), it was held that ‘dross and skimmings’ arising during manufacture of Aluminium is not ‘excisable goods’. They are merely refuse or ashes given out in process of removing impurities from raw material. Hence they are not ‘excisable goods’ as understood in commercial parlance, even if they are sold and they fetch some price. This was followed in CCE v. Tata Iron & Steel Co. Ltd. 2004 AIR SCW 1948 = 165 ELT 386 = 61 RLT 239 (SC 3-member Bench), where it was held that zinc dross and skimmings are merely refuse, scum or rubbish. It is not result of treatment, labour or manipulation, even if it fetches some price in market. Everything which is sold is not necessarily a marketable commodity known to commerce and worthwhile to trade in.

In CC v. Universal Cables 149 ELT 968 (CEGAT 3- member Bench), it was held that dross and skimming of Aluminium obtained in manufacture of Aluminium rods is not excisable. - Departmental appeal dismissed by the Supreme Court on July 9, 1996 - 151 ELT A 175.

However, now CETA has following specific entries with effect from February 28, 2005 - ‘Brass Dross’ (2620 30 10), ‘Aluminium Dross’ (2620 40 10) and slag/dross from manufacture of iron or steel (2619).

In Balaji Enterprises v. CCE 1997 AIR SCW 2026 = 92 ELT 3 (SC) = AIR 1997 SC 2170, it has been observed and noted that whenever things like waste and scrap have been sought to be taxed in the Central Excise Act, specific entries have been made for this purpose. Supreme Court has noted various specific examples from the old tariff in this regard.

Waste is not obtained by any process of manufacturing but in the course of manufacturing and processing to produce the end product. The intention of legislature to cover waste or scrap in relation to manufacture is required to be specifically mentioned in tariff item before liability to pay duty on waste or scrap arises - Plastics Packaging (P.) Ltd. v. CCE - 1991 (51) ELT 271 (Bom HC). In Shree Synthetic Ltd. v. CCE - 1991 (52) ELT 238 (CEGAT), it was held - "Waste is normally not considered as ‘goods’ except where it is deemed to be ‘goods’ by way of legal fiction and specific mention in any provision, rule or the tariff."

‘Waste or scrap’ will be ‘goods’ and hence taxable only if specifically mentioned in CETA (Tariff) - Kamath Packaging (P.) Ltd. v. CCE - 1992 (60) ELT 666 (CEGAT).

Hence, in my view, these may get covered as dutiable with effect from February 28, 2005.

11.10-7 In CCE v. Shyam Traders 2013 (290) ELT 478 (Tri.-Delhi) the Tribunal found that the shortages of raw material detected at the time of visit by the officers were not sufficient to manufacture the quantity of final products, on which the demand stood confirmed by the lower authorities. To confirm the demand based upon the shortage, only the raw material which was not main raw material could not be sustained, especially in the absence of evidence showing procurement of other raw materials required for manufacture of final products.

11.10-8 In CCE v. Power Electrical & Electronics 2013 (293) ELT 305 (Tri.-Delhi) clandestine removal of 10 transformers was alleged. The Tribunal found that at the time of visit of the officers to the factory when the stock of finished goods was checked 10 transformers were found short vis-à-vis the balance of RG-1 Register. The officials of the company recorded that the 10 transformers had been put in the oven for reovening. The Tribunal held that just because there was no entity in the RG-1 Register regarding transfer of 10 transformers from the bonded storeroom to the manufacturing section of the factory for recovering and when this fact was told to the officers, at that time, still they did not verify, it could not be concluded that there was unexplained shortage of 10 transformers.

11.10-9 In CCE v. Beekay Enterprises 2010 (253) ELT 334 (Tri.-Delhi) it was a case of shortage of raw material found at the time of visit of the officers. Neither the show-cause notice nor the reply contained details of stock as per the records so as to assess as to whether the shortage was minimal or significant. The respondent failed to pay an amount equal to the credit taken on such inputs. There was no dispute about liability to pay of excise duty and interest involved for the shortages. However, the submissions of the department to presume such shortages as clandestine removal and to impose penalty under Section 11AC could not be accepted in the absence of evidence corroborating such clandestine removal.

11.10-10 In Alagappa Cements (P.) Ltd. v. CESTAT 2010 (260) ELT 511 (Mad.), the stock verification disclosed 1,214.578 metric tons of cement clinker whileas physical stock available was only 123.500 metric tons. Abnormal shortage of clinkers as held by the Revenue was used in clandestine manufacture and removal of cement. Two officials gave statements expressing ignorance about shortage of clinkers. Onus was on the appellant to satisfactorily explain shortage and defect in maintenance of records. Shortage of clinkers and excess quantity of limestone were sufficient to conclude clandestine manufacture.

Ltd. 2013 (292) ELT 99 (Tri.- Delhi) the confirmation of demand and imposition of penalty were on the ground that the demand could be confirmed only on the basis of excess shrinkage. There was no other evidence of clandestine removal and confirmation of demand on the ground that there had been excess processing loss was not justified. The shrinkage would vary from fabric-to-fabric and in the absence of any allegation by the Revenue that such quantity attributed to shortage was removed clandestinely, confirmation of demand was not warranted.

3.2 Bagasse held non-manufactured by Supreme Court : The Circular aforesaid was challenged successfully in Balrampur Chini Mills Ltd. v. UOI [2013] 30 taxmann.com 175 (Allahabad) and CCE v. DSCL Sugar [2014] 41 taxmann.com 64/43 GST 151 (Allahabad) and also in CCE v. KCP Sugar & Industries Corporation Ltd. - 2015 (321) ELT A223 (A.P.) on ground that even though marketable, Bagasse was non-manufactured product and therefore, not excisable and even payment under rule 6 would not be required. The Department went in appeal before Supreme Court in UOI v. DSCL Sugar Ltd. 2015 (322) E.L.T. 769, wherein it was held as follows :

Facts : Assessee was manufacturing sugarcane and molasses. In the process of manufacture of sugar, sugarcane is crushed, its juice is extracted and Bagasse emerges as residue/waste of sugarcane. Since Bagasse was liable to Nil rate of duty, department argued that it was 'exempted goods' and demanded Cenvat reversal under rule 6(3) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004.

Held :

No manufacture/deemed manufacture : Bagasse is only an agriculture waste and residue and not result of any process; hence, it is not covered in definition of 'manufacture' under section 2(f) of Central Excise Act, 1944. Further, there is no Chapter note or Section note in Central Excise Tariff declaring process in respect of bagasse as amounting to manufacture.

Not excisable, even if deemed to be marketable : Hence, notwithstanding amendment in 2008 in section 2(d) ibid, creating a fiction of deemed marketability, bagasse is not excisable as it is not passing test of 'manufacture'.

Cenvat Rule 6 inapplicable [for period prior to 1-3-2015] : Since bagasse is not excisable, hence, even if NIL-rated, cenvat rule 6 is inapplicable thereto. Therefore, denial of credit on electricity on ground that bagasse is excisable exempted goods, was incorrect.

3.3 Zinc Dross also held to be non-manufactured by Bombay High Court : The Bombay High Court in Hindalco Industries Ltd. v. UOI [2015] 49 GST 429 opined that Aluminium dross and skimmings, etc. not 'manufactured' goods and not liable to duty, even if marketable/bought and sold. The facts and judgment are :

Facts : In course of manufacture of aluminium sheets/coils, aluminium dross/skimmings emerged as byproducts. Department demanded duty thereon arguing that in view of Explanation to section 2(d), said goods were marketable. Assessee argued that 'aluminium dross/skimmings' were not 'manufactured goods' and were not, therefore, liable to duty.

Held : Conditions contemplated under section 2(d) (excisable goods, movability and marketability) and section 2(f) (manufacture) have to be satisfied conjunctively in order to entail imposition of excise duty. Merely because goods satisfy test of being marketed and saleable and merely because goods are listed in tariff, it does not mean that they are 'manufactured goods'. In various judgments, Supreme Court held that 'aluminium dross/skimmings' are not manufactured goods and said view was followed in context of 'zinc dross and flux skimming'. Hence, impugned goods were not manufactured goods and could not, therefore, be charged to excise duty.

United Phosphorus Ltd. 2000 (117) ELT 529 (SC) unless proved otherwise. The Supreme Court in the case of Indian Cable Co. Ltd. (supra) has expressed that marketability is a decisive test for durability. It only means ‘saleable’ or ‘suitable for sale’. It need not be, in fact, marketed. The article should be capable of being sold or being sold to consumers in the market, as it is without anything more. In the absence of a finding, that the goods are ‘marketable’, i.e., saleable or suitable for sale, it could not be said to be a good, which may be subject to excisability.

The Apex Court in the case of Union of India v. Indian Aluminium Co. Ltd. 1995 (58) ECR 612 has reiterated that marketability is a question of fact to be decided on the facts of each case. It was held that it may be possible to recover something from a particular thing, they can, therefore, be sold but that does not make them a marketable commodity. In other words, everything, which is sold, is not necessarily a marketable commodity as known to the commercial world and, it may be worthwhile to trade in. Since marketability test is essentially a question of fact - Hindustan Zinc Ltd. v. CCE 2005 (181) ELT 170 (SC), there must be some serious attempts to go to market and collect proper evidences, but it cannot be established on basis of mere stability. Sufficient proof that product is commercially known is required - Gujarat Nermada Valley Fert. Co. Ltd. v. CCE 2005 (184) ELT 128 (SC) which could not be viewed through a hawker’s eye - Mahindra & Mahindra Ltd. v. CCE 2005 (190) ELT 301 (Trib. - LB) unless the product is capable of being marketed and is known to those who are in the market, as having an identity as a distinct identifiable commodity, that the article is subject to excise duty. Fact that articles fall within Schedule, not make them marketable. Actual sale is not necessary but article must be capable of being sold in market or known in market as good - Gujarat Nermada Valley Fert. Co. Ltd.’s case (supra ). Actual purchase and sale, or fact of their being marketed or their general availability in market is not required to be proved- Mahindra & Mahindra Ltd.’s case (supra).

Article is not eligible to be taxed only because it is having saleable value. CCE v. Indian Aluminium Co. Ltd. 2006 (203) ELT 3 (SC). Mention of an item in an exemption notification is not determinative of its excisability. New Shorrock Mills v. CCE 2006 (202) ELT 192 (Trib. - LB); Indore Wire Co. Ltd. v. Union of India 2006 (203) ELT 179 (SC). Mere listing of an item in the Schedule to the Act is not sufficient to make it excisable - Ahmedabad Electricity Co. Ltd.’s case (supra). Mere mention of item in ISI is also not sufficient - Tata Iron & Steel Co. Ltd. v. Union of India 2004 (164) ELT 372 (SC).

Once marketability of an article is established, the fact that it is not actually sold but is entirely consumed captively or that it is sold only to one or two buyers has no relevance. However, mere manufacturing activity by itself, does not prove marketability. Inter-unit transfer of an item does not prove its marketability. Product produced must be a distinct commodity known in common parlance to commercial community for the purpose of buying and selling - Cipla Ltd. v. CCE 2008 (225) ELT 403 (SC).

Accordingly, articles like storage units, running counters, wall and kitchen units normally not capable to be removed without cannibalizing, are not furniture and not excisable goods - Craft Interiors (P.) Ltd. v. CCE 2006 (203) ELT 529 (SC). The goods, which are removed and used for mandatory quality control test and are destroyed during such test, cannot be considered as amounting to removal and as such do not fall under category of ‘excisable goods’ - CCE v. Tarco Cable Co. Ltd. 2001 (127) ELT A49 (SC). Intellectual property or information technology being an intangible asset if once put on a paper, cassette, diskettes or any other thing to supply the same, fall under the category of ‘excisable goods’ just like drawings, designs, manuals and technical materials - Associated Cement Companies Ltd. v. CCE 2001 (128) ELT 21 (SC).

80. (1) Tetraethyl lead compound shall not be unloaded from a ship unless—

(a)

it is packed in specially constructed steel drums of substantial construction, sealed with an inner and outer bung, and fitted with rolling roofs on to the shell as an added precaution;

(b)

all receptacles containing tetraethyl lead compound are distinctively and durably marked with the words "Tetraethyl Lead Compound Poison"; and

(c)

two sets of protective equipment comprising the following are provided and kept readily available for use in the event of any leakage of tetraethyl lead compound—

(i)

rubber gloves,

(ii)

rubber boots,

(iii)

rubber apron or oilskin suit, and

(iv)

suitable respirator, which should be either of canister type containing minimum of 50cc. of activated charcoal or an airline respirator with an independent fresh air supply.

(2) Following measures shall be taken while unloading tetraethyl lead compound:—

(a)

no receptacle containing tetraethyl lead compound shall be opened within the limits of the port;

(b)

before commencement of the unloading operations, the consignment of tetraethyl lead compound shall be inspected on board the vessel by a responsible person. No tetraethyl lead compound drums showing any sign of leakage shall be unloaded until suitably repaired or placed in a larger receptacle or container offering sufficient precautions from leakage;

(c)

drums containing tetraethyl lead compound shall be discharged under the supervision of a responsible person;

(d)

drums containing tetraethyl lead compound shall be loaded discharged in rope slings with a maximum of two drums at a separate sling for each drum. Hooks shall on no account be used;

(e)

dock workers handling drums containing tetraethyl lead compound shall be provided with heavy gloves of canvas or leather and shall use such gloves; and

(f)

adequate quantities of non-inflammable solvent or kerosene and soap and water to deal with any leakages of tetraethyl lead compound shall be kept readily available where the work of handling of the tetraethyl lead compound is carried on.

(3) Following measures shall be taken in the event of leakage of tetraethyl lead compound:—

(a)

the area on which the leakage of tetraethyl lead compound has occurred (including the outside of a drum) shall be treated as follows:—

(i)

flush with kerosene or some other light oil solvent followed by water. If the surface permits, wash thoroughly with soap working up as much lather as possible, and again flush with water;

(ii)

if it is possible to obtain quickly a supply of common bleaching lime (Ca O Cl2) the area should first be treated generously with a mixture of bleaching lime and water in the form of thin slurry (NEVER use the dry powder) alternatively a five per cent solution of sulphury! chloride (SO2 Cl2) in kerosene may be used;

(b)

if contamination of absorbent material such as wooden flooring, dunnage, or other packing material has taken place, then such material shall, after treatment as above, be removed from the place where tetraethyl lead compound is being handled;

(c)

any clothing which becomes contaminated by tetraethyl lead compound shall be removed immediately and cleaned by repeated rinsing in a non-inflammable dry cleaning fluid;

(d)

if tetraethyl lead compound can be smelled, dock workers not assigned to deal with the leakage of tetraethyl lead compound shall be removed from that place; and

(e)

dock workers assigned to deal with leakage of tetraethyl lead compound shall wear the protective equipment described under sub-regulation 1(c).

(4) Suitable protective clothing shall be provided for handling of tetraethyl lead compound in refrigerated spaces.

Ltd. 2003 AIR SCW 5529 = 134 STC 24 = 158 ELT 3 (SC) (para 29), it was observed, 'Manufacturing process involved treatment, labour or manipulation by the manufacturer resulting in a new and different article. It requires a deliberate skilful manipulation of the inputs or the raw materials. This was not so in case of scrap'.

Waste/scrap generated from sources other than raw materials is not excisable - Indian Petrochemical Corporation Ltd. v. CCE 2006 (198) ELT 193 (CESTAT).

In Kusum Products v. CCE 2003 (156) ELT 900 (CEGAT) also, it was held that burning of coal in boiler is not a process of manufacture and cinder is not dutiable even if it may be sold at a price - same view in Khandesh Extraction v. CCE 2003 (156) ELT 928 (CEGAT).

Waste transformer oil is not excisable goods - Lucas Indian Services v. CCE (2008) 232 ELT 472 (CESTAT).

A manufacturer of beverages cannot be held to be manufacturer of glass and have no intention to manufacture broken glass bottles. No duty is payable on broken glass cleared - Pepsico (I) Holding v. CCE (2008) 231 ELT 487 (CESTAT).

In CCE v. Dhillon Kool Drinks 2001(130) ELT 475 (CEGAT), it was held that waste and scrap arising out of broken bottles through the process of filling, handling etc. is neither generated during the course of manufacture of glass bottles nor it could be considered as a manufactured product. - Departmental appeal dismissed by SC - (2002) 144 ELT A210.

CCE 2007 (210) ELT 219 (CESTAT).

In Alcobex Metals v. CCE (2004) 168 ELT 455 (CESTAT), it was held that 'industrial dust' arising during manufacture of brass or scrap is not excisable', since it is only waste, refuse. It is not manufactured goods - followed in Swastik Power Lines v. CCE 2005 (184) ELT 79 (CESTAT), where it was held that mud containing small quantity of metal is not excisable.

Mixed sweepings of cigarette paper, filter rod, aluminium foil, ribbon etc. arising during manufacture of cigarettes and sold at low prices, is not a manufactured product and not dutiable - CCE v. ITC Ltd. (2008) 221 ELT 543 (CESTAT).

Textile articles : Excise duty of 2% (without CENVAT credit) or 12.5% (with CENVAT credit) is being levied on readymade garments and made up articles of textiles falling under Chapters 61, 62 and 63 (heading Nos. 6301 to 6308) of the Central Excise Tariff except those falling under 6309 and 6310 of retail sale price (RSP) of Rs.1000 and above when they bear or are sold under a brand name. This optional levy would apply to such readymade garments and made up articles of textiles regardless of the composition of the garment/article. However, in respect of readymade garments and made up articles of textiles other than those mentioned above, the optional levy of, 'Nil' (without CENVAT credit) or 6% (with CENVAT credit)? in case of garments / articles of cotton, not containing any other textile material and 'Nil' (without CENVAT credit) or 12.5% (with CENVAT credit)? in case of garments/articles of other composition, as the case may be, shall continue. The SSI exemption for the month of March, 2016 will be Rs.12.5 lakh, subject to fulfilment of other conditions of the Notification No.8/2003-C.E., dated 01.03.2003. 2. Jewellery Excise duty of 1% (without CENVAT credit) or 12.5% (with CENVAT credit) is levied on articles of jewellery [excluding silver jewellery, other than studded with diamonds/other precious stones] with a higher SSI-exemption upto Rs. 6 crore in a year and SSI-eligibility limit of Rs. 12 crore. Thus, a jewellery manufacturer will be eligible for exemption from excise duty on first clearances upto Rs. 6 Crore during a financial year, if his aggregate domestic clearances during preceding financial year were less than Rs. 12 crore. In other words, jewellery manufacturer having aggregate value of clearances in a financial year exceeding Rs. 12 crore, will not be eligible for this threshold exemption in the subsequent financial year. The SSI exemption for the month of March, 2016 for jewellery manufacturers will be Rs.50 lakh, subject to the condition that value of clearances for home consumption from one or more manufacturer from one or more factory or premises of production or manufacture during the financial year 2014-15 should not be more than Rs. 12 crore. Computation for this purpose shall be done in accordance with the provisions of Para 3A of Notification No. 8/2003-CE. For this purpose, a certificate from a Chartered Accountant, based on the books of account, shall suffice. Registration : Registration once applied for shall be granted within two working days, along with simplified registration procedure as prescribed under Notification No. 35/2001-CE. Further, the requirement of post registration physical verification of the premises has been also done away with in this case. Notifications provide for an optional centralized central excise registration for jewellery manufacturers with centralized billing or accounting system. [Notification Nos. 5 and 6-CE(NT), dated 1-3-2016] Moreover, documents being maintained by the jewellery manufacturers for State VAT or Bureau of Indian Standards (in the case of hallmarked jewellery) shall suffice for Excise purposes also. The private records of the jewellery manufacturers, giving details of daily stock for his own purposes, shall be accepted for the purposes of Rule 10 of the Central Excise Rules 2002. Also, jewellery manufacturers will be eligible for a simplified return applicable for optional excise duty of 1%/2% without CENVAT credit under Notification No.1/2011-CE, under Rule 12 of the Central Excise Rules, 2002. Rule 12AA of the Central Excise Rules, 2002 provides that in case of goods falling under Chapter heading 7113, every person (not being an EOU or SEZ unit) who gets jewellery made from any other person, and supplies the raw materials such as gold/silver/gemstones to the job-worker for such manufacture, the duty liability would be on such person who gets articles of jewellery made from the job worker. In such cases, the principal manufacturer (and not job worker) will be required to get Central Excise registered, pay duty and follow other compliance requirements. This will ensure that small artisans/goldsmiths are not required to take any excise registration. The SSIs will be eligible for quarterly payment of duty. Earlier Notification No. 9/2012-C.E. (N.T.), dated 17-3-2012 provided that tariff value in respect of articles of jewellery (other than silver jewellery) [excluding articles of jewellery manufactured from precious metal or old jewellery provided by the retail customer], falling under sub-heading No. 7113 of the First Schedule to the Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985 (5 of 1986), shall be 30% of the transaction value as declared in the invoice. Now, this notification stands rescinded. 3. | Rule 7(4) of CER | 1-3-2016 | The erstwhile rule provided that the assessee shall be liable to pay interest on any amount payable to Central Government, consequent to order for final assessment under sub-rule (3), at the rate specified by the Central Government by notification issued under section 11AA of the Act from the first day of the month succeeding the month for which such amount is determined, till the date of payment thereof. The highlighted words were interpreted in Ceat Ltd. v. CCE [2015] 317 ELT 192 (Bom.) that if differential duty is paid even prior to finalization of provisional assessment, then, no interest can be demanded under Rule 7(4) because amount determined as payable on finalization of assessment order is 'NIL'. Now, this rule is substituted to provide that the assessee shall be liable to pay interest on any amount paid or payable on the goods under provisional assessment, but not paid on the due date specified under sub-rule (1) of rule 8 and the first proviso thereto, as the case may be, at the rate specified by the Central Government, vide, notification under section 11AA of the Act, for the period starting with the first day after the due date till the date of actual payment, whether such amount is paid before or after the issue of order for final assessment. Thus, first of all, interest would arise on already paid amount and further, interest would start from due date of payment. Example : Goods under provisional assessment, cleared in Jan., 2016. Say a provisional duty of Rs. 5000 is paid on the 6th February, 2016 [due date under sub-rule (1) of rule 8]. Further duty of Rs 9000 is paid on the 15th April, 2016, and on the same day the documents for final assessment are submitted by the assessee. Final assessment order is issued on the 18th June, 2016, assessing the duty payable on goods as Rs. 15000. Consequently the assessee pays a duty of Rs. 1000 on the 30th June, 2016. As due date for payment of duty of Rs. 15000 is the 6th February, 2016, hence, in this case : no interest shall be payable on Rs. 5000, interest shall be payable on Rs. 9000 from the 7th February, 2016, till the 15th April, 2016, and interest shall be payable on Rs. 1000 from the 7th February, 2016, till the 30th June, 2016. | Rule 26(1) of CER | 1-4-2016 | Conclusion of proceedings against main assessee, would conclude proceedings against co-noticees : Rule 26(1) provides that any person who : acquires possession of, or is in any way concerned in transporting, removing, depositing, keeping, concealing, selling or purchasing, or in any other manner deals with, any excisable goods which he knows or has reason to believe are liable to confiscation under the Act or these rules, shall be liable to a penalty of upto : (a) duty on such goods or (b) Rs. 2,000, whichever is greater. When proceedings for penalty etc. have been settled against main culprit/noticee under Section 11AC of the Central Excise Act, 1944, then, it is useless to continue proceedings against co-noticees. Now, it is provided that where any proceeding for the person liable to pay duty have been concluded under section 11AC(1)(a)/(d) in respect of duty, interest and penalty (on payment thereof within 30 days from SCN), all proceedings in respect of penalty against other persons, if any, in the said proceedings shall also be deemed to be concluded. However, if adjudication order is passed against main noticee and proceedings are not concluded at SCN-stage, then, penalty against other persons would continue to be levied. This benefit will motivate manufacturers to settle matter at SCN-stage. Other persons would also pressurize in this behalf. |

Waste transformer oil is not excisable goods - Lucas Indian Services v. CCE (2008) 232 ELT 472 (CESTAT).

Floor sweepings - Mixed sweepings of cigarette paper, filter rod, aluminium foil, ribbon etc. arising during manufacture of cigarettes and sold at low prices, is not a manufactured product and not dutiable - CCE v. ITC Ltd. (2008) 221 ELT 543 (CESTAT).

Floor sweepings arising in process of manufacture of soap is waste material including mud, rubbish etc. It is disposed off at nominal value. The goods are not excisable - Kailash Soap v. CCE (2008) 231 ELT 176 (CESTAT).

Floor sweeping during manufacture of biscuits is not 'manufactured' although it has some value - Harinagar Sugar Mills v. CCE (2014) 310 ELT 775 (CESTAT SMB).

Waste of base metal generated by way of sweeping of floor cannot be considered as having been manufactured - Tempo Instruments v. CCE (2008) 225 ELT 444 (CESTAT).

CHAPTER VII

LIFTING APPLIANCES AND GEAR

Construction and maintenance of lifting appliances

.

55. The employer shall ensure at a construction site of a building or other construction work that-

(a)

All lifting appliances, including their parts and working gear, whether fixed or movable and any plant or gear used in anchoring or fixing of such appliances, are-

(i)

of sound construction, sound material, and of adequate strength to serve the purpose for which these are to be used and all such appliances shall be free from patent defects; and

(ii)

maintained in good repair and working condition.

(b)

(i) every drum or pulley around which the rope of any lifting appliance is carried, is of adequate diameter and sound construction in relation to such rope;

(ii) any rope which terminates at the winding drum of a lifting appliance is securely attached to such drum and at least three dead turns of such rope remain on such drum in every operating position of such lifting appliance;

(iii) the flange of a drum project twice the rope diameter beyond the last layer of such rope and if such projection is not available, other measures like anti-slackness guards shall be provided to prevent such rope from coming off such drum;

(c)

Every lifting appliance is provided with adequate and efficient brakes which-

(i)

are capable of preventing fall of a suspended load (including any test load) and of effectively controlling such load while it is being lowered;

(ii)

act without shock;

(iii)

have shoes that can be easily removed for running; and

(iv)

are provided with simple and easily accessible means of adjustment:

Provided that nothing contained in this clause shall apply to steam- winch which can be operated as safely as with brakes as provided in accordance with this clause.

(d)

Controls of every lifting appliance-

(i)

are so situated that the driver of such appliance at his stand or seat has ample room for operating and has an unrestricted view of building or other construction work, as far as practicable, and that he remains clear of the load and ropes, and that no load passes over him;

(ii)

are positioned with due regard to ergonometric considerations for proper operation of such appliance;

(iii)

are so located that the driver of such appliance remains above the height of the heel block during the whole operation of such appliance;

(iv)

have upon them or adjacent to them clear markings to indicate their purpose and mode of operations;

(v)

are provided, where necessary, with a suitable locking device to prevent accidental movement or displacement;

(vi)

move, as far as practicable in the direction of the resultant load movement; and

(vii)

wherever automatic brakes are provided, automatically come to the neutral position in case of power failure.

(g)

Remelting scrap ingots of iron and steel:

Products roughly cast in the form of ingots without feeder-heads or hot tops, or of pigs, having obvious surface faults and not complying with the chemical composition of pig iron, spiegeleisen or ferro-alloys.

(h) Granules :

Products of which less than 90% by weight passes through a sieve with a mesh aperture of 1 mm and of which 90% or more by weight passes through a sieve with a mesh aperture of 5 mm.

(ij)

Semi-finished products :

Continuous cast products of solid, section, whether or not subjected to primary hot-rolling; and other products of solid sections, which have not been further worked than subjected to primary hot-rolling or roughly shaped by forging, including blanks for angles, shapes or sections.

These products are not presented in coils.

(k)

Flat-rolled products:

Rolled products of solid rectangular (other than square) cross-section, which do not conform to the definition at (ij) above in the form of:

–

coils of successively superimposed layers, or

–

straight lengths, which if of a thickness less than 4.75 mm, are of width measuring at least ten times the thickness or if of a thickness of 4.75 mm or more are of a width which exceeds 150 mm and measures at least twice the thickness.

Flat-rolled products include those with patterns in relief derived directly from rolling (for example, grooves, ribs, chequers, tears, buttons and lozenges) and those, which have been perforated, corrugated or polished, provided that they do not thereby assume the character of articles or products of other headings.

Flat-rolled products of a shape other than rectangular or square, of any size, are to be classified as products of a width of 600 mm or more, provided that they do not assume the character of articles or products of other headings.

(l)

Bars and rods, hot-rolled, in irregularly wound coils :

Hot-rolled products in irregularly wound coils, which have a solid cross-section in the shape of circles, segments of circles, ovals, rectangles (including squares), triangles, or other convex polygons (including "flattened circles" and "modified rectangles", of which two opposite sides are convex arcs, the other two sides being straight, of equal length and parallel). Sub-heading Notes :

Reinforced Cement Concrete Pipes

They are not taxable as "Wares made of any metal or alloy other than brass and aluminium".

The pipes are constructed with cement, sand and stone grits, which are reinforced with steel wires and rods. They do not fall in the entry "Wares made of any metal or alloy other than brass and aluminium", because this entry does not cover all wares made of metal. The Hindi version of the notification uses the word "Bartan" for "wares" in the English Notification. Reading the Hindi and English versions of the notification together it becomes clear that the word 'wares' used in the English version has been used in the sense of such wares that are commonly used as utensils. The articles that will not be called "utensils' will not be covered by this entry. The pipes manufactured by the assessee can by no stretch of imagination be called utensils.

In Commissioner of Sales Tax v. Ram Niwas Pushkar Dutt, 1971 UPTC 413 : (1971) 28 STC 736 (All)* (by the Full Bench of Allahabad High Court), the attention of the Bench was not invited to the Hindi version of the notification-dated 21.5.1963. We are unable to read the Full Bench decision as defining the exact significance of the word "wares" as used in the Hindi notification. [Indian Hume Pipe Company v. State of Uttar Pradesh, 1975 UPTC 517 : (1974) 34 STC 230 (All) decided on 10.5.1974 by the Division Bench of the Hon'ble Allahabad High Court]

*Note – In Commissioner of Sales Tax v. Ram Niwas Pushkar Dutt, 1971 UPTC 413 : (1971) 28 STC 736 (All), it was held that weights and measures do not fall in the term "Hardware" because, according to the Court, only those items are included in "hardware" as have something in common with "mill stores" because the Entry under consideration in this case was "Mill stores and hardwares". Hindi version of the said notification read "Mill ke Stores Evam Lohe Ki bani Vastuen". This fact was not brought to the knowledge of the Full Bench in this case. Therefore, this judgment has not been followed by the Division Bench in the case of Indian Hume Pipe Company v. State of Uttar Pradesh, 1975 UPTC 517; (1974) 34 STC 230 (All) while interpreting the meaning of the words "wares".

Iron pallets manufactured and sold by the Assessee to Glaxo Laboratories India Limited for stacking the bags of sugar and wheat do not come within the term "furniture."

12. (1) The owner of different types of ships intended to be recycled within India shall fulfill the following conditions for safe-for- entry or safe-for-hot work, as the case may be, namely:—

(a)

In case of Oil tankers and Chemical tankers, safe for entry and safe for hot work permits are to be obtained for every compartment before actual entry and cutting operations are initiated by ship recyclers.

(b)

The compartment-wise permits as specified under clause (a), shall be required to be obtained in addition to the permission for recycling issued by the competent authority.

(c)

For petroleum oil cargo tankers and petroleum slop tanks, the Petroleum and Explosives Safety Organization/PESO or an authority approved by it shall issue gas free and fit for hot work certificate.

(2) For the purpose of issuing the safe-for-entry and safe-for-hot work permits, inspection shall be carried out by the Safety officer of the Directorate of Industrial Safety and Health/DISH or authorized person of the Directorate of Industrial Safety and Health to ensure the conditions specified under the Fifth Schedule.

(3) In the case of ship recycling process of non - tanker ships, petroleum tankers and slop tankers, the Ship Recyclers shall fulfill the following conditions for safe-for-hot work, namely: —

(a)

Provide portable water hoses with a dedicated water pump with adequate take-off points for attaching additional hoses, for working on the recycling vessel, for immediate water supply in the event of fire, and for wetting the asbestos etc., before its removal from the vessel.

(b)

No naked light or flame or hot work shall be permitted inside a confined space or area, unless it has been made completely free of the flammable material, tested and found safe by a competent person.

(c)

Obtain Naked Light Certificate (Hot Work Permit) as per the rule 68-H of the model rules made under the Factories Act, 1948 (63 of 1948), issued by the relevant authority.

(d)

Keep the area assigned for hot work free from any explosive mixture such that the explosive meter reading is below explosive limit.

(e)

Use only non-sparking tools and flameproof hand lamps protected with guard and safety torches inside such confined space or area for initial inspection, cleaning or other work required to be done for making the area safe.

(f)

Undertake welding, flame cutting and other hot work only on the orders of a competent person after appropriate precautions, as required, are taken to reduce the risk of fire and explosion.

(4) The explosive meter reading of the recycling facility shall be recorded in the work permit by the relevant issuing authority.

(5) Any safe-for-entry or safe-for-hot work certificate or permit shall only be issued by the relevant authorities only after conducting the necessary inspections and satisfying themselves of due compliance of the same, as specified under the Fifth Schedule.

CCE 2012 (285) ELT 274 (Tri. - Ahd.) - The Tribunal found that it was not in dispute that the H.R. coils received by the appellant were exclusively used for manufacturing of MS pipes by availing of exemption Notification No. 6/2002-CE, as amended. It was also undisputed that the appellant had maintained the separate records and also had availed the CENVAT credit of the duty paid on said inputs. Rule 6(1) provides that CENVAT credit shall not be allowed on the quantity of input which is used for the manufacture of exempted goods. The appellants contended that they had not maintained separate accounts asmuchas they had reversed an amount of the 8% of the value of the exempted goods which contention would not hold any water inasmuch as there was nothing on record to show that there was use of the H.R. Coils for dutiable products. An attempt was made by the appellants that they had cleared that MS scrap arising out of utilization of such HR Coils was on payment of duty. By any stretch of imagination, scrap could not be considered as a manufactured product, at least in the case in hand before us. The Tribunal also found that General Manager of the appellant had clearly and categorically stated that the HR Coils which were received by them were used only for the purpose of manufacturing of pipes which were cleared without payment of duty. This being the factual matrix the Tribunal found that the appellant could not claim the benefit of Rule 6(3) by debiting the amount equivalent to 8% of the value of the exempted goods and avail CENVAT credit on the H.R. Coils received by them. On merits the Tribunal did not find any case in favour of the assessee.

6.4-3 In Unn Sugar Complex v. CCE 2013 (293) ELT 236 (Tri. - Delhi) - The appellant manufactured sugar and molasses chargeable to Central Excise duty. They availed CENVAT credit of excise duty paid on inputs. In course of manufacture of sugar during crushing of sugar cane by produce/waste - bagasse emerged. The Department was of the view that since the appellant had not maintained separate accounts and inventory of the inputs used in or in relation to manufacture of dutiable final products - sugar and molasses and exempted final product - bagasse, in accordance with the provisions of Rule 6(3) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, they would be required to pay an amount equal to 8% of the sale value of the bagasse. The Additional Commissioner confirmed the demand with interest and also imposed penalty. The first Adjudicating Authority confirmed the same. The Tribunal held that by no stretch of imagination it could be said that the assessee possibly could have maintained separate accounts for the inputs for the production of sugar and molasses (excisable items) and bagasse. The assessee was liable to pay amount equal to 8% of the sale value of bagasse and confirmed the order.

6.5 Statutory requirement

6.5-1 In Hero Motocorp Ltd. v. CCE 2012 (285) ELT 218 (Tri. - Delhi) - The Tribunal held that on bare reading of Rule 2(k) it was clear that 'input' meant and included accessories of final product cleared along with final product. Rule 138(4)(b) of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1989 made it incumbent on driver of every vehicle to carry the tool kit prescribed by the manufacturer. Since carrying of the tool kit in the vehicle was obligatory for the driver, it could be safely inferred that tool kit was necessary accessory of the motor vehicle because driving of the vehicle without those accessories would be violative of Rule 138(4)(b) of the Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989. Thus, the Tribunal was of the view that the appellants had supplied the tool kit as per the statutory requirements under the Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989 as accessories to be used in relation to the manufacture of vehicle. Thus 'tool kit' was squarely covered by the definition of 'input' under Rule 2(k)(i) of the CENVAT credit Rules and that the appellants had rightly availed of the CENVAT credit in relation to tool kit.

Assuming that process amounts to manufacture, liability to pay duty is of the manufacturer : in this case, job-worker. The job-work charges would form part of the value and since, in this case, the job-work charges are in kind in form of retention of 20 kg. scrap, the value would be determined based on value of scrap retained by the job-worker.

CENVAT CREDIT - REVERSAL ON EXEMPTED SERVICE AND SERVICES COVERED UNDER FULL REVERSE CHARGE ?

6. We are manufacturing goods which are 100% excisable and are also providing Goods Transport Agency's Services, which are exempt as per mega exemption notification (transport of defence and military equipments). When taking and availing cenvat, is it necessary to reverse cenvat on exempted service as per rule 6 of CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 ? Is it necessary to reverse credit, even if service is provided on reverse charge mechanism ? Kindly clarify.

Reversal under rule 6 would apply to exempted services provided by service provider. Hence, it would equally apply to exempt Goods Transport Agency's Services.

However, where services are covered under reverse charge, they cease to be 'output service' and hence, no credit can be availed in respect thereof. Hence, any wrongly taken credit has to be reversed.

7. Whether supply of bed rolls in the trains attracts Service tax before 1-10-2012 and whether there is any abatement of 30% after 1-10-2012 on the same service ? If yes, under which notification ?

Supply of bed rolls in trains is a taxable service and is not eligible for any exemption or abatement. The abatement relates only to 'transport of passengers by railways' and the service in question is altogether different.

SERVICE TAX - OUTDOOR CATERING v. FACTORY CANTEEN

8. If outdoor caterer is providing catering service in a mess within the factory premises : Is the service exempt as per the mega exemption notification ?

Entries 19 and 19A of the Mega Exemption Notification No. 25/2012-ST, dated 20-6-2012 read as follows :

"19. Services provided in relation to serving of food or beverages by a restaurant, eating joint or a mess, other than those having the facility of air-conditioning or central air-heating in any part of the establishment, at any time during the year;";

19A. Services provided in relation to serving of food or beverages by a canteen maintained in a factory covered under the Factories Act, 1948 (63 of 1948), having the facility of air-conditioning or central air-heating at any time during the year."

It appears that mess would be covered by Entry 19A (if maintained as per Factories Act and having AC) or Entry 19 (if non-AC).

Some experts would suggest that mess services are provided by company to employees and not by outdoor caterer and hence, exemption cannot be availed. However, the most important fact to be noted is that 'company has hired outdoor caterer to run mess' in compliance with law and therefore, mess is run/operated by caterer and mess services would thus, be exempt as aforesaid. Employer-company is not the service provider; in fact, it is duty bound to arrange for canteen and canteen/mess services are provided only by the caterer.

They are not covered in "hardwares". They are in fact two rods or one rod bent at two ends so that the two arms of the rod made an opaque angle at the middle portion of the rod.

It is so because it has been held in the case of Commissioner of Sales Tax v. Ram Niwas Pushkar Dutt, 1971 UPTC 413 by the Full Bench of the Allahabad High Court that "what is comprehended within the expression "mill stores and hardwares" are all those articles which whether described as mill stores or hardware have something common with each other.

The view of Division Bench of Hon'ble Allahabad High Court taken in the case of Commissioner of Sales Tax v. Aftab Husain Imdad Husain, 25 STC 477 that, "If the word has been intended to comprehend its wider meaning it would we think be entered as separate entry and not put in the same entry as Mill store…. Hardware referred ordinarily to items made of base metal consisting of building material such as nuts, bolts, hinges, rivets, letches etc.", was endorsed in the case of Ram Niwas Pushkar Dutt (supra).

On the finding that cross arms is used for supporting high-tension electrical lines, they cannot be covered under the entry "Mill stores and Hardware." [Asia Tool Industries v. Commissioner of Sales Tax, 1980 UPTC 50, decided on 30.7.1979 by Allahabad High Court].

2.14-12 Toolings, used for production of refractories, is tangible fixed asset and not consumables and hence should be ac-counted as per AS 10/ICDS-V and not as per AS 2/ICDS-II

Toolings, used for production of refractories, is fixed asset and not consumables and hence the treatment of toolings should be as per AS 10/ICDS-V and not as per AS 2/ICDS-II.

Case Study 2.14.12.1: A company is in the business of manufacturing refractories (a material which retains its strength at high temperatures). The manufacturing process requires that to give shape to refractories, it is required to be filled into 'tooling' (comprised of an outer jacket made by a special metal). These toolings are imported in India. Toolings have a limited useful life of 3 years. As per the present accounting policy, the company treats toolings as consumables having a life of 3 years and accordingly the cost of tooling is amortised over a period of 3 years. Hence, toolings are disclosed under 'inventories'. Whether the present treatment done by company is correct ?

Answer: No. Toolings cannot be treated as inventory (consumables) because consumables are generally consumed in the production process whereas toolings do not get consumed but facilitate production process. Toolings are used in the production of refractories (finished goods) and have a limited useful life. [EAC opinion Query 26 Volume 29 Opinion finalised on 15 Dec 2009] Accordingly, toolings are fixed assets which should be depreciated in accordance with the Act and the Rules.

2.14-13 Whether foodstuffs purchased by company for supply to staff at subsidised rates should be treated as inventory and valued as per ICDS-II?

A company is in the business of manufacturing of tea. The company, to follow existing rules, is required to distribute foodstuff to its employees at concessional rates. The company purchases foodstuff in bulk quantity. The distribution of foodstuff to employees is at subsidized rates (lesser that the bulk cost). Whether ICDs-II applies to stock of such foodstuff?

In accordance with AS 2/ICDS-II, foodstuff cannot be treated as 'inventory'. Rather it is a short term employee benefit as explained by Para 8(d) of AS 15. Valuation of foodstuff should be as follows:-

Foodstuff at the period end should be valued at cost. [Follow AS 2/ICDS-II principles while arriving at the cost]

For the damaged stock, valuation should be lesser of cost or net realizable value. [Follow AS 2/ICDS-II principles]

Since foodstuff is provided at subsidized rates only once the employee renders services, foodstuff for which employees have already rendered services but distribution is pending on the part of the company; such foodstuff should be valued at amount receivable from employee's i.e. subsidized rates. [Because certain portion, i.e. cost (-) subsidized rate, would have already been recognized under AS 15 when the services were rendered by employees].

2.14-14 Empty beer bottles left behind by customer at bar or liquor vend is inventory?

Empty beer bottles left behind by customers at bar or liquor vend are clearly assets of the bar/liquor vend entity as customer has relinquished title by leaving it behind. As these are held for sale in ordinary course of business till they are disposed off, they are clearly 'inventories'.

Whether the empty bottles can be shown as inventory ?

If yes, how the company should value such inventory ?

The Adjudicating Authority reflected the claim on the grounds including infirmities in the cost certificate and doctrine of unjust enrichment. The Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the appeal before the Tribunal. The Tribunal held that Revenue was not disputing the CAS-4 Certificate adopted by the assessee for the payment of duty. However, certain minor discrepancies were being pointed out by the Revenue at the time of grant of refund. The assessee was adopting the price of Rs.18,811.29 per metric ton for payment of duty on their final product. Same cost had to be adopted for the refund purpose also. Ltd. 2014 (304) ELT 84 (Mad.) the High Court held that section 11B of the Central Excise Act, 1944 provided that any person claiming refund of any duty of excise and interest, if any, paid on such duty was required to make an application for refund of such duty and interest, if any, paid on such duty, before expiry of one year from the relevant date in such form and manner as prescribed. However, stipulation of one year would not apply where any duty and interest, if any, had been paid under protest. In the instant case, at the request of the assessee, the assessment was final and not provisional. Thus, the period of limitation would be one year from the relevant assessment year to be counted from the date of final assessment year. The final assessment was made in 1998, claim for refund was filed in May, 2001 and held to be wholly barred by limitation.

Insofar as the instant aspect of the matter was concerned, the Supreme Court was satisfied that there was no question of assessee having recovered the excess amount from the consumers. This was because the assessee throughout asserted that so far as the Tyre Cord Fabrics were concerned, the duty payable was under Heading 59.02 of the classification effective from 01.08.1986 whereunder only basic excise duty was payable.
