Section 65(105)(j) - Clearing and forwarding agents’ services v. Consignment agent

4.3 The assessee had entered into contracts with two steel companies, the TISCO and TRL. As per the said contract the assessee was to take delivery of the steel materials on behalf of the TISCO and TRL from the railway siding. Thereafter, it was to transport said materials to its own premises/godown and sort and stock said materials after weighment in accordance with instructions of the company’s representative. The assessee was to further arrange for and to take all necessary steps for safe custody and protection of steel materials and was to nominate a hub manager in its premises. Further, it had to deliver materials to company’s customers on production of delivery orders and if the hub manager required, the materials would be loaded on the transport vehicles, etc., of the customer or as nominated by the company. The assessee was to bear all the expenses since time of receipt of materials at its premises till these were dispatched and in case of failing to account for the stock, it was liable for consequences. The assessee received consideration of certain sum which comprised of consignment agent service receipts, and receipts towards reimbursement of expenditure, bending and bundling charges and stock verification charges from the said companies in respect of services rendered. The revenue issued a show-cause notice (SCN) on 13-9-2004 and demanded service tax from the assessee for the period 1-9-1999 to 31-3-2004 by stating that services provided by the assessee to its clients fell under the category of ‘Clearing and forwarding agent’. On non-compliance of same the revenue confirmed service tax liability upon the assessee along with penalty and interest. In the instant appeal, the assessee contended that it had acted as a consignment agent which activity was not covered under ‘Clearing and forwarding agent’s service’ and, therefore, it was not liable to pay service tax.

The Tribunal held that according to the Finance Act, 1994, imposing service tax on certain taxable services, any service provided or to be provided by a ‘Clearing and forwarding agent’ to a ‘client’ in relation to ‘Clearing and forwarding operations’ ‘in any manner’ shall be taxable service under section 65(105)(j). Incidence of levy is on the service of ‘Clearing and forwarding operations’, provided measure of tax is ‘value’ of such service. Thus, service provided by a ‘Clearing and forwarding agent’ to his client directly or indirectly in any manner gives rise to a taxable event, provided the service so rendered is ‘Clearing and forwarding operation’. Levy is attracted when there is provision of service: (a) of clearing and forwarding operations; (b) by a ‘Clearing and forwarding agent’; (c) to a client; (d) directly or indirectly; and (e) in any manner.

The notice was opposed on the sole ground that the order-in-original had already merged with the order dated 13-10-2004, hence, on the date of issuance of show-cause notice there was no order-in-original, which could be reviewed by the Commissioner. That contention of the assessee was negatived, and the Commissioner enhanced the penalty. However, the Tribunal allowed the appeal of the assessee. The High Court held that the penalty whole hog was a subject-matter of the challenge before the Commissioner (Appeals), and was also capable of being challenged before the Commissioner (Appeals). Likewise, the Commissioner (Appeals) had jurisdiction to, and was capable of reversing, modifying or affirming the order of penalty also, which was in issue before it. It might be noticed in the instant case, that the order in original imposed a penalty lesser than the one which according to the department was required to be imposed, and the penalty as imposed was challenged. It was well-nigh possible that in appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) could have set aside the order altogether, or could have reduced it as well, while maintaining imposition of penalty, might be rightly, or wrongly. Therefore, on the parameters laid down by the Supreme Court, the superior jurisdiction was capable of reversing, modifying, or affirming the order which was in issue before it, and in the instant case the Commissioner (Appeals) declined to modify, and simply affirmed it. Thus, in the facts and circumstances, the Commissioner could not exercise his power of revision under section 84 to the extent the order of adjudicating authority was found to be erroneous by him and about which no appeal lay at the instance of the revenue, notwithstanding that to the extent the assessee was aggrieved, he had preferred the appeal and the order in appeal had been passed.

In SLR Steels Ltd. v. CCE 2010 (249) ELT 394 (Trib. - Bang.), it is classified in the Explanation 2 to rule 2 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 that the inputs include the goods used in the manufacture of capital goods, which are further used in the factory of manufacturer. In this case, there was no dispute that pollution control equipments and storage tanks were categorized as capital goods in terms of definition in rule 2 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 and that the items in dispute, namely, cement and steel products were used in the construction of the said capital goods. In such circumstances, the said items, namely, cement and steel products were to be treated as inputs in the manufacture of the capital goods, which were, in turn, used within the factory of manufacturer in terms of Explanation to rule 2 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004. Thus, the assessees were entitled to the benefit of CENVAT credit on the said items as inputs and not as capital goods. Hence, the availment of credit on the quantum of cement and steel products used in the manufacture of storage tanks and pollution control equipments was proper and legal and the question of recovery of the credit did not arise.

In Sai Samhita Storages (P.) Ltd. v. CC&CE 2010 (255) ELT 91 (Trib. - Bang.), the appellants were service providers under the category of ‘storage and warehousing services’. They availed CENVAT credit on cement and TMT bars. The department found that the appellants were not eligible to avail CENVAT credit. They issued a show-cause notice for reversal of the amount taken as credit. The appellants contested the same. The lower authority confirmed the demand with interest and also imposed penalties.

The Commissioner (Appeals) rejected the appeal filed by the appellants. The Tribunal held on an analysis of the definition of ‘input’ that it includes goods, which are further used in the factory of the manufacturer. It was argued by the department that the appellants were not a manufacturer. It was undisputed that the appellant were not a manufacturer, but ‘a person’ who was providing output services under the category of ‘Storages and warehouse’ services. It is clear from the definition of the ‘capital goods’ that the credit on the duty paid on tubes and fittings, as well as storage tanks is eligible for availment of CENVAT credit. It was undisputed in this case that the inputs, viz., cement, TNT bars and steel tubes were used for the purpose of construction of storage tanks and for the pipelines for transfer of liquid cargo, and, therefore, the benefit of credit could not be denied to the appellants, as the appellants were using these inputs for manufacture of the capital goods, i.e., storage tanks and pipeline for delivery of the cargo from such storage tank to truck delivery station. The CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 clearly allowed the appellants to take CENVAT credit.

In Vikram Cement v. CCE 2009 (242) ELT 545 (Trib. - Delhi), the Tribunal held that credit on welding electrodes used for repair and maintenance is not available as input.

[2010] 24 STT 497 (New Delhi - CESTAT), the assessees-exporters availed various services from respective service providers for export of their goods and claimed refund of service tax paid on said services, in view of Notification No. 41/2007-ST, dated 17-9-2007. Deputy Commissioner sanctioned refund claim. Revenue, however, after conducting detailed review of service tax payment by service providers, filed review appeals seeking disallowance of certain amounts of service tax refund to assessees on ground that those amounts represented tax on amounts charged for services which were not part of value of impugned services. However, Commissioner (Appeals) upheld order of Deputy Commissioner sanctioning refund.

Held that unless and until, the service tax payment by the service providers is revised by the jurisdictional service tax officers, the service tax refund available to the exporters, who had received those taxable service in connection with export of goods, cannot be revised. The same principle would be applicable to the instant case and unless and until the service tax payment by the service providers is revised by the jurisdictional service tax officers, the service tax refund available to the exporters who have received the taxable services in connection with export of goods, cannot be revised.

SECTION 11AB OF THE CENTRAL EXCISE ACT, 1944 - INTEREST ON DELAYED PAYMENT OF DUTY

7. In the case of Pratibha Processors v. Union of India AIR 1997 SC 138, in paragraph 13, the Supreme Court has observed : "In fiscal statutes, the import of the words—’tax’, ‘interest’, ‘penalty’, etc., is well known. They are different concepts. ‘Tax’ is the amount payable as a result of the charging provision. It is a compulsory exaction of ‘money by a public authority for public purposes, the payment of which is enforced by law. Penalty is ordinarily levied on an assessee for some contumacious conduct or for a deliberate violation of the provision of the particular statute. Interest is compensatory in character and is imposed on an assessee, who has withheld payment of any tax as and when it is due and payable, the levy of interest is geared to actual amount of tax withheld and the extent of the delay in paying the tax on the due date. Essentially it is compensatory and different from penalty—which is penal in character. Generally levy of interest is automatic, even if the default is due to reasonable cause. While levy of interest is generally automatic, in case of penalty the right of being heard has to be given. Also where penalty is also provided separately for the same default in addition to interest, then generally interest will be compensatory and mandatory.

Similarly, in the case of CCE v. International Auto Ltd. [2010] 24 STT 586 (SC), it was held that when differential duty is paid after date of clearance, it indicates short-payment/short-levy on date of removal and, hence, interest which is for loss of revenue, becomes leviable under section 11AB. In this case the assessee was a supplier of auto parts to manufacturers of motor vehicles. Since price difference arose between price on date of removal and enhanced price at which goods were ultimately sold, department sought to recover interest on differential duty paid by the assessee under section 11AB. It was held that the assessee was liable to pay interest on such differential duty.

(3)

Loading and unloading operations

65. (1) No cargo shall be loaded or unloaded by a fall or sling at any intermediate deck unless either the hatch at that deck is securely covered or a secure landing platform of a width not less than that of one section of hatch coverings has been placed across it:

Provided that this regulation shall not apply to any loading or unloading work the whole of which may be completed within a period of half an hour.

(2) No loose gear or any other object shall be thrown in or out of the holds.

(3) During the loading and unloading of bulk cargo a record of all dock workers employed in the hold shall be maintained and produced on demand to the Inspector.

(4) Where necessary cargo shall be secured or blocked to prevent its shifting or falling. In breaking down, precautions shall be taken where necessary to prevent the remaining cargo from falling.

(5) (a) Dragging of cargo shall be done with the ship's winches only when the runner is led directly from the derrick heel block; and

(b) Pulley blocks shall be used to provide a fair lead for the runner so as to prevent it from dragging against obstructions.

(6) If the head room in the hold of a ship for the purpose of stacking and unstaking is less than 1.5 metres, suitable measures shall be taken to guard against accidents.

(7) Loads shall be safely slung before being hoisted. Loose dunnage or debris hanging or protruding from loads shall be removed and suitable means shall be adopted to prevent cargo from falling out.

(8) Cargo-handling bridles, such as pallet bridles, which are to remain attached to the lifting appliance while hoisting successive sling loads, shall be attached by shackles, or other positive means shall be taken to prevent them from becoming accidentally disengaged from the hook of the lifting appliance.

(9) When lifting appliance is operating without a load on the slings—

(a)

slings or chains shall be hooked securely to the appliances before the operators are given signal to move;

(b)

sharp hooks, multiple hooks and claws shall not hang at one end but shall be reeved through slings; and

(c)

the operators shall raise the appliance sufficiently to keep clear off dock workers and objects.

(10) Effective measures shall be taken, by the use of suitable packing or otherwise, to prevent edges of any load from coming into contact with any rope or chain sling which is likely to cause any damage to the rope or chain sling.

(11) Buckets, tubs and similar appliances shall not be loaded above their rims.

(12) No loads shall be lifted at strappings unless such strappings are approved as proper and safe slinging points. Movement of such loads is allowed only if everybody has left the danger zone.

(13) When working with lifting appliances, slopepulling, horizontal dragging and intentional swing of loads and lifting devices are prohibited.

Its claim of Cenvat credit of service tax paid for use of such services was rejected by the department on the ground that services of CHA were engaged in relation to the activity after removal from the factory and in the port area. In the instant appeal, the assessee contended that the definition of ‘input service’ under rule 2(1) is extended one and it includes activities relating to business; that the service of CHA availed by them should be treated as relating to their business activity and, therefore, credit should be extended.

3.The assessee had got certain circles/gardens prepared and put-up signboards for advertising its products. For this purpose, it had availed the services of construction service providers. The assessee claimed construction service as input service and sought credit of service tax paid on such services. The department denied the assessee’s claim on the ground that availing of construction services for the aforesaid purpose could not be treated as part of activity relating to advertising services.

The Tribunal held :

1.In view of decision of the Tribunal in the case of Indian Rayon & Industries Ltd. v. CCE [2007] 6 STT 328 (Mum. - CESTAT), the assessee was eligible to input credit on mobile services.

2.The CHA services availed in respect of export did not have any nexus with the manufacture and clearance of the product from the factory. The business activities, which were sought to be included in the extended definition, could not include the services rendered in the port area. Therefore, the appeal on this aspect was to be rejected.

3.Setting up of circles/gardens away from the factory for the purpose of putting signboards cannot be considered as relating to activity in relation to advertisement. This can lead to a situation where any massive building built away from the factory premises where signboards were also put up can be treated in relation to advertisement of the product. While putting up a signboard is definitely a part of advertisement services, the same cannot be, unrealistically, extended to various activities like setting up circles/gardens with the help of construction service providers. Thus, the Tribunal rejected the assessee’s appeal.

ALLOWABILITY OF PROVISION FOR FORESEEABLE LOSSES UNDER THE MINIMUM ALTERNATE TAX (MAT)

3. Section 115JB of the Act provides for levy of MAT on the 'Book Profits' of a company. In this regard, book profits are to be computed with reference to the profit and loss account prepared in accordance with the provisions of Part-II and Part-III of Schedule VI to the Companies Act and would be subject to adjustments provided for in the Explanation to section 115JB of the Act.

The Explanation 1 to section 115JB of the Act sets out the mechanism for computing the book profits. The Explanation stipulates certain additions and deletions to the net profit to arrive at the book profit. In the current context, clause (c) is relevant, which provides that book profit shall be increased by 'any provision made for meeting liabilities other than ascertained liabilities'.

The issue as to what is a provision made for ascertained liability has been decided in a number of cases. There are several judicial precedents, where the Courts have taken a view (in the context of tax deductibility under section 37 of the Act) that a liability created on the basis of reliable estimates and past experience is an ascertained liability. Reliance in this regard can be placed on the following rulings:

3.1 Rotork Controls India (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2009] 180 Taxman 422 (SC) - In this case in the context of provision for warranty, the Supreme Court held that in this case a contingent liability, for which reliable estimate can be made on the basis of scientific working, is allowable as deduction under section 37 of the Act.

3.2 CIT v. Vinitec Corpn. (P.) Ltd. [2005] 146 Taxman 313 (Delhi) - In this case again in the context of provision for warranty, the Delhi High Court held that provision for warranty created on an acceptable basis was to be allowed as deduction.

3.3 Metal Box Co. of India Ltd. v. Their Workmen [1969] 73 ITR 53 (SC) - In this case, the Supreme Court in the context of provision for gratuity observed that in case a liability is properly ascertained then the same is to be allowed. As mentioned above, this decision of the Supreme Court has been referred to in Jacob Engg. (India) (P.) Ltd.'s case (supra).

3.4 Bharat Earth Movers v. CIT [2000] 245 ITR 428 / 112 Taxman 61 (SC) - In this case, the Supreme Court, in the context of provision for leave encashment created on the basis of a scheme, held that it was eligible for deduction. The Court held that this liability was not a contingent liability as it was capable of being ascertained with a reasonable certainty.

3.5 CIT v. Echjay Forgings (P.) Ltd. [2001] 116 Taxman 322 (Bom.) - In this case, the Mumbai High Court held that the provision for gratuity created on the basis of actuarial valuation could not be regarded as unascertained liability, accordingly, had to be allowed as deduction in computing the book profit.

Further, in the context of MAT computation as well, various judicial precedents have held that provisions which are capable of estimation with a reasonable certainty are allowable, as they are ascertainable and, thus, no adjustment is required for the same while ascertaining 'Book Profit' for MAT computation purposes.

For the purpose of allowability of provision for foreseeable losses under the MAT provisions reference may also be made to the cases of Mazagon Docks Ltd. (supra) and Jacobs Engg. (India) (P.) Ltd. (supra).

6. Rate of DDT should not exceed rate specified in Article 10 in India-Germany DTAA: ITAT

Giesecke & Devrient [India] Pvt Ltd. v. ACIT [2020] 120 taxmann.com 338 (Delhi - Trib.)

The issue before the Delhi Tribunal was:

"Whether Assessing Officer (AO) erred in not extending the benefit of applicable Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement between India and Germany (DTAA) qua the rate of tax on payment of dividend to the shareholder?"

The Delhi Tribunal held that there is no dispute that the liability is on the payer company to pay DDT, but, at the same time, we must not lose sight of the fact that dividend distribution tax (DDT) is part of tax as defined in Section 2(43) of the Act. It must be remembered that this additional Income-tax [DDT] levied u/s 115-0 is a tax on income and definition of "Income" includes dividend.

As per the Income-tax Rules, relevant details regarding payment of DDT have to be provided in the Income-tax return form and have to be disclosed in the Tax Audit Return [Form 3CD]. Further, the Income-tax assessment order read with the Income-tax computation form quantifies DDT liability.

It would not be out of place to mention that the Act does not provide for a separate adjudication/passing of separate order with regard to adjudication of liability of DDT.

Further, the generally accepted principles relating to interpretation of treaties in the light of object of eliminating double taxation does not bar the application of tax treaties to DDT. Thus, the DDT levied by the appellant should not exceed the rate specified in Article 10 in India Germany DTAA.

7. Paragraph substituted in a tax treaty is applicable for entire fiscal year & not from date of its notification

Director of Income Tax (International Taxation) v. Autodesk Asia (P.) Ltd. [2020] 120 taxmann.com 324 (Karnataka)

Assessee filed return of income for the Assessment Year 2006-07 by declaring the taxable income as 'NIL'. The case was selected for scrutiny and it was held that software supplied was chargeable to income tax from royalty and technical services.

The instant appeal was filed by the revenue with regard to the rate of tax under the DTAA for Assessment Year 2006-07.

The revenue submitted that the Notification dated 18-7-2005 issued under section 90 came into force with effect from 1-8-2005. With reference to Section 195(1), the rates in force mean the dates on which credit take place in the account and therefore, AO had rightly applied the rate of tax under the Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement (DTAA).

The assessee contended that from the perusal of Article 4 of the Notification, it was evident that paragraph 12 of Article 12 of India-Singapore DTAA has been deleted and has been substituted by the paragraph which provides for levy of tax on the royalties or fees for technical services at the rate not exceeding 10%. Thus, the Tribunal had rightly held that new provision which was in existence shall apply for the entire fiscal year as defined in DTAA.

The Karnataka High Court held that paragraph 2 of Article 12, which provided for levy of tax on royalties or fees for technical services at the rate not exceeding 12% had been deleted and in its place, the provision which provides for levy of tax on the royalties or fees for technical services at the rate not exceeding 10% had been substituted.

Thus, the substitution had the effect of deleting the old rule and making the new rule operative. Therefore, the Tribunal had rightly determined the rate of tax as substituted in clause 2 of article 12 of DTAA for the entire fiscal year as defined in DTAA and was liable to be taxed at 10%.

SPECIAL SCENARIOS TO WATCH

Inter-Unit Transfers Allowed- Goods can be transferred from one MOOWR unit to another.

Scrap/waste disposal in the domestic market attracts duty; it's waived if exported.

Goods received from SEZs or FTWZs are treated as imports and must follow bonding formalities. Inputs received free of cost must be declared at nominal value and properly recorded.

Goods returning from testing or repairs should be handled as fresh imports or DTA inputs.

CHALLENGES AND FUTURE UNCERTAINTY

While MOOWR is a beneficial scheme, these challenges are hindering its performance.

Complex compliance: Filing multiple BOEs for each DTA sale is time-consuming and complex.

No depreciation is allowed when capital goods are sold in the domestic market—duty is on full import value.

No RODTEP or Drawback: MOOWR-based exports are less competitive given they are not eligible for RODTEP scrips or Drawback. Typically benefits RODTEP and Drawback would be in the range of 4-5% of the value of exported good, which is significant for a lot of exporters.

New concern: The Finance Act 2024 empowered the Government of India to exclude certain goods or operations from the applicability of MOOWR scheme. This adds unpredictability, making long-term planning difficult for businesses relying on this scheme and creating an unease in doing business.

Takeaways

If you are importing raw materials or machinery regularly, consider obtaining a MOOWR license.

Be prepared for higher compliance costs.

Evaluate if loss of RODTEP/Drawback is offset by duty deferment benefits.

MOOWR is one of the most flexible and cash-flow-friendly customs schemes available in India. It's ideal for businesses that import raw material or machinery and sell their finished goods either in domestic market or export market.

Small and Mid-sized manufacturers initially hesitate to register under MOOWR because of compliance worries. But once they set up the systems, the cash flow benefits are too significant to ignore.

Cenvat credit relating to garden maintenance services 5.5 In the case of ISMT Ltd. v. CCE&C [2010] 24 STT 326 (Mum. - CESTAT), the assessee had availed Cenvat credit of service tax paid on garden maintenance service. Same was denied on the ground that said service was not used in or in relation to the manufacture, directly or indirectly in the manufacture of the final products and clearance of final products from the place of removal. On appeal, the Tribunal held as under :

u The definitions of ‘input’ in rule 2(k) and ‘input service’ in rule 2(l) are not at all comparable or pari materia and coverage of the ‘input service’ is definitely wider.

u The definition of ‘input’ is exhaustive and is restrictive in scope. It treats all goods used in or in relation to manufacture of final products or for any other purpose within the factory of production. But certain goods which would be eligible as per definition have been excluded and certain goods which could be interpreted as not includible have been specifically included, i.e., packing material, lubricating oil, accessories, etc. Therefore, all goods other than specified as includible have to be shown to be used in or in relation to manufacture of final product or for any other purpose within the factory of production. In fact, the Apex Court in Maruti Suzuki Ltd. v. CCE 2009 (240) ELT 641 has held that input and capital goods used in captive means are covered by the definition, expanding the scope of definition.

u The Legislature has not used the word in the inclusive part ‘that it is to be used in or in relation of the final product’.

u From the above, it is clear that the intention of the Legislature was that those activities should be in relation to the business.

u It cannot be viewed that a garden is not relating to manufacture. A good garden creates a better atmosphere and environment which increases the working efficiency and the consumer would feel good.

u In view of the above discussion, the assessee was entitled to Cenvat credit availed on the garden maintenance services which were used in or in relation to the manufacture of final products or used in relation to the business activity and, in the instant case, the services used by the assessee were in relation to the business activity and it was entitled to Cenvat credit. Accordingly, the appeal was to be allowed.

Service tax paid/reimbursed to Airport Authority of India for availing of the services of authority such as landing, parking, and x-ray etc.

4.8 The assessee, an aircraft operator, availed credit of service tax paid/reimbursed to Airport Authority of India for availing of the services of authority such as landing, parking, and x-ray in connection with the operation of the aircraft owned by it. The lower authorities denied said credit on the ground that the services were not connected, directly or indirectly, in or in relation to the manufacture of final products and clearance of final products. In the instant appeal, the assessee contended that the aircrafts were used by its officials as conveyance between its plants and were essential for the business purpose and those services were related to business only. On detailed examination of the definition of ‘input service’, it was found that the definition is in two parts.

Part-I includes the services used by the manufacturer whether directly or indirectly in or in relation to the manufacturing of final products and clearance of final products from the place of removal.

And Part-II includes services used in relation to setting up, modernization, renovation or repairs of a factory premises of provider of output services or an office relating to such factory or premises, advertisement or sales promotion, market research, storage up to the place of removal, procurement of inputs, activities relating to business.

The Tribunal held that the contention of the revenue that the definition of input service is to be read as a whole could not be accepted. Further, in the assessee’s own case in Force Motor Ltd. v. CCE [F.O. A/547/08, dated 11-7-2008], the Tribunal had held that the activities specified after the phrase ‘such as’ are only illustrations and examples and not exhaustive. Therefore, an activity other than those illustrated but related to business will also get covered under the definition of ‘input service’. The assessee was a manufacturing unit and according to the above definition, the use of the phrase ‘such as’ would mean inclusion of an activity which is of a kind as of the illustrations. The main issue to be decided in the case was as to whether the services provided by the authority could form a part of the business activities. It was clear that the aircraft which was stationed at airport was used by the assessee for the business activities and that stand was taken by the assessee before the lower authorities, which was not declined by them. Therefore, it was held that the services rendered by the authority and service tax charged by them would get covered under the definition of ‘input services’ as per the rule 2( l).

Compliance with customs regulations is critical when importing second-hand machinery. The Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC) has issued Circular No. 25/2015-Cus., dated 15-10-2015, providing comprehensive guidelines for the import of used machinery:

The import must be accompanied by an inspection/appraisement report by an overseas chartered engineer or equivalent.

If an overseas report is not available, the importer may obtain a report from any of the DGFT-notified agencies in India, or from a locally empanelled chartered engineer at customs stations.

The value of the machinery will be examined in light of the chartered engineer's report, and any doubts regarding the declared value must be justified by the importer.

In cases where significant differences in value arise, customs officers may apply Rule 12 of the Customs Valuation Rules (CVR), 2007 to determine the correct value.

These stringent customs requirements help ensure that the valuation and condition of second-hand machinery are thoroughly assessed before entry into India.

4. Judicial Pronouncements:

Recent judicial rulings provide clarity on the legal treatment of second-hand machinery imports. Some important cases include:

Ratnamani Metal & Tubes Ltd. v. Commissioner of Customs[2022] 143 taxmann.com 180 (Ahd. - CESTAT): The case concerned the confiscation of second-hand office furniture and equipment imported as part of a manufacturing plant. The customs authority denied clearance, arguing that these items did not qualify as capital goods under the Foreign Trade Policy, 2015-2020. The Tribunal ruled in favor of the appellant, stating that the goods met the definition of capital goods and were eligible for import, setting aside the confiscation order.

Warburg Pincus India (P.) Ltd. v. Commissioner of Customs (Imports), Mumbai [Order No. A/86120/2017-WZB/SMB, dated 28-2-2017] : In this case, the appellant imported second-hand furniture and faced confiscation under Section 111(d) of the Customs Act. The tribunal ruled that the furniture qualified as capital goods, allowing the appellant to import them freely under the EXIM policy, thereby overturning the earlier decision of the Commissioner (Appeals).

5. Conclusion:

The import of second-hand machinery presents a practical and cost-efficient solution for Indian startups. However, it is imperative to comply with the relevant provisions of the Customs Act and DGFT guidelines to avoid potential legal hurdles. Businesses should engage with qualified professionals to ensure proper adherence to these regulations, thereby mitigating the risk of penalties and confiscation. By understanding and following the rules, companies can benefit from reduced capital expenditure while maintaining full compliance with Indian import laws.

M. GOVINDARAJAN*

CARGO HANDLING SERVICES - SOME ISSUES

In this article, the author has taken up for discussion different issues in respect of cargo handling services with reference to relevant case-laws.

Definition

1. The Cargo handling services have been subjected to service tax by the Finance Act, 2002, with effect from August 16, 2002. Cargo handling service is defined (as substituted by the Finance Act, 2008 with effect from May 16, 2008) under section 65(23) of the Finance Act, 1994 as loading, unloading, and packing or unpacking of cargo and includes—

u Cargo handling services provided for freight in special containers or for non-containerized freight, services provided by a container freight terminal or any other freight terminal, for all modes of transport and cargo handling service incidental to freight; and

u Service of packing together with transportation of cargo or goods, with or without one or more of other services like loading, unloading, and unpacking

but does not include handling of export cargo or passenger baggage or mere transportation of goods.

The taxable service in relation to cargo handling has been defined under section 65(105)(zr ) as a service provided or to be provided to any person, by a cargo handling agency in relation to cargo handling services.

Exclusion

2. The CBEC Instruction lr. No. F. No. B11/1/2002-TRU, dated August 1, 2002 also indicated that the following services are excluded from the tax net—

u Services provided in relation to export cargo;

u Passenger baggage;

u Mere transportation of goods;

u Services provided in relation to storage of agriculture produce or for goods meant to be stored in cold storage;

u All the services in relation to handling of goods would be appropriately covered under port service and no separate levy will be attracted under cargo handling service;

u Marketing or canvassing for cargo for airlines;

u Service or auction of abandoned cargo;

u Handling of empty containers.

Issues

3. Nearly nine case-laws with different points are covered under the cargo handling services. Those are discussed as under:

u Ridhi Sidhi Transport v. CCE, Belgaum [2009] 18 STT 484 (Bang. - CESTAT) : The appellants had to provide cargo handling services in terms of the agreement entered into by them with Grasim Industries. The receipt for the services is given in the letter of Grasim to the appellants. In terms of the said agreement, the amount to be paid was split up into three categories, viz., rake handling (consisting of loading and unloading expenses) at Rs. 20 per M.T., local transportation charges (from yard to godown) at Rs. 53 per MT and service charges of Rs. 4 per MT. It was the contention of the appellants that the rake handling charges of Rs. 20 per MT were not liable for service tax. The Tribunal held that the contention did not appear to be correct because in terms of the Finance Act, Cargo handling means loading, unloading, packing or unpacking cargo, etc., for all modes of transport. When loading and unloading are integral parts of cargo handling services and when the gross receipt includes the said charges, there is no question of claiming any abatement or arguing that the same is not taxable under the category of ‘Cargo handling service’. The Tribunal held that the appellants did not have a case on merit.

u In re, Bharat Haribhau Salunke [Orders-in-Appeal Nos. PII/PAP/83-88 (Pn.) of 2008, dated 18-6-2008] : The appellant was transporting sugar from sugar house to godown within the factory. It was held that mere transportation of goods is excluded from cargo handling service. Transportation inside the factory is not considered as cargo handling service.

Activity of stitching of sugar bags is not related to loading, unloading, packing or unpacking of goods. Sugar bags cannot be considered as cargo. Impugned activity is not covered under ‘Cargo handling service’. Show-cause notice was issued and confirmed mechanically.

Cargo means goods carried by sea, road or air. Bagasee being residual waste of sugarcane and used as fuel for stream generation cannot be considered as cargo.

Press mud is held as not marketable and non-excisable by the Supreme Court in CCE v. Titawi Sugar Complex 2003 (152) ELT 21. Press mud cannot be considered as goods. Activity of handling press mud is not falling under cargo handling service.

Getting clearance from Committee of Disputes involving inter-departmental litigation is a futile exercise decides the Supreme Court and recalls its earlier orders

In this article, the author has analyzed the Supreme Court’s decision wherein the Court has considered the role of the Committee on Disputes set up by the Government of India for approval of Court cases by this Committee in cases of Public Sector Undertakings and has observed that the objective sought to be achieved by this procedure has not been achieved and the same leads to delays. Hence, the Court has recalled its directions in various orders on this matter. It could be hoped that the Government of India would soon order scrapping of this procedure.

T.N. PANDEY*

Introduction

1. The Supreme Court of India has decided in the case of Electronics Corpn. of India v. UOI [2011] 30 STT 472 that in inter-departmental litigation getting clearance from Committee on Disputes (COD) has not served the objective for which it was introduced and has outlived its utility in the changed scenario and, hence, it has recalled its order in earlier cases requiring COD approval.

Historical background

2. It was decided by the Government of India (GOI) that public sector undertakings of the Central Government and Union of India should not fight their litigation in the Courts. Hence, the Cabinet Secretary, GOI was ‘called upon to handle the matter personally’. Initially, the Committee was called a ‘High Powered Committee’ (HPC).

This was followed by another Committee called ‘Committee of Secretaries’ (COS) and finally christened as ‘Committee on Disputes’ (COD). These Committees were constituted to ensure that resources of the State are not frittered away in intense litigations between the entities of the State which could be best resolved by an empowered Committee - COD. The Committee(s) constituted was/were intended to ensure that no litigation comes to the Court without the parties had an opportunity of conciliation before an in-house Committee. The principle outlined behind the constitution of the Committee was sound, laudatory and unexceptionable. However, over the years, the objective sought to be achieved failed to be realized and led to delays in finalization of disputes. Hence, the entire mechanism in this regard has been reviewed by the Apex Court.

2.1 Facts of the cases before the Supreme Court

(a) Case No. 1 - Electronics Corporation of India Ltd. (‘assessee’ for short) is a Central Government Public Sector Undertaking (‘PSU’). It is registered as a Government company under the Companies Act, 1956. It is under the control of Department of Atomic Energy, Government of India. A dispute had been raised by the Central Government (Ministry of Finance) by issuing show-cause notices to the assessee alleging that the corporation was not entitled to avail/utilize Modvat/Cenvat credit in respect of inputs whose values stood written off. Accordingly, it was proposed in the show-cause notices that the credit taken on inputs was liable to be reversed. Thus, the short point which arose for determination in the present case was whether the Central Government was right in insisting on reversal of credit taken by the assessee on inputs whose values stood written off.

The adjudicating authority held that there was no substance in the contention of the assessee that the write off was made in terms of AS-2. The case of the assessee before the CCE (adjudicating authority) was that it was a financial requirement as prescribed in AS-2; that an inventory more than three years old had to be written off/derated in value; that such derating in value did not mean that the inputs were unfunctionable; that the inputs were still lying in the factory and they were useful for production and, therefore, they were entitled to Modvat/Cenvat credit. As stated above, this argument was rejected by the adjudicating authority and the demand against the assessee stood confirmed. Against the order of the adjudicating authority, the assessee decided to challenge the same by filling an appeal before the CESTAT. Accordingly, the assessee applied before the Committee on Disputes (COD). However, the COD vide its decision dated 2nd Nov., 2006 refused to grant clearance though in an identical case, the COD granted clearance to Bharat Heavy Electricals Ltd. (‘BHEL’). Accordingly, the assessee filed a writ petition in the Andhra Pradesh High Court. The High Court dismissed the petition. Hence, an appeal was filed before the Supreme Court.

What if you could delay paying import duties—and sometimes avoid them completely?

That's the advantage offered by the MOOWR Scheme.

Re-introduced by the Government of India in 2019, the Manufacture and Other Operations in Warehouse Regulations (MOOWR) revamped the 1966 version to align with WTO norms.

Unlike the schemes Advance Authorization (AA), Export Promotion of Capital Goods (EPCG), Export Oriented Unit (EOU), or Special Economic Zone (SEZ), MOOWR does not involve export obligation.

It is suitable for any manufacturer or processor—large or small, domestic or global. There's no restriction on location or investment size.

WHAT MOOWR OFFERS

MOOWR lets manufacturers:

Import capital goods and raw materials without paying customs duty ('duty') upfront

Defer duty on raw materials until finished goods are sold in domestic market.

Save interest: No interest is charged on the deferred customs duty for raw materials component when finished goods are sold in domestic market.

Avoid duty

On raw materials used in finished goods exported

On capital goods re-exported after its lifetime

Defer and avoid duty on waste generated during the manufacture process when the finished goods are sold in domestic market and overseas market respectively.

MOOWR – Case Study

Let's understand MOOWR with a simple illustration before understanding the other nuances.

ABC Technologies obtained MOOWR license in the year 2023. They import sensors for manufacture of finished goods. With MOOWR, they deferred/avoided customs duty.

Machinery

ABC imported machinery worth Rs. 1 crore. Normally, customs duty payable would be Rs. 10 lakhs.

With MOOWR, they paid nothing upfront. They saved Rs. 60k /year in interest—6% of Rs. 10 lakhs.

Ten years later (i.e. after its lifetime), if they export or scrap the machinery, no duty is payable. If sold in India, duty is payable but no interest payable.

Raw material

ABC imported raw material worth Rs. 50 lakhs. No duty was paid at the time of import, though duty payable was Rs. 10 lakhs.

Assuming a timeline of 3 months for conversation of raw material into finished goods and its ultimate sale, interest saving would be at least Rs. 15K —6% * 3* Rs. 10 lakhs/12.

Packing material

ABC imported packaging materials worth Rs. 10 lakhs.

70% of it was used for exported products —no customs duty was paid at the time of import, and such duty shall be waived off upon export.

Customs Duty is payable only on 30% of the packing material used for domestic sales.

More importantly, no interest payable on the Customs Duty payable on the raw materials used manufacture of goods for domestic sales.

Assume a working capital cycle of 3 months, ABC can save interest on packing material worth Rs. 3 lakhs for a period of 3 months.

MOOWR –KEY COMPLIANCE REQUIREMENTS

1.

Import without customs duty- File a bill of entry for warehousing. No duty or IGST is payable upfront.

2.

Manufacture-Use imported and local inputs for manufacture. Pay GST on domestic purchases. Declare input-output norms.

3.

Job Work-Goods can be sent for job work after reaching the MOOWR unit, they must return within 1 year. Tools and molds also can be sent for job work.

4.

Export-Raise GST invoice, e-way bill, and seal goods. Submit export proof within 1 month to the bond officer at jurisdictional customs office.

5.

Sell in India-File bills of entry for home consumption for the raw material component of finished goods.

Example: If inputs consumed in manufacture of finished goods were imported through 5 Bills of Entry (BOE), separate bills of entry for home consumption for such 5 BOE must be filed at the time of sale. This is a huge compliance burden, especially when goods are sourced across multiple consignments.

6.

Records and Compliances

Maintain records for receipt, processing and removal of goods procured

Maintain separate inventory for domestic and imported goods.

Use FIFO method for tracking the goods procured.

Appoint a warehouse keeper who is responsible for day-to-day functioning of the warehouse.

File returns by the 10th of the following month.

SPECIAL SCENARIOS TO WATCH

Inter-Unit Transfers Allowed- Goods can be transferred from one MOOWR unit to another.

Scrap/waste disposal in the domestic market attracts duty; it's waived if exported.

Goods received from SEZs or FTWZs are treated as imports and must follow bonding formalities.

Section 5 of the Foreign Trade Development & Regulation (FTDR) Act, 1992 further empowers the Government to formulate and announce the import and export policy of the country, i.e., the Foreign Trade Policy (FTP).
